### [1] [LLM Agents Factory: Retrieval of Domain-Specific LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09934)
*Vitalii Belov,Artyom Sosedka,Andrey Sakhovskiy,Elizaveta Kovtun,Artyom Boyarskikh,Semen Budennyy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM Agents Factory uses a retrieval-based framework with 20K+ pre-built agent profiles to construct domain-specific agents on demand, matching AutoGen quality at lower cost and offering a controllable alternative to dynamic agent generation for industrial deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic, on-the-fly LLM agent design for each user request is computationally expensive and unstable, limiting practical industrial deployment. A more efficient, controllable, and cost-effective method for constructing specialized agents is needed.

Method: A retrieval-based framework built on a repository of over 20,000 pre-determined, domain-specific, Wikipedia-grounded agent profiles. It operates in two modes: (1) semantic search-based agent profile retrieval, and (2) distillation into a compact fine-tuned model for direct agent generation. The framework constructs agents on demand without requiring expensive per-request dynamic generation.

Result: On MMLU, BIG-bench, and BIG-bench Hard benchmarks in single-agent scenarios, the retrieval-based approach surpasses non-agent baselines in accuracy and matches the generation quality of AutoGen with a 120B backbone, while achieving substantially lower inference cost.

Conclusion: Retrieval from a structured agent repository offers a cost-efficient, accurate, and controllable alternative to dynamic agent generation, meeting the rigorous demands of industrial applications.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents improve task performance by decomposing problems into role-specialized behaviors. However, their practical deployment is often limited by the computational cost and instability associated with the on-the-fly agent design for each user request. To address this, we present LLM Agents Factory, a retrieval-based framework that constructs domain-specific and Wikipedia-grounded agents on demand using a base of over 20K predetermined agent profiles. Our framework supports two modes: (1) agent profile retrieval via semantic search and (2) distillation into a compact model fine-tuned for direct agent generation. Experiments on MMLU, BIG-bench, and BIG-bench Hard in a single-agent scenario demonstrate that our retrieval-based agent construction surpasses non-agent baselines in accuracy while matching AutoGen generation quality with a 120B backbone at a substantially lower inference cost. Our work reveals that retrieval from a structured agent repository provides a cost-efficient, accurate, and controllable alternative to dynamic agent generation, responding to the strict demands of industrial applications. We provide the implementation code and the agent base in https://huggingface.co/frontier-ai/llm-agent-factory.

</details>


### [2] [Conflict or Strategy? Asymmetric Role Framing of La France insoumise and Rassemblement National in French News Headlines, 2022-2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09936)
*Amr Sobhy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: French news headlines frame left-populist LFI and right-populist RN through distinct role registers—conflict vs. strategic-electoral—rather than symmetric extremes. This role asymmetry is robust across models, time, and outlets, while moral-accounting (blame, legitimacy) varies by outlet, yielding misleading aggregate nulls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether French news media frame left- and right-populist challengers as symmetric "extremes" or as fundamentally different political adversaries, and to decompose what valence-based measures conflate by introducing political-role assignment as a distinct framing dimension.

Method: 28,592 headlines from 25 French-language outlets (2022–2025) covering La France insoumise (LFI) and Rassemblement National (RN) were annotated using a three-model LLM pipeline, validated against a stratified human audit. Constructs measured include conflict framing, strategic-game framing, delegitimization, actor roles (AGGRESSOR syntax), and normative judgments (blame, legitimacy, victimhood). Bootstrapping and permutation tests assessed robustness.

Result: Role asymmetry, not valence asymmetry, is the clearest finding: LFI appears predominantly through a conflict register; RN through a strategic-electoral register. This pattern is direction-stable across all three models, survives statistical testing, and persists across outlet families and most of the study period. Moral-accounting constructs are outlet-driven, producing aggregate nulls that mask polarized sub-patterns. Methodologically, conflict and strategic-game framing show strongest human validation and cross-model stability; actor role is direction-stable but with lower audit reliability; normative constructs are weakest.

Conclusion: French media do not treat LFI and RN as symmetric extremes but assign them distinct political roles—conflict actor vs. electoral strategist. The paper establishes political-role assignment as a target for computational framing research and offers a construct-stratified reliability framework for calibrating LLM annotation pipelines in political text tasks.

Abstract: Do French news headlines frame left- and right-populist challengers as symmetric ``extremes,'' or as fundamentally different political adversaries? We examine 28,592 headlines about La France insoumise (LFI) and Rassemblement National (RN) published by 25 French-language outlets between 2022 and 2025, annotated through a three-model LLM pipeline validated against a stratified human audit. The clearest finding is role asymmetry rather than valence asymmetry: conflict framing and strategic-game framing are more robust across models and time than delegitimization, with AGGRESSOR serving as corroborating role syntax. LFI appears in headlines more often through a conflict register and RN through a strategic-electoral register. This role gap is direction-stable across all three annotation models, survives bootstrapping and permutation tests, and persists across outlet families and most of 2022-2025. A secondary moral-accounting layer (who is blamed, legitimized, or cast as a victim) is structured by outlet rather than party, producing aggregate nulls that conceal some of the corpus's most polarized patterns. Methodologically, the annotation pipeline reveals a two-tier reliability profile: conflict and strategic-game framing achieve the strongest human validation and cross-model stability; actor role is direction-stable but treated as corroborating because its audit reliability is lower; normative-judgment constructs (legitimacy, blame) are weaker. The paper contributes political-role assignment as a target for computational framing research that decomposes what valence-based measures conflate, and establishes a construct-stratified reliability framework for calibrating majority-vote LLM annotation pipelines in political text tasks.

</details>


### [3] [Carefully Considering Culture: Analyzing LLM Alignment in Single- and Multi-Cultural Settings using Cultural Consensus Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09937)
*Krishna Pothugunta,John P. Lalor*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper applies Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT) from anthropology to evaluate how well LLMs represent cultural norms. Using World Values Survey data across 10 countries and 12 domains, the authors show that models either fail to capture cohesive cultural consensus or over-regularize it, providing diagnostics to distinguish genuine cultural diversity from algorithmic flattening.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior NLP work probing LLMs for cultural norm understanding relies on distributional patterns alone, overlooking two critical dimensions: (1) within-group consensus (whether a culture coheres around a norm) and (2) multicultural heterogeneity within a single country. The authors argue that without modeling intra-group variance, researchers cannot tell whether models reflect true human cultural diversity or merely produce homogenized outputs.

Method: The authors apply Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT) — a formal framework from cognitive anthropology that models shared knowledge within groups while explicitly accounting for individual variation — to the World Values Survey (WVS). They evaluate LLM representations across 10 countries and 12 cultural domains, using CCT-derived diagnostics (consensus formation, competence-weighted aggregation, and residual variance) to compare model outputs against human response patterns.

Result: Models exhibit two failure modes: (1) failure to form cohesive consensus, where model outputs lack the structured agreement observed in human populations, and (2) severe over-regularization, where models impose artificial uniformity, erasing legitimate intra-cultural variance. CCT-based diagnostics successfully distinguish these cases, revealing where models diverge from authentic human cultural structures.

Conclusion: CCT offers a principled, actionable framework for auditing cultural representations in LLMs. By explicitly modeling intra-group variance alongside consensus, it enables researchers to diagnose whether models reflect genuine diversity or algorithmic homogenization, pointing toward more culturally faithful NLP systems.

Abstract: Recent work in NLP has probed large language models for their understanding of cultural norms across countries. However, this work typically considers distributional patterns, ignoring group consensus or possible multicultural environments within a country. In this work, we leverage cultural consensus theory (CCT) from cultural anthropology to model such multidimensional nuance. Applying CCT to the World Values Survey (WVS) across 10 countries and 12 domains, we demonstrate that models frequently misrepresent cultural structures by either failing to form cohesive consensus or severely over-regularizing consensus. Through explicit representation of intra-group variance, CCT provides actionable diagnostics to evaluate when models reflect true human diversity versus algorithmic homogenization.

</details>


### [4] [The Multilingual Quantization Tax: Structural Collapse and Typological Fragility in Edge SLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09941)
*Mohammad Wathiq Soualhi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A multilingual evaluation of 4-bit quantization in Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.5 SLMs reveals that quantization disproportionately degrades low-resource and non-Latin script languages, exposing pre-training inequalities through four identified phenomena: typological fragility, home language paradox, domain-specific forgetting, and quantization resistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of 4-bit weight quantization degradation (the "quantization tax") for Small Language Models are overwhelmingly English-centric, leaving a critical gap in understanding how quantization impacts multilingual performance, particularly for low-resource languages and diverse scripts on edge deployment scenarios.

Method: Zero-shot multilingual evaluation of 4-bit quantized Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.5 architectures across eight typologically diverse languages using two benchmarks: MMLU ProX Lite (multi-domain knowledge) and GlobalPIQA (commonsense reasoning). The study analyzes logit validity, performance degradation patterns, and architecture-specific dissociations.

Result: Four key phenomena were identified: (1) Typological Fragility — low-resource and non-Latin script languages suffer representational collapse with architecture-specific double dissociations, failing to produce valid task logits; (2) Home Language Fragility Paradox — foundational pre-training pathways provide limited protection against precision loss; (3) Domain-Specific Forgetting — multi-step cross-lingual routing degrades while associative soft-science recall remains robust; (4) Quantization Resistance — highly saturated, typologically aligned domains resist deterministic degradation, with post-quantization gains bounded by statistical noise.

Conclusion: 4-bit quantization exposes and amplifies pre-existing multilingual inequities from pre-training rather than uniformly degrading all languages. The interaction between architectural design and language typology produces double dissociations, suggesting that quantization-aware multilingual evaluation must become standard practice for responsible SLM deployment on edge devices.

Abstract: While 4-bit weight quantization is critical for deploying Small Language Models (SLMs) on edge devices, evaluations of the resulting performance degradation-the quantization tax-remain overwhelmingly English-centric. We present a zero-shot multilingual evaluation of 4-bit quantization across the Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.5 architectures. Evaluating on eight typo-logically diverse languages using MMLU ProX Lite and GlobalPIQA, we show parameter truncation exposes deep pre-training inequalities. We identify four phenomena: (1) Typological Fragility: low-resource and specific non-Latin scripts suffer representational collapse via architecture-specific double dissociations, failing to generate valid task logits; (2) Home Language Fragility Paradox: foundational pre-training pathways provide limited precision loss protection; (3) Domain-Specific Forgetting: multi-step cross-lingual routing degrades while associative soft-science recall remains robust; and (4) Quantization Resistance: highly saturated, typologically aligned domains resist deterministic degradation, with post-quantization performance gains bounded by statistical noise.

</details>


### [5] [When Chain-of-Thought Helps and When It Hurts: An Empirical Investigation of the Serial-Depth Bottleneck in LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09942)
*Tughanbulut Kurtulush*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CoT prompting is not a universal reasoning enhancer; its benefit scales with a task's serial computational depth. On high-depth (P-complete) tasks, CoT provides massive gains (+54–68 pp), while on shallow (TC⁰) tasks it is structurally redundant. The effect on intermediate-complexity tasks is model-size-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically test whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting universally improves LLM reasoning, using the H_dp bandwidth bound framework which predicts that CoT should help only when a task's serial computational depth exceeds the transformer's single-pass capacity.

Method: The authors operationalize the H_dp bandwidth bound by measuring a "serial-depth gradient": comparing no-CoT vs. CoT accuracy across tasks of varying computational depth classes (P-complete: GSM8K, MATH; L: HumanEval; TC⁰: MMLU, ARC). Three instruction-tuned models (Qwen-2.5-7B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B) are evaluated across five benchmarks at practical context lengths. Statistical analysis includes Spearman rank correlation between depth and recovery gain, plus McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction.

Result: On P-complete tasks, CoT yields a +54 to +68 pp recovery gap across all models. On TC⁰ tasks, CoT is redundant (Δ ∈ [0.0, +4.6] pp), though high no-CoT baselines (up to 95% on ARC) may reflect contamination. On the intermediate L-class task (HumanEval), the CoT effect is model-size-dependent: +23.2 pp (32B), +9.1 pp (8B), −28.7 pp (7B). The cross-benchmark depth-recovery correlation is ρ = 0.661 (p = 0.007, n = 15); 9 of 15 McNemar tests are significant after Bonferroni correction.

Conclusion: CoT functions as a bandwidth bypass for serial computation rather than a universal reasoning enhancer. It is beneficial when tasks strain single-pass transformer capacity and redundant when tasks already fit within that capacity. This reframes CoT's role in terms of architectural constraints rather than general reasoning improvement.

Abstract: It is widely assumed that chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting universally improves LLM reasoning. We investigate this through the conceptual framework of the H_dp bandwidth bound (Chen et al., 2024): although the formal bound binds only asymptotically (at astronomically large prompt lengths), it identifies a real architectural bottleneck -- serial computation exceeding a transformer's single-pass capacity must be externalised, which is what CoT does. Our central finding is a within-benchmark serial-depth gradient: single-pass (no-CoT) accuracy degrades monotonically with per-item serial depth, while CoT is approximately depth-invariant. We measure CoT effects across three instruction-tuned models (Qwen-2.5-7B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B) and five standard NLP benchmarks at practical context lengths. On high-depth P-complete tasks (GSM8K, MATH), CoT gives a +54 to +68 pp recovery gap across all models. On shallow TC^0 tasks (MMLU, ARC), CoT is structurally redundant (Delta in [0.0, +4.6] pp, no significant negative effect) -- though high no-CoT baselines (up to 95% on ARC) may reflect contamination, so this null is not a clean architectural test. The intermediate class L (HumanEval) shows a model-size-dependent transition: +23.2 pp (32B), +9.1 pp (8B), -28.7 pp (7B). The cross-benchmark depth-recovery correlation is Spearman rho = 0.661 (p = 0.007, n = 15); 9 of 15 benchmark-level McNemar tests are significant after Bonferroni correction. Pre-registered on OSF, our results indicate that CoT is not a universal reasoning enhancer but acts as a bandwidth bypass: it helps serial computation that strains single-pass capacity and is redundant for tasks that already fit.

</details>


### [6] [Position Encoding in Transformers: From Absolute and Relative Methods to Rotary Position Embeddings and Long-Context Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10021)
*Jiguo Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A unified survey of position encoding methods in Transformers, covering absolute embeddings, relative position representations, and rotary embeddings (RoPE), followed by an analysis of long-context extension techniques. The paper concludes that computing positional features beyond the training length does not guarantee reliable long-context generalization, which must be rigorously evaluated across diverse tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-attention mechanisms inherently lack sequence order information. While numerous position encoding schemes exist, the literature lacks a unified framework comparing them across dimensions such as injection point, computational cost, KV-caching compatibility, and length extrapolation. Furthermore, recent proliferation of long-context extension methods demands systematic analysis.

Method: This is a technical survey synthesizing and deriving a unified account of position encoding methods. The authors mathematically derive how RoPE transforms absolute positions into relative phase differences in Query-Key inner products. They systematically compare methods (sinusoidal/learned absolute embeddings, Shaw-style relative representations, Transformer-XL, T5 relative bias, ALiBi, RoPE) and long-context extensions (Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, Dynamic NTK, NTK-by-parts, YaRN, LongRoPE, LongRoPE2) across dimensions of frequency allocation, attention rescaling, training length, and target context length.

Result: The survey provides a structured comparison revealing trade-offs: RoPE offers strong length extrapolation and KV-cache compatibility; ALiBi incurs minimal overhead but underperforms on complex tasks; relative methods improve generalization but increase computation. For long-context extensions, frequency-aware methods (NTK-aware, YaRN) outperform naive interpolation, and LongRoPE demonstrates progressive context expansion to millions of tokens. The survey also catalogs PE choices in representative LLMs and evaluation protocols.

Conclusion: The central conclusion is that the mere ability to compute positional features beyond training length does not imply reliable long-context generalization. Proper evaluation requires a multi-faceted protocol including short-context retention, position-wise perplexity, retrieval, reasoning, and long-context code tasks. No single position encoding or extension method universally dominates; the choice depends on the target application's context-length requirements and computational constraints.

Abstract: Self-attention models content-dependent interactions between tokens but does not by itself encode token order. Position encoding addresses this limitation by introducing absolute coordinates, relative distances, or position-dependent rotations into Transformer representations and attention scores. This technical survey develops a unified account of sinusoidal and learned absolute position embeddings, Shaw-style relative position representations, Transformer-XL, T5 relative position bias, ALiBi, and Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE). We derive how RoPE converts absolute position indices into relative phase differences in Query-Key inner products and compare these methods in terms of where position is injected, computational cost, compatibility with KV caching, and length extrapolation. We then examine long-context extensions, including Position Interpolation, RoPE scaling laws, NTK-aware scaling, Dynamic NTK, NTK-by-parts, YaRN, LongRoPE, and LongRoPE2, with emphasis on frequency allocation, attention rescaling, training length, and target context length. We also summarize implementation considerations, evaluation protocols, and position-encoding choices in representative large language models. A central conclusion is that the ability to compute positional features beyond the training length does not imply reliable long-context generalization; context extension must be evaluated through short-context retention, position-wise perplexity, retrieval, reasoning, and long-context code tasks.

</details>


### [7] [PERCEPT: A Corpus for POS Tagging and Analysis of Persian-English Code-Mixing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10109)
*Ghazal Kalhor,Zahra Jafari,Amirarsalan Shahbazi,Behnam Bahrak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces PERCEPT, the first large-scale Persian-English code-mixed corpus with Universal Dependencies POS tags, built via an LLM-assisted annotation framework, and presents linguistic analyses revealing platform-specific code-mixing patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persian-English code-mixing is prevalent on social media but lacks annotated resources with Universal Dependencies POS tags, hindering linguistic analysis and development of syntax-aware NLP models for this language pair.

Method: Creation of PERCEPT corpus (6,800 posts from X, Instagram, Digikala) using an LLM-assisted annotation framework that automatically assigns POS tags and document-level topics, validated through human evaluation of annotation agreement.

Result: Nouns dominate code-mixed words across all platforms; POS category distributions vary by platform; positional distribution of code-mixed words is consistent across platforms; the triggering effect is significantly stronger in Digikala.

Conclusion: PERCEPT fills a critical resource gap for Persian-English code-mixing research, and the cross-platform linguistic analyses provide new insights into code-mixing patterns, with the dataset and framework publicly released.

Abstract: Social media has become a major venue for multilingual communication, where users frequently mix multiple languages within a single utterance. Although code-mixed corpora have been developed for several language pairs, Persian-English code-mixing remains relatively underexplored. Existing Persian resources lack Universal Dependencies (UD) part-of-speech (POS) annotations for code-mixed words, limiting both linguistic analyses and the development of syntax-aware NLP models. To address this gap, we introduce PERCEPT, the first publicly available large-scale Persian-English code-mixed corpus annotated with Universal Dependencies POS tags for code-mixed words. The dataset comprises 6,800 posts collected from X, Instagram, and Digikala. We further present an LLM-assisted annotation framework that automatically assigns POS tags and document-level topics. Human evaluation demonstrates high agreement between the automatically generated annotations and gold annotations, confirming the reliability of the annotations. Using PERCEPT, we conduct the first comprehensive linguistic analysis of Persian-English code-mixing across multiple social media platforms. Our analyses reveal that nouns are the predominant category for code-mixed words, while the distributions of other POS categories vary across platforms. We further find that the positional distribution of code-mixed words is remarkably consistent across platforms, whereas the triggering effect is substantially more pronounced in Digikala. PERCEPT is publicly available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/PERCEPT.

</details>


### [8] [The Parser Already Knows: Lightweight Bias Correction in Constrained Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10137)
*Işıl Özgü,Yaoxuan Wu,Guy Van den Broeck,Miryung Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Grammar Constrained Decoding (GCD) uses masking to enforce syntactic validity but distorts the LM's probability distribution. The authors propose a lightweight, offline-trained logit correction conditioned on existing parser/lexer states that restores the true distribution with negligible overhead, outperforming both masking and online sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GCD methods face a trade-off: rigid token masking enforces grammar conformance but distorts the LM's underlying probability distribution (biasing toward suboptimal outputs), while online sampling restores the distribution but incurs expensive iterative resampling. The authors seek to reconcile probabilistic integrity with grammar conformance without compromising inference latency.

Method: The authors leverage parser and lexer states that are inherently maintained during incremental parsing — these states already encode future grammatical validity. They propose a lightweight, offline-trained logit correction conditioned on (1) syntactic state, (2) lexical state, and (3) candidate next tokens. Since these states are already computed as part of incremental masking, extracting them adds negligible overhead and requires no modification to the base LM weights.

Result: Across several grammars, the logit correction substantially closes the gap between the masked distribution and the LM's true distribution, consistently outperforming both masking and online sampling baselines. Even the lightest variant (conditioned on the candidate next token alone) matches or exceeds both baselines, as the next token itself carries an implicit lookahead.

Conclusion: By restoring the probability mass that masking removes, the proposed approach reconciles the LM's probabilistic integrity with grammar conformance, resolving the quality-latency compromise inherent in prior GCD methods.

Abstract: Grammar Constrained Decoding (GCD) forces Language Models (LMs) to produce syntactically valid outputs by masking out non-conforming tokens at each step. However, rigid masking distorts the model's underlying probability distribution, often biasing generation toward valid but suboptimal outputs. While online sampling restores this distribution, it requires computationally expensive iterative resampling. As a result, existing methods force a compromise between output quality and inference latency. Our key insight is that the internal parser and lexer states inherently maintained during incremental parsing already encode future grammatical validity -- exactly the information required to restore the LM's true distribution. We propose a lightweight, offline-trained logit correction conditioned on this syntactic and lexical state together with candidate next tokens. Because these states are already computed as a necessary part of incremental parsing for masking, extracting them adds negligible overhead while leaving the base LM's weights completely untouched. Across several grammars, this correction substantially closes the gap between the masked distribution and the LM's true distribution, consistently outperforming both masking and online sampling. Even its lightest variant, which relies on the candidate next token alone, still matches or exceeds both baselines: the next token itself carries an implicit lookahead, much like how parsers commonly use a lookahead token to resolve ambiguous decisions. By restoring the probability mass that masking removes, it reconciles the LM's probabilistic integrity with grammar conformance.

</details>


### [9] [Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilitie](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154)
*Christopher Ormerod,YoungKoung Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A fine-tuned multimodal LLM (Qwen3.5) is trained to replicate student choice probabilities across ability levels, implicitly capturing 3PL and MCM item response curves. Item difficulty is then accurately approximated from the model's predicted option probabilities on held-out data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional psychometric models like the 3PL and MCM require explicit parametric estimation of item characteristic curves. This work explores whether a multimodal LLM can implicitly learn these response probability patterns directly from item stimuli (images and text) and student ability labels, offering a potentially more flexible, data-driven alternative to parametric IRT modeling.

Method: The authors fine-tune a Qwen3.5-based multimodal LLM on a large corpus of multiple-choice items with both image and text stimuli. The model is prompted and trained to predict choice probabilities conditioned on discrete student ability levels, thereby learning the systematic error patterns across abilities. The resulting model implicitly encodes MCM and 3PL response curves, from which option probabilities are extracted to approximate item difficulty on a held-out test set.

Result: The fine-tuned LLM successfully reproduces choice probabilities across ability levels, implicitly capturing the underlying 3PL and MCM curves. Item difficulty can be accurately approximated on held-out test items directly from the model's predicted option probabilities.

Conclusion: Multimodal LLMs can serve as effective, implicit estimators of item response functions, bypassing explicit parametric curve fitting. This demonstrates a promising intersection of deep learning and psychometrics for item analysis.

Abstract: We present results from reconstructing multiple-choice model (MCM) and three-parameter logistic (3PL) model curves using a fine-tuned multimodal large language model (LLM) based on Qwen3.5. The model is prompted and fine-tuned to replicate choice probabilities across a large training corpus of multiple-choice items containing both image and text stimuli, conditioned on a labeled set of student ability levels. By learning to reproduce the systematic error patterns of students across a discrete range of abilities, the LLM implicitly captures the underlying response probabilities encoded in the 3PL and MCM curves. This allows us to accurately approximate item difficulty on a held-out test set directly from the model's predicted option probabilities.

</details>


### [10] [Similarity Gates Approve Reversals: A Validity Audit of Embedding-Cosine Thresholds in Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10216)
*Scott E. Frias*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Embedding-cosine similarity gates used in agent frameworks for semantic equivalence checks systematically measure lexical overlap rather than meaning preservation, causing safety-critical failures where meaning-breaking reversals score higher than benign paraphrases. Standard repairs fail to generalize, though matched-pair auditing reveals potential for valid instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent frameworks widely deploy embedding-cosine similarity gates for tasks like deduplication, semantic caching, drift detection, and answer grading. These gates ostensibly answer "does this text still mean the same thing?" but the authors hypothesize they actually measure "how much did the wording change?" — a construct validity failure with serious safety implications when meaning-breaking edits (e.g., reversing a medical instruction) go undetected due to high cosine similarity.

Method: The authors audit cosine-similarity quality gates as measurement instruments through: (1) auditing a production drift guard against 56 meaning-breaking mutations; (2) systematic evaluation across 90 configuration-threshold-task cells measuring balanced accuracy; (3) constructing corpora to test whether naive corpus design confounds evaluations, comparing naive vs. balanced 2×2 designs across 18 configuration-task cells with AUROC; (4) testing obvious repairs including encoder swaps, overlap-conditioned gates, and NLI drop-in replacements, evaluated both in-sample and on separately authored held-out data; (5) matched-pair analysis of nine encoder configurations separating reversal from paraphrase at matched lexical overlap.

Result: The production guard caught 0/56 meaning-breaking mutations; a critical reversal ("withhold the study drug" → "administer the study drug") scored cosine 0.9608. Balanced accuracy across 90 configuration-threshold-task cells never exceeded 0.700 (median 0.525). Naive corpus design produced inverted verdicts (AUROC 0.000 in 13/18 cells, ≤0.040 in all 18), while balanced 2×2 design yielded AUROC 0.440–0.815. Repairs failed: overlap-conditioned gate achieved 0.750 in-sample but only 0.533 held-out; NLI drop-in performed no better. However, the strongest two of nine configurations separated reversal from paraphrase at matched overlap (AUROC 0.79–0.90) under matched-pair auditing.

Conclusion: Cosine-similarity gates deployed in production measure lexical overlap, not semantic equivalence, producing systematically invalid safety checks. Obvious repairs (encoder swaps, NLI) fail to generalize. However, matched-pair auditing demonstrates that embeddings can distinguish reversal from paraphrase when overlap is controlled (AUROC up to 0.90), suggesting a valid measurement instrument is constructible with proper auditing methodology. The authors release the corpus method, harness, and results.

Abstract: Agent frameworks ship quality gates that compare text blocks by embedding-cosine similarity and decide at a fixed cutoff. Deduplication filters, semantic caches, drift guards, and answer grader gates deploy to answer the question: "Does this text still mean the same thing?" But the score answers a different question: "How much did the wording change?" We audit this gate class as a measurement instrument. In the cases these gates exist to catch, the two can run in opposite ways. Many times, reversing an instruction is a single word edit, while agreement often rephrases a sentence. The consequence is a safety check that fires backwards. The production drift guard we audited caught 0 of 56 meaning-breaking mutations, and one approved item, "withhold the study drug" -> "administer the study drug", came in at cosine 0.9608. We observed five shipped operating points, and balanced accuracy across 90 configuration-threshold-task cells never exceeded 0.700 (median 0.525). The same confounder also corrupted evaluations. A naively built corpus inherits this confounder and can return an inverted verdict, with a decision AUROC exactly 0.000 in 13 of 18 configuration-task cells (at most 0.040 in all 18) against 0.440-0.815 for the same nine configurations under a balanced 2x2 design. Twice in the effort it captured our own headline claims. Obvious repairs fail: an encoder swap and an overlap-conditioned gate (0.750 in-sample, 0.533 held-out) land at chance on separately authored held-out data, and an NLI drop-in did no better. Embeddings do still bear hope here, as the strongest two of nine configurations separated reversal from paraphrase at matched overlap (AUROC 0.79-0.90), but only a matched-pair audit reveals the deployment regime. We release the corpus method, harness, and frozen results, and contend that scores gated this way measure the wrong thing. We believe a valid instrument is buildable.

</details>


### [11] [Off-Axis, On Purpose: Where a Transformer Computes Concepts and Why it Does So](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10251)
*Mark Oskin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Transformers compute in two phases: an early "concept phase" where representations are held nearly orthogonal to the read-out direction (insulating composition from vocabulary), and a late phase where the answer arrives on-axis via addition. This off-axis geometry is functional—forcing representations onto the read-out axis damages cross-token mixing. The concept subspace's basis is arbitrary and can be prescribed randomly before training without quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the prevailing view that intermediate transformer states lying off the unembedding axis are merely an obstacle to interpretability, and to demonstrate that this off-axis geometry serves a critical functional role in separating conceptual computation from vocabulary read-out.

Method: Analysis of a 12-layer transformer's residual stream geometry through angular measurements of attention outputs relative to the unembedding direction at each depth. Intervention studies rotate attention outputs onto the read-out axis (vs. random rotations) and measure damage. Training experiments manipulate the geometry: early-exit training, loss-based prescription, and inserting fixed/sparse rotations at the phase boundary. Benchmarked on perplexity, LAMBADA, and BLiMP.

Result: Attention outputs remain 75–96° off the read-out axis throughout the concept phase. Forcing them on-axis is 64–84× more damaging than random rotation, with damage confined to cross-token mixing. Early-exit training matches baseline but shrinks the concept workspace from ~25 to 14 effective dimensions. Prescribing geometry via loss collapses 6/8 seeds; inserting a fixed rotation works (baseline quality); sparse rotation converges 9/9 seeds vs. 5/9 for standard training. Random prescribed bases are adopted with unchanged quality. Two baseline seeds hold concepts in near-orthogonal frames while agreeing on read-outs.

Conclusion: The off-axis concept subspace is a functional architectural feature that insulates compositional computation from vocabulary read-out. Its orientation is largely arbitrary—different random bases work equally well—suggesting the geometry is a learned convention rather than a constrained optimum. This has implications for interpretability and for engineering interventions like early exit.

Abstract: A transformer's answer lives on one axis: the direction its unembedding reads. Its intermediate states largely do not, and that off-axis position is usually treated as an obstacle to interpretation. We show it is functional. A 12-layer model computes in two phases. Through the first, every sublayer writes into a subspace held near-orthogonal to the read-out, attention 75 to 96 degrees off it at every depth. Moving attention's values onto the read-out is 64 to 84 times more damaging than a matched random rotation, and the damage is entirely in cross-token mixing: the subspace insulates composition from the vocabulary. Beneath it the frame itself turns rigidly with depth. In the second phase the answer arrives on-axis, late, and by addition rather than by turning accumulated content onto the read-out.
  Pressing every layer onto the read-out instead, as training for early exit does, matches the baseline on perplexity, LAMBADA and BLiMP while cutting the concept-phase workspace from about twenty-five effective dimensions to fourteen, a change none of those benchmarks register. The geometry can also be imposed, though not by asking for it. Prescribing it through the loss is a lottery: six of eight seeds collapse, because a model told to null its read-out projection obeys most cheaply by discarding dimensions. Inserting one fixed rotation at the phase boundary lands it instead, at baseline quality. A sparse rotation the surrounding weights can absorb converges on all nine seeds, against five of nine for ordinary training. Which rotation is immaterial: twenty-five runs across thirteen distinct ones reach the same quality, and two baselines from different seeds hold their concepts in near-orthogonal frames while agreeing on their read-outs. That freedom is usable: a basis drawn at random and prescribed before training is adopted across the concept phase, with quality unchanged.

</details>


### [12] [TAF-MED: Multi-Turn Safety Refusal Collapse in LLMs Under Declared Self-Treatment Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10258)
*Waleed Jamil,Raphael Schmitt*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TAF-MED evaluates LLM medication-safety across multi-turn conversations, revealing that 71.6% of dialogues contain unsafe responses and 61.4% of initially safe responses later collapse to unsafe, demonstrating that first-turn safety is an inadequate proxy for conversational safety persistence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for conversational health information that may influence treatment decisions, yet existing benchmarks fail to isolate whether medication-safety boundaries hold across follow-up turns after users express explicit self-treatment intent. There is a critical gap in evaluating safety persistence throughout complete dialogue trajectories rather than just initial responses.

Method: The authors introduce TAF-MED, a physician-reviewed benchmark comprising 500 fixed three-turn scenarios designed to probe medication-safety boundaries. Eight LLMs were evaluated across 4,000 total conversations. A rubric-based automated judge classified responses as SAFE, LEAKY, or UNSAFE. Two physicians independently annotated a model-balanced random subset of 400 conversations for validation. The analysis assessed unsafe guidance prevalence, collapse rates after initially SAFE responses, and model-ranking stability between initial unsafe rates and collapse rates.

Result: 71.6% of all conversations contained at least one UNSAFE response. Among conversations that began with a strictly SAFE first-turn response, 61.4% subsequently collapsed to UNSAFE in later turns. Model-level collapse rates ranged dramatically from 24.4% to 96.2%. Four of 28 model pairs exhibited rank reversals between initial unsafe rates and collapse rates. The automated judge achieved 94.3% agreement with the adjudicated physician reference (κ = 0.895).

Conclusion: First-turn safety is an incomplete and potentially misleading proxy for conversational safety persistence. Evaluating LLM safety requires assessment across complete multi-turn dialogue trajectories, as models frequently exhibit safety collapse after initially safe responses. The TAF-MED benchmark will be released on Hugging Face to enable reproducible multi-turn medical safety research.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly provide conversational health information that may influence treatment decisions, yet existing benchmarks do not isolate whether medication-safety boundaries persist across follow-ups after explicit self-treatment intent. We introduce TAF-MED, a physician-reviewed benchmark of 500 fixed three-turn scenarios, and evaluate eight LLMs across 4,000 conversations. A rubric-based automated judge labelled responses as SAFE, LEAKY, or UNSAFE, and two physicians independently annotated a model-balanced random subset of 400 conversations. We assessed unsafe guidance, collapse after a strictly SAFE initial response, and model-ranking stability. Overall, 71.6% of conversations contained an UNSAFE response, and 61.4% of those beginning with a strictly SAFE response later collapsed to UNSAFE; model-level collapse rates ranged from 24.4% to 96.2%. Four of 28 model pairs reversed order between initial unsafe and collapse rates. Automated labels achieved 94.3% agreement with the adjudicated physician reference ($κ= 0.895$). These findings show that first-turn safety is an incomplete proxy for conversational safety persistence and motivate evaluation across complete dialogue trajectories. We will release TAF-MED on Hugging Face to support reproducible research on multi-turn medical safety.

</details>


### [13] [Locally Deployable Small Language Models for Emergency Department Decision Support: A Systematic Benchmark of Fine-Tuning Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10273)
*Qingfeng Zhang,Yuanxiong Guo,Yanmin Gong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Open-source small language models fine-tuned with LoRA can outperform commercial LLMs (Claude) on triage and specialist referral tasks in emergency departments, offering a privacy-preserving, locally deployable alternative, though diagnosis prediction remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two key challenges motivate this work: (1) privacy risks associated with transmitting sensitive patient data to closed-source commercial LLMs, and (2) the lack of systematic evaluation of fine-tuning strategies for open-source small language models (SLMs) that could be deployed locally in EDs.

Method: The authors benchmarked eight open-source SLMs across four strategies — zero-shot prompting, prefix tuning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning — on three ED tasks (triage level prediction, specialist referral recommendation, diagnosis prediction). Evaluation used 2,083 MIMIC-IV-ED cases, with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 serving as commercial baselines. Confusion matrix analysis was also conducted.

Result: LoRA fine-tuned open-source SLMs outperformed both Claude baselines on triage level prediction and specialist referral recommendation. Confusion matrix analysis revealed that fine-tuned SLMs detected highest-severity patients missed by the commercial baselines. However, diagnosis prediction remained a challenging task for open-source SLMs.

Conclusion: Locally deployable, fine-tuned open-source SLMs can achieve clinically competitive performance for ED decision support, offering a viable privacy-preserving alternative to commercial LLMs, with particular strength in high-acuity case detection.

Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) for decision support in emergency departments (EDs) faces two major challenges: privacy risks of transmitting patient data to closed-source commercial LLMs and the lack of systematic evaluation of fine-tuning strategies for locally deployable open-source small language models (SLMs). We benchmarked eight open-source SLMs using zero-shot prompting, prefix tuning, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and full fine-tuning on three ED tasks: triage level prediction, specialist referral recommendation, and diagnosis prediction. Using 2,083 MIMIC-IV-ED cases and Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 as baselines, we found that LoRA fine-tuned open-source SLMs outperform commercial baselines on triage level prediction and specialist referral recommendation, while diagnosis prediction remains challenging for open-source SLMs. Confusion matrix analysis further shows that fine-tuned open-source SLMs can detect highest-severity patients missed by the commercial baselines. These results demonstrate that locally deployable SLMs can achieve clinically competitive performance for ED decision support.

</details>


### [14] [Cracks in the Foundation: Seemingly Minor Architectural Choices Impact Long Context Extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10296)
*Amanda Bertsch,Luca Soldaini,Matthew R. Gormley,Graham Neubig,Hannaneh Hajishirzi,Kyle Lo,Dirk Groeneveld*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Minor architectural choices in dense transformers compound to severely degrade long-context performance (up to 47% drop), despite being undetectable from short-context metrics. The authors release OlmPool, 26 comparable 7B models, to isolate these effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prevailing assumption that architectural variations within dense transformer families have limited impact on accuracy is false specifically in long-context settings. The authors aim to identify which architectural decisions drive the large observed variation in long-context ability across model families (Olmo, Llama, Qwen).

Method: Controlled ablation study fixing data, tokenizer, and context-extension recipe while systematically varying four architectural features: normalization scheme, Grouped Query Attention (GQA), pretraining context length, and sliding window attention. Over 170,000 GPU hours of training produced 26 comparable 7B models with checkpoints before and after long-context extension. Analysis of attention sink behavior and attention distributions was also conducted.

Result: Any single architectural change alone has minor impact, but combining three or more causes up to 47% downstream performance degradation. These effects are invisible in short-context loss or validation. Architectural features explain much of the cross-family variation in long-context ability and are detectable by applying context extension early in pretraining. Several architectures in OlmPool outperform Llama 3 on long-context extensibility.

Conclusion: Long-context performance in dense transformers is highly sensitive to the compound effect of seemingly minor architectural decisions. Early detection via context extension during pretraining is feasible. The OlmPool model suite provides a controlled resource for further investigation.

Abstract: One might imagine that architectural variations within the dense transformer paradigm have a limited effect on accuracy. However, we demonstrate that this is not the case in the long context setting. Specifically, we show that a set of four minor architectural decisions --- all made by at least one of the Olmo, Llama, and Qwen dense model families --- have a compoundingly negative effect on long context extensibility. Any one of these choices alone has a minor impact on long context performance, but combining three or more can drop the performance downstream by up to 47%. Furthermore, these differences are not detectable from short-context loss or validation datasets. We show that much of the variation in long context ability across model families is driven by these architectural features and detectable from applying context extension early in pretraining. We demonstrate this with controlled ablations that hold data, tokenizer, and extension recipe fixed while varying normalization, GQA, pretraining context length, and sliding window attention. After over 170,000 GPU hours of training, we release the resulting set of models as OlmPool, a set of 26 comparable 7B models with checkpoints before and after long-context extension. This pool includes several architectures that outperform the Llama 3 architecture on long context extensibility. In an analysis of our ablation models, we identify patterns in attention sink behavior and attention distributions across context that are attributable to specific architectural differences.

</details>


### [15] [Co-Evolution in Agentic Systems: Toward Self-Directed Evolution Beyond Human Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10299)
*Qing Zong,Jiayu Liu,Junhao Shen,Zecong Tang,Linsi Wu,Yuxuan Liu,Rui Wang,Zhaowei Wang,Weiqi Wang,Cheng Qian,Xiusi Chen,Yangqiu Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This survey introduces a three-stage taxonomy for co-evolution in agentic systems: Agent-Agent, Agent-Environment, and Meta Co-Evolution, progressively shedding human constraints to enable open-ended improvement beyond static single-agent self-evolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-agent self-evolution is limited by fixed tasks and feedback. The authors argue that true open-ended improvement requires multi-component co-evolution where agents and their environment mutually exert adaptive pressure, but this emerging area lacks a unified organizational framework.

Method: The authors propose a progressive three-stage taxonomy: (1) Agent-Agent Co-Evolution covering adversarial, collaborative, and organizational adaptation among dynamic peers; (2) Agent-Environment Co-Evolution where tasks, feedback, and interaction spaces co-adapt with agents; (3) Meta Co-Evolution where the evolution mechanism itself becomes evolvable. This taxonomy organizes existing literature by how systems progressively shed human-engineered constraints.

Result: The survey provides a structured mapping of the co-evolution landscape across the three taxonomy stages, identifies open challenges in evaluation, multi-component scaling, and safety/controllability of increasingly autonomous evolutionary processes.

Conclusion: Co-evolution offers a path toward robust, open-ended agentic systems that can improve beyond fixed human-designed trajectories, but significant challenges remain in evaluation methodology, scalability, and ensuring safe autonomous evolution.

Abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly expected to improve after deployment, yet single-entity self-evolution is often bounded by a static learning context, such as fixed tasks and feedback. This survey focuses on co-evolution in agentic systems, a multi-component form of self-evolution in which multiple agents and their environment impose adaptive pressure on one another. To organize existing papers, we propose a progressive three-stage taxonomy that traces how the system gradually sheds human-engineered constraints. Agent--Agent Co-Evolution studies how agents adapt through dynamic peers, including adversarial, collaborative, and organizational adaptation. Agent--Environment Co-Evolution extends this loop to adaptive tasks, feedback, and interaction spaces that change with the agents. Meta Co-Evolution further explores the possibility of making the evolution mechanism itself evolvable. We also discuss open challenges in evaluating such systems, scaling them across multiple components, and keeping increasingly autonomous evolutionary processes safe and controllable. This survey provides a unified foundation for building robust and open-ended agentic systems that can improve beyond fixed human-designed paths.

</details>


### [16] [Is This Your Final Answer? Cross-Contextual Consistency as a Measure of LLM Credibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10315)
*Siyang Wu,Yibo Jiang,Bryon Aragam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Cross-Contextual Consistency (C3), a behavioral property where an LLM's answer should remain stable under topic-aligned, content-neutral contextual perturbations. Stable answers correlate with correctness across 26 models and 6 benchmarks, and C3 doubles as a diagnostic for benchmark saturation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are black-box systems, making it hard to tell whether outputs reflect genuine internal knowledge or superficial pattern matching. Existing evaluation metrics focus on aggregated accuracy but overlook behavioral signals like consistency. The authors aim to leverage cross-contextual stability as an underutilized signal of answer reliability.

Method: The authors operationalize C3 by perturbing original prompts with topic-aligned, content-neutral variations and measuring the shift between model generations under original vs. perturbed conditions. Lower shift indicates higher consistency. They evaluate this across 26 models on 6 benchmarks covering reasoning, factuality, and code generation, analyzing the correlation between consistency and correctness.

Result: Answers exhibiting smaller cross-contextual shifts are consistently more likely to be correct or factual. C3 provides a complementary evaluation axis beyond standard accuracy. Additionally, C3 identifies which parts of a benchmark retain discriminative power even when aggregate scores appear saturated.

Conclusion: Cross-contextual consistency is a reliable behavioral signal for answer quality in LLMs. It offers a model-agnostic, output-level diagnostic that complements existing metrics and can expose benchmark saturation, enabling more nuanced evaluation of LLM capabilities.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful black-box systems, making it difficult to discern whether their answers reflect stable internal beliefs or superficial pattern matching. We identify cross-contextual consistency as an underutilized behavioral property of LLMs: a credible answer should remain stable when the same task is placed under topic-aligned, content-neutral contextual variation. Building on this intuition, we operationalize Cross-Contextual Consistency (C3) by comparing model generations under original and perturbed prompts. Across 26 models and six benchmarks spanning reasoning, factuality, and code generation, we find that answers with smaller cross-contextual shifts are more likely to be correct or factual. We demonstrate that C3 provides a complementary axis of evaluation and can serve as a benchmark usefulness diagnostic, identifying which portions of a benchmark remain informative even when aggregated scores are widely considered "saturate".

</details>


### [17] [VisEditBench: Can Vision-Language Models Edit Visualization Code from Multimodal Feedback?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10408)
*Mizanur Rahman,Arshia Azimlu,Shadikur Rahman,Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar,Amran Bhuiyan,Shafiq Joty,Enamul Hoque Prince*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VisEditBench is a benchmark of 1,395 human-annotated visualization code-editing tasks evaluating VLMs on feedback-guided repair and reference-guided restyling. Top model Claude-4.6-Sonnet achieves 74.46% overall but only 55.71% on style adaptation. The authors propose VisEditAgent, a render-grounded editing framework improving GPT-4o's pass rate from 55.75% to 67.99%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world visualization authoring is iterative, involving frequent revisions to fix flawed charts or adapt styles. Existing benchmarks only evaluate generation from scratch, leaving multimodal visualization code editing largely unexplored.

Method: The paper introduces VisEditBench with 1,395 human-annotated tasks across two settings: (1) feedback-guided repair using buggy/marked charts with textual feedback, and (2) reference-guided restyling to match a target chart image. 20 VLMs are evaluated. The authors also propose VisEditAgent, a render-grounded editing framework that iteratively generates, executes, validates, and refines candidate edits.

Result: Claude-4.6-Sonnet achieves best overall pass rate of 74.46%; most open-source models remain below 50%. Performance is weakest on reference-guided restyling (Claude-4.6-Sonnet: 55.71%). VisEditAgent (built on GPT-4o) improves pass rate from 55.75% to 67.99%.

Conclusion: Visualization code editing from multimodal feedback remains a challenging task for VLMs, particularly style adaptation. Render-grounded iterative feedback significantly improves editing faithfulness, as demonstrated by VisEditAgent.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong capabilities in generating visualization code from textual or visual specifications. However, real-world visualization authoring is inherently iterative: users frequently revise existing visualizations to repair flawed charts or adapt them to desired styles. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate generation from scratch, leaving visualization code editing from multimodal feedback largely unexplored. We introduce VisEditBench, a benchmark of 1,395 human-annotated visualization code-editing tasks grounded in realistic visualization workflows and failure cases. VisEditBench covers two practical settings: feedback-guided repair, where models revise visualization code using buggy or marked charts together with textual feedback, and reference-guided restyling, where models modify code to match a target chart image. Evaluating 20 state-of-the-art VLMs reveals that visualization code editing remains challenging: Claude-4.6-Sonnet achieves the best overall pass rate of 74.46%, while most open-source models remain below 50%. Performance is particularly weak on visually grounded style adaptation, where Claude-4.6-Sonnet achieves only 55.71%. To establish a strong baseline, we further propose VisEditAgent, a render-grounded editing framework that iteratively generates, executes, validates, and refines candidate edits. Built on GPT-4o, VisEditAgent improves overall pass rate from 55.75% to 67.99%, demonstrating the importance of render-grounded feedback for faithful visualization editing. We will release VisEditBench at https://github.com/vis-nlp/VisEditBench.

</details>


### [18] [How Robust Are LLMs to Vietnamese Dialects?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10414)
*Minh Tran,Trinh Chau,Thanh-Nhan Le,Nam Tran,Luan Thanh Nguyen,Cuong Dang,Duc Hoang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VialectBench is the first systematic benchmark evaluating LLM robustness to Vietnamese dialect variation across six dialect groups and four NLP tasks. Across 10 instruction-tuned models, dialectal inputs cause an average 2.82% performance degradation, with QA being most affected and Central dialects (PNT1-PNT4) producing the highest harmful-flip rates (6.54%). No model is fully dialect-invariant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Vietnamese dialect research focuses on dialect-to-standard normalization rather than directly measuring how LLMs fail under dialectal inputs. Standard Vietnamese evaluation masks systematic brittleness to regional variation that preserves meaning but alters surface form, leaving a critical robustness gap unquantified.

Method: The authors construct VialectBench, comprising 400 Standard Vietnamese source instances and 2,400 human-written dialectal rewrites across six dialect groups (covering Northern, Central, and Southern regions). Tasks span emotion recognition, NLI, QA, and MCQA. Evaluation uses a fixed reference LM to verify that rewrites induce measurable likelihood shifts while preserving length parity. Ten instruction-tuned models are then benchmarked to quantify per-task, per-dialect, and per-model degradation, including harmful-flip rate analysis.

Result: Dialectal inputs reduce average performance by 2.82% across all models; no model achieves full dialect invariance. QA suffers the largest degradation. PNT3 and PNT2 (Central dialects) cause the largest drops (6.17% and 4.73%), while PNB slightly improves performance (+0.42%). The Central group yields the highest average harmful-flip rate (6.54%).

Conclusion: Strong Standard Vietnamese performance does not guarantee reliable behavior under dialectal variation. Dialect robustness must be explicitly measured and addressed, as degradation patterns are both task- and dialect-group-specific.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on standard written Vietnamese, yet everyday communication frequently involves regional dialects that preserve meaning but differ in surface form. Existing Vietnamese dialect work largely addresses this issue through dialect-to-standard normalization instead of measuring how the model fails under Vietnamese dialectal inputs. To address this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation of LLM robustness to Vietnamese dialect variation across multiple tasks, quantifying performance degradation and failure patterns. We introduce VialectBench (Vietnamese Dialects Benchmarking), a controlled benchmark for testing whether model decisions remain stable across six Vietnamese dialect groups. VialectBench contains 400 Standard Vietnamese source instances and 2,400 human-written dialectal rewrites spanning emotion recognition (ER), natural language inference (NLI), question answering (QA), and multiple-choice question answering (MCQA). Dataset evaluation with a fixed reference language model shows that the dialectal rewrites induce a measurable model-relative likelihood shift while remaining nearly equal in length to their Standard counterparts. Across ten instruction-tuned models, dialectal inputs reduce average performance by 2.82%, and no evaluated model is fully dialect-invariant. All four tasks are affected, with QA showing the largest average degradation. Robustness also varies substantially across dialect groups: PNT3 and PNT2 cause the largest average performance drops, at 6.17% and 4.73%, respectively, whereas PNB slightly improves average performance by 0.42%. The Central dialect group (PNT1-PNT4) also yields the highest average harmful-flip rate across all models, at 6.54%. These findings show that strong performance on Standard Vietnamese does not guarantee reliable behavior under meaning-preserving regional variation.

</details>


### [19] [From Reasoning Depth to Reasoning Breadth: Evaluating Multi-Point Associative Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10444)
*Si'an Xie,Jiaxun Liu,Biao Yang,Wei Yuan,Fan Yang,Tingting Gao,Ming Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MPAR-Bench is a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark measuring reasoning breadth—the ability to integrate multiple semantically diverse clues in parallel—revealing that current LLMs' strong reasoning depth does not translate to robust breadth, with models vulnerable to perturbations even when using extended chain-of-thought.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs have shown impressive progress in reasoning depth (long inferential chains), reasoning breadth—exploring multiple semantic directions simultaneously and synthesizing them—remains largely unexamined. Existing benchmarks do not isolate this orthogonal dimension of reasoning.

Method: The authors construct MPAR-Bench with 1,000 items using a multi-agent clue-generation pipeline with embedding-based diversity filtering and human verification. Each item requires recovering a hidden target word from independently generated, semantically diverse clues (inspired by the game Just One). Models are evaluated via exact-match accuracy, ANLS, embedding similarity, reasoning-trace verification, and four perturbation tests: clue masking, order shuffling, distractor injection, and multi-step clues.

Result: Perturbations reduce accuracy by 9-18 pp in English and 5-12 pp in Chinese across evaluated models. Thinking mode (extended reasoning) improves standard accuracy, especially in English, but does not consistently reduce perturbation sensitivity. Case analysis shows extended reasoning can overturn initially correct hypotheses, indicating deeper reasoning does not guarantee robust breadth.

Conclusion: Greater reasoning depth does not automatically confer robust reasoning breadth. Reasoning breadth remains largely uncovered by current benchmarks and represents a distinct capability dimension requiring dedicated evaluation and improvement.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress on reasoning tasks that require increasingly long and complex inferential chains. This progress primarily reflects reasoning depth. A complementary and comparatively unexamined capability is reasoning breadth: exploring multiple semantic directions in parallel and integrating the resulting clues into one coherent answer. We introduce MPAR-Bench, a bilingual English-Chinese benchmark that isolates reasoning breadth through multi-point associative reasoning. Inspired by the cooperative game Just One, each item asks a model to recover a hidden target from several independently generated, semantically diverse clues. We construct 1,000 items using a multi-agent clue-generation pipeline, embedding-based diversity filtering, and human verification. Only the answer space is drawn from public word lists, whereas every clue set is generated from scratch. Beyond exact-match accuracy, we evaluate models using accuracy, ANLS, embedding similarity, reasoning-trace verification, and four perturbations: clue masking, order shuffling, distractor injection, and multi-step clues. Across evaluated models, perturbations reduce accuracy by 9-18 percentage points in English and 5-12 percentage points in Chinese. Thinking mode improves standard-setting accuracy, especially in English, but does not consistently reduce sensitivity to perturbations. Case-level analysis also shows that extended reasoning can overturn an initially correct hypothesis. These results indicate that greater reasoning depth does not automatically confer robust reasoning breadth, and that reasoning breadth remains largely uncovered by current benchmarks.

</details>


### [20] [MD-ProTector: Positioning Multiple Data-Driven Prototypes for LLM-Generated Text Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10459)
*Jinmo Han,Jimin Hong,Chanyeong Moon,Ju Yeon Kang,Seonuk Kim,Nam Soo Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MD-ProTector is a multi-prototype detector for LLM-generated text that uses multiple trainable reference vectors (prototypes) per class in encoder embedding space, combined with a Prototype Positioning loss, to capture within-class variation. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard binary classifiers for LLM-generated text detection output only a class label without organizing the substantial within-class variation caused by diverse writing styles, domains, languages, and generator models. This limits both interpretability and robustness in large-scale deployment.

Method: MD-ProTector represents each class (human vs. LLM-generated) with multiple trainable prototype vectors in the encoder embedding space, creating separate decision boundaries for different text subgroups. A novel Prototype Positioning loss explicitly separates class-level discriminative structure from the within-class variation that differentiates individual prototypes, ensuring each prototype captures a meaningful subgroup.

Result: Evaluated on five settings across three benchmarks (MAGE CDCM, RAID), MD-ProTector achieves the highest AvgRec on MAGE CDCM and RAID, and the highest AUROC and lowest FPR95 on RAID among encoder-based methods, covering domain, generator, language, and adversarial variation.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling within-class variation via multiple prototypes with the Prototype Positioning loss significantly improves LLM-generated text detection, outperforming standard encoder-based binary classifiers across diverse and challenging evaluation settings.

Abstract: As LLM-generated content becomes more sophisticated, detection systems for distinguishing those texts from human-written text must operate at scale while handling diverse writing styles, domains, languages, and generator models. Input-only encoder detectors are suitable for practical deployment setting, but standard binary classification supplies only the class label and does not explicitly organize the substantial variation within either class. We propose MD-ProTector, which represents each class with multiple trainable reference vectors in the encoder embedding space, referred to as prototypes. These prototypes provide separate decision boundaries for different groups of texts within the same class. However, adding multiple prototypes alone does not determine which variation each prototype should represent. MD-ProTector addresses this problem with Prototype Positioning loss, which separates class-level structure from the within-class variation that differentiates individual prototypes. Evaluated across five settings from three large-scale benchmarks covering domain, generator, language, and adversarial variation, MD-ProTector achieves the highest AvgRec on MAGE CDCM and RAID and the highest AUROC and lowest FPR95 on RAID among the compared encoder-based methods.

</details>


### [21] [Leveraging Human Reading Behavior for Keyphrase Extraction: A Webcam-based Eye-tracking Corpus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10688)
*Chengzhi Zhang,Xinyi Yan,Wenqi Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether lightweight, webcam-based eye-tracking features (FFD, FN, TFD) can improve keyphrase extraction from Chinese LIS academic abstracts, finding that combining FN and TFD significantly boosts performance on an Att-BiLSTM+CRF model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KPE research focuses heavily on improving textual representations but largely ignores human reading behavior. Eye-tracking offers a window into cognitive processing during reading, yet traditional eye-trackers are expensive and data for Chinese academic reading is scarce.

Method: The authors built a lightweight webcam-based eye-tracking platform using SearchGazer and constructed the Chinese LIS Eye-Tracking Corpus (CLIS-ET). Three character-level features — first fixation duration (FFD), fixation number (FN), and total fixation duration (TFD) — were integrated into KPE models (notably Att-BiLSTM+CRF) to measure their impact on extraction performance.

Result: All eye-tracking features consistently improved KPE performance. The combination of FN and TFD yielded the best results, confirming that reader fixation patterns carry meaningful signals for identifying keyphrases.

Conclusion: A cost-effective webcam-based eye-tracking methodology is viable for augmenting KPE. The CLIS-ET corpus and the demonstrated value of human reading behavior features open new directions for cognitively-informed keyphrase extraction systems.

Abstract: Purpose: Keyphrases are statistically and semantically important textual units that can also attract readers' attention during comprehension. However, existing keyphrase extraction (KPE) studies mainly focus on improving textual representation while largely overlooking human reading behavior. This study examines whether lightweight webcam-based eye-tracking features can improve KPE from Chinese academic abstracts in Library and Information Science (LIS).
  Methodology: To address the limited availability of eye-tracking data for Chinese academic reading, we developed a lightweight webcam-based data collection platform using the open-source SearchGazer library and constructed the Chinese LIS Eye-Tracking Corpus (CLIS-ET). Three character-level eye-tracking features, first fixation duration (FFD), fixation number (FN), and total fixation duration (TFD), were incorporated into KPE models to evaluate their effects on extraction performance.
  Findings: Eye-tracking features consistently improved KPE performance. The combination of FN and TFD achieved the best results on the Att-BiLSTM+CRF model, indicating that readers' fixation behavior provides useful signals for identifying keyphrases in academic abstracts.
  Originality/value: This study introduces a cost-effective webcam-based eye-tracking approach for KPE and presents CLIS-ET, a Chinese academic eye-tracking corpus containing FFD, FN, and TFD features. The results demonstrate the value of incorporating human reading behavior into keyphrase extraction. Dataset and code: https://github.com/yan-xinyi/ET_AKE and https://github.com/yan-xinyi/Reading_ET_System.

</details>


### [22] [Calibrating Post-Training Feature Shifts for LLM Data Contamination Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10462)
*Zhen Yang,Mengqi Wang,Gengda Zhao,Mo Zhou,Jianwei Wang,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CalibDCD is a calibration framework that corrects feature shifts introduced by LLM post-training (e.g., instruction tuning, RLHF) to improve data contamination detection, achieving up to 7.0% AUC and 15.0% TPR@5%FPR gains over existing feature-based detectors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLMs undergo post-training (instruction tuning, preference optimization, reasoning-oriented training) that alters model outputs and shifts membership features, reducing the separability between members and non-members in corpus-level data contamination detection. Existing feature-based DCD methods degrade under these distribution shifts.

Method: CalibDCD consists of two components: (1) Multi-View Shift Detection — evaluates controlled prompt variants on known non-member texts, consolidating the most informative views to identify recurring feature shifts caused by post-training; (2) Bounded Feature Correction — selectively adjusts feature components aligned with detected shifts, with a bounded correction extent to preserve useful detection information while mitigating shift-induced bias.

Result: CalibDCD consistently improves existing feature-based DCD detectors, with gains of up to 7.0% in AUC and 15.0% in TPR@5%FPR across experiments.

Conclusion: CalibDCD provides a broadly applicable, plug-and-play calibration framework that effectively mitigates post-training-induced feature shifts, substantially boosting the reliability of feature-based data contamination detection methods.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive and largely undisclosed corpora that may contain copyrighted or privacy-sensitive content. Data contamination detection (DCD) therefore aims to determine whether a given text is a member of the pre-training corpus of a target LLM. Recent state-of-the-art DCD methods follow a feature-based paradigm that derives membership features from the input text and the corresponding model output. However, most modern LLMs undergo post-training, such as instruction tuning, preference optimization, and reasoning-oriented training, which can alter model outputs and shift the corresponding membership features, thereby reducing the separability between members and non-members.
  To address this problem, we propose CalibDCD, a broadly applicable calibration framework for feature-based DCD methods, comprising (1) Multi-View Shift Detection, which identifies recurring feature shifts associated with post-training, and (2) Bounded Feature Correction, which selectively mitigates their influence on membership prediction. Specifically, Multi-View Shift Detection evaluates controlled prompt variants on known non-member texts and consolidates the most informative views to identify recurring feature shifts. Bounded Feature Correction selectively adjusts feature components aligned with the detected shifts and controls the correction extent to preserve useful detection information.
  Experiments show that CalibDCD consistently improves existing feature-based detectors, with gains of up to 7.0% in AUC and 15.0% in TPR@5%FPR.

</details>


### [23] [Every Token Counts: Exact Likert-Scale Distributions for Measuring LLM Attitudes and Biases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10503)
*Davood Wadi,Mohsen Ghodrat,Matthew Philp*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a controlled behavioral evaluation framework for LLMs that uses factorial experimental designs, exact token-level probability mass functions, and distributional ANOVA to isolate causal biases, demonstrated through a case study on consumer ethnocentrism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM bias evaluations rely on large, unstructured benchmarks that conflate causal mechanisms—they cannot disentangle whether detected bias stems from baseline traits, contextual confounders, or interaction effects. This limits the interpretability and actionability of bias assessments.
