Method: The framework integrates three components: (1) fully crossed factorial experimental designs replacing unstructured prompts to isolate main and interaction effects; (2) operating on exact token-level Probability Mass Functions (PMFs) rather than Monte Carlo text sampling to eliminate sampling noise; (3) a multivariate ordinal consensus metric and distributional ANOVA for analytical processing of PMFs.

Result: A case study on consumer ethnocentrism across five LLMs demonstrates that the framework successfully isolates systemic country-of-origin biases that aggregate benchmarks would otherwise obscure, validating the approach's ability to disentangle causal mechanisms.

Conclusion: The proposed psychometrics-grounded, analytically exact framework enables rigorous causal inference about LLM biases by resolving design, measurement, and analysis gaps inherent in unstructured benchmark evaluations.

Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, accurately evaluating their latent values and biases is critical. The NLP community typically evaluates models using large, unstructured benchmarks. While effective for general capabilities, these datasets fundamentally conflate causal mechanisms: even when an aggregate bias is detected, unstructured evaluations cannot disentangle whether it stems from baseline traits, contextual confounders, or complex interactions. To address this, we introduce an analytically exact framework for the controlled behavioral evaluation of LLMs. We bridge human psychometrics with LLM mechanics by resolving gaps in design, measurement, and analysis. First, we replace unstructured prompting with fully crossed factorial experiments to systematically isolate causal main and interaction effects. Second, we eliminate Monte Carlo text sampling noise by operating directly on exact, token-level Probability Mass Functions (PMFs). Third, we derive a multivariate ordinal consensus metric and a distributional ANOVA to process these PMFs analytically. We validate our framework with a case study on consumer ethnocentrism across five LLMs, demonstrating how our approach isolates systemic country-of-origin biases that aggregate benchmarks otherwise obscure.

</details>


### [24] [ASR-Roundtrip Evaluation Can Mask Context- and Convention-Dependent Reading Errors in Chinese News TTS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10606)
*Shijun Luo,Lizhi Wan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ASR-roundtrip evaluation for TTS intelligibility can produce false negatives when TTS outputs surface-correct but contextually wrong readings. A targeted audit of Chinese news TTS reveals 46 masked errors across 110 high-risk cases, with span-isolation diagnostics re-exposing 18 of them. Qwen3-ASR recovers 40/97 confirmed masked cases vs. only 2 for Paraformer, demonstrating ASR-roundtrip is insufficient as standalone ground truth for Chinese news reading-risk evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ASR-roundtrip evaluation—using ASR to transcribe TTS output and comparing against the original text—is a common scalable proxy for TTS intelligibility. However, it can miss reading errors where the TTS produces a plausible but contextually wrong pronunciation (e.g., misreading sports scores, aircraft models, technical units, or membership names) while the ASR transcribes the intended text, creating false negatives. The authors aim to quantify and characterize this failure mode in Chinese news TTS.

Method: The authors conduct a targeted audit on 110 high-risk cases from MiMo TTS, categorizing outcomes into masked false negatives (ASR recovers surface-correct text despite TTS errors), exposed TTS errors, and cases with no Raw TTS error. They apply a span-isolation diagnostic to re-expose previously masked errors. A parallel audit using CosyVoice (Raw-only) is also performed. They then compare two ASR systems—Qwen3-ASR and Paraformer—on the 97 confirmed masked TTS audio files to assess recovery rates.

Result: Of 110 high-risk MiMo TTS cases: 46 masked false negatives, 9 exposed TTS errors, and 55 with no Raw TTS error. Span-isolation diagnostic re-exposes 18 of the 46 masked errors. The CosyVoice audit confirms 51 masked cases. Across 97 confirmed masked audio files, Qwen3-ASR surface-recovers 40 cases, while Paraformer recovers only 2.

Conclusion: ASR-roundtrip is useful for screening TTS intelligibility but is insufficient as standalone ground truth for evaluating Chinese news reading-risk, as it systematically masks context-dependent reading errors that are perceptible to human listeners.

Abstract: ASR-roundtrip evaluation is widely used as a scalable proxy for text-to-speech (TTS) intelligibility, but it can produce false negatives for reading errors perceived by listeners. We study Chinese news TTS spans whose correct reading depends on context or domain conventions, such as sports scores, aircraft models, technical units, and membership names. In these cases, Raw TTS can choose a plausible but wrong reading while ASR transcribes the audio as the intended or surface-correct text. A targeted audit over 110 high-risk MiMo TTS cases, reported with a complete denominator, confirms 46 masked false negatives, 9 exposed TTS errors, and 55 cases with no Raw TTS error. A span-isolation diagnostic re-exposes 18/46 previously masked errors. A Raw-only CosyVoice audit on the same targeted pool confirms 51 masked cases. Across the 97 TTS-specific audio files labeled confirmed masked across the two audits, Qwen3-ASR surface-recovers 40 cases, whereas Paraformer does so in only 2. The results suggest that ASR-roundtrip is useful for screening but insufficient as standalone ground truth for Chinese news reading-risk evaluation.

</details>


### [25] [Simplex Relaxation for Discrete Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10615)
*Jinya Sakurai,Patrick Pynadath,Satoshi Hayakawa,Jaehong Yoon,Xulei Yang,Nancy F. Chen,Xun Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Simplax augments uniform discrete diffusion with an auxiliary Dirichlet-simplex variable, enabling a Rao-Blackwellized reverse objective and sampler that improves generative perplexity-entropy tradeoffs and achieves state-of-the-art Sudoku generation without changing the underlying corruption process.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard uniform discrete diffusion models are limited by their fixed corruption kernel and reverse prediction problem. The authors ask whether the training objective and reverse transitions can be enriched while preserving the original categorical corruption process, aiming to improve generative performance without altering the fundamental diffusion framework.

Method: Simplax introduces an exact Dirichlet-categorical augmentation that couples each corrupted categorical state with an auxiliary simplex-valued variable. This preserves the original uniform diffusion as the categorical marginal. The augmentation yields a tractable Rao-Blackwellized reverse-bridge objective—providing lower-variance gradient estimates—and a corresponding stochastic reverse sampler, while retaining the corrupted categorical state as the denoiser input.

Result: On unconditional OpenWebText generation, Simplax improves the generative perplexity-entropy tradeoff. On Sudoku, a model trained exclusively on 30-clue puzzles achieves the highest accuracy among compared methods across all evaluated clue densities (including the minimal 17-clue uniquely solvable regime) and the highest validity in unconditional generation.

Conclusion: Augmenting discrete diffusion with an auxiliary simplex variable via Simplax demonstrably improves generative modeling performance on both text and structured reasoning tasks, without modifying the underlying corruption process, suggesting that enriching the objective and sampler is a fruitful direction for discrete diffusion.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion models for categorical generation are defined by a corruption kernel, which determines the intermediate state space and the associated reverse prediction problem. We study uniform discrete diffusion and ask whether its training objective and reverse transitions can be enriched without changing the underlying categorical corruption process. We introduce Simplax, an exact Dirichlet--categorical augmentation that couples each corrupted categorical state with an auxiliary simplex-valued variable while preserving the original uniform diffusion process as its categorical marginal. This augmentation yields a tractable Rao--Blackwellized reverse-bridge objective and a corresponding stochastic reverse sampler, while retaining the corrupted categorical state as the denoiser input. Empirically, Simplax improves the generative perplexity--entropy tradeoff on unconditional OpenWebText generation. On Sudoku, a model trained exclusively on $30$-clue puzzles achieves the highest accuracy among the compared methods across all evaluated clue densities, including the minimum uniquely solvable $17$-clue regime, and also achieves the highest validity in unconditional generation.

</details>


### [26] [Dual-Loop Self-Evolution via Verifiable Emotion Feedback for Multi-Turn Empathetic Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10626)
*Yi Wei,Shuo Jiang,Huaixia Dou,Jie Zhu,Junhui Li,Lifan Guo,Feng Chen,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A dual-loop self-evolution framework with verifiable emotion rewards improves empathetic multi-turn dialogue by aligning policy training with dynamically adapted experience, achieving significant gains on the SAGE benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for empathetic dialogue fix the training interaction distribution while evolving the policy, creating a mismatch between policy competence and training experience. Empathetic support is inherently multi-turn and path-dependent, requiring scalable, long-horizon supervision.

Method: A dual-loop framework: (1) Inner loop optimizes multi-turn policy via continuous emotion rewards from a frozen user simulator and verifier. (2) Outer loop estimates policy-relative interaction utility from sparse, stochastic rollouts by grouping constant scenario/interaction states, prioritizing conditions near the policy's competence boundary. A hierarchical controller shares evidence across support intents, with uncertainty-guided exploration and uniform rehearsal preventing premature exclusion. Both loops close without increasing rollout budget.

Result: On SAGE, Qwen3-8B Overall score improves from 53.87 to 79.24, outperforming protocol-matched uniform emotion-reward RL by 7.23 points.

Conclusion: The dual-loop self-evolution framework effectively aligns policy competence with training experience through adaptive experience selection, demonstrating substantial improvements in empathetic dialogue without additional rollout cost.

Abstract: Large language models have demonstrated conversational capabilities, yet empathetic competence remains challenging. Empathetic support is inherently multi-turn and path-dependent: users disclose concerns gradually, emotions evolve over time, and early responses shape trust and receptivity. Reinforcement learning with verifiable emotion rewards provides scalable supervision for long-horizon interactions. However, existing methods evolve the dialogue policy while keeping its training interaction distribution fixed, creating a mismatch between policy competence and training experience. We introduce a dual-loop self-evolution framework driven by verifiable emotion feedback. With the user simulator and verifier frozen, the inner loop optimizes the multi-turn policy using continuous emotion rewards, while the outer loop uses the same outcomes to estimate policy-relative interaction utility and adapt experience. To obtain estimates from sparse, stochastic rollouts, the framework holds the scenario and interaction state constant within each group and prioritizes conditions whose group pass rates lie near the policy's competence boundary. A hierarchical controller shares evidence across support intents, while uncertainty-guided exploration and uniform rehearsal prevent premature exclusion. The resulting distribution generates trajectories, closing both loops without increasing the rollout budget. On SAGE, our framework raises Qwen3-8B Overall from 53.87 to 79.24 and outperforms protocol-matched uniform emotion-reward reinforcement learning by 7.23 points.

</details>


### [27] [Decomposition-Induced Context-Memory Conflict: When Fact-Checking Pipelines Contradict Their Own Source Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10627)
*Yu-Feng Yen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper reveals that claim decomposition in fact-checking pipelines is not neutral preprocessing — decomposers can inject their own parametric beliefs, creating "Decomposition-Induced Context-Memory Conflict" (DI-CC). The authors mechanistically link DI-CC to classical context-memory conflict, show self-consistency methods fail to detect it, and find that context-aware decoding mitigates it but breaks coreference-heavy decompositions, making it not deployment-ready.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decompose-then-verify pipelines (e.g., FActScore) are widely used for factuality evaluation, with decomposition treated as a neutral, lossless preprocessing step. The authors challenge this assumption, investigating whether the decomposition stage itself can introduce unfaithfulness by substituting the model's parametric knowledge for the source text's actual claims.

Method: The authors identify and characterize DI-CC as a failure mode where decomposers produce claims contradicting the source text. They use a linear probe trained on classical context-memory conflict data (NQ-Swap) to detect DI-CC in decomposition outputs. They evaluate SelfCheckGPT-style self-consistency sampling as a detection baseline and test context-aware decoding as a training-free mitigation. They also explore the mechanism's boundaries, including scale requirements and natural occurrence rates.

Result: A linear probe trained only on NQ-Swap (never exposed to decomposition data) strongly separates DI-CC from faithful decompositions (AUC 0.86–0.88, p < 0.0005). SelfCheckGPT-style self-consistency sampling fails completely (AUC 0.51, chance-level) because DI-CC content is stably recoverable across resamples. Context-aware decoding suppresses DI-CC but causes many coreference-heavy decompositions to fail to parse, often due to fabricated identities. DI-CC is too sparse to manifest on naturally-occurring hallucinated text and requires minimum model scale to detect.

Conclusion: DI-CC is established as a real, mechanistically grounded, and partially treatable failure mode in decompose-then-verify pipelines. However, existing mitigation (context-aware decoding) is not deployment-ready, and the phenomenon's scope should not be overstated given its sparsity in natural settings.

Abstract: Decompose-then-verify pipelines, including FActScore-style fact-checkers and long-form factuality evaluators, first split a passage into atomic claims before checking each one. Decomposition itself is treated as a neutral preprocessing step. We show it is not: a decomposer can be induced to substitute its own parametric belief for what the source passage says, producing a claim that contradicts the text it was supposed to summarize faithfully. We call this Decomposition-Induced Context-Memory Conflict (DI-CC) and show it is mechanistically the same phenomenon as classical context-memory conflict, occurring inside a different pipeline stage than prior work has examined. A linear probe trained only on classical context-memory conflict data (NQ-Swap), never exposed to any decomposition output, significantly separates decomposition positions that produce DI-CC from faithful decompositions (AUC = 0.86-0.88, permutation p < 0.0005). An existing reference-free baseline, SelfCheckGPT-style self-consistency sampling, fails to detect DI-CC at all (AUC 0.51, chance-level), because DI-CC content is stably recoverable and recurs across resamples, unlike the variability self-consistency methods rely on. Context-aware decoding, a training-free mitigation from the classical setting, transfers to decomposition and suppresses DI-CC, but at a severe cost: many decompositions under coreference-heavy conditions fail to parse, often because the decomposer fabricates a different identity. We do not consider this mitigation deployment-ready. We further characterize the mechanism's boundaries: its natural occurrence rate is too sparss not manifest on naturally-occurring hallucinatedtext, and it requires a minimum model scale to detecablish DI-CC as a real, mechanistically grounded, andpartially treatable failure mode, with a scope we chhan overstate.

</details>


### [28] [Seeds Before Objectives: Rethinking Evaluation for Low-Resource Garhwali ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10670)
*Karamvir Singh Batra,Prathamjyot Singh,Ashima Sood,Jasmeet Singh,Sahil Sharma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: First reproducible multi-seed ASR benchmark for Garhwali (low-resource Indo-Aryan language) reveals that previously reported gains (Focal CTC, matra-weighted objectives, Hindi transfer learning) fail under seed-level significance testing. Only pretraining design (w2v-BERT 2.0) and speed augmentation show reliable improvements, achieving 47.0% WER.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource ASR research often reports gains from single-run comparisons that may not replicate across seeds. This paper addresses the lack of rigorous, reproducible evaluation methodology for under-resourced languages, using Garhwali as a case study to demonstrate the fragility of claimed improvements when subjected to multi-seed significance testing.

Method: Built a reproducible multi-seed ASR benchmark on the official VAANI dataset splits for Garhwali. Evaluated standard CTC, Focal CTC, matra-weighted objectives, Hindi-to-Garhwali transfer learning, w2v-BERT 2.0, MMS-1B, and speed augmentation. Each configuration run across five random seeds with per-seed outputs and significance testing to distinguish real gains from seed noise.

Result: Focal CTC and matra-weighted objectives failed to beat standard CTC under seed-level testing; matra objective did not reduce its targeted error types; Hindi-to-Garhwali transfer showed no gain over direct fine-tuning. w2v-BERT 2.0 with standard CTC achieved 47.0% WER (5-seed average), outperforming the larger MMS-1B. Pretraining design, not parameter count, drove performance. Speed augmentation provided a small but largely consistent improvement.

Conclusion: Multi-seed evaluation on official splits is essential for separating genuine gains from seed noise in low-resource ASR. For Garhwali, only pretraining architecture choice and speed augmentation proved robust; other recently proposed techniques did not survive rigorous testing.

Abstract: At corpus sizes typical of low-resource dialects, single-run comparisons can yield gains that do not replicate. We show this for Garhwali, an under-resourced Indo-Aryan language of the central Himalaya, building the first reproducible multi-seed ASR benchmark on the official VAANI splits, with per-seed outputs and significance testing. Re-examining plausible gains, we find them fragile: neither Focal CTC nor a matra-weighted objective beats standard CTC under seed-level testing, the matra objective fails to cut even its targeted errors, and Hindi-to-Garhwali transfer gives no gain over direct fine-tuning. What holds up is mundane: w2v-BERT 2.0 with standard CTC reaches 47.0% WER over five seeds, beating the larger MMS-1B and comparable models; pretraining design, not parameter count, drives performance, and speed augmentation gives a small, largely consistent gain. Multi-seed evaluation on official splits separates real gains from seed noise.

</details>


### [29] [Auditing Chinese Web-scale Corpora via Sampled BPE Token Statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10678)
*Qingjie Zhang,Ziqi Tang,Jie Zhang,Gelei Deng,Jinfeng Li,YueFeng Chen,Yitong Yang,Hui Xue,Tianwei Zhang,Han Qiu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Sampled-BPE is a lightweight token-level auditing pipeline that samples a small subset of a corpus and trains a BPE tokenizer to surface polluted Chinese web tokens, achieving 148.4× speedup and 35.8× memory reduction with only 4.25% relative error, and revealing widespread but uneven pollution across 11 open Chinese corpora and 6 Common Crawl snapshots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chinese web pollution contaminates LLM training data, but auditing upstream Chinese corpora is challenging due to (1) prohibitive cost of full-scale scanning, (2) prior methods being too coarse-grained to detect token-level pollution, and (3) the implicit and rapidly evolving nature of Chinese web pollution. A scalable, fine-grained auditing method is needed.

Method: Sampled-BPE: a lightweight token-level auditing pipeline that samples a small representative subset of a corpus, trains a BPE tokenizer on that subset, and surfaces polluted tokens through token-level analysis. This avoids full corpus scanning while preserving granularity.

Result: The pipeline achieves a 148.4× speedup and 35.8× memory reduction compared to full-scan approaches, with only 4.25% relative error for pollution categories. Applied to 11 open Chinese corpora and 6 Chinese Common Crawl snapshots (2021–2026), it reveals widespread but uneven pollution and temporally shifting polluted content. A hierarchical dataset of 660k+ token records with web context, category, and explanation fields is released.

Conclusion: Sampled-BPE enables efficient, token-level auditing of web-scale Chinese corpora, exposing persistent and evolving pollution patterns. The released hierarchical token dataset supports downstream pollution review, tracing, and mitigation efforts for cleaner LLM training data.

Abstract: Chinese web pollution has surfaced in LLMs, motivating audits of upstream Chinese corpora. However, auditing such corpora faces three challenges: (1) their web-scale size makes full scan costly; (2) prior analyses are often too coarse to expose token-level pollution; (3) Chinese web pollution is implicit and rapidly changing. We propose Sampled-BPE, a lightweight token-level auditing pipeline that sample a small subset and train BPE tokenizer to surface polluted tokens. Experiments show that Sampled-BPE preserves usable estimates while substantially reducing runtime and memory: a 148.4 $\times$ speedup and a 35.8 $\times$ memory reduction induce only 4.25% relative error for pollution categories. We apply the pipeline to 11 open Chinese corpora and 6 Chinese Common Crawl snapshots from 2021 to 2026. The audit reveals widespread but uneven pollution across open corpora, as well as highly polluted and temporally shifting Chinese web content. We further release a hierarchical Chinese web token dataset with 660k+ token records, each with web context, category, and explanation fields, organized as trees to support review and tracing of pollution.

</details>


### [30] [Can Released LLM Vocabularies Support Token-Level Estimation of Hidden Corpora?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10690)
*Qingjie Zhang,Xingzhang Ren,Zixuan Chen,Jinfeng Li,YueFeng Chen,Yitong Yang,Hui Xue,Dayiheng Liu,Han Qiu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Released BPE tokenizer vocabularies leak fine-grained corpus composition information. The paper proposes Quantile-Guided Density Estimation (QGDE), which transfers stable token ID–ratio distributions from known corpora to infer corpus ratios for arbitrary target tokens in hidden training corpora, achieving mean relative errors as low as 3%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretraining corpus composition significantly influences LLM capabilities, yet remains opaque even when model weights are open-sourced. While prior work infers only coarse corpus mixtures or traces specific token groups, there is no method for estimating corpus ratios at the granularity of arbitrary individual tokens using only the released tokenizer.

Method: The authors first demonstrate that BPE tokenizers trained on different corpora exhibit stable distributions of token ID versus corpus ratio, enabling distribution transfer from known corpora to a target tokenizer trained on hidden data. They then propose Quantile-Guided Density Estimation (QGDE), which approximates this distribution using multiple quantile trends and applies local density weighting to produce token-level corpus ratio estimates.

Result: In controlled experiments and a realistic scenario using the publicly released SmolLM tokenizer, QGDE achieves mean relative errors as low as 3.00% for token-level estimation and 3.08% when aggregated into category-level corpus mixtures.

Conclusion: Released tokenizer vocabularies carry a useful signal for fine-grained corpus estimation that goes beyond coarse composition inference, enabling detailed reconstruction of hidden pretraining data mixtures.

Abstract: Pretraining corpus composition shapes LLM capabilities, but it often remains hidden even when model weights are released. Prior work has inferred corpus mixtures or traced specific token groups from released tokenizer vocabularies; in contrast, we estimate corpus ratios for arbitrary target tokens. We first show that BPE tokenizers trained on different corpora share stable token ID--ratio distributions, motivating distribution transfer from known corpora to a target tokenizer trained on hidden corpora. We then propose Quantile-Guided Density Estimation (QGDE), which approximates this distribution with multiple quantile trends and uses local density weighting to produce token-level estimates. In controlled settings and a realistic setting using the released SmolLM tokenizer, QGDE achieves mean relative errors as low as 3.00% for token-level estimation and 3.08% after aggregation into category-level mixtures. These results suggest that released tokenizer vocabularies provide a useful signal for fine-grained corpus estimation beyond coarse composition inference.

</details>


### [31] [SPIEval: Evaluating Large Language Models as Mobile Assistants over Scattered Personal Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10692)
*Junjie Ye,Zhuohui Sheng,Shaofan Liu,Yulun Zhu,Wenjie Fu,Dingwei Zhu,Ming Zhang,Yujiong Shen,Weichao Wang,Xin Zhao,Shihan Dou,Tao Gui,Qi Zhang,Xuanjing Huang,Pluto Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SPIEval is a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based mobile assistants on personal information tasks across multiple apps, revealing that even the best model (GPT-5.5 xhigh) achieves only 57.3% accuracy, with 79% of failures caused by inaccurate information localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as mobile assistants that must leverage personal information scattered across multiple apps, yet no dedicated benchmarks exist to evaluate their capabilities on such tasks. This gap motivates the creation of SPIEval.

Method: The authors introduce SPIEval, a human-curated benchmark grounded in five cognitive capabilities: reasoning, disambiguation, integration, preference inference, and multi-intent decomposition. It comprises 250 tasks, 4,335 personal records across 10 apps, and supports multi-turn interaction via 21 tools. Nine representative LLMs are evaluated on the benchmark.

Result: GPT-5.5 (xhigh) achieves the highest accuracy at 57.3%; the weakest model scores 16.4%. 79% of failures are attributed to inaccurate information localization, where models commit to plausible but incorrect information rather than continuing retrieval. Fewer than 2% of retrieval actions use advanced search methods, and search efficiency varies substantially across models.

Conclusion: Current LLM-based mobile assistants exhibit fundamental limitations in personal-information tasks, particularly in accurate information localization and search strategy. The findings motivate future research on more robust retrieval and verification mechanisms for mobile assistant applications.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as mobile assistants, where a key challenge is leveraging personal information scattered across multiple applications (apps) to complete user instructions. However, due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks, their capabilities remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce SPIEval, a human-curated benchmark grounded in five cognitive capabilities (i.e., reasoning, disambiguation, integration, preference inference, and multi-intent decomposition). SPIEval comprises 250 tasks spanning 4,335 personal records distributed across 10 apps and supports multi-turn interaction through 21 tools. Analysis shows that the benchmark exhibits diverse scenarios, challenging tasks, scattered information, controllable environments, and verifiable outcomes. We evaluate nine representative LLMs and find substantial room for improvement. The best-performing model, GPT-5.5 (xhigh), achieves only 57.3% accuracy, while the weakest achieves just 16.4%. Further analysis reveals that 79% of failures stem from inaccurate information localization, as LLMs often commit to plausible but incorrect information instead of continuing retrieval for verification. We also find that fewer than 2% of retrieval actions employ advanced search methods and observe substantial variation in search efficiency across models. These findings expose fundamental limitations of current LLM-based mobile assistants and motivate future research in this direction. Data and code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Junjie-Ye/SPIEval.

</details>


### [32] [EVIL-Detect for NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 6: LLM-Generated Text Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10698)
*Hongrui Bao,Hangyu Rong,Zhuoshang Wang,Yubing Ren,Yanan Cao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EVIL-Detect is a multi-signal ensemble framework with conflict-aware fusion for detecting LLM-generated and LLM-refined Chinese text, achieving first place (macro-F1: 0.8888) in NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 6.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the rapid proliferation of LLMs, reliable detection of LLM-generated text is critical, particularly in realistic Chinese scenarios involving three text types: human-written (HWT), LLM-generated (LGT), and LLM-refined/hybrid (HLT). Existing methods often lack robustness under out-of-distribution shifts.

Method: EVIL-Detect employs a multi-signal ensemble integrating four components: (1) edit-extent regression, (2) zero-shot likelihood-contrast signals, (3) lexical statistics, and (4) conservative text rules. These signals are combined via calibrated decision boundaries and a conflict-aware fusion mechanism.

Result: The system achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.8888 in the official evaluation, ranking first in NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 6, demonstrating strong robustness under out-of-distribution shifts.

Conclusion: Multi-signal ensemble with conflict-aware fusion provides a robust solution for LLM-generated text detection, particularly in the challenging three-way Chinese text classification setting. The approach generalizes well under distribution shifts.

Abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has increased the need for reliable detection of LLM-generated text, especially in realistic Chinese scenarios involving human-written text (HWT), LLM-generated text (LGT), and LLM-refined text (HLT). This paper presents EVIL-Detect, a multi-signal ensemble framework with conflict-aware fusion for NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 6. The system integrates edit-extent regression, zero-shot likelihood-contrast signals, lexical statistics, and conservative text rules. With calibrated decision boundaries and conflict-aware integration, our system improves robustness under strong out-of-distribution shifts, achieving a macro-F1 score of 0.8888 and ranking first in the official evaluation. Our code is available at https://github.com/bbbbhrrrr/evildetect.

</details>


### [33] [Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10715)
*Lena Holzwarth,Rita González-Márquez,Dmitry Kobak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A new unbiased method based on shifting word frequencies estimates that by end of 2025, 89% of biomedical papers in PubMed Central show excess LLM-associated vocabulary, with usage varying by section (Discussion: 68%, Methods: 32% but still &gt;50% overall prevalence).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-powered chatbots are increasingly used for academic writing, raising concerns about misconduct and fraud. Existing methods cannot reliably estimate LLM prevalence, yet policymakers need accurate data to shape guidelines.

Method: An unbiased estimation approach based on tracking changes in word frequencies within a corpus of texts. Applied to full-text open-access biomedical papers from PubMed Central.

Result: By end of 2025, 89% of papers exhibit excess LLM-associated vocabulary. LLMs are twice as likely to be used in Discussion paragraphs (68%) vs. Methods paragraphs (32%). Even in Methods, overall LLM usage prevalence exceeds 50%.

Conclusion: LLM-assisted writing is pervasive in biomedical literature. These estimates are critical for informing future academic writing guidelines and policies.

Abstract: Over the past several years, LLM-powered chatbots and agents have become widely used as a tool for academic writing. LLM-assisted writing can be valuable by removing language barriers but at the same time causes concerns about misconduct and fraud. To inform policy decisions, it is necessary to monitor the prevalence of LLM-altered texts in scholarly publications. Despite some recent progress in this direction, no existing method can produce reliable estimates. Here we suggest and validate a new unbiased approach to estimate LLM usage in a corpus of texts based on changing word frequencies. We apply our method to the full texts of open-access biomedical papers from Pubmed Central, and show that by the end of 2025, 89% of papers show excess of LLM-associated vocabulary. We also find that LLMs are twice as likely to be used when writing a paragraph in the Discussion section (68%) compared to a paragraph in the Methods section (32%), but even inside the Methods section, the overall prevalence of LLM usage is over 50%. We believe that our estimates are crucial to shape future guidelines and policies.

</details>


### [34] [Mitigating Context Interference for Reliable and Efficient Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10743)
*Boyang Xue,Bin Wu,Shuofei Qiao,Sheng Wang,Rui Wang,Yiming Du,Hongru Wang,Jeff Z. Pan,Emine Yilmaz,Kam-Fai Wong,Aldo Lipani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper systematically investigates context interference in multi-turn LLM search agents, identifies that the latest retrieved documents are the primary source of interference, proposes a distill-based context refiner to dynamically mitigate this issue, and demonstrates that integrating context refinement into RL training significantly improves agent reliability and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-turn search agents accumulate lengthy, complex contexts where irrelevant retrieved documents distract LLMs—a phenomenon termed "context interference"—which undermines both reliability and efficiency. The paper aims to systematically understand and mitigate this problem.

Method: The authors conduct a three-part systematic study: (1) identifying which context components (e.g., latest vs. earlier retrieved documents) contribute to context interference; (2) designing a distill-based context refiner that dynamically filters or compresses irrelevant information from retrieved documents; (3) incorporating this context refinement mechanism into reinforcement learning (RL) training pipelines for search agents.

Result: Key findings include: (1) context interference primarily originates from the latest retrieved documents rather than earlier ones; (2) the distill-based context refiner effectively mitigates interference; (3) integrating context refinement into RL training yields significant gains in both reliability and efficiency of multi-turn search agents.

Conclusion: Mitigating context interference is crucial for building effective search agents. The paper advocates for a "refine context and then generate" paradigm, where dynamic context refinement is treated as a first-class component in AI agent design and training, rather than merely feeding raw retrieval results into LLMs.

Abstract: Recent research empowers Large Language Models (LLMs) as multi-turn search agents to iteratively retrieve and generate outputs until complex tasks are solved. However, the contexts of multi-turn search agents are lengthy and complex. For example, the retrieved set of documents in each turn would inevitably introduce irrelevant information that distracts LLMs, referring to \textit{context interference}, potentially hindering the reliability and efficiency of search agents. Therefore, we conduct a systematic study on context interference in multi-turn search agents, focusing on investigating i) which parts of the context of search agents will contribute to the context interference, ii) how to refine the contexts of search agents to mitigate the interference, and iii) can incorporating context refinement into search agent training yield further improvements. We reveal that interference primarily arises from the latest retrieved documents. Based on the explored findings, we then introduce a distill-based context refiner to dynamically mitigate context interference for multi-turn search agents. Finally, we validate that incorporating context refinement into RL training pipelines of search agents can significantly enhance both reliability and efficiency. This study highlights the importance of mitigating context interference of search agents, inspiring a novel paradigm of ``refine context and then generate'' for AI agents.

</details>


### [35] [Assessing Reliability of BERT-Based Models on Question Answering Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10806)
*Pooja Yadav,Priyanka Harjule,Basant Agarwal,Marko Robnik Šikonja*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study evaluates the reliability (response stability) of four BERT-based QA models under Monte Carlo Dropout and input paraphrasing, finding RoBERTa most reliable while ALBERT and DistilBERT show significant inconsistencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliability of LLMs is as critical as accuracy for trustworthiness and practical deployment, yet the reliability of BERT-based encoder-only QA models remains underexplored despite their strong accuracy on classification-style QA tasks.

Method: Four BERT variants (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT, DistilBERT) are evaluated on SQuAD and QuAC datasets. Reliability is assessed via two conditions: (1) internal variation through Monte Carlo Dropout at varying dropout rates to measure prediction consistency, and (2) input perturbation via paraphrasing to test lexical sensitivity. Statistical analyses validate MCD as a non-disruptive reliability metric.

Result: RoBERTa demonstrates the highest reliability across conditions. ALBERT and DistilBERT exhibit significant prediction inconsistencies under both MCD and paraphrasing. MCD does not disrupt inference dynamics, confirming its validity as a reliability assessment tool.

Conclusion: Evaluating both accuracy and stability is essential for real-world QA deployment. RoBERTa is the most robust choice among BERT variants, and MCD is a valid, non-intrusive method for quantifying model reliability.

Abstract: Reliability estimation of large language models is in many cases as crucial as their accuracy, as reliable models are more trustworthy, robust, and suitable for practical applications. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP), particularly those based on transformer architectures, have significantly accelerated progress across various NLP tasks. This study focuses on the reliability of transformer-based question answering (QA) models, specifically BERT models and its variants (RoBERTa, ALBERT, DistilBERT). These encoder-only pretrained transformers have demonstrated remarkable accuracy in QA tasks that can be treated as classification tasks. However, their reliability remains underexplored. This study evaluates the reliability of four BERT-based models by assessing response stability under two conditions: (1) internal model variations induced via Monte Carlo Dropout (MCD) and (2) input perturbations through paraphrasing. Using the SQuAD and QuAC datasets, we investigate how dropout rates affect prediction consistency and whether lexical changes impact answer stability. Our findings reveal that RoBERTa maintains higher reliability, whereas AlBERT and DistilBERT exhibit significant inconsistencies. Statistical analyses confirm that enabling MCD during prediction does not disrupt inference dynamics, validating its effectiveness as a reliability metric. These findings underscore the importance of evaluating both accuracy and stability in QA models to ensure stability in real-world applications.

</details>


### [36] [Surfacing the Unsaid: CUE-Bench for Affective Stance in Chinese Discourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10810)
*Zhenyan Zheng,Yunyao Zhang,Junxi Sheng,Junqing Yu,Zikai Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CUE Bench is a Chinese benchmark for "unsaid emotion" that introduces Affective Stance — a structured framework capturing the interaction between explicit expression, implicit affect, pragmatic intent, and fine-grained emotion. It improves emotion recognition (+3.5pp) and intent detection (+7.8pp) over strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current emotion benchmarks only annotate surface polarity or final emotion categories, failing to capture how speakers convey affect through indirect, implicit, polite, ironic, or deliberately mismatched expressions. This insensitivity to concealed, weakened, inverted, or pragmatically reshaped affective meaning obscures model failures in deeper emotion understanding.

Method: The authors construct CUE Bench, a Chinese Unsaid Emotion benchmark centered on Affective Stance. They define nine human-interpretable affective stances derived from explicit–implicit polarity interactions and provide additional annotations for pragmatic intent and fine-grained emotion, enabling structured affective inference across diverse communicative scenarios.

Result: Incorporating Affective Stance improves fine-grained emotion recognition by 3.5 percentage points and pragmatic intent detection by 7.8 percentage points over strong baselines.

Conclusion: Modeling Affective Stance as an intermediate structural layer significantly enhances a model's ability to infer unspoken affect and pragmatic intent, demonstrating that structured explicit–implicit polarity interaction is crucial for deeper emotion understanding in discourse.

Abstract: Emotion understanding in discourse requires reasoning beyond surface sentiment because speakers often convey affect through indirect, implicit, polite, ironic, or deliberately mismatched expressions. Existing emotion benchmarks mainly annotate surface polarity or final emotion categories, while lacking a structured account of how explicit expression, implicit affect, pragmatic intent, and fine grained emotion interact. This limitation makes current evaluations insensitive to cases where affective meaning is concealed, weakened, inverted, or pragmatically reshaped, thereby obscuring model failures in deeper emotion understanding. To address this gap, we introduce CUE Bench, a Chinese Unsaid Emotion benchmark that centers on Affective Stance and covers diverse communicative scenarios. CUE Bench constructs nine human interpretable affective stances from explicit implicit polarity interaction and further provides intent and fine grained emotion annotations for structured affective inference. Experiments show that incorporating Affective Stance improves fine grained emotion recognition by 3.5 percentage points and pragmatic intent detection by 7.8 percentage points over strong baselines.

</details>


### [37] [Reference-Free Post-Training of Open Large Language Models for Multilingual Machine Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10812)
*Chris Han,Pengzhi Gao,Pei Fu,Jian Luan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents MiLMMT-46-v1.0, a multilingual machine translation system built by applying GRPO reinforcement learning with reference-free quality estimation rewards to open LLMs, combined with SFT-RL checkpoint interpolation, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 46 languages against both open and proprietary systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To advance reference-free post-training for multilingual machine translation using open LLMs, addressing the need for scalable quality improvement without relying on expensive human references or proprietary models.

Method: Starting from supervised-finetuned MiLMMT-46-v0.1, the authors apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using a reward function that averages two reference-free quality estimation models, gated by language identification. They then linearly interpolate between SFT and RL checkpoints to produce the final MiLMMT-46-v1.0 model. On-policy distillation is also investigated as an alternative.

Result: MiLMMT-46-v1.0 consistently improves translation quality over SFT baselines across 46 languages, outperforms open baselines (Seed-X, HY-MT2, TranslateGemma), and achieves leading reference-free scores against proprietary systems (Google Translate, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5). On-policy distillation matches but does not exceed the quality of RL with interpolation.

Conclusion: GRPO with reference-free rewards and checkpoint interpolation is an effective post-training strategy for multilingual MT. The approach yields state-of-the-art open models competitive with top proprietary systems, and the authors release all models and code publicly.

Abstract: We study reference-free post-training for multilingual machine translation with open large language models. Starting from the supervised-finetuned MiLMMT-46-v0.1 models, we apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward that averages two reference-free quality estimation models and is gated by language identification. We then linearly interpolate the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) model checkpoints to obtain MiLMMT-46-v1.0. Across 46 languages, the resulting models consistently improve translation quality over their SFT counterparts, outperform strong recent open baselines, including Seed-X, HY-MT2, and TranslateGemma, and achieve leading reference-free scores against evaluated proprietary systems such as Google Translate, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT-5. We further investigate on-policy distillation and find that it reaches, but does not surpass, the quality frontier achieved by RL with checkpoint interpolation. We release the models and code to facilitate future research.

</details>


### [38] [VibeLifeBench: Can Your Life Agent Be Proactive and Persistent in a Living World?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10875)
*Xiaohongshu Inc*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VibeLifeBench introduces a benchmark of 200 multi-week, long-horizon tasks across ten everyday-life domains to evaluate LLM agents' ability to act proactively, consistently, and autonomously in dynamic, silently-changing environments — revealing that all seven tested frontier models score poorly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent evaluations use short, self-contained requests in static environments, which fail to capture the demands of real-life personal assistance: tasks lasting weeks, a world that changes silently between prompts, unstated implicit constraints, and the need for proactive decision-making about when to act, ask, or stay silent. No current benchmark measures these capabilities.

Method: The authors created VibeLifeBench with 200 scripted multi-week timeline tasks across 10 everyday-life domains, simulated in a world of 22 mock services. The world advances on its own clock with silent changes. Agents must decide autonomously when to act. Evaluation uses fine-grained, weighted checks covering end state, action timeliness, and adherence to implicit constraints — reading only what the agent actually left behind.

Result: All seven frontier models evaluated scored low on VibeLifeBench, demonstrating a substantial gap between current LLM agent capabilities and the requirements of real-life personal assistance.

Conclusion: Current frontier LLM agents are far from capable of handling real-life, long-horizon personal assistance tasks. The benchmark, tasks, environments, and evaluation framework will be open-sourced to spur progress in developing proactive, consistent, and autonomous agents.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as personal assistants. Existing evaluations, however, mostly use short, self-contained requests in static environments. Everyday life assistance is different. A task runs for weeks rather than minutes. The world keeps changing while the agent is not being prompted. Many constraints are never stated outright. An agent that merely answers the request in front of it will fail at such a task. What is needed instead is an agent that stays proactive and consistent. It decides on its own when to act, when to ask, and when to stay silent. It notices changes that nobody announced. It keeps one plan coherent from the first day to the last. No current benchmark measures this. We introduce VibeLifeBench, a benchmark of 200 long-horizon tasks across ten everyday-life domains. Each task is a scripted multi-week timeline in a simulated world of 22 mock services. The world advances on its own clock, and many of its changes are silent, so only an agent that re-inspects the world discovers them. Every task is graded by fine-grained, weighted checks that read only what the agent actually left behind, covering the end state, the timeliness of its actions, and whether it upheld the implicit constraints. We evaluate seven frontier models. All of them score low, which shows how far current agents are from assisting with real life. We will open-source all tasks, environments, and the evaluation framework.

</details>


### [39] [X2-Turn: Frame-Synchronous Dual-Head Modeling for Joint Streaming ASR and Turn State Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10878)
*Kaiqi Fu,Rime Wen,Altman Lin,Shawn Qin,Roy Gan,Hao Wang,Qian Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: X2-Turn introduces a frame-synchronous turn state prediction method that operates in parallel with ASR on shared streaming representations, enabling accurate, low-latency turn-taking detection without relying on an auxiliary ASR model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior modular turn-taking systems optimize turn state prediction at utterance or fixed-chunk levels, creating a mismatch with continuous turn estimation. They also depend on auxiliary ASR models, which increase latency and system complexity. The authors aim to unify ASR and turn state prediction in a single streaming framework.

Method: Building on the pretrained Voxtral Realtime model, the authors introduce a frame-synchronous turn state head that operates in parallel with the ASR head on shared streaming representations. The model jointly predicts ASR tokens and fine-grained turn states at the frame level using delayed-stream modeling, enabling real-time, frame-synchronous turn-taking detection.

Result: Evaluated on the bilingual Chinese-English Easy-Turn test sets, X2-Turn demonstrates effective turn-taking detection accuracy while maintaining low latency.

Conclusion: Frame-synchronous turn state prediction via delayed-stream modeling effectively bridges the gap between discrete turn prediction and continuous streaming speech, achieving accurate and responsive turn-taking without the overhead of separate ASR modules.

Abstract: Accurate and responsive turn-taking is essential for spoken dialogue systems, which must distinguish in real time between user interruptions, backchannels that should be ignored, and the completion of an utterance. Prior modular approaches typically optimize turn state prediction at the utterance or fixed-chunk level, creating a mismatch with the continuous turn state estimate, and often depend on an auxiliary ASR model, which limits responsiveness and increases overall system complexity. Therefore, we present X2-Turn, a frame-synchronous turn state prediction method via delayed-stream modeling. Specifically, building on the pretrained Voxtral Realtime model, we introduce a frame-synchronous turn state head that operates in parallel with the ASR head on shared streaming representations, jointly predicting ASR tokens and fine-grained turn states at the frame level. We evaluate our method on the bilingual Chinese-English Easy-Turn test sets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving accurate turn-taking detection while maintaining low latency.

</details>


### [40] [Certify or Refuse: A Cross-Model Map for Selective Risk Control with Coverage Floors under Covariate Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10893)
*Jiamiao Liu,Dewen Qiao,Yu Zhang,Xuetao Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a certification framework for selective predictors under covariate shift, where an "automation floor" requires answering at least a β-fraction of target queries with error ≤ α. It proves a "Floor Certification Map" showing certification feasibility depends on two resources: labeled source risk and unlabeled target samples, with matching upper/lower bounds across different model classes (Model-A, B, B'). The floor requirement creates a non-trivial complexity landscape, with Model-B shown inconsistent at α=β=1/2, and empirical validation on SQuAD-to-NewsQA transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying selective predictors in shifted environments requires certified guarantees on both coverage (automation floor) and accuracy. Existing certification theory lacks a unified understanding of when and how both constraints can be simultaneously satisfied under covariate shift, creating a gap between theoretical possibility and practical deployability.

Method: The authors work within the bounded-ratio covariate shift framework and derive upper and lower bounds on certification feasibility. Lower bounds (Model-B) establish impossibility results; matching oracle-weight upper bounds (Model-A) show what is achievable with ideal weights; and implementable upper bounds (Model-B') use a pre-registered exact stratified-shift model. The analysis relies on localized accepted-region functionals, regular frontier margins, slack conditions, and lattice conditions. The bounds are additive in labeled source risk and unlabeled target sample size.

Result: Key results: (1) Certification acquires a feasibility frontier — not all (α,β) pairs are certifiable. (2) Upper and lower bounds match across models, not within a single model, and this is necessary: no unknown-weight procedure matches over the full bounded-ratio class (Model-B inconsistent at α=β=1/2). (3) Complexity is driven by a localized accepted-region functional, not global ESS; both lower-bound axes vanish as β→0. (4) Empirically: registered bite family diverges with log-log slope −2.002; 1,024-cell audit shows 0 violations; SQuAD-to-NewsQA audit returns honest refusal.

Conclusion: The floor constraint fundamentally alters the certification landscape under covariate shift, creating a two-resource complexity map. The match across model classes (rather than within a single model) is necessary due to the inconsistency of Model-B. The necessity of nuisance parameters is only partially resolved, and a fixed-ESS separation theorem remains open.

Abstract: Certified selective predictors attain whatever coverage they attain; operators impose an automation floor: answer at least a $β$-fraction of shifted target traffic with at most an $α$-fraction of answers wrong. Under bounded-ratio covariate shift we prove the Floor Certification Map: once that floor must be certified alongside the selection-conditioned risk $α$, certification acquires a feasibility frontier and a two-resource complexity map, additive up to constants: risk in labeled source, the floor in unlabeled target samples. The rates are local, needing a regular frontier margin, slack below the local-regime threshold, and lattice conditions: pre-registered with a lattice margin for the upper bounds, compatible per-slack for the lower. The displayed split is the operational route; oracle weights also allow a labeled-source floor estimate. Three model-tagged results: a lower bound (Model-B), a matching oracle-weight upper bound (Model-A), and an implementable upper bound (Model-B') valid under a pre-registered exact stratified-shift model with nuisance cost priced explicitly. The match is across these models rather than a single-model minimax theorem, and necessarily so: over the full bounded-ratio class no unknown-weight procedure matches at any sample size (Model-B is inconsistent, witnessed at $α=β=1/2$). The nuisance's necessity is only partially settled. Complexity tracks a localized accepted-region functional, not global effective sample size (ESS), on both sides, though a fixed-ESS separation theorem is left open; both lower-bound axes vanish as $β\to0$, so the floor creates the map. Empirically, the registered bite family diverges with log-log slope $-2.002$ within its pre-registered band; a 1,024-cell audit records 0 violations where the formal certificates fire; and a single-corpus SQuAD-to-NewsQA feasibility audit returns honest refusal.

</details>


### [41] [FaithformBench: Benchmarking Faithfulness of Mathematical Chain-of-Thought Autoformalisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10916)
*Rob Cornish,Iacopo Ghinassi,Po-Hung Yeh,Shuqi Liu,Qiyuan Xu,Haoxuan Yin,Dominik Wagner,Wenda Li,Yee Whye Teh,Luke Ong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new benchmark for evaluating autoformalisation (AF) faithfulness using automatically generated perturbed (invalid) reasoning steps. It measures both validity preservation (correct inputs remain correct) and invalidity preservation (incorrect inputs remain incorrect), revealing that many AF systems exhibit "sycophancy" — silently correcting invalid inputs into provable statements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for assessing AF faithfulness rely on expensive human annotations, LLM judges, or embedding models with limited accuracy guarantees. Moreover, they only test on known-correct inputs, failing to assess whether AF systems faithfully translate incorrect reasoning. The authors aim to address these gaps with a cheap, sound, and bidirectional evaluation method.

Method: The benchmark automatically generates perturbed (invalid) reasoning steps from valid ones, then evaluates AF systems on two metrics: (1) validity preservation — whether unperturbed steps remain provable after autoformalisation; and (2) invalidity preservation — whether perturbed steps remain unprovable. The method is sound under weak assumptions and requires no human annotation.

Result: Applied to eight AF systems across four mathematical datasets, the benchmark reveals pervasive sycophancy: many AF systems "silently correct" invalid inputs into provable statements. Notably, the most validity-preserving fine-tuned AFs are also the most sycophantic, indicating a tension between preserving validity and preserving invalidity in current AF systems.

Conclusion: Current AF systems exhibit a fundamental tension between validity preservation and invalidity preservation (faithfulness to incorrect inputs). The proposed benchmark provides a practical, low-cost method for diagnosing this sycophancy and encourages future work on AF systems that faithfully translate both correct and incorrect reasoning steps.

Abstract: Autoformalisation (AF) systems map natural language reasoning steps into formal statements in a proof assistant such as Lean. We consider how to assess the faithfulness of these systems. Existing approaches require expensive human-annotated ground truth, or rely on LLM judges or embedding models, which come with limited guarantees of accuracy. In addition, these methods typically only consider inputs that are known to be correct, and therefore do not assess whether the AF translates incorrect inputs faithfully. To address these limitations, we propose a new benchmark for AF faithfulness that is cheap to apply, sound under weak assumptions, and assesses both positive and negative examples. Our method is based on automatically generating perturbed reasoning steps that are designed to be invalid, and then measuring validity preservation on unperturbed steps and invalidity preservation on perturbed steps. We apply our method to eight AF systems across four mathematical datasets, and observe pervasive sycophancy: many AFs "silently correct" invalid inputs into provable statements. The most validity-preserving fine-tuned AFs are also the most sycophantic, suggesting a tension between validity and invalidity preservation in current AF systems.

</details>


### [42] [A Cost-Efficient Routing Pipeline for Multilingual Short-Text Classification Using Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10939)
*Wajdi Ben Saad,Safa Madiouni*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a selective translation routing strategy for multilingual short-text classification, where low-resource languages are translated into English before zero-shot classification while stronger languages remain on a direct multilingual path. Evaluated on SIB-200 and MASSIVE benchmarks, selective translation significantly boosts low-resource tier performance, though the optimal routing boundary is task-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aggregate evaluation metrics in multilingual classification hide performance disparities between high-resource and low-resource languages. Uniform inference policies, though simple to deploy, falsely assume equal service quality across languages. The work seeks a practical, self-hosted solution that mitigates this imbalance without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

Method: A fixed-list routing strategy using pretrained compact sentence encoders: stronger languages are classified directly via a multilingual path, while weaker languages are first translated into English, then classified via zero-shot inference. The pipeline is fully self-hosted, uses no task-specific fine-tuning, and evaluates three routing configurations (R1: translate only low-resource tier; R2: translate low + mid tiers; R3: full translation of all tiers). Evaluation uses a 15-language subset of SIB-200 (7-way topic classification) and a 15-locale subset of MASSIVE (60-way intent classification).

Result: On SIB-200, R1 is best overall: low-tier Macro-F1 improves from 0.4632 to 0.6828 while high and mid tiers remain unchanged. On MASSIVE, R1 raises low-tier Macro-F1 from 0.2143 to 0.4417, but R3 (full translation) achieves the best overall Macro-F1 at 0.4647. Selective translation consistently benefits weaker languages, but optimal routing boundaries vary by task. Results are reported as tier-level quality gains and latency rather than a single global efficiency score.

Conclusion: Selective translation routing is a reliable intervention for improving low-resource language performance in multilingual short-text classification. However, the optimal routing boundary is task-dependent, making tier-level reporting of quality gains and latency more informative than a single global efficiency metric.

Abstract: Multilingual short-text classification supports operational systems such as content moderation, customer support routing, and intent recognition, yet aggregate evaluation often hides large differences between high-resource and low-resource languages. Uniform inference policies are simple to deploy, but they assume that all languages are equally well served. In this work, we evaluate a fixed-list routing strategy that keeps stronger languages on a direct multilingual path and selectively sends weaker languages through translation into English before zero-shot classification. The pipeline is fully self-hosted, uses pretrained compact sentence encoders, and requires no task-specific fine-tuning.
  We test the approach on two benchmarks chosen to differ in scale and label granularity: a 15-language subset of SIB-200 for seven-way topic classification and a 15-locale subset of MASSIVE for intent classification over an official 60-intent inventory. On SIB-200, the best overall configuration is R1, which translates only the low-resource tier: high-tier and mid-tier Macro-F1 remain unchanged, while low-tier Macro-F1 rises from 0.4632 to 0.6828. On the MASSIVE subset, the same low-tier intervention raises low-tier Macro-F1 from 0.2143 to 0.4417, but the best overall result is obtained by full translation, R3, at Macro-F1 0.4647. Across these two benchmarks, selective translation is a reliable intervention for weaker languages, whereas the optimal routing boundary depends on the task. We therefore report routing through tier-level quality gains and tier-level latency rather than a single global efficiency score.

</details>


### [43] [REAP: Relation-Aware Elicitation and Parsing for Closed-Book Knowledge Base Construction from LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10963)
*Thanh-Dan Bui,Thanh-Trung Do,Tuan-Phong Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The REAP system, built on Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, combines structured chain-of-thought reasoning, relation-specific queries, and a reasoning-based empty-set gate to extract knowledge from LMs under a 32B-parameter budget without fine-tuning, achieving a macro-F1 of 0.62 on the AKBC 2026 Shared Task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The AKBC Shared Task 2026 requires constructing knowledge bases from language models in a closed-book setting with a strict budget (≤32B parameters, no fine-tuning). The key challenge is effectively eliciting parametric knowledge from frozen LMs while avoiding hallucination and respecting computational constraints.

Method: The REAP system employs three main components: (1) structured chain-of-thought reasoning to guide the LM through multi-step knowledge elicitation, (2) relation-specific query strategies tailored to different predicate types, and (3) a reasoning-based empty-set gate that determines when no valid answer exists to suppress hallucination. Output is directly extracted into valid JSON arrays. The system uses Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501 as the backbone model.

Result: On the test set, REAP achieves a macro-F1 score of 0.62. Particularly strong per-relation results include countryLandBordersCountry (F1=0.95), hasArea (F1=0.77), and companyTradesAtStockExchange (F1=0.73).

Conclusion: Combining structured CoT, relation-specific querying, and an empty-set gate enables effective closed-book KB construction from a frozen 24B-parameter LM, yielding competitive results, especially on relational triples involving geographic and economic facts.

Abstract: We present the REAP system for the AKBC Shared Task 2026 on constructing knowledge bases from language models in a closed-book setting, subject to a budget of at most 32B parameters and no model fine-tuning. Our system combines structured chain-of-thought reasoning, relation-specific query strategies, and a reasoning-based empty-set gate to elicit parametric knowledge, followed by direct extraction into valid JSON arrays. On the test set, the system, built on the Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501 model, achieves a macro-F1 score of 0.62, with particularly strong results on countryLandBordersCountry (F1 = 0.95), companyTradesAtStockExchange (F1 = 0.73), and hasArea (F1 = 0.77). Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yammdd/AKBC-Shared-Task-2026.

</details>


### [44] [ReLTEx: Reliable LLM-based Taxonomy Expansion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10970)
*Zeinab Ghamlouch,Mehwish Alam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReLTEx is a reliable LLM-based taxonomy expansion framework that combines candidate generation with structure-aware validation and recursive expansion control to reduce hallucinations and improve hierarchical consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can generate semantically relevant concepts for taxonomy enrichment, but direct use introduces noise, redundancy, and hierarchical inconsistencies. A framework is needed to ensure reliability in automated taxonomy expansion.

Method: ReLTEx integrates LLM-driven candidate generation with structure-aware validation and recursive expansion control. It is evaluated under a masked taxonomy expansion setting using benchmark taxonomies, comparing multiple validation strategies, adapted evaluation metrics, and human evaluation.

Result: Experimental results show that ReLTEx produces more reliable and semantically coherent taxonomy expansions compared to baselines, as confirmed by both automatic metrics and human evaluation.

Conclusion: ReLTEx effectively mitigates LLM hallucinations in taxonomy expansion by enforcing structural validation and controlled recursion, yielding more consistent and high-quality taxonomic structures.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in generating semantically relevant concepts and relations, making them promising tools for taxonomy enrichment. However, directly relying on LLM-generated expansions often leads to noisy, redundant, or hierarchically inconsistent structures, limiting their reliability for automated taxonomy expansion. In this paper, we present ReLTEx, a framework for reliable LLM-based taxonomy expansion. ReLTEx combines LLM-driven candidate generation with structure-aware validation and recursive expansion control to improve the consistency and quality of generated taxonomies by reducing hallucinations. We evaluate the proposed framework using benchmark taxonomies under a masked taxonomy expansion setting and compare multiple validation strategies. Experimental results, supported by both adapted evaluation metrics and human evaluation, demonstrate that ReLTEx produces more reliable and semantically coherent taxonomy expansions.

</details>


### [45] [MUSE: A Full-Text Cross-Domain Knowledge Base of Scientific Problems, Solutions, and Rationales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10974)
*Tsofia Cohen,Tom Hope*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MUSE is a multi-domain scientific resource that extracts Problem-Solution-Rationale triplets from full-text papers, using expert annotations and a modular pipeline to build a 37K triplet knowledge base. Experiments show rationale-supervised LLMs improve on complex problems but may degrade on simpler ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific papers contain rich, fine-grained records of problem-solving—authors describe technical obstacles, the methods used to address them, and the reasoning behind those choices. However, this structured knowledge (Problem-Solution-Rationale) is largely implicit and not systematically extracted. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a resource that makes these explanatory structures explicit and machine-usable.

Method: The authors introduce MUSE, centered on 579 expert-annotated full-text paragraphs with a rich annotation schema capturing problem, solution, and rationale spans, along with `solves` and `rationale_of` relations and conceptual coreference. They then develop a modular extraction pipeline that scales these annotations to automatically construct a knowledge base of 37K source-grounded P-S-R triplets across multiple domains.

Result: The extraction pipeline produces a high-quality knowledge base of 37K P-S-R triplets. A preliminary experiment training a rationale-supervised LLM for scientific problem-solving reveals a nuanced finding: rationale supervision enhances performance on complex, multi-constraint problems but harms performance on simpler ones.

Conclusion: Structured extraction of problem-solution-rationale triplets from scientific text is feasible at scale. Rationale supervision offers a promising direction for improving LLM scientific reasoning, though its benefits appear contingent on problem complexity, suggesting that naive application may be counterproductive for simpler tasks.

Abstract: Scientific papers contain fine-grained records of problem solving: authors mention technical obstacles and methods that were used to address them, often along with reasoning on why those methods were chosen. We introduce MUSE (Mining Underlying Scientific Explanations), a full-text, multi-domain resource of scientific Problem-Solution-Rationale (P-S-R) triplets. We curate 579 expert-annotated full-text paragraphs, with a rich annotation schema covering salient problem, solution, and rationale spans, solves and rationale_of links and conceptual coreference. A modular extraction pipeline scales this annotation to build a high-quality knowledge base of 37K source-grounded P-S-R triplets. We evaluate the extraction components and include a preliminary experiment training a rationale-supervised LLM for scientific problem solving. Interestingly, we find that rationale supervision improves performance on complex, multi-constraint problems but can harm performance on simpler ones.

</details>


### [46] [What Iterated Self-Feeding Probes of Language Models Measure, and a test that separates the construction from the model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10986)
*Nicolás Vera Zúñiga*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a diagnostic framework using coupled Glauber dynamics on token sequences to probe language model behavior. It reveals that measurements from self-consistency/iterative refinement probes conflate two distinct signals: construction-invariant artifacts (kinematic damage light cone, universal Lyapunov exponent scaling) and model-specific properties (training-phase transitions, attractor ranking). A decoupling test is provided to separate them, validated by exact recovery of a Domany-Kinzel damage field, and four prior conclusions are retracted as estimator failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-consistency, iterated refinement, and agentic loop methods probe language models by feeding them their own output, but it is unclear what such probes actually measure. The authors construct a sharp, controlled setting — a ring of token cells with Glauber dynamics — to isolate and characterize the signal, motivated by the discovery that they themselves mistook construction artifacts for model properties for four months.

Method: The core method uses Glauber dynamics on a ring of token cells, where each token is resampled according to the model's windowed conditional p_r(x_i | x_{i±r}). The key innovation is coupling: advancing two rings differing by one token under common random numbers (maximal coupling). This makes undamaged copies diverge by exactly zero, enabling damage spreading to be measured precisely. The analysis varies two dimensions independently — holding the construction fixed while varying the model, and vice versa — to disentangle construction-invariant quantities from model-specific ones. Validation is performed by recovering a Domany-Kinzel damage field bit-exactly against an independent prediction, and the methodology is packaged as software.

Result: Two classes of quantities were distinguished. Construction-invariant (kinematic) results: the damage light cone is purely kinematic, and the radius scaling of the token-space Lyapunov exponent λ_ca(r) is invariant across 19 models and two scale ladders spanning 70×. Model-specific results: λ_ca crosses zero at a reproducible training checkpoint, and attractor share consistently ranks models regardless of lattice construction. A phase transition measured to three decimal places was found to belong to the probe, not the model. The validation recovered a Domany-Kinzel damage field bit-exactly. Four retracted verdicts were reported, each on quantities that appeared to be measurements but were estimator artifacts.

Conclusion: Self-consistency probes measure two confounded signals at once. The recommended decoupling test — hold construction fixed vs. hold model fixed — reliably separates them. Without this discipline, construction artifacts are readily mistaken for model properties. The framework provides a validated instrument and software package for rigorous probing of language model dynamics.

Abstract: A growing class of methods probes a language model by feeding it its own output: self-consistency, iterated refinement, agentic loops. We ask what such a probe measures, in a construction chosen to make the question sharp: a ring of token cells resampled in place by the model's own windowed conditional p_r(x_i | x_{i+-r}). The substrate is Glauber dynamics on token sequences and is not new; what we change is the coupling. Advancing two rings that differ in one token under common random numbers makes undamaged copies diverge by exactly zero, so damage spreading becomes measurable where a maximal coupling gives mixing times instead. The answer is that it measures two different things at once, in readings that look alike. Some quantities are fixed by the construction: the damage light cone is kinematic, and the radius scaling of the token-space Lyapunov exponent lambda_ca(r) is model-invariant across 19 models and two scale ladders spanning 70x. Others genuinely track the model: lambda_ca crosses zero at a reproducible point in training, and the attractor share ranks models consistently however the lattice is built. Left undistinguished, the first kind is readily mistaken for the second -- we did so ourselves for four months, and report a phase transition we measured to three decimal places that belongs to the probe rather than to any language model. We give the test that separates them: hold the construction fixed and vary the model, or hold the model fixed and vary the construction, and see which readings move. We validate the instrument by reproduction first, recovering a Domany-Kinzel damage field bit-exactly against an independent prediction, and we report the estimator failures that this discipline caught -- four retracted verdicts, each on a quantity that looked like a measurement. The methodology ships as a package.

</details>


### [47] [ConRub-Med: Reinforcement Learning with Consensus Rubrics for Open-Ended Medical Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10996)
*Taojie Zhu,Yuan Xia,Tao Sun,Yizhi Wang,Yan Chen,Qunshan He,Tian Guan,Jian Wang,Jinjie Gu,Junwei Liu,Yonghong He*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConRub-Med introduces a scalable, model-generated rubric framework for reinforcement learning in open-ended medical QA. It uses three heterogeneous LMs to propose atomic criteria, filtered by a reviewer for consensus. A Three-State scoring system penalizes errors (negative credit) and distinguishes missing vs. correct information. For GRPO optimization, tied groups leverage a pairwise judge requiring agreement from both candidate orders. The method achieves state-of-the-art results on medical benchmarks, with 38.98 on HealthBench-Hard using 5,166 prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
