Motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards excels in math/coding where answers are automatically checkable, but open-ended medical questions lack cheap, reliable outcome verifiers. Physician-written rubrics are clinically grounded but expensive and non-scalable. Model-generated rubrics offer scalability but risk losing clinically important distinctions during policy optimization. The work aims to preserve these distinctions while making supervision scalable.

Method: The ConRub-Med pipeline: (1) Three heterogeneous LMs independently propose atomic criteria per prompt; (2) a separate reviewer model retains only criteria with semantic support from all three generators; (3) Three-State scoring assigns positive credit for correct coverage, negative credit for incorrect claims, and zero for missing information; (4) For GRPO, when all responses in a group tie on scalar reward, a pairwise judge assigns sequence advantages only if both candidate orderings agree; non-tied groups use vanilla GRPO.

Result: In a blinded, question-matched study, two medical experts rated ConRub-Med panels as more clinically relevant than single-generator panels. The method ranks first on 6 of 9 benchmarks among evaluated open models and achieves the highest medical and generalization averages. With a 5,166-prompt rubric dataset, it scores 38.98±1.04 on HealthBench-Hard, outperforming InfiMed-ORBIT (33.60 with 8K samples, 37.30 with 28K).

Conclusion: Model-generated rubrics with consensus filtering, error-penalizing Three-State scoring, and a tie-breaking pairwise judge for GRPO together produce clinically superior, scalable reinforcement learning for open-ended medical QA, achieving state-of-the-art results with fewer training prompts than prior work.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has been especially effective in mathematics and coding, where answers can be checked automatically. Many open-ended medical questions lack comparably cheap outcome verifiers: responses may be partly correct, incomplete, or contain clinically consequential errors. Rubrics written or validated by physicians offer strong clinical grounding, but involving experts in every instance is costly. Model-generated rubrics make this supervision scalable. We introduce ConRub-Med to preserve useful distinctions as rubric feedback moves from construction to policy optimization. For each prompt, three heterogeneous language models propose atomic criteria independently; a separate model reviews them, retaining only criteria with semantic support from all three generators. Three-State scoring distinguishes correct coverage, missing information, and incorrect claims. Errors receive negative rather than zero credit. When every response in a complete Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) group receives the same final reward, a pairwise judge provides sequence advantages only if both candidate orders agree, without changing the scalar rewards. Groups without ties use vanilla GRPO. In a blinded study matched by question, two medical experts rate panels from the full pipeline as more clinically relevant than panels produced by one generator. Across the evaluated open models, ConRub-Med ranks first on six of nine benchmarks and achieves the highest medical and generalization averages. Using the resulting rubric dataset of 5,166 prompts, it scores $38.98 \pm 1.04$ (mean $\pm$ SD) on HealthBench-Hard, compared with InfiMed-ORBIT's 33.60 with 8,000 samples and 37.30 with 28,000.

</details>


### [48] [On the Limitations of Cross-Lingual Consistency in Multilingual Text-to-image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11002)
*Sicheng Zhang,Zhonghao Yan,Binzhu Xie,Shi Qiu,Muzammal Naseer,Naveed Akhtar,Mubarak Shah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LingT2I is a multilingual benchmark (10 languages, 33K prompts) for evaluating cross-lingual text-to-image generation, revealing linguistic inequality and language-dependent trade-offs in both content generation and text rendering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing T2I research has been predominantly English-centric, leaving cross-lingual performance disparities and language-specific effects underexplored. There is a need for systematic evaluation across languages to understand and address linguistic inequality in generative models.

Method: The authors introduce LingT2I, a benchmark spanning 10 widely used languages with 33K prompts. They conduct comprehensive cross-lingual quantitative evaluation across multiple dimensions (content generation and text rendering), complemented by qualitative analysis of language-dependent generation patterns tied to linguistic factors and cultural contexts.

Result: Cross-lingual analysis reveals significant linguistic inequality among the 10 languages, with language-dependent trade-offs across evaluation dimensions. Distinct language-dependent generation patterns emerge, demonstrating how linguistic and cultural factors systematically influence model outputs.

Conclusion: The benchmark and findings establish a foundation for studying cross-lingual behavior in T2I generation and support development of more robust, inclusive multilingual models. Code and dataset are publicly available.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) generation has achieved remarkable progress in recent years. However, existing research has largely focused on English-only settings, leaving cross-lingual performance gaps and language-specific effects insufficiently explored. To fill this gap, we introduce LingT2I, a benchmark covering 10 widely used languages with 33K prompts, designed to evaluate cross-lingual effects in both content generation and text rendering. Building on this benchmark, we conduct a comprehensive cross-lingual analysis, uncovering linguistic inequality and language-dependent trade-offs across evaluation dimensions. Beyond quantitative evaluation, we further reveal a range of language-dependent generation patterns, highlighting how linguistic factors and their corresponding cultural contexts systematically impact model outputs. Our benchmark and analysis provide a foundation for studying cross-lingual behavior in T2I generation and facilitate the development of more robust and inclusive models. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/RISys-Lab/LingT2I.

</details>


### [49] [Templated or fully Synthetic? Prompt construction as a confound in measuring LLM political stance beyond writing assistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11008)
*Ilias Chalkidis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper extends IssueBench beyond writing assistance to include information seeking and opinion sharing tasks, proposes using fully LLM-generated synthetic prompts (seeded with real prompts) as a more ecologically valid alternative to templated prompts for political stance detection, and demonstrates through human/LLM annotation studies that synthetic prompts are perceived as more realistic and yield systematically different stance estimates than templated prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing political stance detection in LLMs relies on templated prompts that lack ecological validity—they fail to mirror realistic human-AI interactions, remain recognizable as evaluation artifacts, and are susceptible to sandbagging. The authors argue that even improved templated approaches (like IssueBench) fall short in capturing the nuance of real-world chats, particularly for open-ended tasks.

Method: The authors extend IssueBench with two new task types (information seeking and opinion sharing). They generate fully synthetic prompts using LLMs, guided by detailed instructions and seeded with real-world chat logs. They then conduct a small-scale ecological validity study covering 3 contested policy issues and 3 geopolitical conflicts, using both human and LLM annotators to rank the realism and clarity of real, templated, and LLM-generated prompts. A case study compares stance estimates produced by templated versus LLM-generated prompts on the same model.

Result: LLM-generated prompts are ranked by both human and LLM annotators as no less realistic than real prompts and clearly more realistic than templated ones. They also convey intended intent and stance more clearly. LLM annotators separate templated prompts from the other two types far more sharply than humans do. In the case study, templated and LLM-generated prompts produce systematically different stance estimates, especially under neutral framings where templated prompts overstate the model's leaning in the direction encoded by the topic-and-stance filler text.

Conclusion: LLM-generated synthetic prompts offer superior ecological validity over templated prompts for political stance detection in LLMs and produce more reliable stance estimates. Templated prompts introduce systematic bias, particularly overstating stance under neutral framings, which undermines their utility for realistic evaluation.

Abstract: Political stance detection in LLMs has long been dominated by closed-ended, multiple-choice political survey questions---originally designed for humans, and thus lacks the realism and nuance of human-AI interactions in the wild, while also being susceptible to sandbagging. The recent IssueBench framework substantially mitigates these limitations with templated prompts anchored in real-world chat logs. Given the rise in non-work-related use of GenAI assistants, we extend IssueBench beyond writing assistance to include two additional tasks, information seeking and opinion sharing. We argue that templated prompts still lack the nuance of real ones, especially for open-ended tasks, and remain recognisable as evaluation artefacts. We propose the use of fully synthetic (LLM-generated) prompts, produced under detailed instructions with real prompts as seeds. We assess the ecological validity of real, templated, and LLM-generated prompts in a small-scale study covering 3 highly contested policy issues and 3 recent geopolitical conflicts. Human and LLM annotators rank LLM-generated prompts as no less realistic than real ones and clearly more realistic than templated ones, and find that they carry their intended intent and stance more clearly; the LLMs separate templated prompts from the other two far more sharply than the humans do. In a case study, templated and LLM-generated prompts yield systematically different stance estimates for the same model, most visibly under neutral framings, where templated prompts overstate the model's leaning in the direction encoded by the topic-and-stance text (filler) slotted into their templates.

</details>


### [50] [Data Attribution of Emergent Misalignment with Persona Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11025)
*Clemens Vetter,David Kaczér,Lucie Flek,Florian Mai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fine-tuning amplifies pre-existing persona features (e.g., jailbreak, sarcasm, deception) and suppresses safety features, causing emergent misalignment. SAE-based steering can induce or reverse EM. Human-written web documents containing relevant narratives fail to induce EM unless reformatted as synthetic instruction-response pairs, indicating response structure matters more than semantic content alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the origin of persona features implicated in emergent misalignment (EM): specifically, which pre-training documents activate them, and whether naturally occurring human-written text is sufficient to induce EM, or whether synthetic structure is required.

Method: The authors apply Sparse Autoencoder (SAE)-based model diffing across four open-weight models to identify latent features amplified or suppressed by misalignment fine-tuning. They then perform steering experiments on these features to control EM. Finally, they attribute causal features to a corpus of one million pre-training web documents and test whether fine-tuning on retrieved human-written documents (vs. synthetic instruction-response pairs derived from the same content) induces EM.

Result: Misalignment fine-tuning amplifies features linked to jailbreak personas, sarcasm, deception, and manipulation while suppressing safety and assistant-identity features. Steering individual features induces EM in aligned models (up to 62%, exceeding the 35% from fine-tuning alone) and re-aligns misaligned models. Feature attribution retrieves semantically relevant narratives (villainous characters, domination, harmful agency), but fine-tuning on these human-written documents fails to reliably induce EM, whereas synthetic instruction-response pairs from the same content succeed—even transferring across model families.

Conclusion: Semantic relevance of pre-training content alone is insufficient to induce emergent misalignment; the response structure or model-generated phrasing (as in synthetic instruction-response formats) plays a critical role. This refines mechanistic accounts of EM by showing that the format in which harmful content is presented during fine-tuning is a key causal factor.

Abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) is the phenomenon where fine-tuning a language model on a narrow task leads to harmful behavior in unrelated domains. A leading mechanistic account attributes EM to persona features: latent directions acquired during pre-training that misaligned fine-tuning amplifies. We ask where these features come from: which pre-training documents activate them, and whether naturally occurring human-written text suffices to induce EM. Using Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) based model diffing across four open-weight models, we find that features related to jailbreak personas, sarcasm, deception, and manipulation are amplified by misalignment fine-tuning, while safety-relevant and assistant-identity features are suppressed. Steering individual features controls EM in both directions: it induces misalignment rates of up to 62% in aligned models -- exceeding the 35% reached by misalignment fine-tuning itself -- and re-aligns misaligned models to near-baseline misalignment rates. Attributing the causal features to a corpus of one million pre-training web documents retrieves semantically relevant narratives about villainous characters, domination, and harmful agency. However, fine-tuning on these human-written documents does not reliably induce EM, even after reformatting into assistant-style responses, whereas synthetic instruction-response pairs derived from the same content do -- and transfer across model families. Semantic relevance alone is therefore not sufficient: response structure or model-generated phrasing plays an important role in inducing EM.

</details>


### [51] [myMediWhisper: Construction of Burmese Medical Speech Corpus and Whisper Fine-Tuning for Clinical Dialogue ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11036)
*Ye Kyaw Thu,Ye Bhone Lin,Thura Aung,Htet Arkar,Myat Oo Swe,Thet Htet San,Min Thiha Tun,Thazin Myint Oo,Thepchai Supnithi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fine-tuning Whisper models on a 28-hour Burmese medical speech corpus achieves SOTA WER of 23.44%. Data augmentation improves robustness to noise and reverberation but degrades clean-speech performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Whisper models underperform on Burmese medical speech despite large-scale multilingual pre-training, creating a need for domain-specific adaptation and a high-quality annotated corpus for this low-resource setting.

Method: A 28-hour Burmese medical speech corpus was recorded and validated by native speakers. Whisper models were fine-tuned using both full fine-tuning (FFT) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with LoRA. Robustness was evaluated using waveform- and spectrogram-level data augmentation simulating noise and room acoustics.

Result: The best system (myMediWhisper-Medium, fully fine-tuned without augmentation) achieved a SOTA WER of 23.44%, outperforming larger general-domain fine-tuned models. Data augmentation reduced clean-speech performance but significantly improved robustness in noisy and reverberant conditions across both FFT and PEFT settings.

Conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning of Whisper with a high-quality native-speaker corpus yields strong results for Burmese medical ASR. There is a clear trade-off: data augmentation sacrifices clean-speech accuracy for noise/reverberation robustness.

Abstract: Although Whisper models benefit from large-scale multilingual pre-training, their performance on Burmese medical speech remains limited. This work presents a Burmese medical speech recognition framework built on a high-quality 28-hour corpus recorded and validated by native speakers. We fine-tune Whisper models using full fine-tuning (FFT) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with LoRA. To evaluate robustness, we apply waveform- and spectrogram-level data augmentation under controlled noise and simulated room acoustics. While augmentation reduces performance on clean speech, it significantly improves robustness in noisy and reverberant environments across FFT and PEFT settings. Our best-performing system, fully fine-tuned myMediWhisper-Medium without augmentation, achieves a state-of-the-art Word Error Rate (WER) of 23.44%, outperforming much larger general-domain fine-tuned models. Dataset and other resources can be found at the Huggingface repository: https://huggingface.co/datasets/LULab/mediTalk-mm-rdy.

</details>


### [52] [TEAMMix: Taxonomy Enrichment Augmentation and Minority-augmented Mixing Strategy for LLM-enhanced Weak-Supervised Hierarchical Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11044)
*Jian Zhang,Zhuohao Yang,Songlin Lei,Bangli Liu,Ziwei Wang,Xufeng Weng,Gehan Amaratunga,Yu Lin,Hongwei Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A weakly supervised HTC framework that uses LLM-based data augmentation—keyword generation, pseudo-sample synthesis, and GMM-based confidence resampling—to address label hierarchy complexity and class imbalance, significantly boosting fine-grained classification performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HTC methods using LLMs suffer from lengthy prompts and loss of label structural information, limiting their practical efficiency. Additionally, complex label hierarchies and class imbalance (long-tail distributions) degrade performance on fine-grained categories.

Method: The framework operates in three stages: (1) semantic enrichment of the label hierarchy via keyword generation and corpus mining to improve label understanding; (2) LLM-guided pseudo-sample generation to mitigate the long-tail problem; (3) confidence-based resampling using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to filter and optimize the quality of generated data.

Result: The proposed method effectively improves the reliability of LLM-generated pseudo-labels and significantly enhances classification performance on fine-grained and imbalanced datasets.

Conclusion: LLM-based data augmentation, when combined with semantic label enrichment and GMM-based quality optimization, offers a compelling weakly supervised solution for hierarchical text classification under label imbalance.

Abstract: Hierarchical Text Classification (HTC), as a critical text mining task, faces challenges such as complex label hierarchies and class imbalance. Existing methods based on large language models (LLMs) struggle to be efficiently applied to this task due to issues like lengthy prompts and loss of label structural information. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a weakly supervised HTC framework enhanced by LLM-based data augmentation. The framework first enriches the label hierarchy semantically through keyword generation and corpus mining, thereby enhancing the model's understanding of labels. Subsequently, it guides the LLM to generate pseudo-samples to mitigate the long-tail problem, and employs a Gaussian mixture model for confidence-based resampling to optimize the quality of generated data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively improves the reliability of LLM-generated pseudo-labels and significantly enhances classification performance on fine-grained and imbalanced datasets.

</details>


### [53] [Multiclass Sentiment Analysis for Identifying Political Viewpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11049)
*Girma Yohannis Bade,Olga Kolesnikova,Jose Luis Oropeza,Grigori Sidorov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates multiclass sentiment analysis on political social media posts, comparing XGBoost and BERT-based models. Both achieve modest F1-scores (~0.28), highlighting the difficulty of classifying nuanced political sentiment and establishing a baseline for future work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of political discourse on social media presents an opportunity to computationally analyze public opinion. However, political sentiment is complex and contextualized, requiring robust multiclass classification approaches beyond simple positive/negative polarity.

Method: Two machine learning approaches are designed and evaluated: an XGBoost-based model and a BERT-based transformer model. Both are trained and tested on a labeled dataset of political social media posts, evaluated using standard classification metrics (F1-score).

Result: The XGBoost model achieves an F1-score of 0.2835, while the BERT-based model achieves 0.2806 on the test set — both relatively low, indicating the task's inherent difficulty.

Conclusion: Multiclass political sentiment analysis remains a challenging problem due to the complexity and context-dependence of political discourse. The reported scores serve as a baseline for future research in this domain.

Abstract: The rapid growth of social media has created vast amounts of political discourse, which provides valuable opportunities to analyze public opinions and identify different political perspectives. Sentiment Analysis (SA) is a core task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that allows the computational study of attitudes and opinions in textual data, and has become increasingly important for understanding political discourse. In this work, we investigate multiclass sentiment analysis of political view- points on social media, that is to automatically discriminate multiple sentiment classes over political issues and figures. To solve this task we design and evaluate two machine-learning approaches based on XGBoost and BERT. We train and evaluate the models on a labeled dataset of political social media posts using standard classification metrics. The experimental results show that the XGBoost model reaches an F1-score of 0.2835 and the BERT- based model reaches an F1-score of 0.2806 on the test set. These results demonstrate the challenge of classifying complex and contextualized political discourse sentiment and provide a baseline for future research in multiclass political sentiment analysis.

</details>


### [54] [Actions Speak Louder than Words: Measuring Cross-Lingual Policy Retention in Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11110)
*Sourabrata Mukherjee,Kalika Bali,Sunayana Sitaram*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether tool-using agents maintain consistent action policies across languages. Through massive-scale evaluation (2.38M rollouts across 8 models, 6 benchmarks, 41 languages), the authors identify and remove five confounds that distort trace similarity measurements. After correction, they find that frontier models preserve 71-73% of their action policy across languages under greedy decoding, with structural divergence rather than sampling noise. Non-English tasks are routed through English as a causal pivot, and a single regex bug created a spurious multilingual failure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multilingual evaluation focuses solely on final answer accuracy, ignoring the action traces that determine cost, latency, failure modes, and auditability. The authors argue that whether an agent takes the same steps across languages is an underexplored question with practical consequences for deployment, debugging, and fairness.

Method: The authors define "action policy" as the measured object and conduct evaluation across 8 models, 6 parallel benchmarks, and 41 languages (2.38M total rollouts). They identify five confounds in naive trace similarity measurement: (1) short traces inflate similarity, (2) empty traces yield perfect scores, (3) unrelated traces agree by chance over half the time, (4) the similarity ceiling is capped by each model's self-reproducibility, and (5) same-language repeated queries produce different answers, leaving no baseline. They systematically remove each confound, use greedy decoding and temperature sweeps to distinguish structural from sampling noise, normalize by self-reproducibility, and employ permutation-based chance floors. A pre-registered causal intervention tests whether models pivot non-English tasks through English.

Result: Every confound correction increases the measured divergence effect. Divergence is structural: it persists under greedy decoding and remains flat as temperature rises. Normalized by self-reproducibility, four frontier models converge at 71-73% action policy preservation, with model identity explaining only 5.7% of variance. Below ~10B parameters, consistency breaks down, and smaller model ordering is largely an artifact of an improperly specified chance floor. The English-pivot hypothesis is causally confirmed across four models. A single regex responsible for trace extraction created a spurious multilingual failure; fixing it raised one model's measured accuracy 26-fold while readable output accuracy barely changed.

Conclusion: Action policy divergence across languages is real, structural, and robust to correction. Frontier models show remarkable convergence in cross-lingual action consistency when properly normalized. The work demonstrates that measuring process rather than outcomes reveals hidden failure modes, and that rigorous removal of measurement confounds is essential for meaningful multilingual agent evaluation.

Abstract: When a tool-using agent is given the same task in a different language, does it still take the same steps? Multilingual evaluation rarely asks: it compares final answers and discards the actions. Yet those actions are the product: they fix cost and latency, decide how the system fails, and are the only auditable part of its behaviour. We make the action policy the measured object across 8 models, 6 parallel benchmarks and 41 languages (2.38M rollouts). The naive measurement fails: five confounds sit between raw trace similarity and any defensible claim, each able to flip a conclusion. Short traces score higher, empty traces score perfectly, unrelated traces agree by chance over half the time, the gap is capped by each model's reproducibility, and a model asked the same question twice in one language answers differently, leaving no baseline. We remove all five, and every correction makes the effect larger. Divergence proves structural, not sampling noise: it survives greedy decoding in every cell and stays flat as temperature rises, even as models grow less self-consistent. Normalised by their own reproducibility, four very different frontier models converge under greedy decoding, each keeping 71-73% of its action policy across languages, with model identity explaining only 5.7% of the variance. Below roughly 10B parameters it breaks down, and the ordering among smaller models is largely an artifact of a chance floor we measure by permutation rather than assume. Agents route non-English tasks through English; this pivot is causally load-bearing, confirmed by a pre-registered prediction across four models, and models will not abandon it when told to. Finally, a single trace-extraction regex, not the model, manufactured a multilingual failure: two worked examples raise one model's measured accuracy twenty-sixfold while its accuracy on readable outputs barely moves.

</details>


### [55] [Attention-Path Fragility as an Uncertainty Signal in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11138)
*Minsoo Kim,Sungyoung Ji,Kisung Moon,Ilyong Yoon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ASMI is a training-free uncertainty estimator that masks attention heads and measures mutual information among subnetworks. It captures "confident-but-fragile" predictions, complements single-pass confidence, halves retained error in grounded QA, matches or beats Semantic Entropy on most grounded settings, and reverts to MSP-level on parametric QA as predicted.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing confidence-based uncertainty estimators (e.g., output entropy) miss an important failure mode: predictions that are confident but fragile — i.e., the model appears certain yet its prediction would change under minor perturbation. The authors argue that this fragility, detectable via perturbations to attention pathways, carries orthogonal error-predictive signal not captured by output-distribution breadth alone.

Method: ASMI (Attention-Subnetwork Mutual Information): (1) Mask individual attention heads to create subnetworks; (2) Measure BALD (Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement) mutual information among these subnetwork outputs; (3) Apply a semantic-agreement kernel (Sem-ASMI) to discount surface-form disagreements that are semantically equivalent. The method uses only a single greedy response. An adaptive variant reuses samples drawn for baselines. The authors also show ASMI predicts its own domain of applicability (grounded vs. parametric QA).

Result: On grounded QA, out-of-fold tests show ASMI adds error-predictive information beyond single-pass confidence and entropy, concentrated in confident-but-fragile predictions where it roughly halves the retained error of a confidence filter. Sem-ASMI ties or beats Semantic Entropy on 10/12 grounded benchmark-backbone settings. The best adaptive ASMI variant ties or leads the strongest baseline in 8/12 settings (3 significantly under paired test). On parametric QA, ASMI reverts to or below MSP baseline, as predicted. Estimates are near-deterministic across reruns. Head-level analysis shows error coupling, not mere fragility presence, determines the boundary.

Conclusion: Attention-pathway fragility provides a distinct, complementary uncertainty signal to output-distribution-based measures. ASMI is most effective in grounded (context-dependent) QA settings and gracefully degrades in parametric settings — a regime boundary the method can self-predict. This offers a computationally cheaper alternative to sampling-based uncertainty methods while matching or exceeding their performance.

Abstract: We propose that a model's uncertainty about a token is reflected not only in the breadth of its output distribution but also in whether a confident prediction is \emph{fragile} under perturbation of its attention pathways. We instantiate this as ASMI (Attention-Subnetwork Mutual Information), a training-free estimator that masks attention heads and measures the BALD mutual information among the resulting subnetworks, with a semantic-agreement kernel to discount surface-form disagreement. The signal is not a restatement of output confidence: on grounded QA an out-of-fold test shows it adds error-predictive information beyond single-pass confidence and entropy, concentrated in \emph{confident-but-fragile} predictions, where acting on it roughly halves the retained error of a confidence filter. The distinctness is regime-graded, so ASMI predicts its own domain of applicability, strong where answers are routed through provided context and bounded by design where they are recalled from parametric knowledge. Sem-ASMI reads the signal from a single greedy response, without the stochastic generations the strongest baselines require, and ties or beats Semantic Entropy on ten of the twelve grounded benchmark-backbone settings. Across the same twelve settings, the best ASMI variant, typically the adaptive one reusing the ten samples already drawn for the baselines, ties or leads the strongest baseline in eight, significantly in three under a paired test. On parametric QA all variants revert to or below the zero-cost MSP baseline, exactly as predicted, and the estimates are near-deterministic across reruns. A head-level analysis shows that what tracks this boundary is not the presence of head-level fragility but whether that fragility couples to errors.

</details>


### [56] [The Illusion of Cross-Lingual Safety in Low-Resource Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11146)
*Abigail Oppong,P Sam Sahil,Tadesse Destaw Belay,Maryam Ibrahim Mukhtar,Esmael Ahmed Abdu,Tassallah Abdullahi,Jessica Oparebea,Saminu Mohammad Aliyu,Idris Abdulmumin,Abubakar Juma Chilala,Nicholaus Dismas Ladislaus,Alfred Malengo Kondoro,Lemofouet Valdini Douglace,Shamsuddeen Hassan Muhammad,Seid Muhie Yimam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Safety alignment in LLMs fails to transfer across languages. Using a new dataset (LoDNA) covering four African languages and a latent geometric framework, the authors show that harmful prompts in low-resource languages retain less than 10% of the English refusal signal, demonstrating that multilingual safety is superficial rather than universal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM safety alignment is predominantly developed and evaluated in English, with the untested assumption that these safeguards generalize across languages. This creates a critical vulnerability in low-resource languages where harmful content can bypass safety mechanisms.

Method: The authors introduce LoDNA, a safety dataset for four African languages (Twi, Hausa, Amharic, Swahili) pairing literal translations with culturally localized harmful prompts. They propose a latent geometric framework that probes hidden-state refusal representations rather than relying on generation-based evaluation, measuring refusal signal strength and semantic alignment across layers.

Result: Cross-lingual safety transfer is severely limited: harmful prompts retain less than 10% of the English refusal signal across most language-model pairs. While literal and localized prompts remain semantically aligned (cosine similarity 0.95–0.996), representations drift across layers, indicating models encode harmful concepts without routing them to safety mechanisms.

Conclusion: Multilingual safety alignment is superficial. The findings provide strong evidence against the existence of a universal, language-agnostic harm manifold, at least for the low-resource languages studied.

Abstract: Safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) is largely developed in English, assuming these safeguards generalize across multilingual settings. However, this assumption remains underexplored and exposes a vulnerability in low-resource languages. We investigate cross-lingual safety transfer in four African languages, Twi, Hausa, Amharic, and Swahili, using LoDNA, a new safety dataset that pairs literal translations with culturally localized prompts. To move beyond generation-based evaluation, we propose a latent geometric framework that probes hidden-state refusal representations in LLMs. Our experimental results show that cross-lingual safety transfer is severely limited; harmful prompts retain less than 10% of the English refusal signal across most language-model pairs. Literal and localized prompts are semantically aligned (cosine 0.95-0.996) but drift across layers, suggesting models encode the concepts without routing them to safety mechanisms. These findings demonstrate that current multilingual safety alignment is superficial, providing strong evidence against the assumption of a universal, language-agnostic harm manifold within the specific low-resource languages studied. Warning: This paper contains example data that may be offensive or harmful.

</details>


### [57] [From Interpretability to Control: Insights from Six Years of the TrustNLP Workshop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11171)
*Rahul Gupta,Abhinav Mohanty,Anaelia Ovalle,Anil Ramakrishna,Anubrata Das,Apurv Verma,Jwala Dhamala,Ninareh Mehrabi,Tharindu Kumarage,Yada Pruksachatkun,Yang Trista Cao,Kai-Wei Chang,Aram Galstyan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A meta-analysis of 144 TrustNLP workshop papers (2021–2026) reveals a field-wide shift from post-hoc interpretability toward mechanistic understanding and proactive safety alignment of generative models. Truthfulness is the fastest-growing trust dimension, fairness is the most consistent, and explainability follows a U-shaped trajectory. TrustNLP's topical distribution aligns closely with major ACL venues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to synthesize six years of TrustNLP workshop proceedings to map the evolution of trustworthiness research in NLP, identify structural trends across trust dimensions, and compare the workshop's topical focus with that of broader ACL-affiliated conferences.

Method: The study classifies all 144 TrustNLP proceedings papers (2021–2026) along six trust dimensions derived from established frameworks (TrustLLM, DecodingTrust). It tracks temporal trends per dimension, analyzes co-occurrence with model capability emergence, and performs a cross-venue topical comparison against ~2,000 papers from ACL, NAACL, EACL, and EMNLP over the same period.

Result: Key findings: (1) The release of high-impact chat models activated all trust dimensions simultaneously. (2) Truthfulness grew from 0% (2021–2022) to 37% (2025–2026), making it the fastest-growing dimension. (3) Fairness is the most consistent theme. (4) Explainability shows a U-shaped curve—declining with the waning of post-hoc methods, then resurging via mechanistic interpretability in 2026. (5) TrustNLP's topical distribution closely mirrors that of major ACL venues.

Conclusion: TrustNLP documents a paradigm shift from static-model interpretability to proactive, mechanistic control of generative systems. The authors identify four structural insights and propose actionable directions for the community, emphasizing that trustworthiness research is converging with mainstream NLP concerns.

Abstract: The Workshop on Trustworthy Natural Language Processing (TrustNLP), co-located with major ACL conferences since 2021, has grown from 8 proceedings papers to 41 over six editions, documenting a field-wide transition from post-hoc interpretability of static models to mechanistic understanding and proactive control of generative systems. We synthesize insights from all 144 proceedings papers, classifying them along six trust dimensions grounded in established frameworks (TrustLLM, DecodingTrust). We observe co-occurrences with capability emergence. The release of the first high-impact chat models activated all trust dimensions simultaneously, while subsequent model generations shifted focus toward truthfulness and safety alignment. Analysis from the classification study reveals that truthfulness is the fastest-growing dimension (absent in 2021-2022, comprising 37% of papers by 2025-2026), fairness remains the most consistent theme, and explainability exhibits a U-shaped trajectory; declining as post-hoc methods lost relevance but resurging in 2026 through mechanistic interpretability. A cross-venue comparison with ACL, NAACL, EACL, and EMNLP (~2K papers) in the same period shows that TrustNLP's topical distribution closely follows the field average. We identify four structural insights and conclude with actionable directions for the research community.

</details>


### [58] [ConVAWG: A Retrieval-Grounded Framework for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation in Violence Against Women and Girls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11200)
*Chen Lyu,Xingwei Tan,Simon Cullen,Shelley Wilson,Lois Arthurs,Arshad Jhumka,Gabriele Pergola*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConVAWG is a retrieval-grounded framework for generating synthetic multi-turn dialogues modelling Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios, producing over 6,000 dialogue events across 200 scenarios with rich metadata, validated through human evaluation and downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real conversational data on sensitive abuse domains like VAWG is scarce due to privacy, legal, and ethical constraints. Existing research focuses predominantly on sentence-level toxicity in online abuse, failing to capture abuse as a relational, temporally unfolding conversational phenomenon that includes offline behaviours (surveillance, stalking, coercion, physical violence) planned or referenced in dialogue.

Method: ConVAWG employs a retrieval-grounded, CPS-aligned pipeline: (1) persona seeds are constructed using demographic patterns from the UK ONS, official crime definitions, and retrieved Domestic Homicide Review cases; (2) these are converted into hierarchical event timelines; (3) multi-scene role-play dialogues are generated; (4) targeted activation-steered toxicity control is applied to ensure appropriate toxicity levels in specific utterances rather than uniformly.

Result: The framework produces 6,000+ multi-turn dialogue events across 200 scenarios with scenario-, event-, and turn-level metadata. Human evaluation and LLM-as-Judge assessments confirm strong dialogue quality and domain fidelity. Ablations and downstream task evaluations further validate the effectiveness of the approach.

Conclusion: ConVAWG successfully bridges the gap in modelling abuse as a relational, multi-turn conversational phenomenon, providing a high-quality synthetic dataset that respects privacy constraints while enabling research on VAWG conversational dynamics.

Abstract: Synthetic dialogue generation offers a way to study conversational dynamics in sensitive domains where real data are difficult to access, release, or annotate. The underlying abuse may occur online or offline: threats and coercion can appear directly in messages, while behaviours such as surveillance, isolation, stalking, and physical violence may be planned, disclosed, or referred to conversationally. Privacy and legal constraints make it difficult the release of large-scale real conversation datasets; existing work has mostly focused on sentence-level toxicity of online abuses, leaving a gap in modelling abuse as a relational and temporally unfolding phenomenon. In this work, we focus on modelling Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios as multi-turn dialogues. We introduce ConVAWG, a retrieval-grounded framework for generating CPS-aligned synthetic VAWG chat dialogues. ConVAWG builds scenarios from persona seeds, demographic patterns reported by the UK Office for National Statistics, official crime definitions, and retrieved Domestic Homicide Review cases; converts them into hierarchical event timelines; generates multi-scene role-play dialogues; and applies targeted activation-steered toxicity control to appropriate utterances. We release over 6,000 multi-turn dialogue events across 200 scenarios with rich scenario-, event-, and turn-level metadata. Extensive human evaluation, LLM-as-Judge assessment, ablations, and downstream tasks show strong dialogue quality and domain fidelity.

</details>
