### [59] [N2NMatcher: Towards Inlining-Resilient Binary Decomposition and Module Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10043)
*Ang Jia,He Jiang,Zhipeng Yang,Zhilei Ren,Xiaochen Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: N2NMatcher proposes an inlining-resilient framework for program-level binary code similarity analysis that uses a hierarchical graph neural network to predict anchor functions for stable module decomposition, then matches modules via learned graph embeddings, outperforming existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing program-level binary code similarity analysis methods decompose binaries into modules based on function call graphs (FCGs) and match them via contained functions. However, function inlining—a common compiler optimization—alters both FCG structure and function semantics, rendering decomposition and module matching ineffective. A framework resilient to inlining is needed.

Method: N2NMatcher first empirically investigates whether binaries retain functions that provide stable module boundaries across compilation settings. It then trains a hierarchical graph neural network operating on ACFG-FCG representations (encoding opcode sequences, control-flow structures, and FCG calling context) to predict such boundary functions as anchors. Using these predicted anchors, it performs anchor-bounded decomposition and matches generated modules through learned module graph embeddings.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that N2NMatcher improves both decomposition quality and module matching accuracy compared to existing approaches, enabling more effective program-level binary code similarity analysis.

Conclusion: N2NMatcher provides a robust, inlining-resilient solution for program-level BCSA by learning to identify stable anchor functions for decomposition and leveraging hierarchical graph representations for accurate module matching.

Abstract: Program-level Binary Code Similarity Analysis (BCSA) aims to identify semantically similar code regions across binary programs, serving as a fundamental technique for software plagiarism detection, vulnerability search, and malware analysis. Existing approaches often decompose binaries into modules following the structure of function call graphs (FCGs) and then match these modules by their contained functions. However, function inlining changes both FCG structures and binary function semantics, making existing decomposition and module matching methods less effective.
  In this work, we propose N2NMatcher, an inlining-resilient framework for binary decomposition and module matching. We first conduct an empirical study to examine whether binaries still contain functions that provide stable module boundaries across compilation settings. N2NMatcher learns to predict such functions as anchors using a hierarchical graph neural network that encodes binary ACFG-FCG representations built from opcode sequences, control-flow structures, and FCG calling context. It then performs anchor-bounded decomposition and matches the generated modules using learned module graph embeddings. Experimental results show that N2NMatcher improves both the decomposition quality and module matching accuracy compared to existing works, enabling more effective program-level BCSA.

</details>


### [60] [Exploring Semantic Stability Across Reviews in the Linux Kernel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10101)
*Lucas Ciziks,Paulo Meirelles,Marco Aurélio Gerosa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper measures similarity between initial and final versions of functions across patch revisions in the Linux IIO subsystem. It finds that while overall similarity is near-ceiling (75.3% of functions are never edited), among actually modified functions semantic purpose is largely preserved (mean similarity 0.990 vs. 0.909 baseline). Most change occurs in the first review round, and the paper questions whether near-ceiling similarity reflects genuine preservation of purpose or insensitivity of the measurement tool to small but significant edits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on code review impact studies only the final merged patch without comparing it to the first submission, missing the trajectory of changes across revisions. The authors aim to quantify how much a patch's code actually changes during review, and whether high similarity scores meaningfully reflect preservation of semantic purpose or are artifacts of measurement.

Method: A function-level longitudinal measurement tracking 10,117 function trajectories across numbered revisions of patch series in the Linux IIO subsystem. Similarity scores (likely based on textual or structural metrics) are computed between consecutive versions and compared against a baseline of unrelated function pairs. The analysis controls for compositional effects (functions untouched across revisions) and isolates the first review round vs. later rounds to detect drift patterns and residual effects.

Result: 75.3% of tracked functions are never modified between versions, inflating overall similarity. Among functions with real edits, mean similarity is 0.990 vs. 0.909 baseline. Change concentrates in the first review round; later rounds appear more conservative mainly because they contain more untouched functions. After controlling for this compositional effect, only a small but statistically significant residual effect remains.

Conclusion: Near-ceiling similarity scores in code review trajectories raise an open question: does high similarity genuinely indicate preserved semantic purpose, or does it reflect a measurement tool insensitive to small, localized yet meaningful edits? The work is presented as an initial exploration with outlined next steps for future investigation.

Abstract: Code review is credited with substantially changing a patch's code between its first submission and the version that eventually lands. However, prior work typically studied only the final merged patch without comparing it to the first submission. We present a function-level measurement that tracks 10,117 trajectories (each function followed across the numbered revisions of one patch series) through the patch history of the Linux IIO subsystem, comparing similarity scores against unrelated function pairs as a baseline. A naive reading yields near-total similarity, but this is largely an artifact of composition: 75.3% of tracked trajectories are never textually modified between versions, contributing a trivial 100% similarity that inflates the headline. Restricting to the trajectories with a real edit, semantic purpose is still largely preserved (mean similarity 0.990 vs. a 0.909 baseline), but drift appears to concentrate in the first review round mainly because later rounds contain more functions that nobody touched, not because edits become more conservative over time. After controlling for it, a statistically detectable but small residual effect remains. This points to an open question: whether near-ceiling similarity reflects preserved purpose or a measurement tool that cannot detect the significance of small, localized edits. We present this work as a first look and outline next steps.

</details>


### [61] [One Recipe, Many Harnesses: What Self-Evolution Encodes Across Languages and Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10178)
*Siqi Yang,Qianlan Yang,Yu-Xiong Wang,Saurabh Pujar,Martin Hirzel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates self-evolving agent harnesses, revealing that their gains stem from compensating model-specific behavioral gaps and language-specific engineering demands, rather than mere benchmark overfitting. The evolved knowledge contains a transferable abstract core but requires native re-evolution for ecosystem-specific machinery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on self-evolving harnesses reports only aggregate performance gains without analyzing what evolved artifacts encode. It remains unclear whether improvements reflect benchmark-specific adaptations, language-specific engineering knowledge, or compensation for underlying model limitations. The authors aim to disentangle these factors.

Method: The authors hold a fixed evolution recipe constant across a grid of eight programming languages (using Multi-SWE-Bench) and three base models. Every edit is routed through a typed failure signal and recorded as a falsifiable contract, making each modification attributable post-evolution. The resulting harnesses are systematically analyzed.

Result: Four findings emerge: (1) The loop improves held-out solve rates over baselines in most settings, with two null regions. (2) Gains compensate recoverable execution defects—where defect mass is near zero, gain is near zero. (3) Evolved harnesses share an abstract playbook but instantiate it with nearly disjoint language-ecosystem machinery. (4) The shared core transfers and distills into a universal harness, while the ecosystem margin resists transfer and requires native re-evolution.

Conclusion: Evolved harnesses function as a legible compensation layer shaped jointly by language engineering demands and model behavioral gaps, rather than opaque benchmark-tuned scaffolds. The abstract core is transferable, but ecosystem-specific components require re-evolution.

Abstract: Self-evolving harnesses are closed-loop systems in which an agent inspects its own rollouts and edits its prompts, tools, and memory. They reliably improve coding agents in evaluations, but prior work reports aggregate gains rather than analyzing what the evolved artifacts encode. It therefore remains unclear whether they encode benchmark-specific adaptations, language-specific engineering knowledge, or compensation for limitations of the underlying model. We disentangle these factors by holding an evolution recipe fixed across a grid of eight programming languages (Multi-SWE-Bench) and three base models, and analyzing the resulting harnesses. The recipe routes every edit through a typed failure signal and records it as a falsifiable contract, making each modification attributable after evolution. Four findings emerge. (1)The loop improves held-out solve rates over both a minimal seed and the manually designed mini-SWE-agent scaffold in most cells, but with two null regions. (2)Gains compensate recoverable execution defects, where defect mass is near zero, and gain is near zero; which defect dominates is cell-specific. A harness closes the gap between what a policy can do and what it does. (3)Evolved harnesses share an abstract playbook across languages but instantiate it with almost disjoint language ecosystem machinery. (4)The shared core transfers and can be distilled into one universal harness, while an ecosystem margin resists both and requires native re-evolution. Together, these results recast the evolved harness as a legible compensation layer, shaped jointly by the language's engineering demands and the model's behavioral gaps, rather than an opaque benchmark-tuned scaffold.

</details>


### [62] [Bias Smells in AI Software Development: Recognizing Potential Sources of Fairness Debt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10248)
*Ronnie de Souza Santos,Cleyton Magalhaes,Rodrigo Spinola*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces the concept of "bias smells" — six recurring indicators (Context Oversimplification, Dataset Imbalance, Metrics Inadequacies, Ad hoc Testing, Individual Diversity Unawareness, Homogeneous Team Composition) that signal potential sources of fairness debt in AI-based software projects, identified through an exploratory case study of four AI projects involving 25 professionals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing attention to AI fairness, there is limited empirical evidence on how practitioners recognize potential sources of fairness debt — the long-term consequences of development decisions that reinforce bias and inequities — during the development of AI-based software systems.

Method: An exploratory case study of four AI projects within a single organization, collecting data from 25 professionals via semi-structured interviews and open-ended questionnaires, supplemented by observation of internal communication channels and project documentation. Analysis used iterative qualitative coding, memoing, and constant comparison.

Result: Six recurring bias smells were identified: Context Oversimplification, Dataset Imbalance, Metrics Inadequacies, Ad hoc Testing, Individual Diversity Unawareness, and Homogeneous Team Composition. These span both technical and human/organizational dimensions and signal conditions that may introduce or reinforce bias, contributing to fairness debt.

Conclusion: Bias smells extend the established software smell paradigm into the fairness domain, offering a practical, observable foundation for incorporating fairness considerations into software quality assurance processes.

Abstract: Context: Fairness debt arises from AI development shortcomings that may lead to societal harms. While technical and social debt concern software design decisions and team dynamics, respectively, fairness debt captures the long-term consequences of development decisions that may reinforce bias and inequities in AI-based software systems. Despite growing attention to AI fairness, limited evidence exists on how practitioners recognize potential sources of fairness debt during development. Aim: This study investigates the indicators practitioners recognize as signaling potential sources of fairness debt in AI-based software projects. Method: We conducted an exploratory case study of four AI projects within one organization. Data were collected from 25 professionals through semi-structured interviews and open-ended questionnaires, complemented by observation of internal communication channels and project documentation, and analyzed using iterative qualitative coding, memoing, and constant comparison. Results: We identified six recurring indicators, termed bias smells: Context Oversimplification, Dataset Imbalance, Metrics Inadequacies, Ad hoc Testing, Individual Diversity Unawareness, and Homogeneous Team Composition. These smells span technical and human aspects of software development and signal conditions that may introduce or reinforce bias and contribute to fairness debt. Conclusion: Bias smells extend the software smell paradigm to fairness and provide a foundation for incorporating fairness into software quality assurance through observable indicators.

</details>


### [63] [Enhancing Reliability of Symbolic Execution Tools for Smart Contract Analysis through Rule-Based False Positive Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10265)
*Muhammad Ali Hassan Ahmad,Muhammad Hashim Ali,Muhammad Ali Amer,Muhammad Naiman Jalil,Muhammad Hassan,Affan Rauf*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Mythril, a symbolic execution tool for Ethereum smart contracts, produces many false positives. The authors analyze root causes, devise rule-based heuristics to filter them, and demonstrate significant false-positive reduction without sacrificing true vulnerability detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Smart contract vulnerability detection tools like Mythril suffer from high false-positive rates, wasting developer time and undermining trust. There is a need to both quantify this problem and develop practical mitigation strategies that improve tool reliability without compromising recall.

Method: The authors first empirically demonstrate false-positive prevalence in Mythril's vulnerability reports. They then conduct root-cause analysis of these inaccuracies and design a rule-based filtering approach targeting the most impactful vulnerability categories. The rules are implemented directly within Mythril and evaluated experimentally.

Result: The rule-based approach achieved a significant reduction in false positives while maintaining detection of true vulnerabilities, thereby enhancing Mythril's overall reliability.

Conclusion: Enhancing symbolic execution tools with domain-specific heuristic rules can substantially reduce false-positive rates. Evaluating tools by false-positive rate is as critical as measuring true-positive detection, and rule-based post-processing offers a practical path toward more trustworthy smart contract auditing.

Abstract: A blockchain is a decentralized, secure ledger system that enables transparent and immutable record-keeping, essential for trust and security in digital transactions. Smart contracts are self-executing agreements encoded on a blockchain, enabling different parties to fulfill the terms of the agreement automatically. These contracts trigger corresponding actions when conditions are met, ensuring decentralized and transparent transactions. Writing reliable smart contracts is challenging due to the lack of standardization. To find security vulnerabilities, tools based on various approaches, including symbolic execution, are used. However, these tools often report a large number of false positives, raising concerns about their reliability. The time and effort spent investigating false positives diverts resources from addressing actual vulnerabilities. Therefore, such tools must also be evaluated according to the rate of false positives they exhibit. More importantly, the algorithms and heuristics used by the tools must be enhanced to distinguish between true vulnerabilities and false alarms. In this paper, we first demonstrate the prevalence of false positives in vulnerability reports generated by Mythril, a symbolic execution-based analysis tool for Ethereum smart contracts. We analyze the root causes of these inaccuracies and devise a rule-based approach based on the gained insight to reduce false positives. We implement our rules for the most impactful vulnerabilities in Mythril and assess the effectiveness of our approach. Our results show a significant reduction in false positives without compromising the detection of true vulnerabilities, thus enhancing the tool's reliability.

</details>


### [64] [Comprendia: AI-Augmented Code Comprehension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10290)
*Costain Nachuma,Minhaz F. Zibran*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Comprendia is an Eclipse plugin that unifies interactive dependency graph visualization with LLM-powered code explanation, clone detection, and CVE risk overlays—all grounded in a reproducible, graph-aware callee pruning strategy for auditable prompt generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Program comprehension is challenging due to complex structural dependencies, code duplication, and security vulnerabilities. Existing tools often separate visualization from AI-assisted explanation, lacking traceability between what the developer sees and what the LLM reasons about. Comprendia aims to unify these concerns on a shared graph substrate, ensuring LLM explanations are auditable by grounding them in the same dependency graph the developer navigates.

Method: Comprendia integrates four components on a multi-edge-type dependency graph: (1) interactive graph with search and multiple layouts; (2) Graph-Aware Callee Pruning (GACP), which uses graph distance, inheritance collapse, and edge-type weighting to select relevant callees for constructing reproducible, traceable LLM prompts; (3) a clone-detection overlay that highlights duplication and suggests extract-to-parent refactorings; and (4) a CVE risk overlay using OSV.dev data.

Result: The tool is demonstrated on a Java project with known clones and vulnerabilities, showing that the unified graph substrate effectively supports comprehension while maintaining developer control and producing consistent, auditable LLM explanations across different LLM families.

Conclusion: Comprendia demonstrates that grounding LLM-based code explanation in a visible, navigable dependency graph—via the GACP strategy—yields reproducible, traceable, and developer-controllable program comprehension. The integration of clone and vulnerability overlays further enhances the tool's practical utility within the Eclipse IDE.

Abstract: Comprendia is an Eclipse plugin that integrates structural dependency visualization with LLM-powered code explanation on a shared interactive graph for Java program comprehension. The tool rests on four pillars: (1) a multi-edge-type dependency graph with live search and multiple layouts; (2) LLM explanations grounded in Graph-Aware Callee Pruning (GACP), an auditable strategy that selects relevant callees using the same graph the developer navigates; (3) a clone-detection overlay that highlights duplication and suggests extract-to-parent refactoring opportunities; and (4) a CVE risk overlay powered by OSV.dev. GACP uses graph distance, inheritance collapse, and edge-type weighting to produce prompts that are reproducible across LLM families and traceable to visible graph nodes. We demonstrate Comprendia on a Java project containing known clones and vulnerabilities, showing how the unified graph substrate supports comprehension while keeping the developer in control. Screencast: https://youtu.be/1wlh_RYehzA

</details>


### [65] [Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10450)
*Beichen Huang,Zhenyu Liang,Bowen Zheng,Ran Cheng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Genesis introduces a paradigm where software projects—not agents—are persistent, using recursive worlds and finite-lived agents to achieve long-horizon development. It built a 250k-line Rust-based C compiler in 120+ hours for $44 and reimplemented 100k+ Fortran lines as Rust with up to 6.87x speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex software systems outlast any individual coding agent. Traditional approaches rely on persistent sessions, memories, or managers. The authors propose an alternative: make the software project itself the persistent entity, while agents remain finite-lived, enabling continuous development across agent replacements.

Method: Genesis models software as a persistent recursive world. Each local world is defined by an accepted version and a repository path. Finite-lived agents propose local changes; recursive delegation moves work across paths; only accepted consequences advance the persistent version history. This world-based architecture decouples agent lifespan from project continuity.

Result: Three evaluation scenarios: (1) Formation: built a Rust-based C compiler (~250k tracked lines) from scratch using DeepSeek V4 Flash over 120+ hours, 1,000+ agent episodes, $44 in API costs, passing the complete c-testsuite and most LLVM/Csmith tests. (2) Continuation: using GLM 5.2, compiler development continued seamlessly after repeated agent replacement with full test performance retention. (3) Redevelopment: reimplemented 13 MESA modules (100k+ Fortran lines) as a Rust workspace (~90k Rust lines), achieving median speedups of 1.55–6.87x across six numerical workloads.

Conclusion: Long-horizon software development can be organized around a persistent project rather than persistent agents. The recursive world architecture enables cost-effective, continuous, large-scale code generation and redevelopment across agent turnovers.

Abstract: Complex software systems develop over timescales that exceed the lifespan of any individual coding agent. Most agentic software systems preserve continuity through persistent sessions, memories, managers or shared context. We introduce EvoX Genesis (hereafter, Genesis), which instead makes the software project persistent while allowing local agents to remain finite-lived. Genesis represents software as a persistent recursive world: each local world is situated by an accepted version and a repository path, finite-lived agents propose local changes, recursive delegation moves work across paths, and only accepted consequences advance the persistent version history. We evaluate this organization across formation, continuation and redevelopment. Starting from a repository with no compiler implementation, Genesis used DeepSeek V4 Flash to build a Rust-based C compiler with about 250k tracked lines; the run lasted over 120 hours, archived over 1,000 agent episodes and incurred only US$44 in model-token charges. The compiler passed the complete c-testsuite and most LLVM and Csmith tests. In a separate compiler world generated with GLM 5.2, development continued after repeated agent replacement while retaining full test performance. Genesis also reimplemented 13 MESA modules with over 100k Fortran lines as a Rust workspace with nearly 90k Rust lines; across six numerical workloads, it achieved median speedups of 1.55--6.87x. These results show that long-horizon software development can be organized around a persistent project rather than a persistent agent.

</details>


### [66] [Does the way we write a theory change the program an LLM builds from it? A prospective randomized study of renderer format in LLM theory-to-program translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10314)
*Andre Panossian*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A preregistered randomized experiment tested whether presenting identical theoretical content via structured contracts vs. connected prose changes LLM-generated programs. Across 320 single-shot translations from 5 theories, 2 LLM snapshots, and rigorous randomization inference, both primary hypotheses were NOT_SUPPORTED. Renderer format did not produce the predicted uniform behavioral geometry, establishing a concrete boundary on specification-format effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verbal theories require translation into executable models, but translation forces non-trivial choices about variables, interactions, and interventions. It is unknown whether superficial presentation format (structured contract vs. prose) systematically biases how LLMs operationalize theoretical content into code. Understanding this is critical for reproducible, unbiased theory-to-program translation.

Method: A prospective, preregistered randomized experiment using 16 assignment bits to allocate 32 paired renderer slots between a structured intervention contract and connected prose. Two pinned LLM snapshots generated single-shot programs from five anonymous theoretical accounts in a frozen sparse quadratic language (N=320). A deterministic evaluator measured atomic finite-difference responses (H1) and mixed interaction responses (H2). Two primary endpoints: cross-model matched-distance reduction and closed-set same-account identifiability. Exact randomization inference was used with 27 preregistered support criteria across signed-linear and magnitude-rank pipelines, with a joint support rule requiring both pipelines to pass.

Result: Both H1 and H2 returned NOT_SUPPORTED. Only 19 of 108 criterion evaluations passed (far below threshold). Same-account identifiability AUC ranged 0.469–0.523, against a registered 0.80 threshold. One H2 matched-distance endpoint showed movement in the signed-linear pipeline and survived multiplicity correction, but the magnitude-rank result missed the effect-size floor, failing the joint support rule. Overall, renderer format did not produce uniform, family-invariant, classifiable behavioral geometry.

Conclusion: Specification-format effects in LLM-mediated theory-to-program translation appear bounded; presentation format does not systematically alter the behavioral geometry of generated programs. The study provides a fully auditable randomized experimental framework, datasets, and software for continued investigation of executable formalization.

Abstract: A verbal theory does not run: translating it into an executable model requires choices about variables, interventions, and interactions. We tested whether the presentation of otherwise identical theoretical content systematically changes the programs produced by large language models. In a prospective preregistered randomized experiment, 16 independent assignment bits allocated 32 paired renderer slots between a structured intervention contract and connected prose. Two pinned LLM snapshots translated five anonymous theoretical accounts, yielding 320 preauthorized single-shot programs in a frozen sparse quadratic language. A deterministic evaluator measured atomic finite-difference responses (H1) and mixed interaction responses (H2). Two primary endpoints assessed cross-model matched-distance reduction and closed-set same-account identifiability, with exact randomization inference and 27 preregistered support criteria evaluated across signed-linear and magnitude-rank pipelines. Both H1 and H2 returned the registered verdict NOT_SUPPORTED; only 19 of 108 criterion evaluations passed. Same-account identifiability remained near chance (AUC 0.469-0.523, against a registered 0.80 threshold). One H2 matched-distance endpoint moved and survived multiplicity correction in the signed-linear pipeline, but the corresponding magnitude-rank result missed the registered effect-size floor, so it did not satisfy the joint support rule. Thus renderer format did not produce the uniform, family-invariant, classifiable behavioral geometry predicted in advance. The result places a concrete boundary on specification-format effects in LLM theory-to-program translation and provides a fully auditable randomized design, datasets, and software for studying executable formalization.

</details>


### [67] [Do Personalized Skills Help Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Developer Interaction Histories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10319)
*Shuyan Huang,Kai Du,Andrew Lan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether developer-specific preferences extracted from interaction histories with LLM-powered coding agents can be distilled into reusable "skills" that improve future task performance. Using 206 real-world sessions from 13 developers, the authors find that personalized skills yield only small, inconsistent gains, while generic skills pooled across developers provide the largest and most consistent improvements. Personalization becomes effective mainly when developer preferences appear frequently and have multiple relevant historical examples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As developers increasingly collaborate with LLM-powered coding agents, individual preferences emerge through repeated interactions. Capturing and reusing these preferences could reduce repetitive corrections and enhance collaboration. However, existing work focuses on task-specific skills, leaving open the question of whether developer-specific skills distilled from interaction histories can generalize to future tasks.

Method: The authors propose a framework that (1) generates personalized skills via rule-based bootstrapping and evidence-grounded refinement from interaction traces, and (2) evaluates these skills using a reproducible replay framework with an interactive, trajectory-conditioned LLM-based human developer simulator. The experiment covers 206 real-world developer-agent sessions from 13 developers, comparing personalized skills against no-skill, generic-skill, and other-user-skill baselines.

Result: Personalized skills provide small and inconsistent improvements over the no-skill baseline. In contrast, generic skills pooled across all developers achieve the largest and most consistent gains. Personalized skills only become more effective when developer preferences appear frequently and when histories contain multiple examples relevant to future tasks.

Conclusion: Broadly transferable procedural knowledge (generic skills) proves more robust than developer-specific preference signals. The effectiveness of personalization is contingent on the frequency and relevance of historical preference examples, offering empirical guidance on when developer-specific adaptation is worthwhile.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered agents have rapidly evolved from code-completion tools into solvers of complex software engineering tasks. As developers collaborate with coding agents over time, their preferences emerge through repeated interactions and can be used to adapt agent behavior to better meet individual developers' needs. Capturing and reusing these preferences may reduce repeated corrections and improve developer-agent collaboration. Agent skills provide a lightweight mechanism for transferring experience without modifying model parameters. However, existing work primarily focuses on task-specific skills, and it remains unclear whether developer-specific skills distilled from interaction histories can generalize to future tasks. We propose a framework for extracting reusable developer preferences from interaction traces. It first generates personalized skills through rule-based bootstrapping and evidence-grounded refinement, and then evaluates them using a reproducible replay framework with an interactive, trajectory-conditioned LLM-based human developer simulator. We conduct an experiment on 206 real-world developer-agent sessions from 13 developers and compare personalized skills against no-skill, generic-skill, and other-user-skill baselines. Personalized skills provide small and inconsistent improvements over the no-skill baseline, whereas generic skills pooled across developers achieve the largest and most consistent gains. Further analysis suggests that personalized skills become more effective when developer preferences appear frequently, particularly when their histories contain multiple examples relevant to future tasks. These findings provide empirical insights into when developer-specific personalization is effective and demonstrate that broadly transferable procedural knowledge can be more robust than developer-specific preference signals.

</details>


### [68] [CausalRepair: Bridging the Causality Gap in Large Language Model-Based Automated Program Repair via Dual-Slicing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10613)
*Linhao Wu,Yizhou Chen,Zhen Yang,Pengyu Xue,Dan Hao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CausalRepair is a conversation-driven APR framework that uses a dual-slicing strategy (static + dynamic) to construct minimal causal contexts, enabling LLMs to fix bugs more accurately. It fixes 313 bugs on Defects4J at $0.029 per bug, outperforming SOTA methods like ReinFix and TSAPR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based APR methods suffer from a causality gap: test contexts are noisy/incomplete, and source contexts from static analysis contain irrelevant, unexecuted code. This misleads LLMs from identifying the true root cause of failures.

Method: CausalRepair uses a dual-slicing strategy: (1) context-aware static slicing to purify test semantics, and (2) execution-trace-based dynamic slicing to capture precise runtime dependencies in source code. Together, these construct compact, causally relevant contexts that guide iterative, conversation-driven repair with LLMs.

Result: CausalRepair correctly fixes 313 bugs on Defects4J (V1.2, V2.0) and Defects4J-Trans using DeepSeek-V3, outperforming SOTA approaches (ReinFix, TSAPR). Average repair cost is $0.029 per bug.

Conclusion: Minimal causal context, constructed via combined static and dynamic slicing, significantly improves LLM-based APR by bridging the causality gap, leading to higher fix rates at lower cost.

Abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) has recently benefited from Large Language Models (LLMs), yet their effectiveness heavily depends on repair context. Existing LLM-based APR methods suffer from a causality gap: test contexts can be noisy or incomplete, while source contexts derived from static analysis often contain irrelevant and unexecuted code, misleading LLMs from identifying the true root cause. To address this issue, we propose CausalRepair, a conversation-driven APR framework based on minimal causal context, i.e., the essential dependencies required to explain a failure. CausalRepair employs a dual-slicing strategy: context-aware static slicing purifies test semantics, while execution-trace-based dynamic slicing captures precise runtime dependencies in source code. Together, they construct compact, causally relevant contexts to guide iterative repair. We evaluate CausalRepair on Defects4J V1.2, V2.0, and Defects4J-Trans using DeepSeek-V3. CausalRepair correctly fixes 313 bugs on Defects4J, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches such as ReinFix and TSAPR, while reducing the average repair cost to $0.029 per bug.

</details>


### [69] [A Study of Cursorrules Files in GitHub Open Source Projects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10622)
*Shuang Sun,Jafar Akhoundali,Arina Kudriavtseva,Sengim Karayalcin,Olga Gadyatskaya*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study of 12,110 .cursorrules prompt files from 11,427 GitHub repositories reveals rapid adoption since mid-2024, concentrated in small, low-activity, single-maintainer projects. Content analysis (65-code codebook) shows emphasis on code quality, engineering practices, and project structure, with security underrepresented. Thematic continuity exists between legacy .cursorrules and current .mdc files.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on prompt engineering has focused almost exclusively on dynamic conversational prompts, while static configuration-like prompt files — increasingly used in modern AI-assisted programming tools — remain understudied. Understanding how developers use and maintain these files is essential as AI-assisted coding becomes mainstream.

Method: A mixed-methods empirical study: (1) quantitative analysis of 12,110 .cursorrules files from 11,427 GitHub repositories to characterize distribution, evolution, and maintenance patterns; (2) qualitative analysis of a random sample of 65 prompt files to develop a 65-code codebook capturing developer intent (programming intent, project context, engineering practices, security); and (3) comparison between legacy .cursorrules and current .mdc file formats to assess thematic continuity.

Result: .cursorrules files emerged rapidly from mid-2024, with adoption concentrated in small-scale, low-activity, single-maintainer repositories (suggesting toy/personal projects rather than professional use). Content is dominated by code quality, engineering practices, project structure/configuration, and maintainability guidance; security-related content is notably less frequent. Strong thematic continuity exists between legacy .cursorrules and current .mdc standard files.

Conclusion: Configuration prompt files represent a growing but immature practice in AI-assisted programming, currently skewed toward hobbyist use. The underrepresentation of security guidance is a concern. The thematic continuity between old and new formats suggests that insights from .cursorrules generalize to the evolving .mdc ecosystem, providing a foundation for future research and tool improvement.

Abstract: Prompts are the primary mechanism for communicating with AI agents, and they directly influence the quality and reliability of AI-generated code. As AI-assisted programming becomes widely adopted, modern tools increasingly combine dynamic conversational prompts with static configuration-like prompt files. Despite the growing focus on prompt engineering, prior research has primarily focused on conversational prompts, while prompt files remain understudied.
  To address this gap, we conduct an empirical study of configuration prompt files in Cursor, a widely used AI-assisted code editor. We collect and analyze over 12,110 .cursorrules files from 11,427 GitHub repositories to characterize their distribution, evolution, and maintenance. Complementing this, we perform qualitative analysis on a random sample of 65 prompt files and develop a 65-code codebook capturing how developers express programming intent, project context, engineering practices, and security considerations.
  Our results show that .cursorrules files emerged rapidly from mid-2024. Their adoption is concentrated in small-scale, low-activity, single-maintainer repositories, suggesting toy projects rather than professional development. The content of prompt files is dominated by guidance on code quality and engineering practices, project structure and configuration, and maintainability, while security-related content appears less frequently. Our analysis shows that there is a continuity of themes and topics between the now-legacy .cursorrules files and the current standard .mdc files.

</details>


### [70] [LLM Ensemble Fault Classification for Automotive HiL Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10710)
*Hamza Ouarrad,Mohammad Abboush,Andreas Rausch*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A multi-LLM ensemble framework using compact evidence representations achieves robust, calibrated, and interpretable sensor-level fault classification for automotive HiL validation, with a Top-3 confidence-weighted voting ensemble reaching 0.917 Top-1 accuracy and 0.902 MCC across diverse driving scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automotive Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) validation produces large multivariate test recordings that are difficult to analyze due to reliance on manual review, limitations of rule-based methods, and the need for explainable diagnostics. While ML/DL approaches have advanced fault diagnosis, they suffer from requiring large labeled datasets, poor generalization across operating conditions, and limited interpretability of predictions.

Method: The authors propose an explainable multi-LLM ensemble framework that: (1) constructs compact evidence representations from fault-injection recordings, (2) combines outputs from multiple heterogeneous LLMs via confidence-weighted voting to enhance diagnostic robustness and calibration, and (3) is evaluated on gasoline-engine and electric-vehicle HiL systems across three driving settings and ten single-fault classes. Individual models tested include Mistral Small 24B, Qwen2.5 32B, and Phi-4 14B.

Result: Mistral Small 24B achieves the best single-model performance (0.903 Top-1 accuracy, 0.887 MCC, 0.102 Brier score). The Top-3 ensemble (Mistral Small 24B, Qwen2.5 32B, Phi-4 14B) with confidence-weighted voting improves scenario-averaged results to 0.917 Top-1 accuracy, 0.913 macro F1, and 0.902 MCC, with best calibration among tested strategies. A Top-5 ensemble yields no further improvement, highlighting that model complementarity matters more than ensemble size.

Conclusion: Coordinated multi-LLM reasoning with compact evidence representations provides a viable, robust, calibrated, and engineer-interpretable solution for fault classification in automotive HiL validation, outperforming single-model approaches while maintaining explainability.

Abstract: Automotive HiL validation generates large multivariate test recordings whose analysis remains challenging due to manual review effort, rule-based limitations, and the need for explainable diagnostic decisions. Recent machine-learning and deep-learning approaches have improved fault diagnosis, but they often require large labelled datasets, generalise poorly across operating conditions, and provide limited insight into their predictions. This paper proposes an explainable multi-LLM ensemble framework for sensor-level fault classification in automotive validation. The framework uses compact evidence representations of fault-injection recordings and combines the outputs of heterogeneous large language models to improve diagnostic robustness, ranking quality, confidence reliability, and interpretability. The approach is evaluated on gasoline-engine and electric-vehicle HiL systems across three driving settings and ten single-fault classes. Among the individual models, Mistral Small~24B provides the strongest overall single-model trade-off, achieving 0.903 Top-1 accuracy, 0.887 MCC, and the lowest Brier score of 0.102. The final Top-3 ensemble combines Mistral Small~24B, Qwen2.5~32B, and Phi-4~14B using confidence-weighted voting, improving the scenario-averaged results to 0.917 Top-1 accuracy, 0.913 macro F1, and 0.902 MCC, while also providing the best calibration among the tested ensemble strategies. A Top-5 ensemble does not improve over the Top-3 configuration, indicating that model complementarity is more important than ensemble size. The results show that coordinated multi-LLM reasoning can support robust, calibrated, and engineer-interpretable fault classification for automotive HiL validation.

</details>


### [71] [Conflict Extraction in Probabilistic Datalog Analyses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10755)
*Siyu Chen,Chungha Sung,Xuyang Li,Jingbo Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Probabilistic Datalog analyses can produce mutually inconsistent alarms that cannot co-occur, wasting developer effort. The authors formalize these as minimal unsatisfiable subsets (MUSes) and present PPProbe, a specialized conflict extractor that leverages Datalog derivation graph structure for efficient enumeration, achieving 2.5–24× higher throughput than state-of-the-art MUS enumerators and filtering ~47.7% of inconsistent alarms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Probabilistic extensions of Datalog are used for ranking alarms in static analyses (e.g., pointer analysis, data race detection, side-channel analysis), but marginal probability ranking produces individually plausible yet jointly inconsistent alarms. Developers waste effort investigating alarm combinations that cannot co-occur in any possible world. No existing solution efficiently addresses inconsistency extraction in this domain.

Method: The authors formalize inconsistencies as minimal unsatisfiable subsets (MUSes) and introduce PPProbe, a conflict extractor purpose-built for probabilistic Datalog analyses. PPProbe exploits the structure of Datalog derivation graphs to guide search toward likely conflicts and employs bottom-up UNSAT inference to prune the search space, rather than aiming to improve general-purpose MUS enumeration.

Result: Evaluated on 70 benchmarks across power side-channel analysis, data race detection, semantic diffing, and Bayesian-network inference. PPProbe achieves 2.5× to 24× higher throughput than state-of-the-art MUS enumerators. The identified conflicts provide a conservative estimate of false-positive reduction, filtering out an average of 47.7% of mutually inconsistent alarms.

Conclusion: Domain-specific conflict extraction that exploits derivation graph structure significantly outperforms general-purpose MUS enumeration for probabilistic Datalog analyses, enabling practical filtering of nearly half of all mutually inconsistent alarms.

Abstract: Probabilistic extensions of Datalog enable static analyses such as pointer analysis, data race detection, and side-channel analysis to rank alarms by likelihood, but this added expressiveness also introduces a new challenge absent from deterministic analyses: the final output may contain alarms that are individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent, because marginal probabilities do not guarantee joint satisfiability. As a result, developers may spend effort investigating combinations of alarms that can never co-occur in any possible world. We address this problem by formalizing such inconsistencies as minimal unsatisfiable subsets (MUSes) and introducing PPProbe, a conflict extractor specialized for probabilistic Datalog analyses. Rather than improving MUS enumeration in general, PPProbe exploits the structure of Datalog derivation graphs to guide the search toward likely conflicts and prune the search space through bottom-up UNSAT inference. We evaluate PPProbe on 70 benchmarks from power side-channel analysis, data race detection, semantic diffing, and Bayesian-network inference. The results show that PPProbe achieves 2.5 to 24 times higher throughput than state-of-the-art MUS enumerators, and that the conflicts it identifies yield a conservative estimate of false-positive reduction, filtering out an average of 47.7% of mutually inconsistent alarms.

</details>


### [72] [Extending Triple Graph Grammars to Formalize Complex View Definitions on Families of Models - Long Version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10785)
*Lars König,Jens Kosiol*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper provides a formal semantics for the NeoJoin view definition language using triple graph grammars (TGGs), introduces a skip semantics for TGG rules to handle overlapping queries, and enables automated, formally-guaranteed incremental synchronization between models and views.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: View-based development for complex systems-of-systems requires a view definition language that is both approachable/versatile for diverse developers and formally precise for controlled integration of work across views. Existing approaches lacked a formal foundation enabling automated synchronization with high behavioral guarantees.

Method: The authors equip the NeoJoin view definition language with a formal semantics grounded in triple graph grammars (TGGs). They identify and address a gap—handling overlapping queries—by introducing a novel "skip semantics" for TGG rules, allowing certain prescribed actions to be skipped depending on application context.

Result: The formal TGG-based semantics paves the way for automated, incremental synchronization procedures between models and views with high formal guarantees. The work also serves as a case study demonstrating TGG expressivity and usability, and the skip semantics extension addresses the previously unsupported translation of overlapping queries.

Conclusion: Equipping NeoJoin with TGG-based formal semantics, augmented with skip semantics, successfully bridges the gap between usability and formal rigor in view definition languages, enabling reliable synchronization in complex system-of-systems development.

Abstract: View-based development is an important technique to manage complexity and facilitate cooperation in the development of modern and complex systems of systems. This approach places high demands on view definition languages used in the development process. First, such a language needs to be approachable and extremely versatile so that developers from diverse backgrounds are able to use it and can define views for a diverse set of different tasks. Yet, the language also needs to have a precise and formal semantics so that it is possible to integrate the work performed on various views in a controlled manner to obtain a coherent overall system. In this paper, we continue previous work of equipping the NeoJoin view definition language with a formal semantics that is based on triple graph grammars (TGGs). This paves the way for obtaining automated and incremental synchronization procedures between models and views that come with high formal guarantees for their behavior. Simultaneously, our work serves as a further case study of the expressivity and usability of TGGs. We identify one gap, namely convenient support for the translation of overlapping queries from the view definition language, and tackle that gap by introducing a skip semantics for TGG rules, i.e., allowing to skip certain actions a rule prescribes, depending on the application context.

</details>


### [73] [From Pattern Detection to Composition Analysis in Quantum Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10882)
*Neilson Carlos Leite Ramalho,Erico Augusto da Silva,Anthony Accioly,Higor Amario de Souza,Marcos Lordello Chaim*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents an extended tool for mining quantum software patterns from open-source code, evaluates its accuracy with a vocabulary expansion step (boosting micro-F1 from 0.449 to 0.712), analyzes pattern composition via call graphs stored in a graph database, and releases an open-source pipeline (qpa) with a knowledge base mapping 286 framework components to 61 patterns, maintained by an LLM ensemble.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is little empirical evidence on how quantum software patterns are adopted in practice. The authors aim to quantitatively assess pattern usage, understand how pattern implementations are assembled and co-occur within frameworks, and provide reproducible infrastructure for studying quantum pattern adoption and evolution.

Method: The authors extend a prior pattern-mining tool with two additional matching channels and a vocabulary expansion step. They evaluate accuracy on Qrisp (an unseen framework). They construct composition graphs from calls among high-level framework components associated with patterns and store them in a graph database. These graphs are analyzed to examine pattern assembly, co-occurrence, and direct-vs-indirect usage. They release qpa, a mining pipeline, along with a knowledge base mapping 286 components across five sources to a 61-pattern catalog, maintained by an LLM ensemble classifier.

Result: The vocabulary expansion step improves micro-F1 from 0.449 to 0.712 on Qrisp. All 23 patterns from the prior study occur in practice across 80 projects. Composition graph analysis reveals how patterns are assembled, why they co-occur, and the proportion of detections from direct developer calls versus internal framework calls. The released dataset and knowledge base support reproducible research.

Conclusion: The extended tool with vocabulary expansion significantly improves pattern detection accuracy. Composition graphs stored in a graph database provide valuable insights into pattern usage and assembly. The open-source qpa pipeline, knowledge base, and dataset enable further reproducible studies on quantum software pattern adoption and evolution.

Abstract: Quantum software patterns provide high-level abstractions for building quantum programs, but there is still little empirical evidence on how they are adopted in practice. In prior work, we extended an existing quantum-pattern atlas into a 61-pattern catalog, created a knowledge base that links framework components to those patterns, and built a tool that mines pattern implementations from open-source code. We applied this tool on 80 projects and find that all 23 patterns occur in practice. In this work, we extend the tool with two additional matching channels and a vocabulary expansion step, and execute a quantitative evaluation of its accuracy on Qrisp, a framework not present in the knowledge base, reaching a micro-F1 of 0.712 against 0.449 without the expansion step. We then construct composition graphs that record calls among the high-level framework components associated with patterns and store them in a graph database. We use these graphs to examine how pattern implementations are assembled inside each framework, why patterns co-occur, and how much of a pattern's detection count comes from components called directly by developers rather than introduced through internal framework calls. We release qpa, an open-source mining pipeline, together with the knowledge base, which maps 286 framework components across five sources to the pattern catalog, maintained with the support of an LLM ensemble that classifies newly extracted components, and the resulting pattern usage dataset, to support reproducible studies on the adoption and evolution of quantum patterns.

</details>


### [74] [GitSkills: A Dataset of Agent Skills on GitHub](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10906)
*Giuseppe Destefanis,Daniel Graziotin,Matteo Vaccargiu,Marco Ortu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: GitSkills is a large-scale dataset of 3.8M SKILL.md files from 282K GitHub repositories, designed to empirically study how developers write, reuse, and maintain agent skills — natural-language instruction files for LLM agents that lack traditional software engineering safeguards like compilers or package managers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent skills (SKILL.md files) have proliferated into the millions on GitHub, yet they fundamentally differ from traditional software artifacts: they are natural-language-based, probabilistically selected at runtime, and lack compilers, type checkers, registries, or package managers. No existing dataset captures this phenomenon, leaving open empirical questions about their adoption, reuse, structure, and maintenance.

Method: The authors collected 3,797,117 SKILL.md files from 282,200 public GitHub repositories in July 2026. They retained every file occurrence with repository, path, and content hash; grouped identical files into 1,877,981 distinct contents; and enriched one representative per group with full text, parsed front matter, folder contents, repository metadata, and (for a subset) commit history. The entire dataset is distributed as a single self-contained SQLite file.

Result: The resulting dataset, GitSkills, comprises 3.8M file occurrences deduplicated to 1.88M distinct contents, each enriched with multi-dimensional metadata. It provides the first large-scale empirical foundation for studying agent-skill adoption, reuse, structure, authorship, maintenance, and security.

Conclusion: GitSkills fills a critical gap in software engineering research by providing infrastructure to study a novel, rapidly growing class of software artifacts that operate outside traditional engineering constraints. The SQLite distribution format facilitates broad accessibility for future empirical studies.

Abstract: An agent skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file with instructions for a language-model agent, optionally accompanied by scripts and reference files. The agent loads the skill when it judges that a task matches the skill description. Anthropic introduced the format in October 2025 as an open specification. Nine months later, we find that skill files in the millions sit in public GitHub repositories. Skills are unlike the artifacts the SE research community usually mines: they are written mainly in natural language, a model selects them probabilistically at run time, and no compiler or type checker verifies the selection. They also have no central registry or package manager, so they spread by copying folders between repositories. How developers write, reuse, and maintain skills is therefore an empirical question, and no existing dataset records this population. We present GitSkills, a dataset of 3,797,117 SKILL.md files collected from 282,200 public repositories in July 2026. The dataset retains every file occurrence with its repository, path, and content hash. It groups identical files into 1,877,981 distinct contents and enriches one representative per group with the full text, parsed front matter, folder contents, repository metadata, and, for a subset, the commit history of the file. A single self- contained SQLite file supports research on the adoption, reuse, structure, authorship, maintenance, and security of agent skills.

</details>


### [75] [Understanding the Architecture of Coding Agents: An Exploratory Study Using a Research Prototype](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10934)
*Marco Tulio Valente*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper documents the internal architecture of coding agents, presents Ark (a minimal open-source coding agent for research/education), introduces ArkBench (a 10-task benchmark), and compares Ark's architecture with state-of-the-art agents using a formal taxonomy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the rapid emergence of coding agents as the primary interface for AI-assisted software development, no systematic architectural description of them exists—unlike compilers or operating systems. This gap hinders teaching, research, and experimentation.

Method: The authors document the main architectural components of coding agents (responsibilities, interactions, execution flow); build Ark, a minimal open-source coding agent preserving essential mechanisms while prioritizing simplicity; create ArkBench, a lightweight benchmark of 10 software maintenance/evolution tasks; and evaluate Ark using gpt-5.4-mini, followed by a comparative architectural analysis against state-of-the-art agents using a proposed taxonomy.

Result: Ark successfully solved 8 out of 10 ArkBench tasks with modest token consumption when using gpt-5.4-mini. The architectural comparison situates Ark relative to state-of-the-art coding agents via the taxonomy.

Conclusion: Ark and ArkBench offer a practical foundation for teaching, research, and experimentation on coding agents, filling the architectural description gap and enabling systematic study of this emerging class of AI systems.

Abstract: Coding agents have rapidly emerged as the primary interface for AI-assisted software development. However, despite their growing adoption, relatively little is known about their internal architecture, and no systematic architectural description comparable to those available for compilers or operating systems currently exists. This paper addresses this gap by documenting the main architectural components of coding agents, explaining their responsibilities, interactions, and execution flow. To support this effort, we also present Ark (Agent Research Kit), a minimal open-source coding agent designed for research and education that preserves the essential architectural mechanisms of modern coding agents while emphasizing simplicity and clarity. We also introduce ArkBench, a lightweight benchmark comprising ten representative software maintenance and evolution tasks. Using gpt-5.4-mini, Ark successfully solved 8 of the 10 tasks while requiring modest token consumption. Finally, we compare the architecture of Ark with those of state-of-the-art coding agents using a recently proposed architectural taxonomy. We hope that both Ark and ArkBench provide a practical foundation for teaching, research, and experimentation on coding agents.

</details>


### [76] [Agentic Configuration Management (ACM): A Reference Configuration Model for Governed Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11166)
*Audrey Quessada-Vial*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Proposes Agentic Configuration Management (ACM), a framework-agnostic governance model that normalizes heterogeneous agentic systems into a canonical Configuration Graph, enabling versioning, impact analysis, auditability, and interoperability across LangGraph, CrewAI, and OpenAI Agents SDK.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMOps/AgentOps platforms lack a unified configuration-governance model for heterogeneous agentic systems composed of diverse agents, prompts, tools, models, and workflows that evolve across frameworks and runtimes. This gap hinders reproducibility, auditability, and interoperability.

Method: ACM introduces typed Agentic Configuration Items with immutable revisions/baselines, configuration-runtime separation, lifecycle semantics, dependency-aware impact propagation, and runtime provenance. Native configurations are semantically projected into a canonical Configuration Graph. Impact semantics are formalized as monotone propagation over a finite lattice, proving convergence, termination, and uniqueness of the least fixed point. A Python reference implementation with adapters for LangGraph, CrewAI, and OpenAI Agents SDK validates the approach.

Result: Across 27 governance scenarios and 9 quantitative impact-propagation cases, all three frameworks yielded governance-equivalent ACM representations and reproducible governance outcomes after projection. The formal semantics guarantee convergence and termination of impact propagation.

Conclusion: Common governance semantics can support reproducibility, auditability, dependency analysis, and interoperability across heterogeneous agentic execution abstractions, as demonstrated within the evaluated scope of LangGraph, CrewAI, and OpenAI Agents SDK.

Abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly composed of heterogeneous agents, prompts, tools, models, skills, composite subsystems, policies, and execution workflows whose configurations evolve across frameworks and runtime environments. Existing LLMOps and AgentOps platforms support orchestration and observability but do not provide a common configuration-governance model for representing and governing these systems as coherent, versioned configurations.
  This paper introduces Agentic Configuration Management (ACM), a framework-independent governance and configuration reference model for heterogeneous agentic systems. ACM combines typed and independently versioned Agentic Configuration Items, immutable revisions and baselines, explicit configuration-runtime separation, lifecycle and assurance semantics, dependency-aware impact propagation, and runtime provenance. Heterogeneous native configurations are normalized through semantic projection into a canonical Configuration Graph on which common governance semantics operate.
  We provide a Python reference implementation with adapters for LangGraph, CrewAI, and the OpenAI Agents SDK. The evaluation combines 27 governance scenarios with nine quantitative impact-propagation cases. For the evaluated configurations, the three frameworks yield governance-equivalent ACM representations and reproducible governance outcomes after projection. The impact semantics are formalized as monotone propagation over a finite lattice, establishing convergence, termination, and uniqueness of the least fixed point above the initial impact valuation. These results provide evidence that common governance semantics can support reproducibility, auditability, dependency analysis, and interoperability across heterogeneous agentic execution abstractions within the evaluated scope.

</details>
