### [77] [World-First SEM-based Recovery of Crash EDR Data from the EEPROM of a Severely Damaged SRS Module Using CrashScan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10152)
*Sergei Skorobogatov,Peter Vertal*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A novel, affordable method for recovering data from physically damaged automotive SRS (airbag) modules is presented. Despite catastrophic electrical damage (temperatures exceeding 3000°C) that created visible holes in chip packages and partially vaporized silicon substrates, all EEPROM data was recovered with 100% success. The recovered data enabled full EDR extraction and accident reconstruction using standard tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior to this work, no feasible or affordable solution existed for extracting data from SRS modules whose memory chips suffered permanent mechanical, electrical, or fire damage during accidents. This creates a critical gap in forensic accident investigation.

Method: The authors developed innovative, proprietary sample preparation and imaging techniques to access and read data from a physically damaged Flash EEPROM chip in an SRS module. A donor unit was then used to host the recovered data, enabling standard bench-top EDR extraction via Collision Sciences CrashScan. Failure analysis (microscopy) was also performed to characterize the damage mechanism.

Result: 100% data recovery success was achieved from a real SRS module involved in a severe accident, despite both the processor and Flash EEPROM chip being electrically damaged with visible package holes. The EEPROM array, located only a few hundred micrometers from the vaporized area, retained all bits. Full EDR report and accident reconstruction were completed.

Conclusion: The approach is resilient and practical for recovering data from severely damaged chips. It has broad forensic applicability beyond automotive, extending to medical, aviation, and aerospace industries where data recovery from catastrophically damaged memory is required.

Abstract: This paper introduces fully working and affordable approach to data recovery from automotive SRS (airbag control) module after permanent failure of its data storage memory chip. All essential information was successfully extracted with 100% success rate from a real SRS module after severe accident which resulted in both its Processor and Flash EEPROM chip electrically damaged with visible holes in their packages. Further investigation revealed that the damage was likely caused by overvoltage and subsequent high-current-flow through silicon die of chips. This not only caused some internal metal wires to melt and evaporate but also caused partial evaporation of silicon substrate and the created cavity was filled with melted gold from a bonding wire. This reveals the nature of the failure with local temperatures exceeding 3000°C. Despite to the fact that the on-chip EEPROM array was only a few hundred micrometers away from the damaged area, it did not lose any single bit of information. This proved the approach to be resilient for successful data recovery from severely damaged devices in the future.
  With the donor unit containing the recovered data, standard bench-top EDR extraction was performed using Collision Sciences CrashScan, yielding a full EDR report. The forensic significance of the recovered data, the technical novelty of the methodology, and the complete accident reconstruction are presented and discussed.
  Until now, if because of an accident the memory chip was damaged, there was no feasible or affordable solution for full data extraction or recovery. With the use of innovative and proprietary sample preparation and imaging techniques, it became possible to extract and verify all the data stored inside chips after permanent mechanical, electrical or fire damage. This could help not only automotive but also medical, aviation and aerospace industries.

</details>


### [78] [MarkNull: Model-Agnostic Watermark Removal in AI-Generated Images via On-Manifold Latent Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10166)
*Jie Cao,Qi Li,Zelin Zhang,Xiaodong Wu,Lingshuang Liu,Xiangman Li,Jianbing Ni*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MarkNull is a model-agnostic watermark removal attack that decorrelates latent representations from embedded watermarks using a Noise-Latent Alignment Score (NLAS), achieving near-random bit accuracy (53.14%) without visual degradation, and includes an amortized variant (MarkNull-A) for fast, single-pass inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing watermark removal attacks are either model-specific or degrade image quality severely. There is a need for a realistic, model-agnostic attack that can robustly remove watermarks while preserving semantic fidelity, to expose vulnerabilities in current watermarking paradigms.

Method: The authors observe that watermarked images exhibit statistical dependency between latent representations and embedded initial noise. They introduce the Noise-Latent Alignment Score (NLAS) to quantify this dependency, then formulate an optimization that decorrelates the latent from the watermark. MarkNull-A distills this into a single forward pass for amortized, optimization-free removal.

Result: MarkNull reduces average bit accuracy to 53.14% (near 50% random guessing) across post-hoc, fine-tuning-based, and initial-noise-based watermarking schemes without perceptual degradation. It compromises Google's SynthID-Image, transfers to video watermarking, and MarkNull-A achieves 0.50 s/image with modest overhead.

Conclusion: Model-agnostic latent-space attacks pose a serious threat to current watermarking methods. An attack detection mechanism is proposed as a defense, underscoring the need for watermark designs resilient to such manipulation.

Abstract: Digital watermarking has emerged as a critical technique for provenance and copyright attribution in AI-generated imagery, yet its robustness against realistic, model-agnostic removal attacks remains poorly explored. Existing attacks either succeed only against specific generative models or achieve removal at the cost of severe visual degradation. In this paper, we propose MarkNull, a model-agnostic watermark removal attack via on-manifold latent manipulation. MarkNull is grounded in a key observation: watermarked images exhibit a strong statistical dependency between the generated latent representation and the embedded initial noise. To quantify this dependency, we introduce the Noise-Latent Alignment Score (NLAS) and formulate an optimization objective that selectively decorrelates the latent representation from the embedded watermark while preserving semantic fidelity. Extensive evaluations across different categories of watermarking paradigms, including post-hoc, fine-tuning-based, and initial-noise-based schemes, demonstrate that MarkNull reduces average bit accuracy to 53.14%, approaching random-guessing (50%), without perceptible image degradation. To further improve scalability, we propose MarkNull-A, an amortized, optimization-free variant that distills the attack into a single forward pass, achieving 0.50 s/image with modest computational overhead. Notably, our attacks successfully compromise Google's SynthID-Image system while preserving high visual quality and transfer effectively to video watermarking. Finally, we present an attack detection mechanism as a defensive counterpart to MarkNull and MarkNull-A, highlighting the necessity of developing watermark designs resilient to model-agnostic latent-space attacks.

</details>


### [79] [Withholding the Completing Chunk: Deterministic Pair-Completion Guardrails for Streaming LLM Output](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10279)
*Christopher M. Frost*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper addresses the streaming language model output moderation problem by proposing a deterministic mechanism that withholds text chunks only when a pair of lexical predicates are both satisfied, providing exact release-boundary control as a backstop (not replacement) for semantic moderation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Streaming LLM output creates a dilemma: complete-response moderation is too late (toxic text already escaped), while repeated partial-text classification is expensive and semantically unstable. The authors seek a lightweight, deterministic, and exact alternative for narrow safety policies.

Method: The authors construct a narrow deterministic guard where each danger signature is a conjunction of two lexical predicates. The guard scans the accumulated prefix before every chunk release and withholds only the first chunk that makes both predicates observable (pair completion). They evaluate across four signature families, eight chunk sizes, and 32 mechanism trials, with comparisons including full-prefix scanning, complete buffering, windowed scanning (512-char), chunk-local scanning, and a calibrated Llama Guard 3 1B baseline. Human-derived safe responses and jury-labelled unsafe responses are used for safety coverage testing.

Result: The pair-completion mechanism matched the buffered scanner in all 32 trials, correctly withholding every pair-completing chunk. Full-prefix scanning and complete buffering detected all 128 configured pairs; a 512-character window detected 96/128; chunk-local scanning detected only 38/128. Fixed lexical pairs flagged 0/338 safe responses and 0/394 unsafe responses, confirming narrow coverage. Llama Guard 3 1B classified 310/338 safe as safe and 202/394 unsafe as unsafe. Repeated-prefix scanner latency on 16,384-character responses ranged from 13.261 ms to 829.640 ms depending on chunk size.

Conclusion: Pair-completion offers an exact, low-latency release-boundary backstop for small fixed policies but is not a substitute for semantic moderation, as confirmed by its zero detection on real unsafe content versus Llama Guard's meaningful coverage.

Abstract: Streaming language-model output creates a release-timing problem: complete-response moderation acts after streamed text has escaped, whereas repeated semantic classification of partial text can be costly and unstable. We study a narrow deterministic construction in which each committed danger signature is the conjunction of two lexical predicates. The guard scans the accumulated prefix before every release and withholds the first chunk that makes both predicates observable. Across four signature families, eight chunk sizes, and 32 mechanism trials, streaming decisions matched the buffered scanner and withheld every pair-completing chunk; eight single-predicate controls passed. In a separate 512-trial strategy comparison, full-prefix scanning and complete buffering detected all configured pairs, a 512-character window detected 96/128, and chunk-local scanning detected 38/128. Fixed pairs flagged 0/338 human-derived safe responses and detected 0/394 jury-labelled unsafe responses, confirming narrow rather than general harm coverage. A calibrated official Llama Guard 3 1B baseline classified 310/338 safe responses as safe and 202/394 unsafe responses as unsafe. Repeated-prefix scanner time on 16,384-character responses ranged from 13.261 ms to 829.640 ms across tested chunk sizes. Pair completion is therefore an exact release-boundary backstop for a small fixed policy, not a substitute for semantic moderation.

</details>


### [80] [From Prompt Injection to Web Exploitation: Revisiting Classic Vulnerabilities in LLM-Integrated Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10281)
*Spiros Tsigkopoulos,Christoforos Ntantogian*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper systematizes a new class of attacks called LLM-mediated web attacks, where attacker-controlled input passes through an LLM before reaching traditional web sinks (SQL, XSS, SSTI, etc.). The LLM acts as a mediation layer or confused deputy rather than introducing vulnerabilities itself. A case study (TicketOracle) evaluates LLM2SSRF across seven LLMs, revealing model-dependent susceptibility, and the authors propose layered mitigations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly embedded in web applications as chatbots, tool-calling pipelines, and agents, where user input can influence backend actions (database queries, HTTP requests, file operations, API calls). Despite growing adoption, the security implications of LLMs as intermediaries between user input and traditional web-application sinks remain under-systematized, motivating a structured analysis of this emergent attack surface.

Method: The authors introduce and taxonomize eight representative LLM2X attack variants (LLM2SQLi, LLM2XSS, LLM2SSTI, LLM2CommandInjection, LLM2IDOR, LLM2CSRF, LLM2XXE, LLM2SSRF), mapping how attacker input traverses the LLM mediation layer to traditional sinks. They implement TicketOracle, a Flask-based LLM-integrated web application, to experimentally evaluate LLM2SSRF across five attack scenarios and seven LLMs, measuring susceptibility variation.

Result: The LLM generally does not create the underlying vulnerability; it serves as a mediation layer or, in tool-enabled settings, a confused deputy that relays attacker influence into trusted downstream components. Experimental results show substantial variation in LLM2SSRF susceptibility across the seven tested models, indicating that exploitation depends on both insecure application architecture and model-specific behavioral traits.

Conclusion: LLM-mediated web attacks represent a distinct and practically relevant threat class requiring defense-in-depth. The paper proposes mitigation strategies spanning four layers: prompt-level (e.g., input/output sanitization instructions), model-level (e.g., fine-tuning, guardrails), application-level (e.g., least-privilege tool design, output validation), and network-level (e.g., egress filtering).

Abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly integrated into web applications through chatbots, tool-calling pipelines, and agentic workflows. In these systems, user input may influence not only generated text, but also backend actions such as database queries, HTTP requests, file operations, template rendering, or API calls. This paper introduces LLM-mediated web attacks, a class of attacks in which attacker-controlled input is transformed by an LLM-integrated application and then reaches traditional web-application sinks. We systematize this attack surface through representative LLM2X variants, including LLM2SQLi, LLM2XSS, LLM2SSTI, LLM2CommandInjection, LLM2IDOR, LLM2CSRF, LLM2XXE, and LLM2SSRF. Our analysis shows that the LLM usually does not create the underlying vulnerability itself; rather, it acts as a mediation layer, and in some tool-enabled settings as a confused deputy, carrying attacker influence into components that trust model-generated or model-influenced content. As an experimental case study, we implement TicketOracle, a Flask-based LLM-integrated web application for evaluating LLM2SSRF across five attack scenarios and seven LLMs. Our results show substantial variation in susceptibility across models, suggesting that exploitation depends both on insecure application architecture and model-specific behavior. We conclude with mitigation strategies across the prompt, model, application, and network layers.

</details>


### [81] [Beyond Detection Accuracy: Measuring Explanation Cost, Stability, and Utility for Resource-Aware IoT Intrusion Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10349)
*Abdurrahman Tolay*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The study jointly evaluates predictive accuracy, explanation cost, local stability, and selective explanation for IoT intrusion detection, finding that XGBoost offers the best overall predictive profile and lowest TreeSHAP cost, while Random Forest provides superior explanation stability and the lowest false-positive rate. Selective explanation can yield 15–32% compute savings depending on coverage thresholds and class prevalence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior machine-learning intrusion-detection research treats explanation generation as a computationally free post-processing step, ignoring the real-world operational trade-offs between predictive effectiveness, explanation cost, local explanation stability, and selective invocation — particularly in resource-constrained IoT environments.

Method: A leakage-safe CICIoT2023 corpus was constructed using exact 39-feature hashing, non-finite-value handling, exact-feature deduplication, conservative label-collision removal, and deterministic hash-level partitioning. Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated on both natural and balanced test distributions. TreeSHAP computational cost was measured, local explanation stability was assessed under prediction-preserving perturbations, and validation-calibrated policies were used to allocate explanation workload selectively.

Result: XGBoost provided the strongest overall predictive profile; Random Forest achieved the lowest false-positive rate. At 5,000 samples, TreeSHAP took 700.759 s for Random Forest versus 1.471 s for XGBoost. Random Forest exhibited the strongest base-level explanation stability, while XGBoost maintained high rank and directional consistency but with greater top-feature turnover and attribution-magnitude drift. On the balanced test, ~90% false-negative explanation coverage enabled 28–32% compute savings; ~95% coverage enabled 15–23% savings. Savings were substantially smaller under the attack-heavy natural prevalence.

Conclusion: Operationally useful explainable IoT intrusion detection depends on a multi-dimensional assessment encompassing predictive quality, explanation cost, local stability, workload prevalence, and selective invocation — not on detection accuracy alone.

Abstract: Machine-learning intrusion-detection studies commonly emphasize predictive accuracy while treating explanation generation as a computationally free post-processing step. This study jointly evaluates predictive effectiveness, explanation cost, local explanation stability, and selective explanation for binary Internet of Things (IoT) intrusion detection. A leakage-safe CICIoT2023 corpus was constructed using exact 39-feature hashes, non-finite-value handling, exact-feature deduplication, conservative label-collision removal, and deterministic hash-level partitioning. Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated on natural and balanced test distributions. TreeSHAP cost was measured, stability was assessed under prediction-preserving perturbations, and validation-calibrated policies were used to allocate explanation workload. XGBoost provided the strongest overall predictive profile, while Random Forest produced the lowest false-positive rate. At 5,000 samples, TreeSHAP required 700.759 s for Random Forest and 1.471 s for XGBoost. Random Forest showed the strongest overall base-level explanation stability; XGBoost retained high rank and directional consistency but showed greater top-feature turnover and attribution-magnitude drift. On the balanced test, about 90% false-negative explanation coverage permitted 28-32% compute savings, while about 95% coverage permitted 15-23% savings. Savings were much smaller under the attack-heavy natural prevalence. These results show that operationally useful explainable IoT intrusion detection depends on predictive quality, explanation cost, local stability, workload prevalence, and selective invocation rather than detection accuracy alone.

</details>


### [82] [Synthesizing Probabilistic Saturating Counters with Differentially Private Formal Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10521)
*Zhiming Chi,Lutan Zhao,Depeng Liu,Yong Li,Pengfei Yang,Bow-Yaw Wang,Rui Hou,Cheng-Chao Huang,Andrea Turrini,Lijun Zhang,Naijun Zhan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper formally analyzes probabilistic saturating counters (PSCs) for branch predictors using differential privacy (DP), modeling PSCs and Prime+Probe attacks as probabilistic Moore machines to derive optimal attack strategies and formal DP guarantees, then synthesizes PSC parameters that achieve target DP while maintaining competitive prediction accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical saturating counters in branch predictors are deterministic and vulnerable to side-channel attacks (e.g., Prime+Probe), where an attacker can manipulate counter state to infer a victim's branch direction. While PSCs have been proposed as a mitigation, existing evaluations are purely empirical and lack formal security guarantees.

Method: The authors model PSCs and Prime+Probe attack strategies as probabilistic Moore machines, derive optimal attack strategies, and quantify attacker distinguishing power using differential privacy (DP). They then synthesize parameters for an enhanced PSC satisfying a target pure DP guarantee and evaluate utility via stationary misprediction rate validated on benchmark programs.

Result: The synthesized PSCs provide formal DP security guarantees while retaining competitive prediction performance compared to both deterministic and existing probabilistic saturating counters. Theoretical misprediction rates are validated empirically on benchmark programs.

Conclusion: A formal DP framework can be successfully applied to the PSC primitive under the Prime+Probe observation model, yielding PSC designs with provable security against side-channel leakage. End-to-end security for full branch predictors under repeated or adaptive attacks remains future work.

Abstract: Branch predictors improve instruction-level parallelism in modern processors and are commonly modeled using saturating counters. However, classical saturating counters are deterministic and thus vulnerable to side-channel attacks: an attacker can manipulate the counter state and infer the branch direction of a victim process. Probabilistic saturating counters (PSCs) have been proposed to mitigate this leakage by randomizing counter updates, but existing evaluations are mainly empirical. In this paper, we give a formal analysis based on differential privacy (DP): we model PSCs and the corresponding Prime+Probe attack strategies as probabilistic Moore machines, derive optimal attack strategies, and quantify the attacker's distinguishing power through DP. Our DP guarantee applies to the PSC primitive under the Prime+Probe observation model; end-to-end security for a full branch predictor under repeated or adaptive attacks is an important direction for future work. We then synthesize parameters for an enhanced PSC that satisfies a target pure DP guarantee. To evaluate utility, we derive the stationary misprediction rate and validate the theoretical predictions on benchmark programs. Compared to deterministic and existing probabilistic saturating counters, the synthesized PSCs provide formal security guarantees while preserving competitive prediction performance.

</details>


### [83] [On Understanding, Identifying, and Mitigating Vulnerabilities in Agentic Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10530)
*Md Jafrin Hossain,Mohammad Arif Hossain,Nirwan Ansari*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic literature review (85 papers) reveals LLM agent security research is attack-heavy (3.9:1), dominated by perception-layer vulnerabilities (66%), while action-layer threats like tool misuse and sandbox escape are critically understudied despite real-world risks. The authors propose a four-layer taxonomy and identify seven open containment problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have evolved into autonomous agents with real-world privileges (API calls, file modification, database queries), where a single compromised reasoning step can cause unauthorized access or cascading failures. The security research community has not kept pace with this paradigm shift, motivating a comprehensive landscape assessment.

Method: PRISMA 2020 systematic literature review across six databases, screening 743 records and retaining 85 papers (2023–2025) on agentic LLM security. Quantitative analysis of attack vs. defense ratios, vulnerability distribution, and proposal of a four-layer taxonomy (perception, brain, action, interaction) mapping 13 vulnerability types.

Result: Attack research outnumbers defense 3.9:1. Perception-layer vulnerabilities dominate at 66% (prompt injection, jailbreaking, adversarial perturbations), while action-layer vulnerabilities (tool misuse, code injection, sandbox escape) comprise only 4.7%. Code execution security accounts for 3.5%, tool-augmented agents 12%. Root cause identified as architectural coupling with weak inter-layer isolation.

Conclusion: The field suffers from a severe mismatch between research focus and real-world risk. Seven open problems center on containment, with the core issue being architectural coupling that allows vulnerabilities to propagate across layers. Urgent need for action-layer and defense-oriented research.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have undergone a shift from stateless conversational interfaces to autonomous agents capable of multi-step planning, tool invocation, code execution, and maintaining persistent memory. When these agents operate with real-world privileges---calling APIs, modifying files, and querying databases---a compromised reasoning step can trigger unauthorized data access, irreversible state changes, or cascading failures, yet the security research community has not kept pace. To quantify the state of the field, we conducted a systematic literature review under PRISMA 2020 guidelines across six databases, screening 743 records and retaining 85 papers (2023--2025) on agentic LLM security. Attack research outpaces defense work by 3.9:1. Perception-layer vulnerabilities (prompt injection, jailbreaking, adversarial perturbations) dominate, accounting for 66\% of papers, while action-layer vulnerabilities (tool misuse, code injection, sandbox escape) appear in only 4.7\%, misaligned with real-world risk. Code execution security accounts for 3.5\%, and tool-augmented agents 12\%. We contribute a four-layer taxonomy mapping 13 vulnerability types across perception, brain, action, and interaction layers, and identify seven open problems centered on containment. Agentic LLM insecurity stems from architectural coupling, where weak isolation allows vulnerabilities to propagate across layers.

</details>


### [84] [Trigger the Straggler: Load Hijack on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10614)
*Rui Zhang,Wenbo Jiang,Hongwei Li,Zihan Wang,Rui Zhang,Chaoshun Zuo,Jianfei Sun,Guowen Xu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Load Hijack is a supply-chain attack where a malicious model provider poisons a MoE checkpoint's router weights so that a private trigger input concentrates token assignments on experts co-located on a single GPU, creating a straggler that degrades serving performance, while ordinary inputs route normally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expert parallelism in MoE serving exposes a supply-chain vulnerability: a malicious checkpoint provider could manipulate router weights to selectively degrade performance. The challenge is achieving conditional behavior — routing concentration only on triggered inputs while preserving normal routing on clean inputs — which is difficult because optimizing for trigger-conditioned expert assignment tends to bleed into ordinary-input routing.

Method: Load Hijack uses a three-stage optimization procedure: (1) a trigger-conditioned loss that maximizes token assignment to target experts co-located on one GPU when the trigger is present, (2) a regularization term that keeps ordinary-input routing close to the clean reference router, and (3) a balancing mechanism that resolves the inherent conflict between these two objectives, preventing the trigger-optimized bias from leaking into normal routing behavior.

Result: Across three MoE families and four corpora, Load Hijack directs 92.3%–95.6% of triggered token assignments to target experts. In live expert-parallel serving, triggered traffic yields 1.43× time-to-first-token and 0.86× throughput compared to ordinary traffic, demonstrating effective trigger-controlled performance degradation with minimal impact on clean inputs.

Conclusion: Poisoned routers can function as trigger-controlled device schedulers, selectively degrading MoE serving performance. This motivates the need for checkpoint audits that verify routing distributions and runtime load characteristics before deployment.

Abstract: Expert parallelism (EP) is a common strategy for serving large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models across multiple GPUs by distributing experts among devices. Router decisions then determine both which experts process each token and which GPUs execute the resulting work. This procedure exposes a supply-chain attack surface in the serving schedule. We introduce Load Hijack, in which a malicious model provider modifies only a checkpoint's router weights, distributes the poisoned checkpoint, and retains a private trigger. When the trigger appears, the poisoned router concentrates token-to-expert assignments on experts co-located on one GPU. The resulting load makes that GPU a straggler and forces peer devices to wait, while routing on ordinary inputs remains near the clean reference. We find this conditional behavior difficult to achieve because an objective that rewards target-expert use on triggered inputs can also bias ordinary-input routing toward the same experts. To resolve this conflict, Load Hijack employs a three-stage optimization procedure that produces strong trigger-dependent concentration while keeping ordinary-input routing close to the clean reference. Across three MoE families and four corpora, Load Hijack directs 92.3% to 95.6% of triggered token assignments to the target experts. In live EP serving, triggered traffic produces 1.43x the time-to-first-token and 0.86x the throughput measured under ordinary traffic. These results show that poisoned routers can act as trigger-controlled device schedulers and motivate checkpoint audits of routing and runtime load.

</details>


### [85] [A Lightweight Fault-Detection Scheme for Barrett Modular Multiplication Using Multiple Conditional Reduction Paths](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10736)
*Rourab Paul,Paresh Baidya,Krishnendu Guha,Amlan Chakrabarti*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Statistical Reduction Monitoring (SRM) method to protect Barrett Modular Multiplication (BMM) units in PQC and FHE hardware accelerators against both intentional (SCA, Trojans) and unintentional (aging) faults, achieving efficient fault detection with minimal hardware overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Polynomial multiplication relies heavily on BMM units in lattice-based PQC (Kyber, Dilithium) and FHE (BGV, BFV, CKKS) schemes. These BMM units are vulnerable to intentional faults from Side-Channel Attacks and Hardware Trojans, as well as unintentional faults from aging and environmental factors. Such faults can cause information leakage and compromise system security, creating a need for lightweight protection mechanisms.

Method: The authors employ a Statistical Reduction Monitoring (SRM) method to protect the BMM unit. SRM monitors the statistical properties of the modular reduction process to detect anomalies indicative of faults, covering both random and burst fault patterns.

Result: The proposed SRM approach incurs minimal hardware overhead while providing efficient detection of both random and burst faults in the BMM unit.

Conclusion: SRM offers a cost-effective, hardware-friendly countermeasure for protecting BMM units in PQC and FHE accelerators against a broad spectrum of faults, enhancing overall system security without significant performance or area penalties.

Abstract: Polynomial multiplication is the most resource-, time-, and energy-critical operation in lattice-based Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) schemes. Lattice-based PQC schemes such as Kyber and Dilithium have already been standardized, while lattice- based FHE schemes such as BGV, BFV, and CKKS are widely recognized as leading candidate in FHE area. Barrett Modular Multiplication (BMM) for polynomial multiplication is widely adopted in PQC and FHE hardware accelerators due to its hardware friendly nature and efficient modular reduction capabilities. However, Side-Channel Attacks (SCAs) and Hardware Trojans may introduce intentional faults, while aging and various other factors can cause unintentional faults. These faults may target the BM M unit, one of the most critical components of PQC and FHE infrastructures, potentially leading to information leakage and compromising system security. In this paper, we employ a Statistical Reduction Monitoring (SRM) method to protect the BM M unit against such adversarial conditions. The proposed approach incurs minimal hardware overhead while providing efficient detection of both random and bur

</details>


### [86] [A Gateway Architecture for Enterprise MCP Authentication: Unifying Heterogeneous Auth, Identity Delegation, and the User / Non-User Persona Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10760)
*Suraj Kumar,Amy Wang,Srinivasan Manoharan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MCP's rapid enterprise adoption created a governance crisis due to fragmented authentication. This paper presents a centralized MCP gateway deployed in production that provides unified authentication, authorization, and auditing across all MCP servers via a novel two-axis auth model, multiple SSO grants, and three end-to-end identity flows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explosive enterprise adoption of MCP — from zero to dozens of internally built MCP servers within a year — led to each team independently implementing authentication (or none at all). This produced a fragmented landscape with no consistent way to authorize callers, audit actions, or offboard employees across the fleet, creating an urgent governance crisis.

Method: A centralized MCP gateway acting as a single aggregation, governance, and authentication layer in front of all downstream MCP servers. The system employs: (1) a two-axis authentication model (persona: interactive user vs. automated non-user × credential type: no-auth, static/dynamic API key, PKCE, client credentials, platform app-context); (2) a gateway authentication layer with three enterprise SSO grants and three token-provisioning models (BYOT, GYOT, delegated OAuth via RFC 8693); (3) three end-to-end identity flows (User-to-OAuth2, Non-user-to-Service-Account, User-to-Service-Account); and (4) an evolutionary deployment path from CDN/WAF/edge perimeter to private MCP tunnels and enterprise connectors.

Result: The architecture is deployed in production, successfully fronting dozens of MCP servers across heterogeneous clients including web, desktop, custom-SDK, and low-code platforms, providing unified governance across the entire MCP fleet.

Conclusion: Centralizing MCP authentication and governance through a gateway architecture resolves the fragmentation crisis caused by decentralized, ad-hoc MCP server deployment. The proposed two-axis model and token-provisioning patterns provide a reusable blueprint for enterprises scaling MCP adoption securely.

Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the de-facto interface for connecting LLM agents to enterprise tools, and adoption has been explosive: within a year, large organizations went from zero to dozens of internally built MCP servers. That speed created a governance crisis. Each team implemented authentication independently -- some with no auth, some with API keys, some with full OAuth -- producing a fragmented landscape with no consistent way to authorize callers, track who did what, or offboard a departing employee across the fleet. This paper reports an industry deployment that resolves the crisis with a centralized MCP gateway: a single aggregation, governance, and authentication layer that fronts every downstream MCP server.
  We make four contributions grounded in production experience. First, a two-axis authentication model crossing persona (interactive user vs. automated non-user) with credential type (no-auth, static/dynamic API key, PKCE, client credentials, platform app-context). Second, a gateway authentication layer supporting three enterprise SSO grants and three token-provisioning models: Bring-Your-Own-Token, Generate-Your-Own-Token, and delegated OAuth via RFC 8693 token exchange. Third, three end-to-end identity flows -- User-to-OAuth2, Non-user-to-Service-Account, and User-to-Service-Account -- composing client, gateway, and server. Fourth, the deployment evolution from CDN/WAF/edge perimeter to private MCP tunnels and enterprise-wide connectors. The architecture is in production, fronting dozens of MCP servers across web, desktop, custom-SDK, and low-code clients.

</details>


### [87] [Strategies to Avoid Illegal Data Access](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11153)
*Muhammad Mubeen,Arslan Bisharat,Giri Anandhi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper examines three core strategies for preventing unauthorized data access in organizations: technological solutions (firewalls, intrusion detection systems, encryption), employee training (phishing awareness, password hygiene), and policy enforcement (usage guidelines, compliance, regular review).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data security is a top priority for companies of all sizes, and the increasing sophistication of technology heightens the risk of unauthorized data access. Businesses must adopt proactive measures to safeguard their data against these evolving threats.

Method: The study adopts a multi-layered, qualitative approach, examining three interdependent methods: (1) deployment of technological safeguards—firewalls as perimeter defense, intrusion detection systems for anomaly alerting, and encryption for data-at-rest/in-transit protection; (2) employee education programs targeting threat recognition (phishing, malicious websites) and proper security hygiene (password management); and (3) establishment and periodic review of organizational data security policies with defined usage guidelines and noncompliance consequences.

Result: The integration of technological solutions, staff training, and robust policy enforcement collectively enables organizations to prevent unauthorized data access, reduce the risk of data breaches, and maintain regulatory compliance.

Conclusion: A holistic security posture combining technology, human capital development, and governance frameworks is essential. Organizations that implement this tripartite strategy can effectively mitigate unauthorized access risks and sustain compliance with regulatory requirements.

Abstract: For companies of all sizes, data security is a top priority. The chance of unauthorized data access increases as technology develops. To prevent unwanted access to their data, businesses must be proactive. This study examines technology solutions, personnel training, and policy enforcement as methods to prevent unauthorized data access. Data may be protected from illegal access using technological solutions like firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and encryption. Intrusion detection systems notify the administrator when suspicious behavior is found, while firewalls serve as a protective border between the internal network and the internet. Even if data is intercepted, encryption makes sure it is safe. Another effective method of avoiding unauthorized data access is employee education. Employees must be taught how to spot hazards like phishing emails and shady websites and react to them. Additionally, they should be taught the right way to utilize passwords and other security precautions. To secure data, organizations should create and implement policies. Policies should set out appropriate data and system use guidelines and provide repercussions for noncompliance. Policies should be evaluated regularly to ensure that they are current and useful. Businesses may prevent unwanted access to their data by installing technology solutions, training staff, and enforcing regulations. Organizations may reduce data breach risk and maintain regulatory compliance by taking these precautions. ...

</details>
