### [88] [Do LLM Recommenders Know When They're Hallucinating? Auditing Confidence Calibration in Catalog Faithfulness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10008)
*Srijith Ravikumar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: LLM recommenders hallucinate out-of-catalog items at catalog-dependent rates (0–8.4%), but all models exhibit systematic under-confidence (67–86% verbalized confidence vs. 92–100% accuracy). This under-confidence, an elicitation mismatch, makes conformal abstention ineffective for reducing hallucinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior audits of LLM recommenders treat out-of-domain (OOD) recommendation as a binary metric without investigating whether models are aware of their hallucinations. The authors aim to jointly audit hallucination rates and verbalized-confidence calibration to understand if confidence scores can be leveraged to mitigate hallucinations.

Method: Joint audit of four zero-shot LLM recommenders (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6) across three catalogs (MovieLens-25M, Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys, Yelp Open Dataset), stratified by item popularity. Metrics: OOD@10 (hallucination rate), ECE, Brier score, and reliability diagrams for confidence calibration. Tested conformal abstention thresholds over verbalized confidence.

Result: Hallucination rates are catalog-dependent: 0–0.2% (MovieLens), 4.5–8.3% (Amazon), 2.2–8.4% (Yelp). Confidence is materially miscalibrated even at 0% hallucination (ECE up to 0.223). All models are systematically under-confident (verbalized confidence 67–86% vs. 92–100% accuracy). Conformal abstention reduces hallucination by at most 0.7pp at 4–21pp coverage cost, as under-confidence fails to separate correct from hallucinated items.

Conclusion: The under-confidence observed is best explained as an elicitation mismatch: "Just Ask" prompts elicit generic recommendation-quality ratings, not catalog-membership probabilities. The authors recommend audits report calibration alongside OOD and use catalog-anchored elicitation.

Abstract: LLM recommenders for top-$K$ item suggestion regularly emit titles outside the target catalog. Prior audits measure this as a binary out-of-domain rate; none ask whether the model knew it was hallucinating. We jointly audit hallucination rate (OOD@10) and verbalized-confidence calibration (ECE, Brier, reliability) for four zero-shot LLM recommenders from four independent vendors (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6), not grounded or fine-tuned systems, across three catalogs (MovieLens-25M, Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys, Yelp Open Dataset), stratified by item popularity. Hallucination is catalog-dependent (0--0.2\% on MovieLens, 4.5--8.3\% on Amazon, 2.2--8.4\% on Yelp), but verbalized confidence is materially miscalibrated even when hallucination is zero (ECE up to 0.223 on MovieLens despite 0\% OOD). All four LLMs are systematically \emph{under}-confident across all twelve cells, verbalizing a mean of 67--86 on items they recommend with 92--100\% accuracy. This is the opposite of the over-confidence usually emphasized in LLM-hallucination work. The under-confidence is best read as an \emph{elicitation mismatch}: ``Just Ask'' elicits a generic recommendation-quality rating, not a catalog-membership probability. A conformal abstention threshold over verbalized confidence reduces hallucination by at most 0.7\,pp across $α\in \{.05, .10, .15, .20\}$, at 4--21\,pp of coverage cost: the under-confident channel cannot separate correct items from hallucinations, so the threshold mostly removes correct items. We recommend that audits of LLM recommenders report calibration alongside OOD, and use catalog-anchored elicitation rather than generic confidence prompts.

</details>


### [89] [ConnectionMind: Leveraging Social Networks and Large Language Models for Personalized Recommendation at Meta](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10187)
*Haoyu Han,Yuming Liu,Lei Huang,Lizhu Zhang,Jiliang Tang,Xiangjun Fan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: ConnectionMind is a production recommendation framework at Meta that integrates heterogeneous social graphs with LLMs, using a two-stage SFT+RL training strategy to enable graph-reasoning-based personalization, achieving a 0.43% improvement in video watch time in online A/B tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern social media recommendation requires modeling complex multi-relational social structures (friendships, groups, creators) and heterogeneous content (text, video). Traditional models either omit these social signals or treat them independently, lacking the reasoning capability to integrate multi-relational context for fine-grained personalization.

Method: ConnectionMind constructs a heterogeneous graph connecting users, items, friends, groups, and creator pages. It formulates recommendation as a graph reasoning problem — discovering personalized paths from users to candidate items — using an LLM-based policy to reason over graph structures. Training employs a two-stage strategy: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on large-scale user-item interaction trajectories, followed by (2) end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) to refine social graph reasoning for personalization.

Result: ConnectionMind outperforms representative baselines on multiple real-world datasets. In production deployment at Meta, online A/B tests demonstrated a 0.43% improvement in video watch time, confirming measurable real-world impact.

Conclusion: Tightly integrating social network structure with LLMs via graph reasoning is both feasible and effective at production scale. The SFT+RL training paradigm successfully enables LLMs to reason over heterogeneous social graphs for recommendation, yielding statistically and practically significant gains in a live industrial system.

Abstract: Modern recommendation systems on social media platforms such as Meta must model complex social relationships, including friendships, group memberships, and creator interactions, alongside massive and heterogeneous content such as text and video. Traditional recommendation models, however, often omit these signals or treat them independently, lacking the reasoning capability to integrate multi-relational context for fine-grained personalization. We present ConnectionMind, a production-ready recommendation framework that tightly integrates the social network structure with large language models (LLMs) to enable scalable, interpretable, and reasoning-aware personalization in Meta. ConnectionMind constructs a heterogeneous graph connecting users, items, friends, groups, and creator pages, and formulates recommendation as a graph reasoning problem: discovering personalized paths from users to candidate items. An LLM-based policy is employed to reason over these graph structures and guide recommendation decisions. To train the system at scale, ConnectionMind adopts a two-stage learning strategy. We first perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on large-scale user-item interaction trajectories to initialize the reasoning policy, followed by end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) to refine the model's ability to reason over social graphs for personalized recommendation. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ConnectionMind compared to representative baselines. More importantly, ConnectionMind has been deployed in Meta's large-scale recommendation pipeline and has been evaluated through online A/B tests, achieving a 0.43% improvement in video watch time. These results demonstrate measurable real-world impact in a production recommendation system.

</details>


### [90] [Sequential Modality Dropout for Robust Multi-Modal Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10240)
*Guanqun Yang,Wenlong Zhang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SMD is a training-time dropout technique that independently erases entire modality streams (image/text) across a user's history, dramatically improving robustness to missing modalities at inference without sacrificing full-modality accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world product catalogs often have missing images or text, yet multi-modal sequential recommenders trained on complete data degrade severely when modalities are unavailable at serving time. Existing methods lack robustness to this modality incompleteness.

Method: Sequential Modality Dropout (SMD): during training, each modality stream is independently dropped with probability p for the entire user interaction sequence, forcing the model to rely on whichever modalities remain. An optional cross-modal reconstruction loss further aligns representations across modalities. The method requires only ~4 lines of code and is architecture-agnostic.

Result: Across four backbones (MM-SASRec, IISAN, MISSRec, fMRLRec) on four Amazon domains, SMD improves text retention by 1.0–3.2x with no loss in full-modality HR@10. Under 95% per-item missing rate, retention is 61% vs. 22% (2.8x improvement). Cross-modal reconstruction pushes retention from 90% to 98% under severe text missingness.

Conclusion: SMD is a simple, lightweight, architecture-agnostic modification that makes multi-modal sequential recommenders robust to realistic missing-modality scenarios, substantially closing the gap between training assumptions and deployment conditions.

Abstract: Multi-modal sequential recommenders assume every item carries every modality, but real product catalogs often miss images or text, and a model trained on complete data loses much of its recommendation accuracy when a modality is unavailable at serving time. We propose Sequential Modality Dropout (SMD): during training, each modality stream (image and text) is independently erased with probability p for an entire user interaction history, so the model learns to predict the next item without relying on any single modality. We measure robustness by retention, the fraction of a model's full-modality accuracy (HR@10) that survives when a modality is removed at test time. Across four backbones (MM-SASRec, IISAN, MISSRec, and fMRLRec) on four Amazon domains, SMD raises text retention by 1.0 to 3.2x at essentially no cost to full-modality accuracy; under an extreme 95% per-item missing rate, it retains 61% of HR@10 versus 22% without (a 2.8x improvement). An optional cross-modal reconstruction loss further lifts retention from 90% to 98% on a simple additive backbone under severe text missingness. SMD is a four-line, architecture-agnostic change that makes multi-modal sequential recommenders robust to the missing modalities they actually encounter in deployment.

</details>


### [91] [DualSpectralCF: Training-Free Sign-Aware Spectral Collaborative Filtering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10247)
*Guanqun Yang,Tong Qi,Xiaoxue Han*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: DualSpectralCF is a training-free framework that incorporates explicit negative feedback into spectral collaborative filtering, achieving significant accuracy gains (up to +32.6% Recall@20) while running 7.7–155.3× faster than learned sign-aware methods like SIGformer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two gaps exist in recommender systems: (1) sign-aware recommenders exploit explicit negative feedback for accuracy gains but require expensive gradient-based training; (2) training-free spectral CF methods are fast and competitive but only use positive interactions. The authors aim to unify these lines of work by bringing sign-awareness to spectral CF without sacrificing its training-free nature.

Method: DualSpectralCF introduces two components that attach to any spectral backbone of the form r̂_u = F(M) r_u: (1) a signed input signal r_u^± that encodes explicit dislikes alongside likes, and (2) a signed item-item operator M^± that blends like-together and dislike-together similarity. The framework is backbone-agnostic and introduces only two scalar hyperparameters (γ, κ). It is instantiated on ChebyCF, GF-CF, and Turbo-CF.

Result: Every DualSpectralCF instance matches or beats its unsigned backbone across all 5 sign-aware benchmarks. Recall@20 lifts reach +32.6% with tuned (γ, κ) and +1.9% to +16.0% at fixed defaults. The family runs 7.7–155.3× faster than SIGformer while retaining 70.7–90.7% of its accuracy. Sign-awareness benefits cold-start users most, with up to +29.2% Recall@20 on Epinions users with 1–5 training items.

Conclusion: DualSpectralCF successfully bridges training-free spectral CF and sign-aware recommendation, demonstrating that explicit negative feedback can be leveraged without gradient-based training, yielding strong accuracy improvements especially for cold-start users, all while maintaining orders-of-magnitude speed advantages over learned competitors.

Abstract: Real-world recommendation platforms routinely collect explicit negative feedback such as 1-star reviews, hate-button clicks, distrust between users, and very-low watch-ratio videos. Learned sign-aware recommenders exploit this signal for clear accuracy gains, but only at the cost of gradient-based training. In parallel, a line of training-free spectral collaborative filtering methods matches or beats learned graph recommenders at a fraction of the cost, yet operates on positive interactions alone. We bridge these two lines with DualSpectralCF, a training-free framework of two components that attach to any spectral backbone of the form $\hat{\mathbf{r}}_u = F(\mathbf{M}) \mathbf{r}_u$: a signed input signal $\mathbf{r}_u^{\pm}$ that encodes the user's explicit dislikes, and a signed item-item operator $\mathbf{M}^{\pm}$ that blends like-together and dislike-together similarity. The framework is backbone-agnostic and adds just two scalar hyperparameters. We instantiate DualSpectralCF on ChebyCF, GF-CF, and Turbo-CF, and evaluate on five sign-aware benchmarks: every instance matches or beats its unsigned backbone on all 5 datasets, with Recall@20 lifts up to +32.6% with backbone-specific $(γ, κ)$ tuning and +1.9% to +16.0% for DualSpectralCF-Cheby at the fixed default $(γ= -0.5, κ= 0.1)$, and the family runs 7.7 to 155.3$\times$ faster than SIGformer while reaching 70.7% to 90.7% of its accuracy. Sign-awareness helps most for cold-start users, with up to +29.2% Recall@20 on Epinions users with 1 to 5 training items.

</details>


### [92] [GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10257)
*Ying Li,Shradha Sehgal,Arjun Rao,Rein Houthooft,Yaochen Zhu,Ashish Rastogi*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Netflix presents GenRec, a two-phase LLM-backed recommendation ranker. Phase 2, the paper's focus, transitions from a traditional discriminative ranker to an LLM-driven approach using verbalized user histories. Despite fewer training examples and input signals, GenRec achieves statistically significant offline and online gains. The work highlights a paradigm shift from feature engineering to context engineering and from bespoke architectures to shared foundation backbones, with practical serving insights under cost constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs offer richer modeling of users, content, and context in natural language, but deploying them as production rankers requires overcoming challenges: aligning LLM outputs with business metrics, managing inference costs, and transitioning from heavily engineered feature pipelines to verbalized context. The authors aim to demonstrate that an LLM-backed ranker can be practically deployed and outperform a mature production discriminative ranker.

Method: GenRec's Phase 2 involves post-training an in-house Netflix foundation LLM (adapted from open-source in Phase 1) with recommendation-specific data, labels, and reward signals. Key design elements include: (1) input verbalization and context engineering to represent user history and context in natural language; (2) construction of post-training data with ranking-oriented labels; (3) reward integration for aligning the ranker with long-term member satisfaction; (4) a prefill-only inference architecture for cost-constrained serving. Evaluation is conducted via large-scale A/B testing against the production ranker.

Result: In large-scale A/B tests, GenRec achieved statistically significant gains on both offline and online metrics compared to the current production ranker, despite using substantially fewer Phase-2 labeled training examples and input signals than the traditional discriminative model.

Conclusion: LLM-backed recommenders can outperform traditional discriminative rankers even with fewer features and labels. The paradigm shifts from feature engineering to context engineering and from bespoke architectures to shared foundation backbones. Practical deployment is feasible under real-world resource constraints using techniques like prefill-only inference.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping recommender systems by enabling richer modeling of users, content, and context directly in natural language. At Netflix, we are exploring this direction through GenRec, an LLM-backed recommendation ranker built on top of an in-house foundational LLM. GenRec follows a two-phase framework: Phase 1 adapts an open-source LLM to Netflix data, developing deep understanding of the catalog and member behavior while balancing capabilities such as content understanding and instruction following. Phase 2 post-trains this foundation model with recommendation-ranking specific data, labels, and reward signals, aiming to align the ranker with business requirements and long-term member satisfaction.
  This paper focuses on Phase 2 and the transition from a traditional discriminative ranker with thousands of engineered features to an LLM-backed ranker driven by verbalized user histories and context. We describe our design for input verbalization and context engineering, post-training data construction, reward integration, model architecture, and a cost-constrained serving design based on a prefill-only inference approach. We report results from a large-scale A/B test comparing GenRec against the current production ranker model, where we show that a GenRec model trained with substantially fewer Phase-2 labeled training examples and input signals can achieve statistically significant gains in offline and online metrics. We discuss how LLM-backed recommenders could shift the recommendation paradigm: from feature engineering to context engineering, and from bespoke architectures to shared foundation backbones. We also outline practical lessons for serving such systems under real-world resource constraints.

</details>


### [93] [Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering: Rethinking Graph Collaborative Filtering as Tree Collaborative Filtering with Curvature-Aware Propagation Depth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10297)
*Jinfeng Xu,Zheyu Chen,Ziyue Peng,Shuo Yang,Jinze Li,Wenhao Yuan,Jian Chen,Edith C. H. Ngai*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: NTCF proposes node-specific propagation depths in Graph Collaborative Filtering based on a Ricci-curvature proxy derived from local degree imbalance, theoretically generalizing NGCF and preventing over-smoothing on peripheral nodes while better exploring hubs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniform propagation depth in GCF ignores heterogeneous local connectivity: peripheral nodes suffer over-smoothing while hub nodes are under-explored. A node-adaptive depth mechanism is needed.

Method: NTCF models each node's neighborhood as a rooted tree, computes a closed-form local-degree-imbalance score as a discrete Ricci-curvature proxy, and assigns node-specific propagation depths. The framework strictly generalizes NGCF and can serve as a drop-in backbone for self-supervised models.

Result: NTCF outperforms widely used GCF backbones and, when integrated into advanced self-supervised models as a replacement backbone, yields further performance gains across three public datasets.

Conclusion: Node-specific depth scheduling via curvature-based scoring effectively addresses the over-smoothing/under-exploration trade-off in GCF, offering both theoretical guarantees and practical performance improvements.

Abstract: Graph Collaborative Filtering (GCF) has become the dominant paradigm in modern recommender systems by modeling user-item interactions as a bipartite graph and propagating embeddings through a fixed number of message-passing layers. However, applying a uniform propagation depth to every node ignores a fundamental property of real interaction graphs: nodes differ substantially in their local connectivity, so peripheral nodes quickly suffer from over-smoothing while hub-like nodes remain under-explored beyond their immediate neighborhood. In this paper, we revisit GCF from a tree-structured perspective and propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF), a framework that re-interprets each node's local neighborhood as a rooted tree and assigns a node-specific propagation depth based on a closed-form local-degree-imbalance score that serves as a discrete Ricci-curvature proxy. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that (i) NTCF strictly generalizes NGCF, degenerating to NGCF when all curvature-induced depth adjustments vanish (a lower bound on its representation power), and (ii) the curvature-aware schedule retains strictly more discriminative information at deep layers on positively-curved (peripheral) nodes than uniform-depth propagation. NTCF can achieve higher performance than most widely used GCF backbone models and can be integrated into existing advanced self-supervised models as a backbone, replacing their original backbone to achieve enhanced performance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of NTCF.

</details>


### [94] [Persona Conditioning as an Assessor-Sensitivity Probe for LLM-Based IR Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10385)
*Samaneh Mohtadi,Pietro Bernardelle,Joel Mackenzie,Gianluca Demartini*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper investigates how persona-conditioned framing of LLM-based relevance assessors affects judgment reliability and system ranking stability in IR evaluation. Using five distinct assessor personas across six LLMs, the study finds structured sensitivity — judgments shift in strictness and emphasis rather than reversing wholesale, with smaller models showing greater instability and certain system types (neural rankers, RAG pipelines) being disproportionately affected.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as relevance assessors in IR evaluation, but the impact of assessor framing (via personas) on judgment reliability and downstream system comparison remains poorly understood. The authors aim to diagnose whether persona conditioning introduces systematic biases that could undermine evaluation validity.

Method: The authors instantiate five task-oriented assessor personas (intent interpretation, domain expertise, contrastive judgment, evidence verification, global search-quality assessment) drawn from PersonaHub and NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA, alongside a standard UMBRELA baseline. They evaluate six LLM backbones on TREC DL20 and RAG24 benchmarks, measuring agreement with baseline judgments, system-ranking preservation (Kendall's τ), and local rank-displacement analysis to identify which systems and system types are most sensitive to persona shifts.

Result: Judgments remain close to baseline while exhibiting shifts in strictness, evidential threshold, and interpretation emphasis rather than widespread relevance reversals. High-capacity models preserve system-ranking agreement; smaller models amplify persona-induced instability. Sensitivity concentrates on specific systems — neural ranking/reranking systems on DL20 and RAG-oriented pipelines on RAG24. Persona source matters less than assessor role and model capacity.

Conclusion: Persona-conditioned judging serves as an effective controlled sensitivity probe for stress-testing LLM-based IR evaluation pipelines. It can identify systems whose evaluation outcomes are sensitive to assessor framing, enabling more robust evaluation design without requiring persona conditioning as a mandatory practice.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as relevance assessors in information retrieval (IR) evaluation, raising questions about how assessor framing affects judgment reliability and downstream system comparison. We study persona conditioning as a diagnostic mechanism for exposing LLM assessor sensitivity. Using task-oriented personas drawn from two complementary sources (PersonaHub and NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA), we instantiate five assessor roles emphasizing intent interpretation, domain expertise, contrastive judgment, evidence verification, and global search-quality assessment, compared with a standard UMBRELA baseline. Across six LLM backbones on TREC DL20 and RAG24, our analyses reveal structured rather than uniform assessor sensitivity. Judgments usually remain close to the baseline while shifting assessment strictness, evidential threshold, or interpretation emphasis rather than producing widespread relevance reversals. At the system level, high-capacity models preserve system-ranking agreement, while smaller models amplify persona-induced instability. Local rank-displacement analysis shows sensitivity concentrates on particular retrieval systems and system types, especially neural ranking/reranking systems on DL20 and RAG-oriented pipelines on RAG24. Persona source matters less than assessor role and model capacity. These findings position persona-conditioned judging as a controlled sensitivity probe for stress-testing LLM-based IR evaluation pipelines and identifying systems whose evaluation outcomes are sensitive to assessor framing.

</details>


### [95] [Post-Calibration Reliability Reranking of Relevance Decisions via Label-wise Monotone Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10406)
*Inwoo Tae,Yongjae Lee*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Proposes Label-wise Monotone Reliability Projection (MRP), a method that learns label-specific monotone functions mapping calibrated confidence to correctness reliability, enabling better reranking by residual risk without altering predicted labels or probabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-hoc calibration aligns confidence with average correctness but fails to address reliability differences that persist across different predicted labels within the same confidence level. This leads to over-trusting wrong predictions or unnecessarily deferring correct ones in retrieval systems.

Method: MRP learns label-wise monotone functions that map calibrated confidence scores to correctness reliability while preserving original predicted labels and class probabilities. The resulting reliability score enables reranking of fixed predictions according to residual risk. The approach is evaluated across six information access relevance datasets with multiple post-hoc calibrators, with structural ablations isolating label-wise residual reliability from global confidence remapping.

Result: MRP improves both reliability reranking and average fallback utility while maintaining full-coverage accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Structural ablations confirm gains stem from label-wise residual reliability rather than global confidence remapping.

Conclusion: MRP effectively addresses the gap where equally calibrated confidence scores can mask differing label-dependent reliability, offering a practical post-hoc improvement for information access retrieval systems without compromising existing calibration or accuracy.

Abstract: Web search, product search, and question-answering retrieval systems often assign a relevance label and confidence score to each query-candidate pair. The relevance label describes how well a page, product, or passage matches the query, while the confidence often guides downstream use or fallback decisions. Post-hoc calibration is therefore needed because misaligned confidence can make systems over-trust wrong predictions or unnecessarily defer correct ones. However, calibration mainly aligns confidence with average correctness, and does not remove predicted-label-dependent reliability differences that remain within the same calibrated confidence level. We address this gap with Label-wise Monotone Reliability Projection (MRP), which learns label-wise monotone functions that map calibrated confidence to correctness reliability while preserving the original predicted labels and class probabilities. The resulting reliability score reranks fixed predictions according to residual risk. Across six information access relevance datasets and multiple post-hoc calibrators, MRP improves reliability reranking and average fallback utility while preserving full-coverage accuracy and ECE. Structural ablations show that the main gains come from label-wise residual reliability rather than from global confidence remapping. We further analyze when MRP reliability scores can be embedded back into top-label probability geometry, showing that this projection is useful as a compatibility analysis but is distinct from the main reliability-reranking objective. The implementation will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [96] [Towards Efficient Reasoning in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10447)
*Linh Dieu Le,Tong Chen,Shazia Sadiq,Hongzhi Yin,Ming Jin,Junliang Yu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes REAM, a training-free model merging framework that fuses slow-thinking and fast-thinking recommender models at the granularity of individual attention heads to compress reasoning traces, achieving up to 24.3% reduction in reasoning length without sacrificing recommendation accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Slow-thinking LLM-based recommenders achieve high accuracy via step-by-step reasoning, but their reasoning traces are overly verbose, inflating inference costs with little accuracy benefit. Existing compression methods either require costly retraining (training-based) or are brittle and hard to scale (inference-time). Model merging offers a training-free alternative by blending slow- and fast-thinking models in a shared parameter space, but existing merging techniques use uniform coefficients that fail to capture the heterogeneous nature of reasoning across model components.

Method: REAM performs fine-grained model merging at the attention-head level. Each attention head in the slow-thinking model receives a distinct merge coefficient determined by two criteria: (1) its contribution to critical reasoning evidence, and (2) its sensitivity to parameter change. This selective, head-wise blending injects the concise behavior of the fast-thinking model into the slow-thinking model, pruning verbose reasoning while preserving decision-critical reasoning pathways.

Result: Experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that REAM reduces reasoning length by up to 24.3% and outperforms competitive model merging baselines in maintaining recommendation accuracy.

Conclusion: Head-level model merging is an effective, training-free strategy for compressing reasoning in LLM-based recommender systems, achieving a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off by selectively transferring concise reasoning behavior from fast-thinking to slow-thinking models.

Abstract: Large language model-based recommender systems are increasingly adopting slow-thinking models that generate step-by-step reasoning before making predictions, often achieving higher accuracy than fast-thinking models that predict directly. However, their reasoning traces are often unnecessarily verbose, increasing inference costs without commensurate accuracy gains. Existing training-based approaches to reasoning compression often incur substantial adaptation costs, while inference-time methods are brittle and difficult to scale. These limitations motivate model merging as a promising training-free direction for transferring specialised behaviours between models in a shared parameter space. In particular, merging a slow-thinking model with a fast-thinking counterpart provides a natural mechanism for balancing recommendation accuracy and reasoning conciseness. To this end, we propose, to our knowledge, the first model merging framework for reasoning compression in recommender systems. Unlike conventional merging methods that apply uniform merge coefficients across model components, our method performs fine-grained merging at the level of individual attention heads, capturing heterogeneous patterns in recommendation reasoning. Each attention head is assigned a distinct merge coefficient according to its contribution to critical reasoning evidence and its sensitivity to parameter change, enabling selective injection of the concise behaviour of the fast-thinking model into the slow-thinking model and reducing reasoning verbosity without compromising recommendation quality. Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that our method reduces reasoning length by up to 24.3% while outperforming competitive model merging baselines in maintaining recommendation accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/linhledieu/REAM.

</details>


### [97] [When Do Anchor-Based Pointwise LLM Rerankers Help? Retriever Quality, Statistical Scope, and Anchor Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10528)
*Utshab Kumar Ghosh,Shubham Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper reproduces and stress-tests anchor-based pointwise LLM reranking (GCCP/PAGC). After recovering eight undocumented implementation details to reproduce reported results, the authors find that while contrastive scoring is robust, complex anchor construction and score combination with pointwise relevance are unnecessary or only narrowly beneficial—gains depend on the retriever strength and simpler anchors work equally well.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Anchor-based pointwise LLM reranking promises cross-document context at pointwise cost, but the original GCCP/PAGC evaluation leaves unclear which components actually drive performance gains and under what conditions. A controlled stress test is needed to disentangle the contributions of contrastive scoring, anchor construction, and score aggregation.

Method: The authors first attempt to reproduce GCCP/PAGC from the paper text alone, achieving only 0.24 nDCG@10 vs. the reported 0.66. They identify and recover eight undocumented implementation details, yielding reproduction within 1.6% of reported results. Using this validated implementation, they conduct a controlled component-level stress test manipulating: (1) contrastive vs. standard pointwise scoring, (2) score combination strategies, (3) anchor construction complexity, (4) first-stage retriever type (BM25 vs. dense E5), and (5) LLM backbone variants including a 4-bit quantized 72B model.

Result: The contrastive scoring mechanism is robust under rigorous statistical correction. However, combining contrastive scores with standard pointwise relevance scores only helps with BM25 retrieval and yields negligible benefit with stronger dense retrievers like E5. The complex anchor construction method is unnecessary—a simpler interleaving of top-ranked sentences matches or outperforms it across datasets. These findings hold across different LLM backbones.

Conclusion: Anchor-based pointwise reranking is effective, but gains derive primarily from contrastive scoring rather than complex aggregation or anchor construction choices. Benefits appear under narrower conditions than originally suggested, with retriever strength and anchor simplicity being key moderating factors.

Abstract: Anchor-based pointwise LLM reranking scores each candidate against a shared reference passage to recover cross-document context at pointwise cost. We study when this actually helps, using GCCP/PAGC as a representative method. Our study is reproduction-first. We use reproduction as a starting point for a controlled component-level stress test of anchor-based pointwise reranking. Our initial reimplementation, based only on the paper text, achieves 0.24 nDCG@10 instead of the reported 0.66, revealing that several undocumented implementation details are necessary to reproduce the method. After identifying and recovering eight such details, we reproduce the reported results within 1.6% and use the validated implementation for controlled analysis.
  We find that the core contrastive scoring idea is robust under rigorous statistical correction. However, two design choices held fixed in the original paper are less reliable. First, we find that combining the contrastive score with the standard pointwise relevance score helps when the first-stage retriever is BM25, but gives little or no benefit when the first-stage retriever is a stronger dense model such as E5. Second, the paper's more complex method for constructing the anchor is unnecessary. A much simpler anchor, built by interleaving the top-ranked sentences, matches or outperforms it across datasets. These findings are consistent across different LLM backbones, including a 4-bit quantized 72B model. Overall, anchor-based pointwise reranking is effective, but its gains come mainly from contrastive scoring rather than from the more complex aggregation and anchor-construction choices, and they appear under narrower conditions than the original evaluation suggests.

</details>


### [98] [Multi Interests for Joint Search-Recommendation Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10535)
*Xiangchen Pan,Wei Wei,Huakang Niu,Zhicong Cheng*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes MIJSR, a multi-interest-based mixed sequential modeling framework that jointly models search and recommendation behaviors by extracting fine-grained user interests from both structural (subsequence-based) and semantic (query-clustering-based) perspectives, with adaptive fusion for multi-task prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cross-domain unified modeling frameworks for search and recommendation overlook the expression of diverse user interests in different scenarios within mixed behavior sequences. The authors identify a gap in capturing fine-grained, multi-faceted interests that manifest differently across search (active) and recommendation (passive) behaviors.

Method: MIJSR consists of three modules: (1) Cross-domain behavior fusion using contrastive learning to align query and item representations; (2) Multi-interest mining from structural (subsequence partitioning with masks to extract search, recommendation, and cross interests) and semantic (query-based clustering for semantic segmentation of mixed sequences) perspectives; (3) Multi-task prediction using adaptive fusion of multiple interests with side information via a progressive layered extraction model.

Result: Extensive experiments on two open-source datasets demonstrate that MIJSR enhances accuracy in both search and recommendation tasks by extracting users' multi-interests at a fine-grained level.

Conclusion: Fine-grained multi-interest extraction from mixed search-recommendation sequences, incorporating both structural and semantic perspectives, significantly improves the joint modeling of user preferences across search and recommendation domains.

Abstract: Search and recommendation are crucial for understanding user preferences. More and more studies are attempting to jointly model search behavior and recommendation behavior, by integrating user active search and passive recommendation behavior data to better mine user preferences. However, although existing cross-domain unified modeling frameworks can effectively compensate for the differences in behavior between domains, they overlook the expression of interests in different scenarios under mixed sequences. In this study, we propose a multi-interest-based mixed sequential modeling framework MIJSR, which performs multi-interest mining and adaptive integration on search recommendation mixed sequences from both structural and semantic perspectives. Specifically, our model can be roughly divided into three modules: cross-domain behavior fusion, multi-interest mining, and multi-task prediction. Firstly, we align the representations of query and item through contrastive learning training. Then, we extract the multi interests of the mixed behavior sequence from both structural and semantic perspectives. Structurally, we extract search interests, recommendation interests, and cross interests through subsequence partitioning and mask settings; In terms of semantics, we use the semantic information of queries for clustering and perform semantic segmentation on mixed sequences to construct semantic multi interests. Finally, the adaptive fusion of multiple interests is combined with other side information to use a progressive layered extraction model for multi-task prediction. Extensive experiments on two open-source datasets have shown that our model can further enhance its accuracy in search and recommendation by extracting users' multi interests at a fine-grained level. Codes are available at https://github.com/pxcstart/MIJSR.

</details>


### [99] [DistilVDR: A Compact End-to-End Visual Document Retriever via Dual-Student Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10636)
*Zhuchenyang Liu,Ziyi Wang,Yao Zhang,Yu Xiao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: DistilVDR distills a 524M-parameter single-vector visual document retrieval system from an 8B teacher using bilateral cosine alignment loss, achieving 86.9% of teacher performance with 15.6× smaller index size and an order-of-magnitude faster indexing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual document retrieval models are large (multi-billion parameters), slow to index at corpus scale, and expensive to serve. Prior compression methods either train a smaller multi-vector encoder from scratch or distill only the query side, failing to produce a compact end-to-end single-vector retriever.

Method: DistilVDR employs a 524M asymmetric encoder-only student distilled bilaterally from a frozen 8B vision-language teacher. The training uses a pointwise cosine alignment loss operating purely in the teacher's embedding space, requiring no relevance labels, negative sampling, or contrastive terms. The architecture is asymmetric: the document side receives concentrated visual capacity, while the query side is kept lightweight at 70M parameters. Two variants (HiRes and Fast) differ only in the document encoder's visual-tile budget.

Result: DistilVDR-HiRes achieves 61.74 average NDCG@5 on ViDoRe v1+v2+v3 (86.9% of the 8B teacher) and leads all reproduced sub-1B baselines on the high-resolution-sensitive v3 benchmark. DistilVDR-Fast attains 59.98 with a 3× smaller visual-token budget. Both variants store one million documents in a 15.6× smaller index than the strongest sub-1B multi-vector baseline and index the corpus an order of magnitude faster.

Conclusion: Bilateral distillation into an asymmetric encoder-only architecture is an effective route for compressing large VDR models into compact, high-performance single-vector retrievers, enabling practical full-corpus indexing without sacrificing retrieval quality.

Abstract: Visual document retrieval (VDR) is dominated by multi-billion-parameter models that are slow to index at full corpus scale and expensive to serve. Prior compression routes either train a smaller multi-vector encoder from scratch or distil only the query side; neither yields a compact single-vector retriever end-to-end. We present DistilVDR, a 524M end-to-end VDR system distilled bilaterally from a single 8B vision-language teacher under a pointwise cosine alignment loss. All supervision comes from the frozen teacher's embedding space, which was itself trained with relevance supervision, so the student objective needs no relevance labels, negative sampling, or contrastive term. We match VDR's text-query and image-document input asymmetry with an asymmetric encoder-only student that concentrates visual capacity on the document side and keeps the query side at 70M parameters. We release two variants that share the same encoders and training and differ only in the document encoder's visual-tile budget: DistilVDR-HiRes attains 61.74 average NDCG@5 on ViDoRe v1+v2+v3 (86.9% of the 8B teacher) and leads every reproduced sub-1B baseline on the high-resolution-sensitive v3 benchmark, while DistilVDR-Fast attains 59.98 at a 3 times smaller visual-token budget. Both variants store one million documents in a 15.6 times smaller index than the strongest sub-1B multi-vector baseline and index the corpus an order of magnitude faster. The code is available at https://github.com/Ryenhails/NanoVDR.

</details>


### [100] [ENTLORE: A Graph-Grounded Benchmark for Latent Organizational Reasoning in Enterprise Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10679)
*Akrin Zheng,Alexander Wu,Alaia Liu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: ENTLORE is a benchmark for enterprise QA that focuses on "latent organizational reasoning"—recovering implicit relations across heterogeneous business documents. Built from real enterprise data with audited truth graphs, it contains 2,341 documents and 907 questions. Even with gold document retrieval, 30.4% of latent reasoning questions remain unanswered, highlighting a fundamental gap beyond document recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-source QA benchmarks test composition of stated facts along predefined answer paths, rather than the recovery of implicit organizational relations that are absent from the corpus. Routine enterprise documents contain work by-products where required relations remain implicit across heterogeneous sources, necessitating "latent organizational reasoning" capability that current benchmarks fail to evaluate.

Method: The ENTLORE framework constructs benchmarks by reconstructing an audited enterprise world from three source types: routine documents, organizational tables, and operational records. Versioned organizational conventions certify derived relations in a truth graph, yielding complete golden answers and proof certificates. The release withholds private structure and target relations, exposing only the document corpus. The benchmark evaluates 56 model/access configurations across three question types: explicit lookup, cross-source composition, and latent organizational reasoning.

Result: Structuring the world as an induced entity graph or navigable knowledge base yields the strongest deployable results. Performance gaps are striking: with gold documents supplied, 30.4% of latent questions remain unanswered, versus 12.6% for explicit and 6.2% for compositional questions. This demonstrates enterprise QA depends critically on whether implicit organizational relations become usable, not merely on document recall.

Conclusion: Enterprise QA success hinges on making implicit organizational relations usable—a capability current systems lack. ENTLORE provides the first principled benchmark isolating this gap, showing that even perfect retrieval leaves substantial headroom on latent reasoning tasks. The benchmark and framework are publicly released.

Abstract: Enterprise question answering is framed as retrieving internal documents and generating grounded answers. Routine enterprise records, however, are work by-products in which required organizational relations remain implicit across heterogeneous sources. Existing benchmarks provide realistic multi-source evidence, but often materialize a predefined answer path and therefore test the composition of stated facts rather than recovery of a target relation absent from the corpus. We call the latter capability latent organizational reasoning.
  We introduce ENTLORE, a graph-grounded benchmark construction framework that reconstructs an audited enterprise world from routine documents, authoritative organizational tables, and operational records. Versioned organizational conventions certify derived relations in a truth graph, enabling complete golden answers and proof certificates. The aligned anonymized release exposes only the document corpus while withholding private structure and target relations. ENTLORE contains 2,341 documents from three source types and 907 questions spanning explicit lookup, cross-source composition, and latent organizational reasoning, evaluated across 56 model and access configurations. Structuring the released world as an induced entity graph or navigable knowledge base gives the strongest deployable results. Yet supplying gold documents still leaves 30.4% of latent questions unanswered, versus 12.6% and 6.2% for explicit and compositional questions. Enterprise QA therefore depends not only on document recall, but also on whether implicit organizational relations become usable. The benchmark, data, and code are publicly available at ENTLORE.

</details>


### [101] [Deciding When to Rely on Visual Information: Gated Multimodal Fusion in Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10700)
*Natalija Glisovic,Danica Kragic,Martin Tegner*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: VisGate introduces an adaptive gating framework for multimodal sequential recommendation that makes item-level decisions about when to incorporate visual signals, based on item embeddings and user context. The learned gate reveals that visual utility varies across items, increases under interaction sparsity, and correlates with visual distinctiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal sequential recommenders fuse visual and collaborative signals uniformly, treating visual features as equally informative for all items and users. The authors argue this is suboptimal: visual utility is not a fixed item property but a latent contextual variable dependent on both the item and the user's interaction history.

Method: VisGate employs an adaptive item-level gating mechanism conditioned on item embeddings and the user's current sequence context to decide when visual features should contribute. Visual representations are learned via a contrastive objective over sequential co-occurrence patterns, preserving complementarity with collaborative embeddings rather than forcing alignment into a shared space.

Result: VisGate achieves competitive recommendation performance. The learned gate reveals three key findings: (1) visual utility varies significantly across items, (2) visual utility increases under interaction sparsity when collaborative signals are weak, and (3) visual utility correlates with visual distinctiveness in semantically meaningful ways.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates the importance of fine-grained, context-aware fusion and modality complementarity in multimodal recommendation. It further shows that item-level visual utility can be both estimated and interpreted through learned gating behavior, turning the gate itself into a measurement tool for understanding when and why visual information benefits recommendation.

Abstract: Multimodal sequential recommender systems commonly fuse visual and collaborative signals uniformly, treating visual features as generically informative regardless of item or user context. We argue that visual utility, defined as the contribution of visual signals to recommendation quality, is a latent contextual variable that depends on both the item and the user's interaction history rather than a fixed item property. To model this variability, we introduce VisGate, a framework that makes adaptive item-level fusion decisions conditioned on item embeddings and the user's current sequence context. Visual representations are learned through a contrastive objective over sequential co-occurrence patterns, preserving complementarity with collaborative embeddings rather than aligning them into a shared space. Beyond achieving competitive recommendation performance, VisGate's learned gate serves as a measurement tool for understanding when and why visual information is beneficial. Our analyses show that visual utility varies across items, increases under interaction sparsity when collaborative signals are weak, and correlates with visual distinctiveness in semantically meaningful ways. Together, these findings highlight the importance of both fine-grained fusion and modality complementarity, while demonstrating that item-level visual utility can be estimated and interpreted through learned gating behaviour.

</details>


### [102] [TimeRoute: Time-Aware Modality Routing and Diffusion for Multi-Modal Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10983)
*Pengyu Zhang,Yangqin Jiang,Klim Zaporojets,Congfeng Cao,Paul Groth*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TimeRoute introduces a diffusion-based multi-modal recommender that dynamically adjusts modality fusion weights over time using a temporal-aware modal router and a FiLM-conditioned dual-stream denoising graph reconstructor to handle modality relevance drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Different modalities (text, image, audio) drift in relevance at different rates across temporal contexts, creating a modality time-scale mismatch. This mismatch causes users to need different modality proportions over time, and irrelevant modalities can inject outdated or misleading signals into recommendations. Prior work uses globally shared fusion weights, which fail to adapt to these temporal shifts.

Method: TimeRoute consists of two core components: (1) A temporal-aware modal router that maps each user's aggregated behavioral features to a personalized, time-dependent modality distribution, replacing static global fusion weights. (2) A diffusion-based graph reconstructor conditioned on temporal profiles via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), with dual-stream long-term and short-term denoising heads that suppress outdated modality edges before they enter the propagation graph.

Result: Experiments on TikTok, Amazon-Baby, and Amazon-Sports datasets show consistent improvements up to 9.8% in Recall@K, Precision@K, and NDCG@K over strong baselines across 10-seed paired tests.

Conclusion: TimeRoute effectively addresses modality time-scale mismatch in multi-modal recommenders by coupling temporal-aware modality routing with diffusion-based graph denoising, yielding significant performance gains across diverse datasets.

Abstract: Multi-modal recommenders fuse collaborative signals with item modalities such as text, images, and audio, but the usefulness of each drifts over time and at different rates. For example, chocolate purchases typically guided by textual ingredient cues can shift toward visual packaging and ambient audio around Valentine's Day. This modality time-scale mismatch gives rise to two coupled challenges: (1) users require different modality proportions across temporal contexts, and (2) less relevant modalities are more likely to introduce outdated or misleading signals into the recommender. We address both challenges within a unified diffusion-based recommender, TimeRoute. A temporal-aware modal router maps each user's aggregated behavioral features to a personalized modality distribution, replacing the globally shared fusion weights used in prior work. The diffusion-based graph reconstructor is then conditioned on the same temporal profile through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) with dual-stream long- and short-term denoising heads, suppressing outdated modality edges before they enter the propagation graph. Experiments on TikTok, Amazon-Baby, and Amazon-Sports demonstrate consistent improvements of up to 9.8\% in Recall@K, Precision@K, and NDCG@K over strong baselines across 10-seed paired tests. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TimeRoute.

</details>


### [103] [Sona Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11015)
*Sona Team,Alexandr Udeneev,Aleksei Krasilnikov,Alexey Nadtochiy,Andrey Semenov,Andrey Tsyrkunov,Anna Krivonos,Anna Lipkina,Artem Matveev,Daniil Burlakov,Daniil Leschev,Daria Tikhonovich,Denis Burshtein,Ekaterina Dmitrieva,Eugene Krofto,Grigorii Khlystov,Ilya Murzin,Kirill Golovko,Ksenia Sycheva,Leonid Dmitriev,Mariia Rozaeva,Mariia Ulianova,Mikhail Sandul,Nikolai Savushkin,Oleg Sorokin,Roman Odobesku,Semyon Panenko,Sergei Liamaev,Sergei Makeev,Vadim Shilov,Veronika Ivanova,Viktor Yanush,Vladimir Baikalov,Vladislav Dodonov,Vladislav Tytskiy*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Sona is a single-model generative recommender for Yandex Music that unifies candidate generation and ranking using a shared user representation. It replaced a 15+ stage cascade, achieving significant uplifts in active users (+4.53%), listening time (+6.30%), and likes (+11.42%) in live A/B tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Replace a complex, multi-stage production recommendation cascade (15+ candidate generators, pre-ranking, ranking models using hundreds of hand-engineered features) with a single jointly trained model that simplifies serving while improving recommendation quality.

Method: Sona uses an encoder that transforms chronological user engagement sequences into hidden states, shared by an autoregressive decoder (for next-token-prediction generation) and a Ranking Module. Training couples generation and ranking via joint next-token-prediction and distillation objectives, with a larger Teacher Ranker providing targets during training but not serving. No hand-engineered features are used — only logged event fields and learned item representations.

Result: In an online A/B test on Yandex Music's "My Vibe" smart speaker surface, Sona achieved statistically significant uplifts: +4.53% Active Users (primary metric), +6.30% Total Listening Time, +11.42% Likes. The Active Users uplift was 2.35× the improvement previously delivered by Argus (the prior strongest model).

Conclusion: A single jointly trained generative model can replace a mature multi-stage recommendation cascade while simultaneously improving recommendation quality on live traffic, as demonstrated by Sona's significant and incremental metric gains.

Abstract: We introduce Sona, a single-model generative recommender for Yandex Music. In an online A/B test, Sona replaced the entire production cascade, comprising more than 15 candidate generators followed by pre-ranking and ranking models that consume hundreds of features, including signals from large transformer models such as Argus and target-attention scorers, while significantly improving key engagement metrics.
  The architecture of Sona unifies candidate generation and ranking around a shared user representation. Its encoder transforms the user's chronological sequence of logged engagement events into hidden states consumed by both the autoregressive decoder and the Ranking Module. The next-token-prediction and distillation objectives jointly update the encoder, coupling generation and ranking through the same user state. Neither Sona nor its Teacher Ranker uses hand-engineered features; both operate on logged event fields and learned item representations. In the final Sona configuration, the larger teacher supplies ranking targets during training but is absent from serving, leaving the encoder, decoder, and Ranking Module as a single deployed model.
  We evaluate Sona in an online A/B experiment using live traffic from My Vibe on smart speakers, one of Yandex Music's largest recommendation surfaces. Relative to the production control, Sona produced statistically significant uplifts of 4.53% in Active Users, the primary metric, 6.30% in Total Listening Time, and 11.42% in Likes. These effects were incremental to improvements retained from preceding deployments. The Active Users uplift was 2.35 times the increment previously delivered by Argus, the strongest model deployed on this surface before Sona. These results show that a single jointly trained model can replace a mature multi-stage recommendation cascade while improving recommendation quality on live traffic.

</details>


### [104] [Self-Knowledge Retrieval Augmented Generation Framework for Patent Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11030)
*Jian Zhang,Songlin Lei,Zhuohao Yang,Bangli Liu,Ziwei Wang,Xufeng Weng,Gehan Amaratunga,Yu Lin,Hongwei Wang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A self-knowledge RAG framework that enables LLMs to autonomously extract key technical entities and construct hierarchical ontological structures from patent queries, integrating FAISS retrieval with generative matching to improve patent retrieval and matching accuracy without costly domain-specific fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional patent matching methods struggle with complex patent structures, dense terminology, and multi-modal information. Existing LLM-based approaches require expensive domain-specific pretraining or instruction tuning, incurring high labeling costs and risking catastrophic forgetting. While RAG introduces external knowledge, it fails to fully exploit LLMs' capacity to automatically parse patents and mine deep semantic relationships.

Method: A self-knowledge RAG framework that guides LLMs to autonomously extract key technical entities and construct hierarchical ontological structures from patent matching queries for query expansion and precise retrieval. The approach integrates FAISS vector retrieval with a generative matching mechanism, leveraging self-knowledge to enhance understanding of patent innovations.

Result: The proposed method demonstrates outstanding performance on real-world patent datasets, validating its effectiveness and application potential.

Conclusion: The self-knowledge RAG framework effectively addresses the limitations of existing patent matching approaches by enabling autonomous knowledge extraction and structured reasoning, achieving significant improvements in retrieval and matching accuracy without the drawbacks of domain-specific fine-tuning.

Abstract: Patent retrieval and matching based on large language models (LLMs) play a vital role in intellectual property protection. However, due to the complex structure of patent documents, dense technical terminology, and multi-modal information, traditional methods struggle to accurately identify subtle differences between patents. Existing LLM-based patent matching approaches typically rely on domain-specific pretrained or instruction tuning, which often entail high manual labeling costs and catastrophic forgetting. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods introduce external knowledge they fail to fully leverage LLM's capability to automatically parse patents and mine deep semantic relationships. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a self-knowledge RAG framework that guides LLMs to autonomously extract key technical entities and construct hierarchical ontological structures from patent matching queries, thereby enabling query expansion and precise retrieval. The method integrates the FAISS retrieval with a generative matching mechanism, leveraging self-knowledge to enhance the model's understanding of patent innovations and significantly improve retrieval and matching accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the outstanding performance of the proposed method on real-world patent datasets, validating its effectiveness and application potential.

</details>


### [105] [Role of Personality in Conversational Information Seeking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11164)
*Abdisalam Abukar,Junchen Fu,Chengli Zhai,Joemon M. Jose*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This study investigates how assistant personality (extraverted, conscientious, neutral), user personality (Big Five), and task type jointly shape conversational information seeking. A within-subject experiment (N=26) found that assistant personality is behaviorally distinct, affects trust and delegation in a task-dependent manner, and that users strongly prefer style choice over a single optimized personality—positioning personality as a context-sensitive design variable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for conversational information seeking, where dialogue shapes how users articulate constraints, ask follow-ups, verify claims, and gauge sufficiency. Despite this, there is little understanding of how user personality, assistant personality, and task context interact to influence these dialogues, motivating an empirical investigation of personality as a controllable interaction design variable.

Method: A controlled within-subject study with 26 participants. Assistant personality (extraverted, conscientious, neutral) and task type were experimentally manipulated; user personality was measured via Big Five. Each participant completed three information-seeking tasks (exploratory travel planning, comparative smartphone shopping, verification-sensitive health/diet) under all three assistant conditions. Data comprised conversation logs, behavioral traces, post-interaction questionnaires, an exit questionnaire, and Big Five scores.

Result: Assistant conditions were behaviorally distinct: the extraverted assistant produced longer turns, the conscientious assistant elicited higher user word share and more turns, and the neutral baseline sat between. The strongest finding was a significant task-by-assistant interaction effect on trust and delegation—preferred style varied by task. No single assistant personality was globally superior, but participants strongly preferred having style choice or adaptation.

Conclusion: Assistant personality functions as a context-sensitive interactional design variable rather than a globally optimizable system property. Designers of LLM-based conversational systems should support dynamic personality adaptation or user-selectable styles rather than pursuing a one-size-fits-all personality.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information seeking, where users find, compare, and evaluate information through dialogue. In this role, the assistant does more than retrieve or generate content: it shapes how users articulate constraints, ask follow-up questions, verify claims, and decide when an answer is sufficient for action. Yet little is known about how user personality, assistant personality, and task context jointly influence these interactions. We examine personality as a controllable variable in conversational information seeking and study its effects on user behaviour and interaction quality. We conducted a controlled within-subject study in which assistant personality and task type were experimentally varied, while participant personality was measured using Big Five scores. Twenty-six participants each completed three information-seeking tasks under three assistant personality conditions: extraverted, conscientious, and neutral. Tasks covered exploratory travel planning, comparative smartphone shopping, and verification-sensitive health and diet information seeking. Data included conversation logs, behavioural traces, post-interaction questionnaires, an exit questionnaire, and Big Five measures. The assistant conditions were behaviourally distinct: the extraverted assistant produced longer turns, the conscientious assistant elicited higher user word share and more turns, and the neutral baseline fell between them. The strongest effect was a task-by-assistant interaction on trust and delegation, with preferred styles varying by task. No global winner emerged, but participants strongly preferred style choice or adaptation. These findings position assistant personality as a context-sensitive interactional design variable rather than a globally optimisable system property.

</details>


### [106] [Are We Really Making Progress in Group Recommendation? Unmasking the Tie-Breaking Illusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11190)
*Song-Duo Ma,Pu-Jen Cheng*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper reveals that recent group recommendation methods suffer from evaluation bias due to sigmoid-induced score compression causing tied top scores, which makes standard top-K metrics unreliable. A tie-aware evaluation protocol is proposed, showing that many reported improvements shrink substantially under fair comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent group recommendation methods report strong benchmark improvements, but the authors question whether these gains reflect genuine advances. They identify a systematic evaluation bias: training-time score compression (via sigmoid before BPR) inflates ties in top scores, making deterministic tie-breaking at evaluation unreliable, thereby distorting HR@K and NDCG@K metrics.

Method: The authors revisit representative group recommendation methods (and baselines) on CAMRa2011 and Mafengwo datasets. They propose a tie-aware evaluation protocol that computes the exact expectation of HR@K and NDCG@K under uniform random tie-breaking. They also analyze the effect of the additional sigmoid as implicit margin smoothing and explore temperature-scaled BPR as an alternative that retains optimization benefits without severe tie inflation.

Result: Under tie-aware evaluation, many previously reported improvements shrink substantially, and the relative ranking of methods can change markedly. Temperature-scaled BPR retains much of the sigmoid's benefit without inducing severe tie inflation.

Conclusion: Tie-aware evaluation is crucial for establishing reliable progress in group recommendation. The interaction between score compression and tie-breaking is a previously overlooked confound that can produce misleading performance comparisons.

Abstract: Recent group recommendation methods have reported strong improvements on standard benchmarks, but it remains unclear whether these gains always reflect genuine advances in modeling group preferences. In this paper, we show that several recent methods are affected by a systematic evaluation bias caused by the interaction between training-time score compression and evaluation-time deterministic tie-breaking. Specifically, an additional sigmoid transformation before the BPR objective can greatly increase tied top scores, making top-K metrics such as HR@K and NDCG@K highly sensitive to how ties are resolved. We revisit recent representative methods and their baselines on CAMRa2011 and Mafengwo under both group and user recommendation settings, and evaluate them with a tie-aware protocol that computes the exact expectation of HR@K and NDCG@K under uniform random tie-breaking. Our results show that many previously reported improvements shrink substantially under tie-aware evaluation, and the relative ranking of methods can change markedly. We further show that the additional sigmoid may act as implicit margin smoothing during optimization, and that temperature-scaled BPR can retain much of this benefit without inducing severe tie inflation. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of tie-aware evaluation for establishing reliable progress in group recommendation. The code is available at https://github.com/songduoma/TieAwareGroupRec.

</details>

### [107] [Closed-Loop LLM Co-Pilots for Digital Agriculture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09949)
*Serge Kernbach*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a closed-loop framework where LLMs autonomously interpret multi-modal phytosensor data and control hardware actuators to optimize plant growth in vertical farms, demonstrating up to 35% faster production cycles and 67.9% energy savings through AI-discovered cultivation strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evolve LLMs from passive data analysis tools into autonomous agents capable of direct, closed-loop control of complex biological systems, reducing dependency on human-in-the-loop analysis and expert labor while improving the cost-to-value ratio in digital agriculture.

Method: A framework integrating a 49-channel phytosensor network (multispectral, electrochemical, dielectric modalities) with an LLM that (1) provides real-time natural-language interpretation of plant physiology, (2) evaluates biophysical data to trigger hardware actuators, and (3) executes closed-loop control for microclimate optimization, phenotyping, and controlled stress induction. Validated across vertical farm and single-plant setups, with production-scale agents performing multi-parameter optimization of biomass, chlorophyll, and energy use via modulated full-spectrum, 450 nm, and 660 nm lighting at 2-hour intervals.

Result: In minimal-time mode, the system reduced the production cycle by 35% versus periodic control. In energy-optimization mode, it achieved 18% energy reduction with only marginal time increase by exploiting physiological inertia via light pulses. Most notably, agents autonomously discovered a dark-induced chlorophyll accumulation strategy yielding 67.9% energy savings.

Conclusion: LLMs can serve as autonomous co-pilots for digital agriculture, transforming into direct AI-biology interfaces that lower computational and expert-labor constraints while enabling novel, unforeseen cultivation strategies.

Abstract: This study evaluates the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex biological systems, evolving from data analysis to autonomous, AI-guided experimentation. The framework is driven by data from a 49-channel phytosensor network, encompassing multispectral, electrochemical, and dielectric modalities. To enhance accessibility, the system provides real-time natural-language interpretation for both specialists and non-experts. However, its core advantage lies in the transition from human-in-the-loop analysis to autonomous control. Processing biophysical data, the LLM evaluates plant physiology and triggers hardware actuators to optimize microclimates, execute phenotyping protocols, or induce controlled stress scenarios. This closed-loop architecture establishes a direct AI-biology interface, enabling data-driven exploration of complex biosystems and ecologies. The framework was validated across three case studies, based on a vertical farm and a single-plant setup and deciphered complex micro- and macro-fluctuations in plant physiology. Agents in a production-scale deployment executed multi-parameter optimization, balancing biomass accumulation, chlorophyll content, and energy consumption. The LLM processed biosensing telemetry to modulate full-spectrum, 450 nm, and 660 nm lighting at 2-hour intervals. Compared to periodic control, the system in minimal-time mode reduced the production cycle by 35%. In the energy-optimization mode, it reduced energy consumption by 18% with only a marginal increase in cultivation time, exploiting physiological inertia via light pulses. Finally, the agents autonomously developed an unforeseen strategy of dark-induced chlorophyll accumulation, resulting in a 67.9% energy saving. This framework transforms LLMs into autonomous co-pilots for digital agriculture, improving the cost-to-value ratio and lowering computational and expert-labor constraints.

</details>


### [108] [SPOTting the Future: Lookahead Explanations for Deep Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09967)
*Tamar Gozlan,Claudia V. Goldman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SPOT is a model-agnostic, sampling-based framework that constructs interpretable finite-horizon trees from DRL policies by simulating action sequences, enabling inspection of action preferences and downstream behaviors beyond single-step explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DRL agents achieve strong performance but lack interpretability. Existing methods like single-timestep feature attribution cannot reveal how action preferences evolve over multi-step horizons or expose downstream consequences of decisions.

Method: SPOT takes a trained policy and an environment simulator, then builds a finite-horizon tree by recursively sampling actions from the policy, simulating successor states, and recording empirical action probabilities at each node. The tree captures the policy's action distribution and its propagation over time.

Result: Formal guarantees prove SPOT asymptotically recovers the policy's unique most probable action and characterize disagreement behavior under high-entropy policies. A case study in SUMO-RL traffic-signal control demonstrates that SPOT reveals policy preferences, alternative future trajectories, and downstream behaviors invisible to single-timestep attribution methods.

Conclusion: SPOT provides a principled, simulator-based tree representation that makes DRL policy behavior transparent across multiple timesteps, offering richer interpretability than static single-step explanations.

Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents achieve strong performance in complex environments, yet their decision-making processes remain difficult to interpret. We introduce SPOT (Sampling Policy Observation Tree), a novel model-agnostic, sampling-based framework for interpreting DRL policies. Given access to the policy and an environment simulator, SPOT constructs an interpretable finite-horizon tree by sampling actions and recursively simulating the resulting successor states. The tree provides an empirical representation of the policy's action preferences and their possible downstream evolution. We provide formal guarantees establishing SPOT's asymptotic recovery of the policy's unique most probable action and characterizing its disagreement behavior under high-entropy policies. We demonstrate SPOT in the SUMO-RL traffic-signal control domain. The case study illustrates how its tree-based representation can be used to inspect policy preferences, compare alternative future trajectories, and reveal downstream behaviors that are not visible through single-timestep feature-attribution methods.

</details>


### [109] [MIDAS: Mutual Information Disentanglement with Uncertainty-Aware Fusion for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09986)
*Yuhua Wen,Yingying Zhou,Qifei Li,Yingming Gao,Zhengqi Wen,Jianhua Tao,Ya Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MIDAS is a unified framework for multimodal sentiment analysis under incomplete modalities. It uses variational multivariate Gaussian latent variables, disentangles shared/exclusive factors via a minimax mutual information objective, and employs uncertainty-aware fusion using posterior variance as reliability weights. It achieves strong gains across multiple incomplete-modality benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal sentiment analysis methods assume full modality availability. Real-world settings often have missing or corrupted modalities, and current solutions relying on data imputation and heuristic constraints fail to extract task-relevant information effectively from incomplete multimodal data.

Method: MIDAS models each modality as multivariate Gaussian latent variables via variational inference, decomposing them into shared and exclusive factors. A minimax objective minimizes mutual information (MI) between shared and exclusive spaces (for stable disentanglement) while maximizing MI among shared spaces across modalities (for semantic alignment). An uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism uses posterior variance as a reliability indicator to adaptively weight latent features during integration.

Result: Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate that MIDAS achieves strong and consistent performance gains over competitive baselines across a wide range of incomplete settings.
