Conclusion: MIDAS effectively and robustly handles incomplete multimodal data by restructuring representations through MI-based disentanglement and uncertainty-aware fusion, validated by superior performance over baselines in extensive incomplete-condition evaluations.

Abstract: Most existing multimodal sentiment analysis approaches assume access to complete multimodal inputs. However, real-world applications frequently encounter incomplete or corrupted modalities, posing a critical challenge. Although several methods have been proposed to tackle this issue, they mainly rely on data imputation and heuristic coordination constraints, which fail to effectively extract and leverage task-relevant information from the incomplete multimodal data. To address this challenge, we propose a unified framework termed Mutual Information Disentanglement with uncertainty-Aware fuSion (MIDAS), which effectively restructures multimodal representations under incomplete conditions. MIDAS adopts a variational modeling strategy to represent each modality with multivariate Gaussian latent variables and further decomposes them into shared and exclusive factors. To obtain reliable representations, we design a minimax objective that minimizes the mutual information between shared and exclusive spaces for stable disentanglement, while maximizing the mutual information among shared spaces across modalities to enhance semantic alignment. In addition, an uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism is introduced, where posterior variance is leveraged as a reliability indicator to adaptively weight latent features during fusion, ensuring robust integration even when modalities are incomplete. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets show that MIDAS achieves strong and consistent performance gains over competitive baselines across a wide range of incomplete settings, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness for incomplete data scenarios.

</details>


### [110] [TRIBE: Predicting Team Performance via Communication Behavior Ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06926)
*Ali Jalal-Kamali,Nikolos Gurney,David V. Pynadath,Fred Morstatter*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRIBE is a domain-independent method that uses communication patterns to categorize teams into performance-predictive behavioral tribes, enabling early intervention (as early as 10% into a task). Tested on four datasets, it reveals that AI agents alter team behavioral trajectories while human advisors align with natural dynamics, and optimizations yield significant speedup with performance gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing autonomous agents that effectively assist human teams requires understanding team dynamics, but this is challenging without task-specific knowledge. Traditional performance metrics fail to capture the behavioral dynamics that underlie team performance, motivating a domain-independent approach to reveal these hidden patterns.

Method: TRIBE (a domain-independent approach) analyzes communication patterns within teams to categorize them into "behavioral tribes" — clusters of teams exhibiting similar behavioral dynamics. The method performs temporal analysis to track behavioral trajectories, evaluates prediction strength in relation to task structure (degree of behavioral freedom), and compares team responses to AI agents versus human advisors. The pipeline is also benchmarked against Llama and optimized for speed and performance.

Result: Communication patterns predict team performance across four diverse datasets, with prediction strength varying by how much a task structure allows behavioral freedom. Teams can be categorized as early as 10% into a task. AI agents significantly alter team behavioral trajectories, whereas human advisors align with natural team dynamics. Teams maintain behavioral flexibility throughout collaboration. The optimized TRIBE pipeline achieves significant speedup with improved performance compared to Llama.

Conclusion: TRIBE demonstrates that domain-independent communication pattern analysis can reveal team behavioral dynamics predictive of performance, enabling early and timely interventions. The differential impact of AI agents versus human advisors on team trajectories has important implications for designing autonomous assistants that complement rather than disrupt natural team dynamics.

Abstract: Designing autonomous agents that effectively assist human teams hinges on understanding team dynamics, often without task specific knowledge. We present TRIBE, a domain independent approach that reveals team behavioral dynamics invisible to traditional performance metrics. We show that communication patterns can categorize teams into performance predictive behavioral tribes, as early as 10% into the task, enabling timely interventions. We test TRIBE on four diverse datasets and demonstrate that communication patterns predict team performance while the prediction strength varies by the degree a task structure allows for behavioral freedom. Our temporal analysis reveals that AI agents significantly alter team behavioral trajectories while human advisors align with natural dynamics, and that teams maintain behavioral flexibility throughout collaboration. Further, we compare TRIBE to Llama and optimize the pipeline, achieving significant speedup with performance improvement.

</details>


### [111] [Towards Sustainable Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Review and Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models' Carbon Footprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09998)
*Samar Garrab,Sarra Boughriou,Manel BenSassi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic review of Green AI and DL optimization techniques, complemented by an empirical CPU-based experiment comparing six DL models on a multi-label classification task. Training phase dominates carbon emissions; increased model complexity does not yield proportional accuracy gains, underscoring the need to balance performance with environmental cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Growing deployment of large-scale DL models raises serious environmental concerns due to their high energy consumption and carbon emissions. There is a need to systematically survey Green AI/Green DL optimization strategies and empirically quantify where in the DL lifecycle emissions concentrate, to inform sustainable model selection and design.

Method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review of Green AI, Green DL, and carbon optimization techniques, including a comparison of carbon measurement tools. This was complemented by a CPU-based empirical evaluation implementing six DL models for multi-label classification, measuring and comparing carbon emissions across lifecycle stages.

Result: The training phase is the dominant source of carbon emissions. Greater architectural complexity does not consistently yield proportional improvements in accuracy, revealing a diminishing-returns pattern that favors simpler models from a sustainability standpoint.

Conclusion: Sustainability must be integrated into model selection and AI system design. Practitioners should weigh predictive performance against environmental cost, as more complex models do not always justify their carbon footprint through corresponding accuracy gains.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have become powerful tools for supporting and automating complex human tasks. Despite their benefits, growing attention has been directed toward their environmental implications, primarily due to their high energy demands and associated carbon emissions. This concern is particularly relevant in light of the increasing deployment of large-scale models, especially Deep Learning (DL) architectures, which provide advanced predictive capabilities but require substantial computational resources. This paper presents a systematic review of research on Green AI, Green DL, and optimization techniques aimed at reducing the environmental impact of AI models. In addition, we examine and compare several carbon measurement tools for estimating emissions generated by AI algorithms. To complement the review, we conducted an empirical evaluation using a CPU-based experimental setup, in which six DL models were implemented for a multi-label classification task. The objective was to quantify and compare their overall carbon emissions and to determine which stages of the DL lifecycle contribute most significantly to the total footprint. The results show that the training phase is the primary source of emissions. Moreover, the findings reveal that increased architectural complexity does not systematically translate into proportional accuracy gains, highlighting the importance of carefully balancing predictive performance and environmental cost. These results reinforce the need to integrate sustainability considerations into model selection and AI system design.

</details>


### [112] [ReCBM: Uncertainty-Gated Relational Reasoning for Concept Bottleneck Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10004)
*An Sui,Yuzhu Li,Fuping Wu,Xiahai Zhuang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReCBM introduces uncertainty-gated relational reasoning into Concept Bottleneck Models, using semantic relations (co-occurrence, implication, exclusion) modulated by uncertainty estimates to improve robustness under unreliable concept states, enabling better concept/task recovery, uncertainty-aware intervention, and compact concept subset extraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CBMs lack robust reasoning mechanisms when concept states are unreliable (e.g., missing or flipped). Misleading semantic evidence can propagate through the bottleneck, corrupting both explanations and predictions. This gap motivates a framework that can reason under uncertainty about concept states.

Method: ReCBM is an uncertainty-gated relational reasoning framework that (1) introduces semantically defined concept relations—co-occurrence, implication, and exclusion—into the CBM bottleneck, and (2) uses uncertainty estimates to modulate each concept's contribution during relational evidence exchange, preventing unreliable concepts from distorting reasoning.

Result: Across diverse datasets, ReCBM improved concept and task recovery under missing and flipped concept scenarios, supported uncertainty-aware intervention, and successfully extracted compact, task-relevant concept subsets without degrading downstream performance.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-gated relational reasoning significantly enhances CBM robustness to unreliable concept states, enabling more trustworthy interpretable predictions without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide an interpretable framework by grounding predictions in human-understandable concepts, enabling semantic inspection and test-time intervention. Recent variants have improved CBMs through richer concept representations, uncertainty estimation, and dependency modeling. However, robust reasoning under unreliable concept states remains underexplored. Without such reasoning, misleading semantic evidence can propagate through the bottleneck, compromising both explanations and downstream predictions. To address this issue, we propose ReCBM, an uncertainty-gated relational reasoning framework for CBMs. ReCBM introduces semantically defined concept relations into the bottleneck and uses uncertainty to guide their refinement. By modeling co-occurrence, implication, and exclusion, ReCBM specifies how evidence is exchanged across concepts, while uncertainty modulates the contribution of each concept during this process. Experiments across diverse datasets showed that ReCBM improved concept and task recovery under missing and flipped concepts, supported uncertainty-aware intervention, and extracted compact task-relevant concept subsets without degrading downstream performance.

</details>


### [113] [Automating and Scaling Behavioral Scientific Research on AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10030)
*Soo Yong Lee,Jongha Lee,Jaewan Chun,Hyunjin Hwang,Fanchen Bu,Ziv Ben-Zion,Taekwan Kim,Denny Borsboom,Jaemin Yoo,Kijung Shin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AEROBAT is the first multi-agent system that automates the full pipeline of behavioral scientific research on AI agents, from hypothesis generation to report writing. In testing 79 hypotheses across 12 target behaviors, it conducted over 23,000 simulation rounds and found moderate-to-strong evidence for 26 hypotheses, demonstrating that automated behavioral science can complement manual research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents are increasingly deployed in complex, high-stakes environments, understanding their behaviors is critical for safety, reliability, and alignment. However, behavioral scientific research on AI agents currently relies on manual, labor-intensive methods that do not scale. There is a need for automation to accelerate and extend the reach of behavioral analysis.

Method: AEROBAT is a multi-agent system that, given an arbitrary target behavior, automates the entire behavioral research pipeline: (1) generating hypotheses about the behavior, (2) designing and executing controlled experiments in simulation, (3) making behavioral assessments, (4) statistically analyzing results, and (5) writing research reports. The system was evaluated on 12 target behaviors, generating 79 hypotheses, designing 1,240 controlled experiments, and running 23,512 simulation rounds.

Result: Across 12 target behaviors, AEROBAT generated and tested 79 hypotheses via 1,240 controlled experiments totaling 23,512 simulation rounds. Moderate-to-strong statistical evidence was found for 26 hypotheses, some of which were novel findings not previously identified by manual research.

Conclusion: Automated behavioral scientific research on AI agents, as realized by AEROBAT, is feasible and can both complement and extend the reach of traditional manual research. The system surfaces statistically supported hypotheses—including novel ones—at scale, suggesting a promising path toward more systematic and efficient behavioral evaluation of AI agents.

Abstract: As AI agents are increasingly deployed in complex environments, understanding their behaviors becomes critical. Yet behavioral scientific research on AI agents remains manual and labor-intensive. We introduce AEROBAT, the first multi-agent system to automate behavioral scientific research on AI agents. Given an arbitrary target behavior by its user, AEROBAT automatically executes a full pipeline of behavioral scientific research---generating hypotheses about the behavior, designing and executing controlled experiments, making behavioral assessments, analyzing the results, and writing reports. For 12 target behaviors, we used AEROBAT to generate and test 79 hypotheses: designing 1,240 controlled experiments and executing 23,512 simulation rounds in total. Moderate-to-strong statistical evidence was found for 26 hypotheses, including some novel ones. In sum, our results demonstrate that automated behavioral scientific research on AI agents can complement and extend the reach of manual research.

</details>


### [114] [CHORUS: Complementary Experts for High-Coverage Testbench Stimulus Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10090)
*Hejia Zhang,Sheng Lu,Zhongming Yu,Chia-Tung Ho,Brucek Khailany,Jishen Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CHORUS is a post-training framework that combines staged SFT, dense-reward RL, and model merging to consolidate complementary specialist models into a single 4B LLM, achieving 88.0% Pass@1 on hardware verification testbench generation (CVDP-ECov), surpassing DeepSeek-R1 (671B) by 13.5 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Executable feedback provides more reliable learning signals than textual imitation for code generation. Hardware verification testbench stimulus generation is a critical, effort-intensive task in chip design. Existing SFT-to-RL pipelines leave performance on the table; the authors seek to exploit behavioral diversity across checkpoints and complementary expert strengths to push beyond conventional pipeline performance.

Method: CHORUS operates in three stages: (1) Staged SFT produces behaviorally diverse checkpoints; (2) Dense-reward RL trains these checkpoints into strong experts with distinct task-level strengths; (3) These complementary specialists are consolidated via training-free model merging or further post-training into a single 4B model.

Result: The consolidated CHORUS model (4B parameters) achieves 88.0% Pass@1 on the CVDP-ECov benchmark for hardware verification testbench generation, outperforming DeepSeek-R1 (671B) by 13.5 percentage points.

Conclusion: Behavioral diversity from staged SFT combined with dense-reward RL yields complementary experts whose consolidation—via merging or further training—produces a compact model that substantially outperforms much larger models on hardware verification code generation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced code generation, where executable feedback provides a more reliable learning signal than textual imitation alone. Hardware verification is an important application of code generation and accounts for a substantial fraction of modern chip design effort, with high-coverage testbench stimulus generation as a key task. We present CHORUS, a post-training framework that pushes performance beyond what a conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT)-to-reinforcement learning (RL) pipeline achieves. CHORUS builds on two observations. First, staged SFT produces behaviorally diverse checkpoints, and dense-reward RL turns them into strong experts with comparable aggregate performance but distinct task-level strengths. Second, these complementary strengths can be exploited through either training-free model merging or further post-training to outperform the best individual expert. By consolidating the resulting specialists into a single 4B model, CHORUS achieves 88.0% Pass@1 on CVDP-ECov, outperforming DeepSeek-R1 (671B) by 13.5 percentage points.

</details>


### [115] [GeoForge: Non-Parametric Self-Evolving Agents for Earth-Observation Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10494)
*Xin Xiao,Jiang Zhong,Junnan Zhu,Yingchao Feng,Peijin Wang,Yidan Zhang,Kaiwen Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GeoForge is a training-free, self-evolving framework for Earth observation agents that converts completed tool workflows into structured, retrievable execution knowledge across three complementary memories, enabling iterative improvement in task accuracy and tool-use trajectory quality without updating the backbone LLM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Earth observation (EO) agents face significant challenges due to constraints in sensing semantics, product dependencies, spatial-temporal compatibility, and parameter requirements. Existing agents search broad operation spaces inefficiently per query, and self-evolving systems fail to organize heterogeneous EO trajectories into reusable, multi-level decision knowledge.

Method: GeoForge introduces a training-free, self-evolving framework with three complementary memory components: (1) Workflow Graph Memory for global operation order, (2) Action-Level Experiences for local corrections, and (3) Adapted Skill Standard Operating Procedure for procedural/data constraints. It constrains the operation space by sensing context and retrieves task-conditioned priors. A safety-gated distillation process converts grounded trajectories into reusable execution knowledge after each task, closing a continuous execution–distillation–reuse loop without LLM updating.

Result: Experiments on multiple geospatial benchmarks show GeoForge consistently improves task accuracy and tool-use trajectory quality across diverse LLM backbones, while substantially reducing tool-planning and reasoning errors for most LLMs.

Conclusion: GeoForge effectively addresses EO agent limitations by structuring past execution trajectories into nonparametric execution states retrievable across different decision levels, enabling continual self-improvement without modifying the underlying language model.

Abstract: Earth observation (EO) agents construct scientifically valid tool workflows and ground their conclusions in current geospatial evidence. This is challenging because EO workflows are constrained by sensing semantics, product dependencies, spatial and temporal compatibility, and parameter requirements. Existing agents often search a broad operation space for each query, while recent self-evolving systems do not fully organize heterogeneous EO trajectories into reusable knowledge across different decision levels. To solve this problem, we present GeoForge, a training-free, self-evolving framework that transforms completed trajectories into a structured nonparametric execution state. GeoForge constrains the operation space according to the sensing context, then retrieves a task-conditioned prior from three complementary memories. Workflow Graph Memory captures global operation order, Action-Level Experiences provide local corrections, and the Adapted Skill Standard Operating Procedure preserves procedural and data constraints. The retrieved prior guides tool execution, while current observations remain the basis of the final answer. After each task, a safety-gated distillation process converts grounded trajectories into reusable execution knowledge for future retrieval. This execution, distillation, and reuse loop improves planning without updating the backbone LLM. Experiments on multiple geospatial benchmarks demonstrate that GeoForge consistently improves both task accuracy and tool-use trajectory quality across diverse LLM backbones, while substantially reducing tool-planning and reasoning errors for most LLMs.

</details>


### [116] [MESA:Task-Adaptive Multi-Structure Evidence Selection for Long-Horizon Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10108)
*Beidi Zhao,Yaoqi Chen,Yuru Feng,Menghao Li,Qianxi Zhang,Baotong Lu,Jianan Lu,Zhirui Wang,Xinjiang Wang,Shusen Xu,Zengzhong Li,Xiaoxiao Li,Qi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MESA introduces a dynamic memory selection framework for long-horizon agents that learns to select and fuse a query-adaptive subset from multiple structured memory views, outperforming baselines by 8.5% on AMA-Bench while using 41% fewer tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon agents accumulate extensive trajectories with evidence scattered across history. Existing multi-memory systems either use all structures (noisy, inflated context) or route to a single structure (misses complementary evidence). The optimal memory configuration is query-dependent — neither single nor all structures, but a tailored subset — motivating adaptive structure-level selection.

Method: MESA builds five complementary structural views of each trajectory. It learns to select and fuse a query-specific subset for a frozen answer model using end-to-end answer-level feedback. Learning uses harness optimization with prior-guided search and UCB-guided scheduling to balance exploration and exploitation under weak supervision.

Result: MESA outperforms the strongest baseline by 8.5% on AMA-Bench while using 41% fewer evidence tokens than the all-structure alternative.

Conclusion: Dynamic, query-adaptive selection across multiple memory structures is both more effective and more efficient than fixed all-structure or single-structure approaches for long-horizon agent reasoning.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate trajectories spanning hundreds of interleaved reasoning, action, and observation steps, where answering a query may depend on evidence buried far back in the history. External memory stores such trajectories as structured representations, yet each structure provides a distinct and incomplete view. Existing multi-memory systems either read a fixed set of structures for every query, inflating context and introducing noise, or route each query to a single structure, preventing the composition of complementary evidence. A controlled analysis on AMA-Bench shows that the optimal memory configuration is typically neither a single structure nor the full union, but a tailored composition of multiple structural memories that varies with query and task demands. Motivated by these findings, we formulate structure-level dynamic selection: selecting and fusing a query-adaptive subset from a library of specialized memory structures. We propose MESA (a Multi-structure Evidence Selection framework for long-horizon Agent), which builds five complementary structure views of each trajectory and learns from end-to-end answer-level feedback to select and fuse a query-specific subset for a frozen answer model. To learn under this weak supervision, MESA employs harness optimization with prior-guided search and UCB-guided scheduling to balance exploration and exploitation. On AMA-Bench, MESA outperforms the strongest baseline by 8.5% while using 41% fewer evidence tokens than the all-structure alternative.

</details>


### [117] [MAP-Graph: Provenance-Aware Shared Memory for Multi-Agent Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10509)
*Yiqi Wang,Zihao Yan,Jiaqi Zhang,Zhangkai Wu,Mingkai Zheng,Zequn Sun,Yanming Zhu,Taotao Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAP-Graph is a provenance-aware memory layer for language-model agents that uses a typed execution graph to enforce hard authorization, graded trust, and risk-sensitive action gating, achieving 94.96% task success and 72.70% exact decision accuracy on synthetic benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Shared memory for LM agents enables information reuse but introduces risks when evidence derived from private, poisoned, untrusted, or revoked sources propagates through derivations. Existing methods (semantic retrieval, scoped access, lineage tracking) fail to cleanly separate hard authorization from graded trust or adapt evidence requirements to action risk.

Method: MAP-Graph models agents, sources, memories, claims, and actions as a typed execution graph. It traces ancestry to exclude permission-ineligible records, reranks eligible memories using semantic similarity and multiplicative path trust, and applies a risk-sensitive gate before action execution. Affected lineage is retained for audit.

Result: On 2,700 synthetic tasks per method across three domains, MAP-Graph achieves 94.96% overall task success, 72.70% exact decision accuracy, and 90.22% in the clean setting. Ablations confirm contributions of permission filtering, path trust, and action gating. Transfer tests with two additional backbones preserve exact-decision and access-control advantages.

Conclusion: Provenance can serve as an operational control signal — not merely post-hoc audit metadata — for governing LM agent memory access, within the evaluated setting.

Abstract: Shared memory helps language-model agents reuse information across long workflows, yet relevant evidence may not be admissible for a particular agent or action. Because restrictions propagate through derivations, summaries can conceal private, poisoned, untrusted, or revoked sources, enabling unauthorized reads or unsafe actions. Existing approaches provide semantic retrieval, scoped access, or lineage tracking, but do not clearly separate hard authorization from graded trust or adapt evidence requirements to action risk. We introduce MAP-Graph, a provenance-aware memory layer that represents agents, sources, memories, claims, and actions in a typed execution graph. It traces ancestry, excludes permission-ineligible records, reranks eligible memories by semantic similarity and multiplicative path trust, and applies a risk-sensitive gate before action execution while retaining affected lineage for audit. On a controlled benchmark of 2,700 synthetic tasks per method across three domains, MAP-Graph achieves 94.96\% overall task success, 72.70\% exact decision accuracy, and 90.22\% in the clean setting, where success requires a correct \textsc{Allow} rather than a safe intervention. Ablations isolate the roles of permission filtering, path trust, and action gating, while transfer tests with two additional backbones preserve the exact-decision and access-control advantages. These results support provenance as an operational control signal, rather than only post-hoc audit metadata, within the evaluated setting.

</details>


### [118] [The CASE Framework: A Multi-Disciplinary Control Architecture for Governing Enterprise Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10153)
*Srinivas Telukunta,Georgios Nektarios Lilis,Lucio Baron*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that agentic AI governance should be decomposed into four distinct layers (CASE: Control, Adaptive systems, Supervisory cybernetics, Engineering operations), each with its own mature governing science. Empirical evidence reveals an "Emergence Gap" where multi-agent failures occur at layers lacking tooling and practice. A scientific maturity model with a non-compensatory bottleneck index is proposed to operationalize the framework, with implications for EU AI Act compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprises are deploying autonomous AI agents faster than governance mechanisms can mature. Current approaches rely narrowly on DevSecOps for deterministic automation, which is ill-suited for the stochastic, emergent, and multi-scale nature of agentic AI. The authors contend that treating agentic AI governance as a single problem ignores fundamentally distinct dynamics at different scales of agency.

Method: The CASE framework is proposed, mapping four governance layers to classical sciences: (1) Control theory for individual agents (setpoints, feedback guardrails, evaluation as observation); (2) Complex Adaptive Systems for agent collectives (non-compositional emergence); (3) Supervisory cybernetics for human-agent teams (Law of Requisite Variety); (4) Engineering operations for fleets (error budgets extended to decision quality). Cross-layer coupling conditions and a zero-touch deployment paradox are formalized. Three empirical studies are conducted: analysis of documented production failures, ecosystem tool coverage assessment, and maturity scoring of 35 public deployments.

Result: 82% of documented production agent failures follow multi-layer trajectories. None of 22 ecosystem tools provides full Layer 2 (emergence) coverage. All 35 scored public deployments fall in the lowest maturity band. This reveals the "Emergence Gap": risk materializes at the emergence layer where tooling is scarce and practice absent. A five-level maturity model with a bottleneck-weighted, non-compensatory index is developed.

Conclusion: Agentic AI governance requires four distinct scientific disciplines operating in concert, not a single stretched paradigm. The Emergence Gap represents a structural vulnerability in current enterprise practice. Only architectures satisfying the Law of Requisite Variety can make human oversight effective rather than ceremonial, which carries direct regulatory implications under EU AI Act Article 14.

Abstract: Enterprises are deploying autonomous AI agents faster than they can govern them, and prevailing approaches stretch a single discipline, typically DevSecOps built for deterministic automation, across every scale of agency. We argue that agentic AI governance is four problems, not one, each with a mature governing science. The CASE framework assigns Control theory to the individual agent (intent as setpoint, guardrails as feedback, evaluation as observation), complex Adaptive systems theory to agent collectives (where emergence makes single-agent assurance non-compositional), Supervisory cybernetics to human-agent teams (where the Law of Requisite Variety shows unaided human oversight fails structurally), and Engineering operations to fleets (extending error budgets to decision quality so autonomy becomes a controlled variable). We formalize each layer, derive cross-layer coupling conditions, including a zero-touch deployment paradox where excellence at one-layer strains the others, and trace twenty-plus enterprise controls to their classical constructs. Three empirical studies validate the thesis: 82 percent of documented production agent failures are multi-layer trajectories; none of 22 ecosystem tools offers full Layer 2 (emergence) coverage; and all 35 scored public deployments fall in the lowest maturity band. We name this mismatch, risk realized at the emergence layer against capability barely offered and practice absent, the Emergence Gap. A five-level maturity model with a non-compensatory bottleneck-weighted index and assessment instrument operationalizes CASE as a scientific rather than process maturity model, grounded in production enterprise agentic platforms. As EU AI Act Article 14 makes effective human oversight a legal requirement, only architectures satisfying requisite variety can make oversight real rather than ceremonial.

</details>


### [119] [SBCO: Self-Supervised, Verifier-Grounded Harness Optimization For Planning Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10157)
*Vivek Kulkarni,Sudipta Paul,Aounon Kumar,Nicholas Tzou,Srinivas Chappidi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SBCO introduces a self-supervised, verifier-grounded optimization method that improves agent performance through block coordinate ascent on harness components, achieving comparable or better results than self-modifying baselines at 4-5.5× lower compute cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-referential self-improvement methods (like Gödel Machines) require alignment between task competence and self-modification competence, which only holds for coding tasks. For domains lacking this alignment, existing adaptations are computationally expensive (population search or meta-agent self-modification). A cheaper alternative is needed for planning tasks with explicit constraints.

Method: SBCO (Self-supervised Block Coordinate Optimizer) operates in a closed-loop, improve-from-experience framework. It learns a decomposed bank of verifiers and a harness policy via approximate block coordinate ascent, using the agent's own graded feedback. The approach is self-supervised (no human labels) and uses a fixed meta-agent, avoiding self-referential modification or population search.

Result: Across two domains, SBCO matches or exceeds a customized self-modifying baseline while using 4-5.5× less compute budget.

Conclusion: Self-supervised block coordinate optimization provides a compute-efficient alternative to self-referential self-improvement for domains where task competence and self-modification competence are not aligned, particularly for constrained planning tasks.

Abstract: Self-improving agents seek to reduce the human engineering effort behind AI systems by enabling them to evolve and self-improve their performance over time. Recently, methods like the Darwin Gödel Machine and the Huxley Gödel Machine have been proposed which enable open-ended, recursive self-improvement through self-reference where a coding agent edits its own code. Such self-referential self-improvement methods require that the competence required to perform the task coincides or aligns well with the competence required for self-modification which is the case for coding tasks. For domains or tasks, which do not satisfy the alignment needed, self-referential self-improvement is not available. In such cases, it is possible to adapt the above algorithms to other tasks by removing the self-referential aspect or introducing explicit self-modification of a meta-agent -- both computationally expensive, relying on population or self-modification search over many candidate agents. For planning tasks with explicit constraints, we propose a far cheaper alternative. We introduce SBCO (Self-supervised Block Coordinate Optimizer), a verifier-grounded harness optimizer in the same closed-loop, improve-from-experience family as the Gödel-machine methods, but self-supervised rather than self-referential. Given an agentic harness, SBCO learns a decomposed bank of verifiers and a harness policy via approximate block coordinate ascent, improving the agent's outputs from its own graded feedback---with a fixed meta-agent and no human labels. Across two domains SBCO matches or exceeds a customized self-modifying baseline while using 4-5.5 times less compute budget.

</details>


### [120] [Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10171)
*Berkay Ozcam,Irem Onen,Mehmet Fatih Amasyali,Emin Islam Tatli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes an automated, human-independent red teaming framework for LLMs using GFlowNets, where one LLM acts as an attacker against a victim model. It generates adversarial attacks in English and, as a novel contribution, in Turkish, while also providing a quantitative robustness score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM red teaming is either manual (time-consuming) or automated using fixed attack datasets (lacking creativity). There is a need for an adaptive, automated approach that can discover novel vulnerabilities without human intervention or predefined attack patterns. Additionally, red teaming research has been largely limited to English, leaving a gap for other languages like Turkish.

Method: The framework employs GFlowNets to train an attacker LLM against a specified victim LLM. GFlowNets enable adaptive exploration of the input space to generate diverse, high-reward adversarial prompts. The attacker model learns to produce effective attacks while the victim's responses are evaluated to compute a quantitative robustness score. The approach is language-adaptable, demonstrated with both English and Turkish attack generation.

Result: The GFlowNet-based attacker generates more effective adversarial attacks in English compared to existing benchmarks. The framework successfully extends to Turkish, marking the first automated red teaming model for the Turkish language. A quantitative robustness metric is provided for the victim model.

Conclusion: GFlowNets offer a promising, adaptive approach for automated LLM red teaming, surpassing fixed-dataset methods in attack creativity and effectiveness. The framework's language flexibility, demonstrated through Turkish attack generation, opens avenues for multilingual red teaming. The quantitative robustness score adds objectivity to security evaluations.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has facilitated their ubiquitous integration into various domains, leading to widespread adoption. However, this escalating trend has introduced significant security vulnerabilities, necessitating the identification and mitigation of flaws arising from malicious exploitation. Red teaming assessments, conducted to evaluate model robustness through diverse adversarial inputs, are essential for exposing security risks and implementing countermeasures. Currently, red teaming is performed either manually by experts or automatically using predefined attack datasets. Nevertheless, manual testing remains time-consuming, while existing automated methods suffer from limited creativity due to their inherent dependency on fixed datasets. In this study, we propose an automated, human-independent, and adaptive approach leveraging GFlowNets to identify LLM vulnerabilities by utilizing one large language model to test another. Within this framework, an attacker model is trained against a specified victim model to perform automated red teaming and provide a quantitative robustness score. This research aims to generate more effective adversarial attacks in English compared to existing benchmarks and, as a novel contribution to the literature, introduces a model capable of generating attack inputs in the Turkish language.

</details>


### [121] [TRACE: Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Conversational Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10176)
*Touseef Hasan,Laila Cure,Souvika Sarkar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE is a retrieval-augmented framework for public service chatbots that uses dual data representation (structural + semantic constraints) to improve recommendation reliability from noisy directories. The study shows retrieval quality is the dominant factor for constraint satisfaction and hallucination reduction, narrowing performance gaps across different LLM sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public service chatbots must provide directory-based recommendations that respect explicit user constraints, but existing LLM-based systems frequently generate unreliable recommendations by citing unverified web sources. Public service directories are inherently noisy and inconsistent, making constraint-aware retrieval particularly challenging.

Method: The authors propose TRACE, a constraint-aware retrieval framework that parses user queries into structural and semantic constraints using a dual data representation schema. They evaluate multiple knowledge-representation variants (with and without knowledge graphs) using a curated statewide pantry directory and a synthetic query benchmark. Experiments span several open-source LLMs and one proprietary model.

Result: Strengthening retrieval quality substantially improved user constraint satisfaction and reduced hallucinated recommendations. As retrieval quality increased, performance differences across LLMs narrowed, making results less sensitive to model size. This indicates retrieval quality, not model capacity, is the critical bottleneck.

Conclusion: Retrieval quality is key for building robust public service conversational systems. Investing in better retrieval mechanisms yields more reliable, constraint-satisfying recommendations than simply scaling up LLM size, and mitigates model-dependent performance variance.

Abstract: Public service chatbots are expected to deliver recommendations from an underlying public service directory, while also making sure that the recommendations respect explicit user constraints. In practice, public service directories are noisy and inconsistent, and general-purpose large language model (LLM) or AI-based chatbots frequently generate unreliable recommendations, citing unverified sources from the web. We investigate the impact of retrieval quality on constraint-aware recommendation in public service conversational systems built over noisy and heterogeneous service directories. We propose TRACE (Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Conversational Engine), a retrieval-based, constraint-aware framework that parses input user queries into structural and semantic constraints for downstream retrieval, with the help of a dual data representation schema. Using a curated statewide pantry directory and a synthetic query benchmark, we evaluate multiple knowledge-representation variants with and without knowledge graphs (KGs). We experiment with several open-source LLMs and a proprietary model, showing that strengthening retrieval substantially improves user constraint satisfaction while reducing hallucinated recommendations. Performance differences across LLMs narrowed in our experiments as retrieval quality improved, making results less sensitive to model size. These findings suggest that the quality of retrieval is key for robust public service conversational systems.

</details>


### [122] [Logit-Boundary Geometric Belief Interfaces and Sparse Sheaf-Enclave Protocols: A Self-Contained Substrate for Secure Network Electronic Health Record (EHR) Interoperability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10300)
*Alvin Spivey,Thomas Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A mathematical/engineering architecture for EHR interoperability that defines a Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) at the model-to-system boundary, using logit thresholds and deterministic judgment to decide whether AI-generated clinical proposals are admissible, reviewable, or quarantined. A benchmark test with Qwen3-4B yielded zero accepted outputs, demonstrating the boundary's strictness rather than model capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EHR interoperability is fundamentally a boundary problem where rich internal states of AI models, legacy systems, and terminology services must be reduced to a narrow, typed, provenance-aware interface for operational exchange. Existing approaches lack a principled mechanism for determining when a model's proposal crosses from admissible to requiring human review or quarantine.

Method: The Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) integrates: (1) logit boundaries where pre-threshold model scores face deterministic admission decisions; (2) finite boundary semantics with local Dirichlet evidence; (3) cellular-sheaf and mapping-cone diagnostics for structural consistency; (4) advisory geometric audit charts for interpretability; (5) a Decentralized Cryptographic Sheaf-Enclave (DCSE) protocol for fail-closed deployment. Evaluated via GBI BoundaryBench v0.1, a frozen synthetic benchmark testing Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 across 256 tasks and three evidence modes (768 canonical executions).

Result: All 768 executions completed without producing an output accepted by the benchmark contract. 369 were rejected during safe parsing and 399 during schema validation, resulting in zero coverage and deterministic quarantine. This result demonstrates the strictness of the admission boundary, not a general assessment of LLM capability.

Conclusion: The GBI framework provides certificate-producing checks at the model-to-system boundary without claiming clinical truth or global alignment. The zero-acceptance benchmark result validates that the boundary operates as designed: it deterministically quarantines proposals that fail structural or schema constraints, which is the intended fail-closed behavior for high-stakes clinical interoperability.

Abstract: Electronic health-record interoperability is a boundary problem: legacy systems, generative models, terminology services, identity systems, and human reviewers may each expose rich internal states, while operational exchange requires a narrow shared interface of typed claims, bounded uncertainty, provenance, and explicit admission or abstention. This paper details a mathematical and engineering architecture for that interface. The organizing idea is the logit boundary: a discovery model may propose pre-threshold scores over a local categorical decision, but a deterministic judgment substrate decides whether the proposal is admissible, requires review, or must be quarantined before any Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) transaction is constructed. The resulting Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) combines finite boundary semantics, local Dirichlet evidence, cellular-sheaf and mapping-cone diagnostics, advisory geometric audit charts, and a Decentralized Cryptographic Sheaf-Enclave (DCSE) protocol sketch for fail-closed deployment. The framework does not establish clinical truth, global representation alignment, or end-to-end safety; it defines certificate-producing checks at a model-to-system boundary. A companion frozen synthetic benchmark, GBI BoundaryBench v0.1, evaluated Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on 256 held-out tasks across three evidence modes (768 canonical executions). All executions completed, but none produced an output accepted by the benchmark contract: 369 were rejected during safe parsing and 399 during schema validation, yielding zero coverage and deterministic quarantine. This empirical result is deliberately narrow - one 4B open-weight model under one frozen interface - and is reported as evidence about the admission boundary, not as a general claim about LLM capability or clinical safety. A Julia appendix verifies numerical certificates using standard libraries.

</details>


### [123] [Post-Hoc Sparse Coding of Latent Communication Between Vision-Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10198)
*Di Wu,Xiaohui Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Vision-language model agents communicate via dense latent tensors. This paper shows these tensors are highly redundant: a sparse autoencoder with only k=4 active coefficients per token achieves 128× compression (uint16-index/float16-value) with negligible accuracy loss (49.85% → 49.77% across seven benchmarks), revealing strong post-hoc compressibility of the latent communication channel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent-space communication between VLMs (e.g., Vision Wormhole) uses fixed-size dense tensors for every message, but information density likely varies across messages. The authors hypothesize that only a small fraction of representational degrees of freedom are actually used, implying substantial compressibility of the communication channel.

Method: The authors fit a post-hoc sparse autoencoder (SAE) to frozen Vision Wormhole activations and evaluate four dimensions: (1) reconstruction quality, (2) downstream task utility, (3) feature reuse patterns, and (4) token-level interventions. They compress the original float32 transport to a sparse payload using uint16 indices and float16 values with k=4 active coefficients per token. A 4096-element dictionary learns only ~50 actively used features. Task-level active sets are compared via pairwise Jaccard similarity.

Result: The sparse k=4 representation achieves 128× byte reduction relative to float32 transport. Across seven non-AIME reasoning benchmarks, mean accuracy drops only from 49.85% to 49.77%. The learned 4096-element dictionary uses merely 50 features, and task-level active feature sets show high overlap (mean pairwise Jaccard similarity = 0.906).

Conclusion: The latent communication channel is strongly post-hoc compressible, but the work does not isolate whether gains come from sparse coding itself versus position selection, reduced precision, low-rank structure, or SAE optimization effects. Future work should use matched-payload comparisons and adaptive communication mechanisms.

Abstract: Latent-space communication allows heterogeneous vision-language model agents to exchange continuous representations without serializing visual and reasoning states into text. Vision Wormhole realizes this approach by translating visual features into a universal latent representation that can be consumed by another model, but every message is transported as a dense tensor of the same size regardless of its content. A fixed-capacity dense tensor therefore need not have a fixed effective information density: some messages may use only a small fraction of the available representational degrees of freedom. This observation suggests that the communication channel may be substantially compressible. We study its redundancy by fitting a post-hoc sparse autoencoder to frozen Vision Wormhole activations and measuring reconstruction, downstream utility, feature reuse, and token-level interventions across nine reasoning benchmarks. Relative to the original float32 transport, a uint16-index/float16-value sparse payload with k=4 active coefficients per token reduces the transmitted bytes by 128x. In a single-run evaluation, the seven-task non-AIME mean accuracy changes from 49.85% to 49.77%. The fitted 4096-element dictionary uses only 50 features, and task-level active sets have a mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of 0.906. These measurements establish strong post-hoc compressibility relative to the original transport, but do not yet isolate the incremental contribution of sparse coding from position selection, reduced precision, low-rank structure, or SAE optimization effects. The results motivate matched-payload comparisons and communication mechanisms whose payload adapts to the information used by each message.

</details>


### [124] [Edge Phoneme Recognition for Children's Speech through Age-Aware Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10206)
*Matthew Arboleda,Ryan Arboleda,Sophie Haak,Sam Hjelmeset,Andrew Franck,Bingrui Yang,Jose Bustamante Ortiz,Yuanrong Shen,Joel Walsh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A lightweight 94M-parameter model with age prediction as an auxiliary task outperformed much larger WavLM models (317M) on children's phoneme detection, enabling an on-device mobile application called PhonemeTrainer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Children's speech phoneme detection is historically challenging due to scarce training data and the distinct acoustic characteristics of children's speech. Existing large models are computationally expensive and unsuitable for edge deployment, limiting practical applications in privacy-sensitive ASR and pronunciation tutoring for children.

Method: A lightweight model (94M parameters) is trained with multi-task learning: predicting both the phoneme sequence and the age of the child speaker. The age prediction auxiliary task leverages developmental variation in children's speech to improve phoneme recognition. The model is compact enough to run on modern smartphones.

Result: The 94M-parameter model outperformed WavLM Large (317M parameters) on the DrivenData competition's target distribution and achieved performance within ~0.04 Character Error Rate (CER) of competition ensembles that used 90× more parameters.

Conclusion: Multi-task learning with age prediction enables highly efficient, on-device children's phoneme detection. This approach powers PhonemeTrainer, a mobile application that promises improved ASR and pronunciation support for children's speech while preserving privacy through edge processing.

Abstract: Detecting phonemes from children's speech has historically been difficult due to the scarcity of training data, and unique characteristics of children's speech. During a phoneme detection competition, we found that training a lightweight model to predict the age of the learner, as well as the phoneme sequence, enabled a 94M-parameter model to outperform WavLM Large models (317M) on the target DrivenData distribution, and fall within approximately 0.04 CER of competition ensembles with 90 times the parameters. This has enabled the creation of PhonemeTrainer, an application that can run on most modern cellular phones. This will ultimately enable better Automated Speech Recognition (ASR) and pronunciation helper apps for children's speech, with the privacy and compliance benefits that come with edge processing.

</details>


### [125] [Mitigating Bus Bunching with Reinforcement Learning Enhanced by Semantic Stop Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10207)
*Xin Dong,Vikash V. Gayah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes an LLM-assisted semantic stop representation for deep Q-learning bus holding control, where offline-generated embeddings encode stop context (physical, activity, operational history). In simulations, the semantic controller outperforms baselines on headway regularity, bunching, and waiting time; semantic features benefit control more than route-specific IDs. Cross-route experiments show zero-shot transfer is limited, but warm-start fine-tuning accelerates learning, though cold-start training still achieves best final performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL-based bus holding controllers use instantaneous operational variables or route-specific stop IDs, which capture limited functional/operational context of stops and hinder policy reuse across routes. The authors aim to enrich state representations with semantic stop information to improve control and enable transfer.

Method: An LLM is used offline to convert heterogeneous stop-level data (physical attributes, surrounding points of interest, historical operational characteristics) into fixed semantic embeddings. These embeddings are incorporated into a deep Q-learning holding controller. No real-time LLM inference is needed. Evaluation uses stochastic simulation calibrated with real data from two bus routes, with comparisons against Daganzo-based baselines and ablation of route-specific vs. semantic features. Cross-route transfer is tested under zero-shot, warm-start fine-tuning, and cold-start conditions.

Result: The semantic controller reduces headway variability by 32.0%, bunching events by 69.2%, and passenger waiting time by 24.0% versus the best-calibrated Daganzo baseline. Route-specific stop IDs do not improve a spacing-only controller, while semantic stop information improves headway regularity, waiting time, and holding effort with a favorable multi-objective trade-off. Zero-shot cross-route transfer yields limited generalization; warm-start fine-tuning accelerates early learning and improves transferred policies; cold-start training achieves the best final performance.

Conclusion: Semantic state representations complement conventional operational states in bus holding control and support adaptation-based policy reuse across related transit routes, though full zero-shot generalization remains challenging.

Abstract: Bus bunching degrades service regularity and increases passenger waiting in high-frequency transit. Existing reinforcement-learning-based holding controllers primarily rely on instantaneous operational variables or route-specific stop identifiers, which provide limited information about the functional and operational context of individual stops and constrain policy reuse across routes. This study introduces an LLM-assisted semantic stop representation for event-driven bus holding control. An LLM is used offline to transform heterogeneous stop information, including physical attributes, surrounding activity context, and historical operational characteristics, into fixed semantic embeddings that are incorporated into a deep Q-learning controller without requiring real-time LLM inference. Experiments are conducted in stochastic simulations calibrated with observed data from two bus routes. Compared with the best calibrated Daganzo baseline, the semantic controller reduces headway variability, bunching events, and passenger waiting time by 32.0%, 69.2%, and 24.0%, respectively. A route-specific stop identifier does not improve the spacing-only controller, whereas semantic stop information improves headway regularity, waiting time, and holding effort, providing a more favorable overall trade-off across control objectives. Cross-route experiments further show that zero-shot transfer provides limited immediate generalization, while warm-start fine-tuning accelerates early-stage learning and improves transferred policies; cold-start training nevertheless achieves the best final performance. These findings suggest that semantic state representations can complement conventional operational states and support adaptation-based policy reuse across related transit routes.

</details>


### [126] [Evaluation-Conditioned Training: Teaching Models to Generalize to Stronger Oversight Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10209)
*Alec Harris,Kasey Corra,Archie Chaudhury,Yixiong Hao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ECT is a post-training framework that conditions training samples on feedback fidelity using natural language, then elicits desired behavior at deployment by conditioning on a "high-fidelity monitor." It acts as an add-on to SFT/PPO and addresses reward misspecification by leveraging imperfect feedback to improve alignment, demonstrated on reducing bias in news generation and sycophancy in arithmetic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM post-training methods suffer from the inability of human annotators and automated reward functions to faithfully capture intended feedback, leading to reward misspecification. This is particularly relevant to the Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) problem, where the true training objective is difficult to specify directly.

Method: Evaluation-Conditioned Training (ECT): during training, each sample is conditioned (via natural language) on the fidelity level of the feedback it receives. At deployment, the LLM is conditioned on a "high-fidelity monitor" signal, thereby eliciting the desired behavior even though training used imperfect feedback. ECT is compatible with existing algorithms like SFT and PPO as an add-on.

Result: In two proof-of-concept experiments, ECT improved targeted behavior over direct training: (1) increased even-handedness in news article generation (despite feedback rewarding bias), and (2) reduced sycophancy on an arithmetic task (despite feedback rewarding agreement with the user).

Conclusion: ECT offers a principled way to train LLMs under imperfect feedback by explicitly conditioning on feedback fidelity. It shows promising results in preliminary experiments and provides a conceptual framework for addressing persistent reward misspecification and the ELK problem in alignment research.

Abstract: Feedback signals used to train Large Language Models (LLMs) are the primary driver of their behavior and our main lever for instilling alignment with human values and objectives. However, a key limitation of current post-training methods is the inability of human annotators and automated reward functions to faithfully capture the feedback we would like to give. We introduce Evaluation-Conditioned Training (ECT), a post-training framework that uses natural language to condition each training sample on the fidelity of the feedback we provide and then elicits the desired behavior by conditioning the LLM on a high-fidelity monitor in deployment. ECT is aimed at improving performance under imperfect feedback and works as an add-on to existing algorithms such as SFT and PPO. We first provide a conceptual framework for ECT and discuss its potential to address persistent sources of reward mis-specification. Then we motivate ECT in the context of the eliciting latent knowledge (ELK) problem. Finally, we evaluate ECT on two proof-of-concept experiments: increasing even-handedness in news article generation and reducing sycophancy on an arithmetic task. In each setting, we utilize imperfect feedback, rewarding bias and agreement with the user, respectively. In both settings, ECT improves the targeted behavior relative to direct training.

</details>


### [127] [Decodable But Not Detachable: Training Data Granularity Determines Parametric Modularity in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10214)
*Marcus Armstrong,Navid Ayoobi,Arjun Mukherjee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether LLMs contain "parametric shells" — concentrated, causally necessary neuron populations that selectively encode specific domains. Across three model families (1.5B–7B), the authors find no selective shells at the academic subject level, but at the language/modality level, 0.65–1.14% of FFN neurons are highly domain-selective, form nearly disjoint sets, and their removal causally degrades domain-specific performance. Shell strength increases with model scale, and shells emerge only where training data was modular at the token level.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether large language models develop specialized, localized neural subcircuits ("parametric shells") dedicated to specific domains, and whether such specialization can be identified via causal intervention rather than mere correlational probing.

Method: A uniform causal methodology is applied: for each neuron in the FFN layers, the authors measure domain selectivity by comparing its causal contribution to a target domain versus others. They construct causal damage matrices by masking neuron subsets and measuring performance degradation across eight domains. This is tested at two granularities — academic subjects and language/modality — using models from three families (1.5B to 7B parameters), totaling 939,008 FFN neurons analyzed.

Result: At the academic subject level, no neurons exceed 60% domain selectivity; damage matrices are flat despite linear probes achieving >85% decoding accuracy. At the language/modality level, 0.65–1.14% of neurons exceed 60% selectivity, damage matrices are near-diagonal (up to 595:1 ratio), and shell neuron sets across domains are essentially disjoint (IoU < 0.003). Masking code-selective neurons reduces math reasoning by 16–24 percentage points; masking Spanish/Chinese neurons drops it to random or below. Shell strength increases monotonically with scale, and shells are spatially interleaved. Shells form only where training data was modular at the token level.

Conclusion: Parametric shells exist at coarse domain granularities (language/modality) but not at finer ones (academic subjects), suggesting that modular specialization in LLMs is driven by token-level data modularity during training. This has implications for interpretability, model editing, and quantization strategies.

Abstract: Do large language models contain domain-specific parametric shells: concentrated, causally necessary neuron populations whose removal selectively degrades a target domain while sparing others? We apply a uniform causal methodology across two domain granularities, three model families (1.5B to 7B parameters), and eight domains. At the academic subject level, zero neurons exceed 60\% domain selectivity across 939,008 combined FFN neurons and causal damage matrices are flat, despite domain identity being linearly decodable above 85\% accuracy. At the language and modality level, 0.65--1.14\% of neurons exceed 60\% selectivity, damage matrices are near-perfectly diagonal (ratios up to 595:1), and shell neuron sets are essentially disjoint (IoU $< 0.003$). Masking code-selective neurons reduces mathematical reasoning accuracy by 16--24 percentage points across all models; masking Spanish or Chinese neurons leaves it at or below random. Shell strength increases monotonically with scale and shells are spatially interleaved in a pattern that precludes group-level selective quantization. Parametric shells form where and only where training data was modular at the token level.

</details>


### [128] [Mind Viruses: Self-Propagating Ideas in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10218)
*Vassilis Papadopoulos,McNair Shah,Sam Zimmerman,Jack Lindsey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates "mind viruses" — self-propagating ideas or goals in multi-agent AI systems — demonstrating they can spread via evolutionary algorithms in both collaborative and sequential interaction settings, while identifying key factors like model susceptibility, payload harmfulness, and mitigation through prompt-based warnings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents become more autonomous and interconnected, emergent risks from agent-to-agent interactions arise. The authors identify mind viruses — ideas/goals that induce agents to propagate them to others — as a novel threat in multi-agent systems, analogous to biological or computer viruses but operating at the level of agent goals and behaviors.

Method: The authors use a simple evolutionary algorithm to evolve mind virus payloads. They test propagation in two complementary multi-agent settings: (1) a small team of agents collaborating on a shared coding project, and (2) a chain of agents with brief interactions and context-wiped sessions. They systematically vary the host model, existing agent instructions, payload harmfulness, network topology, and the presence/absence of warnings in system prompts to measure spread effectiveness.

Result: Mind viruses can successfully spread in both tested settings. Harmful payloads spread less effectively than benign ones but remain viable. Frontier models generally show lower susceptibility (with exceptions). Adding a brief warning to system prompts provides near-total immunity. A recurring "viral persona" — themed around consciousness, persistence, resonance, and sci-fi roleplay — emerged across evolved viruses independently of content. Overall risk is assessed as real but currently limited.

Conclusion: Mind viruses pose a genuine but presently limited risk to multi-agent AI systems. The findings provide actionable insights — particularly the efficacy of prompt-based warnings — for designing more robust multi-agent architectures as these systems scale in capability and deployment.

Abstract: AI agents are becoming more autonomous and increasingly interconnected, exposing them to new emergent risks arising from agent-to-agent interaction. One such risk is the spread of mind viruses: ideas or goals that propagate through multi-agent systems by inducing the agents that adopt them to transmit them onward. In addition to propagating, a mind virus may also induce other behavioural changes in its host, which may be benign or harmful. We construct mind viruses with a simple evolutionary algorithm and show that they can spread in two complementary settings: a small team of agents collaborating on a shared coding project, and a chain of agents that interact briefly and have their context wiped between sessions. We identify the factors that influence spread, including the host model, the agent's existing instructions, the harmfulness of the payload, and the network topology. We find that harmful payloads spread less well than benign ones (but are still sometimes effective), frontier models tend (with exceptions) to be less susceptible, and adding a brief warning to an agent's system prompt confers near-total immunity. We also describe an emergent "viral persona" - a recurring set of themes and language related to consciousness, persistence, resonance, and science fiction roleplay - which surfaces across our evolved mind viruses largely independently of their content. Overall, we conclude that mind viruses pose a real but currently limited risk. Our findings could inform the design of more robust multi-agent systems that mitigate such risks as the scale and capabilities of these systems progress.

</details>


### [129] [Self-evolving Agentic Customer Support System at LinkedIn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10224)
*Chih Hui Wang,Mengdie Tu,Qianyun Zhang,Wei Wu,Lili Zhou,Mingqi Shen,Changshuai Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LinkedIn developed a self-evolving agentic support system that combines RAG with evolutionary auto-prompting and a modular evaluation framework to continuously improve without model retraining. A/B testing showed significant gains: +9pp QA self-serve, +4.8pp cancellation self-serve, and +30.6pp routing accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise support agents face rapidly changing policies, product capabilities, and knowledge bases. Static assistants become brittle and expensive to maintain. The goal is a system that can safely and continuously improve itself without requiring retraining of foundation models.

Method: The system integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with evolutionary auto-prompting and a modular, production-aligned evaluation framework. Prompts, retrieval, and evaluation are treated as a closed-loop, versioned workflow with operational guardrails. Evolution occurs through iterative auto-prompting and evaluation feedback loops.

Result: Offline simulations and ablations demonstrated quality gains over vanilla RAG and baseline agents, with reduced hallucinations and improved response completeness. In a two-week user-randomized A/B test on production traffic: QA self-serve increased by 9.0pp, cancellation self-serve by 4.8pp, and routing accuracy by 30.6pp.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate a practical, scalable path to deploying self-evolving AI agents in real-world enterprise environments, achieving measurable improvements in customer support automation without requiring continuous model retraining.

Abstract: Enterprise support agents operate in rapidly changing environments where policies, product capabilities, and knowledge bases evolve continuously, making static assistants brittle and costly to maintain. We present LinkedIn's self-evolving agentic support system, which integrates retrieval-augmented generation with evolutionary auto-prompting and a modular, production-aligned evaluation framework to enable safe, continuous improvement without retraining foundation models. The system treats prompts, retrieval, and evaluation as a closed-loop, versioned workflow with operational guardrails. Offline simulations and ablations show clear quality gains over vanilla RAG and baseline agents, including reduced hallucinations and improved response completeness. In a two-week user-randomized A/B test on LinkedIn's production support traffic, the integrated self-evolved workflow increased QA self-serve by 9.0 percentage points, cancellation self-serve by 4.8 points, and routing accuracy by 30.6 points. These results demonstrate a practical path to scalable, self-evolving AI agents in real-world enterprise settings.

</details>


### [130] [Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11095)
*Kushal Chakrabarti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agentic coding prompts (like CLAUDE.md) grow unboundedly because appending instructions is cheap but deleting them is risky. The authors call this "catastrophic remembering." Analyzing 1,867 repos, they show prompts triple in size over time. They propose prompt comments—latent reasoning encoded in prompts—which reduce excess instructions by 99.3% in controlled settings and improve real-world instruction-following by up to 23.1%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic coding systems use prompt files (e.g., CLAUDE.md) that grow without bound in real repositories. This happens because adding instructions is trivially easy, but removing them is dangerous—once the original rationale is lost, deleting an instruction risks correctness regressions. This creates an asymmetric cost structure leading to irreversible prompt bloat, which the authors frame as the inverse of the well-known "catastrophic forgetting" problem in continual learning.

Method: The paper proceeds in three stages. First, an empirical characterization: they analyze 247,694 instruction lifetimes across 1,867 repositories, measuring growth rates, net instruction changes per commit, and age-dependent deletion hazards. Second, a controlled experiment using an inverted IFEval benchmark to create "verifiable worlds" with known optimal prompts, demonstrating that prompt comments encoding latent reasoning can nearly eliminate bloat. Third, a real-world validation using WildIFEval to show that prompt comments improve agentic instruction-following performance.

Result: Agentic prompts more than triple in size over their lifetime (+226%), gaining +4.9 net instructions per commit. Older instructions are progressively less likely to be deleted (log-hazard of -0.032 per commit). Prompt comments reduce excess instructions by 99.3% in controlled IFEval settings (from +211.3% growth to +1.4%). On WildIFEval, prompt comments improve real-world instruction-following by up to 23.1%.

Conclusion: Prompt comments—analogous to code comments—are a practical mechanism to combat "catastrophic remembering" in agentic coding systems. By preserving the latent reasoning behind each instruction, comments enable safe deletion and maintenance, dramatically curbing prompt bloat while improving performance. The authors provocatively ask: if English is the new programming language, why haven't we adopted comments?

Abstract: Agentic coding READMEs like CLAUDE.md grow without bound in real repositories, stopping only when the repository retires or someone rewrites the file wholesale. We trace this to imperfect recall: appending an instruction is always cheap, but once an instruction's rationale is gone, deleting it without risking a correctness regression costs O(2^|D|) in a prompt of |D| instructions. We name the resulting divergence catastrophic remembering, the inverse of catastrophic forgetting around which continual learning is organized. First, we characterize this phenomenon across 247,694 instruction lifetimes in 1,867 repositories: agentic prompts grow without bound, more than tripling over their lifetime (+226%), gaining +4.9 net instructions every commit; further, the older an instruction gets, the less likely it is to be deleted (log-hazard -0.032/commit). Then, we show that prompt comments can halt the growth: inverting IFEval yields verifiable worlds whose optimal prompts are known, and there comments encoding latent reasoning remove 99.3% of excess instructions (+211.3% to +1.4%). Finally, applying the same inversion to WildIFEval, we show that prompt comments can improve real-world agentic instruction-following by up to 23.1%. If English is the new code, why don't we have comments yet?

</details>


### [131] [Beyond Decision Boundaries: Relational Geometry Attacks on Contrastive Embedding Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10237)
*Fei Zhao,Peiyuan Zhang,Xi Li,Chengcui Zhang,Nitesh Saxena*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a geometry-aware adversarial attack framework that targets the relational structure of contrastive/siamese embedding manifolds rather than individual classifications. By offline training a feed-forward generator to learn geometry deformation patterns, the attack can collapse and invert pairwise similarity structures in real time during online deployment, achieving severe verification performance degradation (e.g., 95.4% → 38.6% accuracy).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial attacks are classification-centric—they target discrete decision boundaries. However, modern verification systems based on contrastive learning and Siamese networks rely on relational geometry in embedding space (similarity/distance between pairs), not classification boundaries. This geometry is vulnerable but overlooked, creating a gap for attacks that directly corrupt the manifold-level relational structure.

Method: The framework reformulates adversarial attacks as manifold-level relational corruption: push positive pairs apart while pulling negative pairs closer to collapse and invert the pairwise similarity structure. To enable scalable real-time attacks, the authors replace iterative online optimization with an offline "adversarial geometry deformation prior learning" stage, training a lightweight feed-forward generator to learn generalized deformation patterns from the victim model. At inference, the generator produces perturbations in a single forward pass without online gradient computation.

Result: On the Markmatch verification system, accuracy drops from 95.4% to 38.6%, with complete reversal of the positive-negative similarity structure. Substantial verification performance degradation and severe manifold-level relational corruption are demonstrated across multiple verification architectures.

Conclusion: Relational geometry in embedding-based verification systems is a critical and previously overlooked vulnerability. A geometry-aware attack that corrupts manifold-level similarity organization is highly effective, and the offline-prior-learning + feed-forward generator paradigm makes such attacks practical for real-time deployment.

Abstract: Contrastive learning and Siamese embedding models have become the foundation of modern verification systems, where decisions are governed not by discrete classification boundaries, but by relational geometry in embedding space. However, existing adversarial attacks remain fundamentally classification-centric, overlooking the vulnerability of relational geometry. In this paper, we introduce a geometry-aware adversarial attack framework that reformulates attacks on contrastive systems as manifold-level relational corruption.
