Instead of targeting individual predictions, the proposed framework systematically distorts similarity organization within the embedding manifold by pushing positive pairs apart while simultaneously pulling negative pairs closer, ultimately collapsing and inverting pairwise similarity structure. To enable scalable deployment, we shift iterative online optimization into an offline adversarial geometry deformation prior learning stage and train a lightweight feed-forward generator that learns generalized geometry deformation patterns from the victim model. Once trained, the generator produces adversarial perturbations through a single forward pass without requiring online gradient computation, enabling real-time online attacks against similarity-based verification systems. Experimental results across multiple verification architectures demonstrate substantial degradation of verification performance together with severe manifold-level relational corruption. On the Markmatch verification system, the proposed attack reduces accuracy from 95.4% to 38.6% while completely reversing the positive-negative similarity structure.

</details>


### [132] [Beyond Detection: Evaluating Defensive LLMs Against AI-Generated Social Engineering in Live Turn-by-Turn Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10239)
*Yuqiao Xu,Osama Zafar,Alexander Nemecek,Erman Ayday*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formalizes "trust-chain localization" to evaluate whether LLM-based defenders against generative-AI-powered social engineering can identify structural sources of risk. Testing five defender models on a 300-case online-housing corpus reveals that safe-looking behavior is insufficient: intervention rates vary wildly (0–96.3%), and protective action is frequently decoupled from correct structural diagnosis. The authors argue that live scam resistance must separately measure intervention, timing, structural localization, and false-positive behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI makes social-engineering attacks more fluent, adaptive, and scalable, heightening the need for LLM-based defenders that protect users during ongoing interactions. The core question is whether such defenders genuinely identify the structural source of risk (why a trust interaction fails) or merely react to surface cues. Existing evaluation paradigms risk conflating safe-looking surface behavior with genuine defensive understanding.

Method: The authors formalize *trust-chain localization* — identifying whether an interaction fails at one of four structural loci: actor authority, asset control, verification sufficiency, or transaction path. They construct a controlled 300-case online-housing corpus spanning 20 scenario families, legitimate cases, four structural failure modes, and three surface conditions. Five defender models are evaluated in both stateful turn-by-turn and one-shot static settings, yielding 1,500 model-case evaluations per protocol (3,000 total).

Result: No model produced explicit unsafe compliance, but intervention rates ranged from 0% to 96.3%. Protective action and correct structural localization were frequently decoupled — models sometimes intervened while identifying the wrong trust component, or recognized a structural failure without taking protective action. Asset-control failures proved a major localization bottleneck. Surface sensitivity varied across models, and live-static performance differences were model-dependent.

Conclusion: Safe-looking behavior alone is insufficient for evaluating LLM-based scam defenders. Robust live scam resistance requires separate measurement of intervention, timing, structural localization, and false-positive behavior. The trust-chain localization framework provides a finer-grained lens for auditing whether defenses understand *why* an interaction is unsafe, not merely that it appears suspicious.

Abstract: Generative AI makes social-engineering attacks more fluent, adaptive, and scalable, increasing the need for LLM-based de- fenders that can protect users during ongoing interactions. We ask whether such defenders identify the structural source of risk or merely react to surface cues. We formalize trust-chain localization: identifying whether an interaction fails at actor authority, asset control, verification sufficiency, or transaction path. We construct a controlled 300-case online-housing corpus spanning 20 scenario families, legitimate cases, four structural failure modes, and three surface conditions. Five defender models are evaluated on the same corpus in state- ful turn-by-turn and one-shot static settings, yielding 1,500 model-case evaluations per protocol and 3,000 in total. No model produced explicit unsafe compliance, yet defensive effectiveness varied sharply: intervention rates ranged from 0% to 96.3%. Protective action and correct structural localization were frequently decoupled, with models sometimes intervening while identifying the wrong trust component or recognizing a structural failure without taking protective action. Asset-control failures were a major localization bottleneck, surface sensitivity varied across models, and live-static differences were model-dependent. These findings show that safe-looking behavior alone is insufficient; live scam resistance must separately measure intervention, timing, structural localization, and false-positive behavior.

</details>


### [133] [Interpreting Language Model Hidden States at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10260)
*Jordan Pettyjohn,Mansi Sakarvadia,Nathaniel Hudson,Daniel McKenzie,Kyle Chard,Ian Foster*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OmniLens introduces a scalable lens framework for interpreting LLMs by combining low-rank translators and Subset-KL training, enabling dense, model-wide activation analysis on LLaMA-3.3-70B at a fraction of prior costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing trained-lens methods are prohibitively expensive: affine translators scale quadratically with model width and full-vocabulary KL training dominates memory, restricting prior work to models ≤20B parameters and narrow component types.

Method: OmniLens employs two independent scaling techniques: (1) low-rank translators that make parameter growth linear in model width (up to 98.4% reduction), and (2) Subset-KL training with a Top-k mode for memory savings (up to 70%) and an importance-sampled variant preserving unbiased full-KL gradients. These allow a dense ensemble of 482 lenses across all component types (residual stream, attention, MLP) on LLaMA-3.3-70B.

Result: OmniLens achieves 6x the coverage of residual-stream-only designs at the same depth. Model-wide analysis reveals that components where a behavior is most visible are not necessarily those where intervention is most effective, and the most effective interventions lie outside the attention heads studied in prior lens work. Three case studies (prompt-injection detection, multi-hop memory injection, toxicity localization) reproduce key published results at substantially lower cost.

Conclusion: OmniLens demonstrates that scalable, model-wide lens-based interpretability is feasible on large-scale LLMs, enabling richer causal insights by covering all component types rather than cherry-picked subsets.

Abstract: Lens methods interpret large language models (LLMs) by mapping intermediate activations to the output vocabulary, revealing how next-token predictions develop through the network. Trained lenses remain expensive: affine-translator parameters grow quadratically with model width, while exact, full-vocabulary Kullback--Leibler (KL) training dominates memory. Consequently, prior trained lenses have been applied to models of at most 20B parameters and remain tied to particular component types. We present OmniLens, which applies a single lens family to any model-width activation, whether residual stream, attention, or MLP, and combines two independent scaling techniques. First, low-rank translators make per-lens parameter growth linear in model width and reduce trainable parameters by up to 98.4%. Second, Subset-KL materializes only selected vocabulary logits: its Top-k mode cuts peak training memory by up to 70%, while its importance-sampled variant retains unbiased stochastic gradients for the full KL. These savings enable a dense ensemble of 482 lenses for LLaMA-3.3-70B, providing 6x the coverage of a residual-stream design at the same depth. Model-wide coverage then reveals what single-component lenses cannot: the components where a behavior is most visible need not be those where intervention is most effective, and the most effective interventions lie outside the attention heads examined by prior lens studies. Across three case studies (prompt-injection detection, multi-hop memory injection, and toxicity localization), OmniLens reproduces key published results at substantially lower cost.

</details>


### [134] [Neuroevolution Arena: Nested Ecological Evaluation of Update-and-Inheritance Regimes across Neural Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10323)
*Yuxu Ge,Yifei Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Neuroevolution Arena, a GPU-accelerated platform for evaluating neural-network controllers in spatial ecological settings. Using a nested evaluation protocol with three update regimes and two architectures over 50,000 generations, the study finds that training fitness rankings poorly predict ecological performance, with winners varying across artifacts and contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Competitive artificial-life systems often rank trained controllers inconsistently between training and ecological evaluation. The authors aim to expose rather than conceal sources of variation arising from training-run artifacts versus evaluation contexts, addressing a gap in how neuroevolution studies report and interpret controller performance.

Method: The authors present Neuroevolution Arena with an audit-tracked nested evaluation protocol. Three update-and-inheritance regimes (EvoEvo, EvoRL, RLRL) are crossed with two neural architectures, run for 50,000 generations across three independent training runs per condition (18 total runs). One elite controller per run enters a frozen-evaluation design with 198 computational jobs. Pairwise outcomes are assessed across three seed-defined ecological contexts (two cooperation-permitting, one attack-permitting) within aligned training-run blocks, with n=3 independent runs per condition.

Result: RL-enabled regimes (EvoRL, RLRL) achieve higher recorded training fitness than EvoEvo, but pairwise ecological outcomes reveal architecture-conditioned majority patterns and substantial artifact dependence. Six-way winners differ across artifacts and contexts, and the prespecified survival endpoint exhibits a complete floor effect.

Conclusion: The nested protocol effectively separates training-run artifacts from evaluation contexts, demonstrating that training fitness is an unreliable proxy for ecological performance. The study advocates for evaluation designs that expose rather than conceal the distinct sources of variation in neuroevolution research.

Abstract: Competitive artificial-life systems can rank trained controllers differently under training and ecological evaluation. We present Neuroevolution Arena, a GPU-accelerated spatial ecology of independently parameterized neural-network cells, and an audit-tracked nested evaluation protocol. Three implementation-specific update-and-inheritance regimes (EvoEvo, EvoRL, and RLRL) are crossed with two neural architectures for 50,000 generations in three independent training runs per condition. One saved elite-controller artifact from each of the 18 runs enters an aligned-run frozen-evaluation design comprising 198 computational jobs. Pairwise effects average three seed-defined ecological contexts (two cooperation-permitting and one attack-permitting) within each aligned training-run block; the independent level remains n = 3 runs per condition. RL-enabled regimes attain higher recorded training fitness than EvoEvo, whereas pairwise outcomes show architecture-conditioned majority patterns and substantial artifact dependence. Six-way winners vary across artifacts and contexts, and the prespecified survival endpoint has a complete floor. We contribute a nested protocol that separates training-run artifacts from evaluation contexts and exposes, rather than conceals, their different sources of variation.

</details>


### [135] [Toward a Theory of Value in AI Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10327)
*Andrew Smart,Shazeda Ahmed,Jackie Kay,Jimmy Tobin,Kris Shrishak,Abeba Birhane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes 94 AI value alignment research papers, finding that most fail to define "human values," instead relying on preferences as a reductive proxy. This risks collapsing complex cultural concepts into binary choices. The authors warn that the shift toward synthetic data and autoraters may foreclose alternative methods for contesting and enacting values in foundation models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To critically examine how the AI value alignment field conceives of, operationalizes, and evaluates "human values," given that vague or unexamined conceptions of values can undermine alignment efforts and mask important philosophical commitments.

Method: Annotation and qualitative analysis of 94 value alignment research papers to discern their implicit theory of values, examining definitions (or lack thereof), technical operationalization, and evaluation practices.

Result: The majority of papers do not define values; they overwhelmingly rely on preferences as a stand-in, reducing culturally situated concepts to binary choices. A trend toward synthetic data and autorater approaches for alignment and evaluation risks closing off alternative, contestatory methods for enacting values.

Conclusion: Making the philosophical commitments underlying AI value alignment explicit is essential for bringing specificity and underrepresented perspectives to the debate on whether and how AI can address human values.

Abstract: Can AI systems be aligned to human values? The popularization of large language models (LLMs) and multi-modal foundation models has seen a rise in harms spanning from toxic speech and hallucinations to AI agents executing unauthorized actions. Within the field of AI safety, these harmful instances are often framed as the alignment problem, or of models being misaligned with human values. Researchers have responded by pursuing applied and theoretical AI value alignment efforts, often without specifying what they mean by human values. How does the field of AI value alignment conceive of human values? How are these conceptions of values technically operationalized and evaluated? What does the emergent theory of value from this field signify for the future of AI? We annotated 94 value alignment research papers to discern their implicit theory of values in AI. The majority do not define values, relying heavily on preferences as a stand in that runs the risk of reducing complex culturally situated concepts down to binary choices. As researchers dispense with using human annotators for model training and evaluation, turning instead to synthetic data and autorater approaches to aligning and evaluating models, we identify the potential to close off alternative methods for contesting and enacting values in foundation models. In making AI value alignments philosophical commitments explicit, we seek to bring great specificity and under explored perspectives in the debate on whether and how AI can address human values.

</details>


### [136] [Hierarchical Compositionality for An Assistive AI Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10330)
*Tianyi Fu,Mohan Sridharan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hierarchical compositional architecture for AI agents that resolves referential ambiguity by combining human-validated semantic feature norms, compositional hierarchies learned from interaction history, and heuristic reasoning over domain axioms, semantic compatibility, salience, and user preferences—consistently outperforming data-driven baselines while adapting to individual user profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLM-based AI agents are resource-intensive, opaque, and prone to arbitrary decisions in novel situations. The authors aim to revisit foundational AI principles—particularly hierarchical compositionality and heuristic reasoning—that are underutilized in current methods, applying them to the fundamental problem of referential ambiguity in human-agent interaction.

Method: Domain objects are represented using primitive attributes from human-validated semantic feature norms. A hierarchical combination of attributes and concepts is automatically identified from limited observed interaction history. The agent disambiguates references by reasoning over this compositional hierarchy, domain dynamics axioms, semantic compatibility models, session salience, and user-specific thematic preferences, requesting human clarification when confidence is insufficient.

Result: The proposed approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data-driven baselines and demonstrates effective adaptation to specific user profiles.

Conclusion: Hierarchical compositionality combined with heuristic reasoning provides a principled, transparent, and effective alternative to purely data-driven methods for referential disambiguation in assistive AI agents, enabling user-specific adaptation without the resource and opacity costs of large-scale models.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly being developed to assist humans in various applications, and Large Language Models and other deep network architectures are considered to be state of the art for such agents. These methods are impressive stochastic predictors, but they are resource-hungry, opaque, and known to make arbitrary decisions in novel situations due to the narrow set of underlying representation and processing choices. Our work seeks to explore the design of architectures for such AI agents based on core principles that can be traced back to the early pioneers of AI but are not fully utilized in modern AI methods. We do so in this paper in the context of the core problem of AI agents addressing ambiguity in the objects being referred to by the human participants. Humans address such ambiguity by heuristically leveraging compositional knowledge of domain context and the preferences of the other human participants. Drawing inspiration from this observation, we describe an architecture that embeds the principle of hierarchical compositionality and uses simple heuristics to achieve the desired disambiguation. Specifically, domain objects are represented in terms of primitive attributes drawn from human-validated semantic feature norms, and a hierarchical combination of attributes and concepts automatically identified from a limited observed history of interactions of an assistive agent with specific users. The assistive agent then achieves the desired disambiguation by reasoning with knowledge of this compositional hierarchy; axioms governing domain dynamics; and models of semantic compatibility, session salience, and user-specific thematic preference, requesting human clarification when necessary. Experiments show that our approach consistently outperforms state of the art data-driven baselines, supporting adaptation to specific user profiles.

</details>


### [137] [Nutrition Data Infrastructure for the AI Era: Operationalizing FAIR for Agent-Mediated Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10363)
*Lin Liao,Peng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NDS is a FAIR-compliant infrastructure that resolves data ambiguities in nutrition research, enabling AI agents to perform auditable, reproducible analyses through description resolution, typed crosswalks, and versioned machine-readable interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents can accelerate nutrition research but are hampered by ambiguities in underlying data—identity (which dataset version?), semantic (what does a field mean?), and release (which release is being used?)—making analyses non-reproducible and non-auditable.

Method: NDS operationalizes FAIR principles through three mechanisms: (1) description resolution for release-specific record findability, (2) typed crosswalks that connect independently released resources with explicit semantic contracts, and (3) machine-readable interfaces exposing versioned sources and crosswalks. Evaluation uses food-description benchmarks, external/blinded crosswalk assessments, and a person-level glycemic-index reproducibility experiment comparing pinned NDS inputs against open-web reconstruction.

Result: NDS achieves strong held-out accuracy on food-description benchmarks, outperforms the best published LM result on NutriBench, produces defensible crosswalk links while rejecting unsupported mappings, and yields identical outputs across models and repeated runs in the glycemic-index analysis—unlike unstable open-web reconstruction.

Conclusion: Agent-mediated nutrition research fundamentally requires a new class of data infrastructure that solves data identity, search, and crosswalk—FAIR alone is insufficient without operationalization for machine agents.

Abstract: AI agents can accelerate nutrition research, but their analyses inherit the identity, semantic, and release ambiguities of the underlying data. We present Nutrition Data Service (NDS), source-preserving infrastructure that operationalizes FAIR for automated use: description resolution makes release-specific records findable; typed crosswalks connect independently released resources; machine-readable interfaces expose versioned sources and crosswalks, making analyses by AI agents replayable and auditable. On food-description benchmarks, NDS shows strong held-out accuracy and outperforms the best published language-model result on NutriBench. External and blinded crosswalk evaluations show that its typed contract favors defensible links and rejects unsupported mappings. In a person-level glycemic-index analysis, pinned NDS inputs produce identical outputs across models and repeated runs, while open-web reconstruction remains unstable. The central result is that agent-mediated nutrition research requires a new data infrastructure for data identity, search, and crosswalk.

</details>


### [138] [DSAgentBench: Can Agents Automate End-to-End Data-Science Workflows in Real Computer Environments?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10366)
*Mizanur Rahman,Mohammed Saidul Islam,Ridwan Mahbub,Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar,Shafiq Joty,Enamul Hoque Prince*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSAgentBench is the first benchmark for evaluating AI agents on end-to-end data-science workflows in real computer environments. It comprises 275 tasks spanning the full data-science lifecycle and uses a deterministic evaluator for analytical correctness. The best model (Claude-4.6-Sonnet) achieves only 56.70% success, while all open-source agents fall below 1%, revealing a large capability gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks lack real-computer interaction and fail to evaluate whether agents can execute complete, multi-stage, multi-tool data-science workflows in realistic operating environments. They do not capture the coordinated use of notebooks, IDEs, terminals, browsers, and databases that real-world data science demands.

Method: The authors introduce DSAgentBench, a benchmark with 275 diverse tasks covering the entire data-science lifecycle (wrangling, exploration, modeling, visualization, validation). Each task requires grounding decisions in intermediate outputs and coordinated multi-tool use. Evaluation uses a deterministic evaluator that verifies analytical correctness, visual outputs, and model performance—not merely code execution.

Result: Experiments with 15 closed- and open-source models show Claude-4.6-Sonnet as the strongest at 56.70% task success. All open-source agents remain below 1%, frequently failing at tool orchestration, OS grounding, and multi-step reasoning.

Conclusion: A substantial capability gap exists between current agentic systems and real-world data-science workflows. DSAgentBench provides a foundation for developing grounded, verifiable, autonomous data-science agents.

Abstract: Real-world data science involves long-horizon workflows that span data wrangling, exploration, modeling, visualization, and validation, and require coordinated use of tools such as notebooks, IDEs, terminals, browsers, and databases within real operating environments. Yet existing benchmarks lack real-computer interaction and do not evaluate whether agents can execute complete end-to-end data-science workflows in realistic computing environments, failing to capture the multi-stage, multi-tool nature of data-science practice. We introduce DSAgentBench, the first benchmark to evaluate whether agents can automate full data-science workflows inside real computer environments. DSAgentBench contains 275 diverse tasks covering the entire data-science life-cycle, reflecting the complexity and tool coordination required in practice. Each task requires grounding decisions in intermediate outputs and coordinated tool use, and includes a deterministic evaluator that verifies analytical correctness, visual outputs, and model performance rather than code-only execution. Our extensive experiments with 15 closed- and open-source models show that even the strongest agent, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, achieves only 56.70% task success, while all open-source agents remain below 1%, frequently failing at tool orchestration, OS grounding, and multi-step reasoning. These results reveal a substantial capability gap between current agentic systems and real data-science workflows, positioning DSAgentBench as a foundation for developing grounded, verifiable, autonomous data-science agents. We release DSAgentBench at https://github.com/vis-nlp/DSAgentBench.

</details>


### [139] [Hidden in Plain Sight: Diffusion-Based Unrestricted Robotic Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10393)
*Jiahui Han,Yuhui Yao,Xin Wang,Jiafei Cao,Mingxuan Zhang,Danfeng Shan,Huiqi Deng,Guanchu Wang,Xia Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DURA is a diffusion-based adversarial attack that generates visually natural patches to manipulate VLA models, working in both white-box and black-box settings, exposing safety risks in physically deployed robotic systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing attacks on VLA models rely on pixel-space perturbations or white-box access, producing noticeable artifacts and limiting real-world deployability. The adversarial robustness of VLA models in physical robotic systems remains underexplored, posing safety risks.

Method: DURA leverages a pretrained diffusion model's latent trajectory to optimize adversarial patches that appear visually natural. It supports both white-box and black-box settings; the black-box variant requires only predicted actions from the victim model. The attack steers the robot toward attacker-specified target actions.

Result: Extensive simulation and real-world physical experiments demonstrate DURA consistently outperforms existing adversarial attack methods against VLA models.

Conclusion: The findings reveal significant safety vulnerabilities in physically deployed VLA models and highlight the urgent need for stronger defenses against unrestricted adversarial attacks.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong capabilities in controlling robots across diverse manipulation tasks. However, their adversarial robustness remains largely underexplored, and exploiting this weakness can lead to physical-world harm. Existing attacks on VLA models often rely on pixel-space perturbations or white-box access, resulting in noticeable artifacts and limited deployability in real-world robotic systems. In this work, we propose DURA, a diffusion-based unrestricted robotic attack that generates visually natural adversarial patches for VLA models. DURA supports both white-box and black-box attack settings, where the black-box setting requires only the predicted actions of the victim model. By optimizing along the latent trajectory of a pretrained diffusion model, DURA generates visually natural patches while steering the robot toward attacker-specified target actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and the real physical world show that DURA consistently outperforms existing methods. Our findings expose a safety risk for physically deployed VLA models and call for stronger defenses.

</details>


### [140] [Threat-guided Policy-aware Scene Perturbation for Safe Autonomous Driving with Online Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10403)
*Xincong Hu,Lei Ou,Maosen Li,Jingtao Zhang,Liguo Hou,Zongzhang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TPSP introduces a policy-aware scene perturbation method for safe RL-based autonomous driving that selectively perturbs critical objects guided by threat-level differences, achieving strong safety performance on NAVSIM v2 with ~4M km of simulated driving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online RL struggles with safety due to the long-tailed distribution of real-world driving: dangerous/rare interactions are hard to encounter. Existing scene generation methods optimize separately from the evolving policy, failing to model how perturbations relate to the current policy's specific weaknesses and learning needs.

Method: TPSP consists of three components: (1) a policy-aware scene encoder that captures interactions between policy behavior and surroundings; (2) selective perturbation of critical objects rather than uniform scene modifications; (3) a threat-guided optimization strategy that evaluates perturbed scenes via threat-level differentials between policy rollouts on original vs. perturbed scenes, prioritizing safety-critical scenes with higher training value.

Result: TPSP improves safety learning efficiency on NAVSIM v2 with approximately 4 million kilometers of simulated driving data. Ablation studies show policy-aware targeted perturbations yield more informative safety-critical experiences than random or policy-unaware strategies, enabling safer driving under limited interaction budgets.

Conclusion: Policy-aware, threat-guided scene perturbation is an effective paradigm for safe online RL in autonomous driving. By aligning scene generation with the policy's current weaknesses, TPSP produces more informative training data and achieves strong safety outcomes even with constrained interaction budgets.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promising performance in autonomous driving, yet ensuring the safety of online RL policies remains challenging due to insufficient exposure to safety-critical driving scenes. The long-tailed nature of real-world traffic situations makes dangerous and rare interactions difficult to encounter through conventional sampling, limiting the ability of RL policies to learn robust safety behaviors. Existing methods improve training diversity by synthesizing challenging scenes or adversarial situations. However, these approaches typically optimize scene generation objectives separately from the evolving policy, without explicitly modeling how generated perturbations relate to the current policy's weaknesses and learning needs. In this paper, we propose Threat-guided Policy-aware Scene Perturbation (TPSP) for safe autonomous driving with online RL. TPSP introduces a policy-aware scene encoder to capture the interaction between policy behaviors and surrounding environments, enabling scene perturbation aligned with the current policy. Based on this representation, TPSP selectively perturbs critical objects rather than applying uniform modifications across the scene. Furthermore, we develop a threat-guided optimization strategy that evaluates perturbed scenes through threat-level differences between policy rollouts on original and perturbed scenes, guiding the generation of safety-critical scenes with higher training value. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that TPSP improves safety learning efficiency, achieving strong safety performance on NAVSIM v2 with approximately 4 million kilometers of simulated driving data. Ablation studies verify that policy-aware targeted perturbations provide more informative safety-critical experiences than random or policy-unaware strategies, enabling safer driving under limited interaction budgets.

</details>


### [141] [Long-Horizon AI Research for Grothendieck Constant: A Case Study in Human-AI Mathematical Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11195)
*Alan Li,Rahul Saha,Anton Xue,Swarat Chaudhuri,Adam Klivans,Pravesh K Kothari,Raghu Meka*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A case study on using an AI research system to improve bounds on the Grothendieck constant, yielding new tighter bounds while discussing AI's strengths, weaknesses, and optimal conditions for mathematical discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing use of AI in mathematics research, there is little clarity on how to deploy AI effectively. The authors aim to demonstrate and analyze practical AI-assisted mathematical discovery through a concrete, high-profile problem.

Method: The authors conducted an extensive case study employing an AI research system to tackle the Grothendieck constant bound problem. The AI system generated insights that domain experts evaluated as novel, leading to improved lower and upper bounds.

Result: The best known bounds on the Grothendieck constant were tightened to: 6π/11 ≤ K_G ≤ π/(2 log(1+√2)) − 10⁻⁴. These improvements were directly achieved through AI-generated insights.

Conclusion: AI can contribute novel, expert-level insights in pure mathematics research when deployed under ideal conditions. The paper provides a reflective account of both capabilities and limitations, offering guidance on fostering conditions for AI-driven breakthroughs.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly used in mathematics research, but it is often unclear how to use them effectively. Towards this, we present an extensive case study of how AI was used to improve bounds on the Grothendieck constant $K_G$, which captures the hardness between combinatorial problems and their continuous relaxations. Specifically, while the precise value of $K_G$ is not known, we recently tightened the best known bounds to \[
  \frac{6π}{11}
  \;\le\;
  K_G
  \;\le\;
  \fracπ{2\log(1+\sqrt2)} - 10^{-4}. \] Crucially, these improvements were achieved using an AI research system that could arrive at insights deemed novel by domain experts. We give a detailed discussion of our experience using AI for mathematics research, particularly touching upon its strengths and weaknesses, as well as our experience with creating ideal conditions for AI to arrive at breakthrough insights.

</details>


### [142] [Reasoning Shortcuts and Value Symmetries: What Symmetry Permits, Architecture Realizes, and Optimization Selects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10420)
*Xin Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper critiques and refines a prior framework for analyzing reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems via automorphism groups. It reveals that the original definition fails on heterogeneous benchmarks, introduces a hierarchy of componentwise symmetries, proves six transitivity theorems, establishes complexity results for symmetry detection in circuits, gives an exact Boolean classification, and empirically shows that weakly supervised models exclusively find shortcuts at levels the theory flags as non-transitive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A prior framework by Takemura, Inoue, and Nishino used automorphism groups to analyze when reasoning rules "pin down" intended concepts, but left a central open question. This paper identifies a critical flaw: the framework's key definition (one shared permutation per position) does not apply to heterogeneous benchmarks it was evaluated on. The work aims to correct the theory and provide rigorous conditions under which symmetries explain or fail to explain reasoning shortcuts.

Method: The authors introduce a componentwise symmetry hierarchy that properly handles heterogeneous domains, prove six theorems establishing sufficient conditions for transitivity and its failure (including a Free Slot Lemma), conduct complexity-theoretic analysis (coNP-completeness, Σ₂^p placement, monotone circuit results), derive an exact classification for Boolean domains (automorphisms explain everything iff the solution set is an affine coset), and empirically validate predictions using weakly supervised models across eleven rule families with fifteen pre-specified predictions.

Result: The original framework produces 90.91% unexplained pairs on CLE4EVR due to padding artifacts, while the componentwise hierarchy reports 0%. Unexplained-pair rates span 0–99.9999% across rule families, tracking provable structure. All 94 observed shortcuts fall at levels the theory flags as non-transitive; 48 certified-transitive levels produce none. Twelve typed-ambiguous levels yield no shortcuts, separating what symmetry permits from what optimization selects.

Conclusion: The componentwise symmetry hierarchy correctly captures when rules pin concepts down, resolving the earlier framework's central open question. The theory tightly predicts where neurosymbolic shortcuts can and cannot arise, with empirical results matching theoretical predictions and all data traceable to released artifacts.

Abstract: Reasoning shortcuts are solutions of a neurosymbolic system's rules that produce correct predictions through unintended concepts. A recent framework of Takemura, Inoue, and Nishino analyzes them through an automorphism group of value relabelings and asks, as its central open question, when rules pin concepts down. We first show that the framework's key definition, one shared permutation applied at every position, does not apply as stated to any of the four heterogeneous benchmarks it was evaluated on, and that the most direct embedding, padding domains to a common size, produces confident false pathology: 90.91% of solution pairs reported unexplained on CLE4EVR, where every well-defined member of the hierarchy we introduce reports 0%, and the padded verdict's content rotates with configuration-file ordering. Re-measuring eleven rule families under fifteen pre-specified predictions (thirteen confirmed), unexplained-pair rates span 0% to 99.9999% and track provable structure: six theorems give sufficient conditions for transitivity and its failure, including a Free Slot Lemma certifying Kandinsky's pathology from syntax alone. For circuit-given rules, deciding symmetry-inertness of a coordinate is coNP-complete; nontrivial-automorphism existence is coNP-hard under randomized reductions, lies in $Σ_2^p$, is not $Σ_2^p$-complete unless PH collapses, and on monotone circuits is coNP-complete outright. In the Boolean case transitivity is classified exactly: automorphisms explain everything iff the solution set is an affine coset. Weakly supervised models place all 94 observed shortcuts at the one level the componentwise theory flags and none at the 48 it certifies transitive; twelve typed-ambiguous levels produce none, separating what symmetry permits from what optimization selects, and a dual-head control replicates the geography. All numbers trace to released artifacts.

</details>


### [143] [Recovering Wasted Compute in Autoresearch Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10424)
*Au Kwok Chun,Abhigyan Acherjee,Amrutha Rao,Zaiqian Chen,Kazem Meidani,C. Bayan Bruss,Micah Goldblum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies four common failure modes in autoresearch agents applied to tabular data — redundant bug-fixing, hyperparameter tuning neglect, inadequate tree-search exploration, and unused data analysis — and demonstrates that targeted agentic design interventions (global debug consultant, prompt/control enhancements, refined tree-search) yield substantial performance gains without changing the underlying language model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoresearch systems are attracting major industry investment for automating ML research, but their core modeling pipelines suffer from systematic inefficiencies when applied to tabular datasets. The authors aim to diagnose these failure modes and show that agent design, rather than scaling the underlying LLM, can unlock significant performance improvements.

Method: The authors study the modeling pipeline of autoresearch agents, catalog four specific failure modes through empirical observation, and then propose and evaluate targeted interventions: (1) a global debug consultant that propagates discovered runtime constraints across all branches of the search tree, (2) prompt-level and control-level enhancements, and (3) refined tree-search algorithms that improve exploration.

Result: The interventions successfully recover wasted compute. Large gains in autoresearch agent performance are achievable through agentic design improvements alone, with the underlying language model held fixed.

Conclusion: Agentic design — encompassing debugging strategies, search algorithms, and prompt/control mechanisms — is a critical and underappreciated lever for improving autoresearch systems, independent of advances in the base language model.

Abstract: A slew of recent works develop agents for solving research problems end-to-end, a paradigm increasingly referred to as autoresearch. Such agents have inspired large industry investment, motivated by their potential to automate time-consuming human labor and customize machine learning solutions for specialized applications. In this paper, we study the modeling pipeline at the core of these autoresearch systems and identify common failure modes when they are applied to tabular datasets: (1) they waste compute resolving the same bugs over and over again; (2) they often fail to tune hyperparameters even when they have a large remaining compute budget; (3) the tree-search algorithms that power them do not explore; and (4) they perform data analysis, mimicking the humans whose data they are trained on, but do not use that analysis to make downstream decisions. We explore targeted interventions and find that a global debug consultant that shares discovered runtime constraints across all branches of the search tree, prompt- and control-level enhancements, and refined tree-search algorithms successfully recover wasted compute. Our results show that large gains in autoresearch agent performance are achievable through agentic design alone, holding the underlying language model fixed.

</details>


### [144] [Conversational versus Dashboard Explainable AI for UAV Intrusion Detection: An Empirical Study of Operator Trust and Reliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10434)
*Cong Chi Nguyen,Trang Mai Xuan,Vu-Duc Ngo,Kim-Ngan Thi Nguyen,Trong-Nghia Nguyen,Thien Van Luong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A conversational XAI interface powered by LLMs was compared against a traditional dashboard for UAV intrusion detection auditing. The conversational interface improved perceived usefulness but reduced appropriate self-reliance, revealing a trade-off between usability and over-reliance in human-AI collaboration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Black-box ML-based IDS for UAV networks suffer from interpretability challenges due to high-dimensional multimodal cyber-physical data. Static dashboards struggle to convey complex feature relationships in an inspectable manner, motivating the need for more adaptive, on-demand explanation interfaces.

Method: A controlled between-subjects experiment comparing two XAI interfaces: (1) a Conversational XAI interface driven by an LLM allowing natural-language on-demand investigation, and (2) a traditional static XAI Dashboard. Participants performed post-incident auditing tasks, with outcomes measured on understanding, trust, and reliance.

Result: The conversational interface was rated significantly more useful than the dashboard and facilitated easier information synthesis. However, it led to lower appropriate self-reliance — participants were less likely to verify AI advice when the IDS was incorrect, indicating over-reliance on natural-language explanations.

Conclusion: A trade-off exists between interaction usability and appropriate reliance in XAI for UAV intrusion auditing. Designers should incorporate cognitive forcing functions into seamless conversational interfaces to mitigate over-reliance while preserving usability benefits.

Abstract: Machine learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) have demonstrated superior performance in securing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. However, the 'black-box' nature of these models, combined with the high dimensionality of multimodal cyber-physical data, poses significant interpretability challenges. Static visualization dashboards may struggle to present complex relationships among multimodal cyber-physical features in a form that is easy for operators to inspect and interpret. To address this, we propose a Conversational XAI interface powered by Large Language Models (LLM) to facilitate on-demand investigation. In a controlled experiment with participants, we systematically evaluated the impact of this conversational interface versus a traditional XAI Dashboard on operator understanding, trust, and reliance during post-incident auditing tasks. Our results suggest that the conversational interface was perceived as more useful than the dashboard, potentially because it helped participants access and synthesize relevant information more easily. However, this benefit was accompanied by a lower level of appropriate self-reliance, indicating a potential risk of over-reliance. One possible interpretation is that the natural-language responses made the AI advice easier to accept, which may have reduced participants' tendency to verify the underlying evidence when the IDS was incorrect. These findings point to a potential trade-off in human-AI collaboration for UAV intrusion auditing: interaction mechanisms that improve perceived usability may also increase the risk of inappropriate reliance. We conclude by discussing design implications for future XAI systems that balance seamless interaction with cognitive forcing functions to foster appropriate reliance.

</details>


### [145] [Continuous Interaction Diffusion: A Diffusion-Native Runtime for Asynchronous Tool-Augmented Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10438)
*Yuhang Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CID extends diffusion language models with a native tool-use architecture that overlaps tool calls with denoising, enabling earlier evidence exposure, latency hiding, and reduced redundant computation — without requiring fully serialized tool calls before interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive models fit tool use naturally via stop-and-resume generation, but diffusion language models (dLLMs) — which iteratively refine outputs in parallel — are constrained by this sequential pattern. Forcing tool decisions before reasoning stabilizes, delaying observations until calls complete, and introducing redundant refinement and execution harms both accuracy and inference efficiency.

Method: CID introduces a three-channel architecture: (1) a read-only fact channel, (2) a thought channel represented by a Typed Cognitive Tensor, and (3) a display channel. Perceptual bindings allow external reads to launch as soon as information needs emerge — before textual/JSON calls are fully serialized — while denoising continues. Returned results are projected into the evolving thought state and can revise prior cognition and display regions. Persistent bindings reuse static results and refresh dynamic sources. The paper formalizes the architecture, runtime, training objectives, and an evaluation protocol, focusing on read-only tools.

Result: This first paper presents no empirical performance claims; it focuses on formalizing the CID architecture, runtime, training objectives, and evaluation protocol for task quality and end-to-end efficiency.

Conclusion: CID offers a diffusion-native alternative to sequential tool interaction, designed to expose evidence earlier, overlap tool latency with computation, reduce duplicate external work, and preserve useful computation after new evidence arrives. The paper establishes the conceptual and formal groundwork for future empirical validation.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external tools to access up-to-date information, perform computation, and interact with the outside world. For autoregressive models, tool use naturally fits the generation process: the model emits a tool call, waits for the result, and then continues generating. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), however, reason by repeatedly refining many parts of their output in parallel, making this stop-and-resume interaction pattern unnecessarily restrictive. It can force tool decisions before the model's reasoning has stabilized, delay useful observations until a discrete call finishes, and introduce redundant refinement and tool execution, potentially hurting both task accuracy and inference efficiency.
  We introduce Continuous Interaction Diffusion (CID), a diffusion-native model--runtime architecture that integrates tool interaction into iterative denoising. CID separates a model-read-only fact channel, a thought channel represented by a Typed Cognitive Tensor, and a display channel. Information needs can emerge before a textual or JSON call is fully serialized, allowing perceptual bindings to launch external reads while denoising continues. Returned results are projected into the evolving thought state and can revise earlier cognition and display regions. Persistent bindings reuse static results without repeated external execution and refresh changing sources when needed. CID is designed to expose evidence earlier, overlap tool latency with model computation, reduce duplicate external work, and preserve useful computation after new evidence arrives. We formalize the architecture, runtime, and training objectives, and define an evaluation protocol for task quality and end-to-end efficiency. This first paper focuses on read-only tools and makes no empirical performance claims.

</details>


### [146] [Rationale-Guided Learning for Multimodal Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10448)
*Sujung Oh,Jung Uk Kim,Sangmin Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RGL transforms multimodal emotion recognition in conversation into a cognitively-inspired reasoning task by decomposing emotional reasoning into Intuitive, Contextual, and Integrative facets based on dual-process theory. Using MLLM-generated rationales as training guidance, it achieves SOTA on IEMOCAP and MELD without MLLM overhead at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MERC approaches treat emotion recognition as a direct input-output mapping problem, ignoring the causal reasoning process humans naturally employ when interpreting emotions from multimodal cues.

Method: The RGL framework leverages dual-process theory to decompose emotional reasoning into three facets: Intuitive (System 1, immediate perception), Contextual (System 2, situational analysis), and Integrative (synthesis). An MLLM is used offline to generate structured rationales, which are encoded as memories to guide model training by aligning internal representations with human-like reasoning patterns. The MLLM is not used at inference time.

Result: RGL achieves state-of-the-art performance on IEMOCAP and MELD benchmarks. Internal features can effectively retrieve semantically correct rationales for unseen test samples, validating the model's rationale reasoning capabilities.

Conclusion: Rationale-guided learning successfully bridges the gap between direct mapping and human-like causal reasoning in MERC, offering both performance gains and interpretability without inference-time overhead from large models.

Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversation (MERC) requires understanding complex interactions between verbal and non-verbal cues. However, most existing approaches fundamentally treat this as a direct input-output (multimodal cues-emotion labels) mapping problem, overlooking the causal reasoning that humans use when interpreting emotions. We propose rationale-guided learning (RGL), a novel framework that transforms MERC into a cognitively-inspired reasoning task. Based on dual-process theory, we decompose emotional reasoning into three facets: Intuitive (immediate perception, System 1), Contextual (situational analysis, System 2), and Integrative (synthesis of both). We leverage an MLLM offline to generate structured rationales, which are encoded as memories to guide model training via aligning internal representations with human-like reasoning patterns. Our final model operates without any MLLM overheads at inference time. Experimental results show that RGL achieves state-of-the-art performance on the IEMOCAP and MELD benchmarks. Further, for interpretation, we demonstrate that the model's internal features effectively retrieve semantically correct rationales for unseen test samples, validating its rationale reasoning capabilities.

</details>


### [147] [Quantum Incremental Learning with Mixed State Prototypes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10464)
*Yu Wu,Qianli Zhou,Xinyang Deng,Wen Jiang,Kang Hao Cheong,Witold Pedrycz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A quantum incremental learning framework using trainable mixed-state prototypes is proposed, enabling sequential class addition without expanding circuit width, leveraging mixed-state representational power and Hilbert-Schmidt distance for efficient classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NISQ-era quantum neural networks face hardware-limited circuit width, and traditional quantum classifiers are bottlenecked by the number of orthogonal basis states, restricting their ability to handle continually growing class categories in incremental learning scenarios.

Method: The framework uses a shared quantum backbone with trainable mixed-state prototypes. New classes are incorporated by adding class prototypes rather than increasing circuit width. Mixed-state prototypes offer richer representation than pure-state counterparts, and their decomposable calculation enables lower production costs and convenient Hilbert-Schmidt distance metric for classification.

Result: Simulations demonstrate high-dimensional feature concentration with minimal qubits, lower computational complexity, and robust representation in incremental learning tasks compared to classical baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed quantum incremental learning framework effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting under parameter/memory constraints by using mixed-state prototypes, showing promise for scalable quantum continual learning on NISQ devices.

Abstract: Incremental learning models are required to learn new classes sequentially without catastrophic forgetting, while operating under parameter and memory constraints. In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, although quantum neural networks offer advantages in feature mapping, hardware limitations restrict circuit width. Furthermore, traditional quantum classifiers are constrained by the number of orthogonal basis states, limiting their capacity to accommodate a continually growing number of categories. Thus, we introduce a novel quantum incremental learning framework based on trainable mixed-state prototypes. Its original design incorporates new classes by adding class prototypes rather than increasing the circuit width of the shared quantum backbone. The use of mixed-state prototypes is another key contribution, since they have representation capabilities to represent information than a single pure-state prototype. And the decomposable mixed-state calculation provides lower production costs and a convenient Hilbert-Schmidt (HS) distance metric for classification. Simulation results show that our model achieves high-dimensional feature concentration using a minimal number of qubits, while demonstrating lower computational complexity and robust representation in incremental learning tasks compared with classical baselines.

</details>


### [148] [RLMOpt: Adaptive Prompt Optimization via Recursive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10471)
*Subhash Bangalore Satheesha,Nirvik Pande,Deepthi Duddempudi,Bharath Dandala*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RLMOpt is a prompt optimizer where the search strategy itself is driven by a recursive language model agent operating in a tool-based environment. It outperforms GEPA across four benchmarks with fewer rollouts and shorter prompts, and shows that optimization gains depend on seed-prompt headroom rather than search budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt optimizers rely on a fixed, predefined optimization procedure (e.g., genetic algorithms, iterative refinement). The authors argue that making the search policy itself language-model-driven could yield more adaptive, efficient, and effective optimization by leveraging the LM's reasoning to decide which candidates to explore, how to allocate evaluation budget, and when to stop.

Method: RLMOpt employs a recursive language model (RLM) agent that interacts with a tool-based environment. The agent inspects task information, analyzes failure cases, generates candidate prompts, allocates evaluation budget across candidates, and decides when to terminate search. A deterministic harness complements the agent by enforcing objective scoring, Pareto-based selection among candidates, and regression constraints (ensuring new prompts do not underperform the seed).

Result: In a single-seed matched comparison across four benchmarks (Chia, HotpotQA, IFBench-2025, BFCL), RLMOpt achieved the best held-out score on all four and a higher four-task mean (0.610 vs. 0.589 for GEPA). Across 11 benchmark-seed comparisons, RLMOpt outperformed GEPA in 9, never once underperforming its seed, while GEPA fell below its seed twice. RLMOpt used fewer search rollouts and produced prompts 27-79% the size of GEPA's. Additionally, optimization gains were primarily determined by seed-prompt headroom, not search budget.

Conclusion: RLMOpt demonstrates that a language-model-driven search policy can surpass fixed algorithmic optimizers in both effectiveness and efficiency. The findings reframe efficient prompt optimization as a problem of reliably reaching the headroom available in the seed prompt with minimal search, rather than simply scaling compute or iterations.

Abstract: Prompt optimizers automate the search for prompts that improve language-model performance, but existing methods rely on a predefined optimization procedure: the algorithm determines which candidates to explore and how the search progresses, while the language model generates or refines prompt proposals. We introduce RLMOpt, a prompt optimizer that makes the search policy itself language-model-driven through a recursive language model (RLM). The RLM agent operates over a tool-based environment, inspecting task information, analyzing failures, generating candidates, allocating evaluation budget, and deciding when to stop. A deterministic harness complements the agent by enforcing objective scoring, Pareto-based selection, and regression constraints.
  We evaluate RLMOpt across four benchmarks spanning structured clinical information extraction (Chia), multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA), verifiable instruction following (IFBench-2025), and multi-turn tool-calling agents (BFCL). In a matched comparison at a single seed, RLMOpt obtains the best held-out score on all four benchmarks and leads the four-task mean (0.610 against 0.589 for GEPA). Repeating each benchmark across seeds yields 11 matched benchmark-seed comparisons, in which RLMOpt outperforms GEPA in 9 cases. Across all 11 runs, it never produced a prompt that underperformed its seed, whereas GEPA fell below its starting point twice. It is also more efficient, achieving these results with fewer search rollouts while producing prompts that are 27-79% the size of those produced by GEPA.
  Our results further show that optimization gains are determined primarily by the headroom available in the seed prompt, rather than by the search budget. Efficient optimization therefore depends on reaching the available headroom reliably and with minimal search

</details>


### [149] [Evaluating Rational Contracting in Natural Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10475)
*Bhavyesh Sajja,Max Kleiman-Weiner,Roger Zimmermann,Tan Zhi-Xuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current LLM-based agents can negotiate contracts reliably under low uncertainty, but under high uncertainty they fail to produce efficient, satisfiable, or mutually beneficial agreements, and frequently behave uncooperatively during execution by violating terms for extra profit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-based AI agents open new possibilities for negotiating and executing complex, time-extended, contingent natural language contracts, but existing evaluations are limited to one-off exchanges and simple games, ignoring the rich space of incomplete contracting and the trustworthiness qualities required for real economic activity.

Method: The authors propose a rational framework for natural language contract negotiation and performance in uncertain multi-step environments, with metrics for rational and cooperative play. They instantiate this in ContractSim, a two-player multi-turn supplier contract simulation across six environments and three settings (catering, hotel cleaning, AI hosting), varying environmental and inter-player uncertainty.

Result: LLM agents reach agreements reliably and negotiate efficient contracts under low environmental uncertainty. Under high uncertainty, they often fail to produce satisfiable, efficient, or mutually beneficial contracts. Agents also frequently act uncooperatively during execution, violating contract terms for additional profit even when contracts are easy to satisfy.

Conclusion: Significant room remains for improving language agents' ability to negotiate, interpret, and execute contracts both rationally and cooperatively, particularly under uncertainty.

Abstract: The emergence of language-based AI agents promises to transform the scope of machine economic activity. Instead of just proposing bids or following hard-coded protocols, such agents can be used to negotiate and execute agreements in open-ended natural language. However, most evaluations of these abilities have focused on one-off exchanges or simple economic games, leaving open the rich space of time-extended, contingent, and incomplete contracts made expressible by language; they also focus on raw profit, without measuring the qualities required for trustworthy contracting. We address this by formulating a rational framework for how agents should negotiate and perform natural language contracts in uncertain multi-step environments. Within this framework, we develop metrics and baselines for quantifying rational and cooperative play. To evaluate how agents perform at such contracting, we instantiate our framework in ContractSim, an evaluation suite where two players negotiate and execute a multi-turn supplier contract under environmental and inter-player uncertainty. Across six environments and three supplier settings (catering, hotel cleaning, and AI hosting) we find that current LLM-based agents reach agreement reliably, and negotiate efficient contracts when environmental uncertainty is low. However, under high uncertainty, they often fail to negotiate satisfiable, efficient, or mutually beneficial contracts. They are also frequently uncooperative when executing contracts, violating contract terms for additional profit even when contracts are easy to satisfy. These findings highlight room for improvement in the design of language agents that can negotiate, interpret, and execute contracts both rationally and cooperatively.

</details>


### [150] [Multi-Granular Rationale-Guided Molecular LLM for Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10480)
*Junwoo Park,Minyoung Shin,Cheol Soon Lee,Sujee Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MR-MoL is a molecular LLM that uses a GNN to identify and rank influential substructures, serializing them as rationale text for the LLM to read alongside SMILES and molecular graphs, improving molecular property prediction transparency and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing molecular LLMs encode molecular information implicitly through SMILES or graphs, making substructure contributions opaque. Retrieval-augmented methods add external context but fail to provide the internal substructure-level cues that chemists actually reason over when assessing molecular properties.

Method: MR-MoL employs a fine-tuned GNN that scores substructures via masking to identify the most influential ones for a given property. These are serialized as a ranked, direction-tagged rationale spanning three granularity levels: Murcko scaffolds with side chains, BRICS fragments, and functional groups. The LLM then reads this rationale alongside the SMILES sequence and 2D molecular graph for property prediction.

Result: On eight MoleculeNet tasks, MR-MoL achieves the best overall results among generalist models and narrows the gap to specialist models tuned per task. Five diagnostic analyses confirm the model actively reads the rationale: prediction is shaped by direction, rank, and substructure content, and the attributions reproduce known structure-property relationships.

Conclusion: Exposing GNN-derived substructure attributions directly to an LLM as internal evidence is both feasible and effective, offering a more interpretable and performant approach to molecular property prediction that aligns with how chemists reason.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely applied across chemical tasks, such as molecular property prediction, which underpins drug discovery. Molecular LLMs represent a molecule through several modalities, notably a 1D SMILES sequence or a 2D molecular graph. Both encode molecular information implicitly, so the contribution of individual substructures remains opaque. Retrieval and augmentation methods add context, but from external sources. However, the cues chemists reason over are the internal substructures that drive a property up or down. We propose MR-MoL, a multi-granular rationale-guided molecular LLM that supplies this evidence directly. A fine-tuned GNN scores each substructure through masking, and the most influential ones are serialized as a ranked, direction-tagged rationale that the LLM reads alongside the SMILES sequence and molecular graph. The rationale spans three levels of granularity: Murcko scaffolds with their side chains, BRICS fragments, and functional groups. This is, to our knowledge, the first method to expose GNN-derived attributions to an LLM as evidence for property prediction. On eight MoleculeNet tasks, MR-MoL achieves the best overall results among generalist models and narrows the gap to specialist models tuned for each task. Five diagnostics further confirm that the model reads the rationale rather than merely benefiting from its presence. Its direction, rank, and substructure each shape the prediction, and its attributions reproduce known structure-property relationships.

</details>


### [151] [Predicting Space Groups of Double Perovskites by LLM with Dynamic Few-Shot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10483)
*Jongwon Park,Inhyo Lee,Junhyeong Lee,Seunghwa Ryu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DyRIS is an LLM-agent framework that predicts space groups for double perovskites using diversity-enhanced few-shot retrieval and rule-guided inference. It tackles severe class imbalance by limiting dominant space group influence and incorporating crystallographic domain knowledge (B/B' ordering, quantitative indicators, bias control), achieving superior performance on minority space group classes compared to CrabNet and PyCaret baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Double perovskite space group prediction is hindered by strongly imbalanced datasets where dominant (major) space group classes overshadow underrepresented (minor) ones. Existing methods struggle with these minority classes, motivating a solution that balances retrieval diversity with domain-specific crystallographic reasoning.

Method: DyRIS combines three components: (1) diversity-enhanced dynamic few-shot prompting that retrieves relevant in-context examples while preventing overrepresentation of major SGs; (2) rule-guided inference incorporating B/B' cation ordering, quantitative indicators, and major-SG bias control; and (3) a final ranking mechanism to produce Top-3 SG candidates from a given DP composition. The framework operates as an LLM-agent system.

Result: On 3,528 thermodynamically filtered DP entries at 0.5 training-data ratio, DyRIS achieves competitive overall accuracy, the best Overall Top-1 macro-F1, and best performance on all Minor-SG metrics. Minor-SG Top-1 accuracy improves by 3.26 percentage points over CrabNet, and Minor-SG Top-3 accuracy surpasses the strongest PyCaret baseline. Ablations confirm each component (diversity retrieval, quantitative indicators, bias control, B/B' ordering) contributes positively. The rule-guided inference step cannot be easily substituted by conventional classifiers or rankers.

Conclusion: Combining retrieval-based LLM reasoning with crystallographic domain knowledge is a promising approach for space group prediction in imbalanced materials datasets, particularly for improving performance on underrepresented classes.

Abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer broad compositional tunability, but predicting the space groups (SGs) of stable structures remains difficult because available datasets are often strongly imbalanced toward dominant SG classes. We refer to dominant SG classes as major SGs and underrepresented classes as minor SGs. We introduce Dynamic and Diversity-enhanced Few-shot Retrieval and Rule-Guided Inference for Space-Group Prediction (DyRIS), an LLM-agent-based framework that predicts ranked SG candidates from a given DP composition. DyRIS uses diversity-enhanced dynamic few-shot prompting to retrieve relevant in-context examples while limiting the dominance of frequently represented SGs. It further incorporates rule-guided inference based on B/B' cation ordering, quantitative indicators, and major-SG bias control to refine and rank the final Top-3 SG candidates. We evaluate DyRIS on 3,528 thermodynamically filtered DP entries and compare it with composition-based and descriptor-based baselines. At a training-data ratio of 0.5, DyRIS achieves competitive overall accuracy while obtaining the best Overall Top-1 macro-F1 score and the best performance across all Minor-SG metrics. DyRIS improves Minor-SG Top-1 accuracy by 3.26 percentage points relative to CrabNet and achieves higher Minor-SG Top-3 accuracy than the strongest PyCaret-based baseline. Ablation studies show that diversity-enhanced retrieval, quantitative indicators, major-SG bias control, and B/B' ordering information each contribute to prediction performance. Additional experiments show that the final rule-guided inference step is not easily replaced by conventional classifier- or ranker-based models. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining retrieval-based LLM reasoning with crystallographic domain knowledge for SG prediction in imbalanced materials datasets.

</details>


### [152] [INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10492)
*Rose Niousha,Minwoo Kang,Narges Norouzi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INSIDE is a student modeling framework that fine-tunes LLMs to simulate both student actions and their underlying reasoning via internal dialogue grounded in Bloom's Taxonomy, achieving up to 57.9% reasoning alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based simulators reproduce observable student actions but fail to capture the underlying cognitive reasoning behind those actions. In educational contexts, identical submissions can stem from different reasoning processes, and this gap limits the validity of student simulation for applications like tutoring system evaluation.

Method: INSIDE (INTERNAL STUDENT DIALOGUE) is a student modeling framework that fine-tunes LLMs on paired "think traces" and actions. It generates internal dialogue structured around Bloom's Taxonomy across three dimensions: cognitive, affective, and action. The approach involves collecting student reasoning traces, mapping them to Bloom's Taxonomy categories, and fine-tuning models to jointly produce both internal reasoning and observable actions.

Result: INSIDE improves simulation fidelity along two axes: (1) action fidelity — matching the code generation patterns of real students, and (2) reasoning alignment — achieving the highest alignment score across models, up to 57.9%. It outperforms baseline prompting frameworks on both metrics.

Conclusion: Modeling both student actions and their internal reasoning via Bloom's Taxonomy-grounded internal dialogue significantly improves the fidelity of LLM-based student simulation, advancing the state of educational simulation tools.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based simulators often reproduce observable actions but fail to capture the underlying reasoning behind them. In education, where student simulation is increasingly used for various applications such as evaluating tutoring systems, this gap is especially pronounced. Two students may submit identical submissions for entirely different reasons. We present INTERNAL STUDENT DIALOGUE (INSIDE), a student modeling framework that fine-tunes LLMs not only to act like students but also to think like them. INSIDE generates internal dialogue grounded in Bloom's Taxonomy across cognitive, affective, and action dimensions, and fine-tunes models on paired think traces and actions. We baseline against different prompting frameworks and evaluate on two axes: fidelity of simulated actions and quality of generated internal dialogue. Our evaluations show that INSIDE improves simulation fidelity in both action fidelity, matching code generation of real students, and reasoning alignment, achieving the highest alignment across models up to 57.9%.

</details>


### [153] [From Faulty Memories to Corrected Actions: Dependency-Guided Rollback Repair for Memory-Augmented Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10502)
*Caili Yu,Yiqi Wang,Jiaqi Zhang,Yiqun Duan,Mingkai Zheng,Zhangkai Wu,Kaize Shi,Taotao Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes dependency-guided rollback repair for recovering language-model agents after memory failures. Builds a typed memory-to-action provenance graph to selectively deactivate faulty memories and replay only affected computation, achieving 85.3% recovery on controlled benchmarks vs. 77.3% for best competitor, while preserving all benign memories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent memory in LM agents introduces durability of errors: faulty records propagate through reasoning, tool use, and subsequent writes. Existing defenses either delete suspicious memories (leaving propagated effects active) or reset/replay the full trace (destroying benign state and wasting computation). A targeted recovery mechanism that excises faulty memories while preserving unaffected work is needed.

Method: Dependency-guided rollback repair constructs a typed memory-to-action graph from runtime provenance, traces explicit downstream dependencies, preserves candidates with independent trusted support, deactivates unsupported memory state, and selectively replays only answer-relevant affected computation.

Result: On a 150-case controlled benchmark (3 tool-use domains, 4 failure types), achieves 85.3% recovery vs. 77.3% best competitor; removes all diagnosed faulty memories, preserves all benign memories, with modest LLM-call cost. On a 50-case LongMemEval-V2 stress test, achieves 68.0% recovery vs. 54.0% best competitor, with highest claim invalidation F1 of 0.669 vs. 0.603.

Conclusion: Dependency-guided rollback repair offers a strong recovery--cost trade-off: it does not guarantee uniformly better trace reconstruction but effectively repairs faulty memory state while preserving benign memory, outperforming competing recovery methods on both controlled and stress-test benchmarks.

Abstract: Persistent memory lets language-model agents reuse information across sessions, but it also makes errors durable: a poisoned, stale, or misattributed record can alter reasoning, tool use, answers, and subsequent memory writes. Existing defenses mainly detect or delete suspicious memories, or revise the current response. Deleting the source leaves already propagated claims, actions, and derived memories active, whereas resetting the store or replaying the full trace destroys benign state and repeats unnecessary computation. We therefore formulate \textbf{post-failure memory recovery: } \textit{given a failed execution and diagnosed faulty memories, recover both the answer and persistent state while retaining unaffected work.} Our \textbf{dependency-guided rollback repair} builds a typed memory-to-action graph from runtime provenance, traces explicit downstream dependencies, preserves candidates with independent trusted support, deactivates unsupported memory state, and selectively replays only answer-relevant affected computation. We evaluate this approach on a 150-case controlled benchmark spanning three tool-use domains and four memory failure types, and on a 50-case trajectory-derived stress test adapted from LongMemEval-V2. On the controlled benchmark, it achieves 85.3\% recovery versus 77.3\% for the best competing recovery method, removes all diagnosed faulty memories, preserves all benign memories, and requires only selective replay with modest LLM-call cost. On the adapted subset, it reaches 68.0\% recovery versus 54.0\% for the next best method, while also achieving the highest claim invalidation F1, 0.669 versus 0.603. Overall, the results do not imply uniformly better trace reconstruction, but show that dependency-guided rollback repair provides a strong recovery--cost trade-off while repairing faulty memory state and preserving benign memory.

</details>


### [154] [MEGA: Self-Evolving Agent Optimization Infrastructure via Wisdom Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10504)
*Jung Hwan Lee,Kyu Ho Lee,Gwang Hoon Yoo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MEGA is a self-evolving infrastructure that treats agent optimization and knowledge evolution as a unified process. It operates in three layers: (1) distilling reusable wisdom from agent sessions via behavioral clustering and A/B validation, (2) decomposing assets into atomic PCR units within a typed Wisdom Graph with compositional reasoning (deductive, abductive, inductive), and (3) multi-agent collaborative optimization with controlled evaluation to attribute improvements.
