Operational evidence from Layer 3 drives self-evolution of both curation strategies and optimization trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to improving coding agent systems suffer from three gaps: they optimize without accumulating transferable knowledge, they accumulate knowledge without compositional reasoning over it, and they lack mechanisms for knowledge to self-evolve through operational evidence. The central challenge has shifted from building individual agents to building infrastructure that systematically improves them.

Method: MEGA employs a three-layer architecture. Layer 1 distills reusable wisdom from agent sessions using behavioral-pattern clustering and empirical A/B validation, producing durable assets. Layer 2 decomposes these assets into atomic PCR (Primary-Context-Resultant) units within a typed Wisdom Graph, applying deductive, abductive, and inductive reasoning to expand implicit relations, then assembles execution plans via compositional retrieval that surfaces bridging knowledge beyond embedding similarity. Layer 3 performs multi-agent collaborative optimization over heterogeneous workflows (code nodes, LLM calls, tool-using agents) with controlled evaluation that eliminates data variance to attribute improvement effects to specific strategy changes. Evidence from Layer 3 feeds back to drive self-evolution of curation strategies and optimization trajectories.

Result: The architecture yields an infrastructure where optimizing an agent system and evolving the guiding knowledge are unified into a single, self-reinforcing process. Durable assets accumulate across optimization cycles, compositional reasoning guides subsequent optimizations, and operational evidence continuously refines both accumulated wisdom and governing reasoning.

Conclusion: MEGA demonstrates that a self-evolving infrastructure can close the loop between agent optimization and knowledge evolution, turning each optimization cycle into a knowledge-accumulating, reasoning-driven, evidence-refining process. This shifts the paradigm from building individual agents to building systems that systematically improve themselves over time.

Abstract: As coding agents increasingly handle implementation, the central challenge shifts from building individual agents to building an infrastructure that systematically improves them. Current approaches optimize agent systems without accumulating transferable knowledge, accumulate knowledge without compositional reasoning over it, and lack a mechanism for that knowledge to self-evolve through operational evidence. MEGA (Meta Evaluation-Grounded Adaptation) addresses these gaps as a self-evolving infrastructure: each optimization cycle produces durable assets, compositional reasoning over those assets guides subsequent optimization, and operational evidence refines both the accumulated wisdom and the reasoning that governs it. Layer 1 distills reusable wisdom from agent sessions through behavioral-pattern clustering and empirical A/B validation, transforming each process into a durable asset. Layer 2 decomposes these assets into atomic PCR (Primary-Context-Resultant) units within a typed Wisdom Graph and performs deductive, abductive, and inductive reasoning to expand implicit relations; it then assembles context-specific execution plans through compositional retrieval that surfaces bridging knowledge unreachable by embedding similarity alone. Layer 3 performs multi-agent collaborative optimization over heterogeneous agent workflows (code nodes, LLM calls, and tool-using agents), attributing improvement effects to specific strategy changes through controlled evaluation that eliminates data variance. Evidence fed back from Layer 3 drives the self-evolution of both the curation strategies that govern wisdom composition and the optimization trajectories accumulated across runs. The result is an infrastructure in which optimizing an agent system and evolving the knowledge that guides optimization are one and the same process.

</details>


### [155] [RadFusion: Towards Threshold-Controllable Radiology Report Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10505)
*Ying Jin,Noel C. F. Codella,John Corring,Mu Wei,Dinei Florencio,Eric Horvitz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RadFusion introduces threshold-controllable radiology report generation by fusing a multi-label classifier with a VQA-based generator, then using an LLM to reconcile them. This enables ROC-based validation and operating-point selection for different clinical scenarios, improving sensitivity by 6.9% and specificity by 20.7% over uncontrolled generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated radiology report generation models offer no control over the sensitivity-specificity trade-off, yet clinical contexts vary: emergency triage requires high sensitivity to avoid missed findings, while confirmatory interpretation demands high specificity to prevent unnecessary interventions. A single fixed report cannot adapt to these different requirements, nor does it support the ROC-based validation expected for regulatory clearance.

Method: RadFusion combines three components: (1) a multi-label classifier providing per-disease confidence scores, (2) a VQA-based report generator producing detailed finding descriptions, and (3) an LLM that rewrites the final report so that stated diagnoses align with the classifier's decisions at a user-selected threshold, while remaining grounded in the generator's descriptive content.

Result: On MIMIC-CXR, sweeping the threshold and mapping generated reports back to class labels reproduces the classifier's ROC curve, demonstrating quantitative verifiability. Sensitivity improved by 6.9% at matched specificity, and specificity improved by 20.7% at matched sensitivity compared to uncontrolled generation.

Conclusion: RadFusion makes radiology report generation clinically adaptable, quantitatively evaluable through ROC analysis (supporting regulatory clearance), and diagnostically more reliable than uncontrolled generation.

Abstract: Automated radiology report generation is advancing rapidly in response to the shortage of radiologists, yet unlike a perception model, existing generation models offer no control over the sensitivity-specificity trade-off of their diagnostic content. Such control is essential because clinical scenarios diverge: emergency triage prioritizes sensitivity to reduce missed findings, whereas confirmatory interpretation emphasizes specificity to limit unnecessary interventions. A single fixed report can neither adapt to these scenarios nor support the ROC-based validation widely expected for regulatory clearance. We introduce RadFusion, a framework that equips report generation with threshold controllability. Our method fuses a multi-label classifier, which provides per-disease confidence scores, with a VQA-based report generator, which describes medical findings in detail; an LLM then rewrites the report so that its stated diagnoses follow the classifier's decisions at the selected threshold while staying grounded in the generator's descriptions. On MIMIC-CXR, the performance of RadFusion conforms to the classifier's ROC curve: sweeping the threshold and mapping the reports back to class labels reproduces the classifier's validated ROC performance. This conformance makes generated reports quantitatively evaluable through ROC analysis, strengthening the case for regulatory clearance, and enables operating-point selection that matches report behavior to clinical context. Moreover, combining the two model types improves diagnostic accuracy over uncontrolled generation: sensitivity increases by 6.9% at matched specificity, and specificity by 20.7% at matched sensitivity. These results show that RadFusion makes report generation clinically adaptable, quantitatively verifiable, and diagnostically more reliable.

</details>


### [156] [Measuring Semantic Abstractness of SAE Features via Nonlocality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10537)
*Chuqiao Lin,Shivaji Sondhi,Xiao-Liang Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Feature Nonlocality (FNL), an entropy-based metric measuring how dispersed a sparse autoencoder feature's influence is across token positions. FNL correlates with feature abstractness, distinguishing contextual reasoning features from token-level ones. Applications include auditing jailbreak mitigation features (revealing most are low-FNL positional features) and improving MATH-500 accuracy via steering high-FNL features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for evaluating SAE feature abstraction levels—autointerp-based semantic descriptions and causal steering utility—fail to fully capture whether a feature is a surface-level lexical pattern or a genuinely high-level concept. A reliable, LLM-independent metric is needed to distinguish these cases for proper evaluation of mechanistic explanations.

Method: Feature Nonlocality (FNL) is defined as the entropy of the normalized per-position influence on an SAE feature's activation. The per-position influence is computed by summing activation contributions across tokens at each position. High FNL indicates influence distributed broadly across positions (contextual/high-level), while low FNL indicates concentrated influence (token-level). The metric is validated against LLM-based proxy metrics of semantic abstractness.

Result: FNL correctly distinguishes context-dependent from token-driven features in 73–84% of randomly drawn pairs. In jailbreak mitigation auditing, most effective features were low-FNL positional features rather than intent-recognizing ones. Steering high-FNL features in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B improved MATH-500 accuracy by 4.6 points over baseline and outperformed low-FNL steering, though gains are model-specific.

Conclusion: FNL provides an LLM-independent, label-free, correlational witness of SAE feature abstraction level, with practical applications in evaluating mechanistic explanations and selecting features for interventions like steering and jailbreak mitigation auditing.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have helped uncover mechanistic explanations for LLM behaviours such as reasoning, jailbreaking etc., via understanding the corresponding task-relevant and causally effective features. To evaluate such mechanistic explanations, downstream studies must distinguish surface lexical features from genuinely high-level ones. However, neither an autointerp-based semantic description nor causal steering utility fully resolves the abstraction level of a feature. To this end, we introduce \emph{Feature Nonlocality} (FNL), defined as the entropy of the normalized per-position influence on an SAE feature's activation. We report that FNL correlates with existing LLM-based proxy metrics of feature semantic abstractness, and successfully distinguishes context-dependent reasoning features from token-driven ones, correctly assigning the higher FNL to the contextual feature in $73$--$84\%$ of randomly drawn pairs that consist of one contextual and one token-level feature.
  We demonstrate two downstream applications. We audit SAE-based features used for jailbreak mitigation and find surprisingly that most effective features are positional features with low FNL rather than genuinely recognizing harmful intents.
  We report that steering high-FNL features in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B improves MATH-500 accuracy by $4.6$ points over the unsteered model and outperforms steering low-FNL features, though the gains are model-specific. We conclude that FNL provides an LLM-independent, label-free, correlational witness of the abstraction level of an SAE feature, with applications in evaluating mechanistic explanations as well as selecting features for downstream interventions.

</details>


### [157] [SKILLER: Language-Level Reinforcement Learning for Reusable Skill Extraction in Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10538)
*Chenhao Dang,Siyuan Xiong,Conghui He,Weijia Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILLER is an RL framework that uses a strong LLM as actor-critic to automatically generate agent skills tailored for small open-source models, achieving significant performance gains (up to 20.4 pp) while drastically reducing inference costs compared to closed-source alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent harnesses (e.g., Codex, OpenClaw) rely on expensive closed-source models. While open-source models on consumer GPUs offer cost advantages, automatically generating effective skills tailored for these compact models remains an unsolved practical challenge.

Method: SKILLER is a natural-language-driven RL framework where a strong model serves as both actor and critic, the small-model agent system acts as the environment, and all RL signals (rewards, policy updates) are propagated entirely via natural language. This enables automatic generation of executor-specific skills.

Result: On five benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B, SKILLER outperforms three open-source and one closed-source skill generation/evolution methods by 4.3–20.4 pp (9B) and 1.8–13.3 pp (4B). It matches strong closed-source performance on single-skill tasks in SkillsBench.

Conclusion: SKILLER demonstrates that RL-driven, NL-mediated skill generation can unlock near-closed-source performance from small open-source agent models, offering a cost-effective path for real-world agent deployment.

Abstract: Agent skills represent a standardized format for packaging procedural knowledge and domain expertise, serving within agent harness systems as an essential mechanism to continually constrain a language model's behavior space for repeatable, high-quality task execution. However, because strong closed-source models entail high inference costs, current popular agent harnesses, such as Codex and OpenClaw, remain prohibitively expensive when deploying these skills to accomplish real-world tasks. The rapid capability enhancement of open-source models deployable on consumer-grade GPUs presents a compelling opportunity to drastically reduce these costs by leveraging skill-based behavioral constraints. Nevertheless, automatically generating effective skills tailored specifically for such compact models remains a significant practical challenge. To address this, we propose SKILLER, a natural-language-driven reinforcement learning framework designed to automatically generate executor-specific skills for small models, which employs a strong model as the actor and critic, treats the small-model agent system as the environment, and propagates all reinforcement learning signals entirely via natural language. Extensive experimental evaluations across five relevant benchmarks using Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B demonstrate that SKILLER outperforms three open-source and one closed-source skill generation or evolution methods, achieving absolute gains ranging from 4.3 to 20.4 percentage points for the 9B model and 1.8 to 13.3 points for the 4B model, while remarkably matching the performance of strong closed-source models on single-skill tasks in SkillsBench. The project is available at https://github.com/DANG-ai/SKILLER.

</details>


### [158] [Reinforcement Learning-Based Laser Cutting Machine Parameter Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10549)
*Khanh Quan Pham,Majid Kundroo,Geunwoo Ban,Seongho Bae,Taehong Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL²C, a Q-learning-based algorithm with epsilon-greedy policy and dynamic environment adaptability, optimizes laser-cutting parameters for optical films, reducing taper size, film wastage, optimization steps (up to 12.5%), and processing time (up to 81.8%) compared to existing RL methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional trial-and-error methods for tuning laser-cutting parameters (focal length, laser power) for different optical films are slow, inaccurate, and wasteful, necessitating an automated, adaptive optimization approach.

Method: The RL²C algorithm employs Q-learning with an epsilon-greedy exploration policy to dynamically optimize cutting parameters. A dynamic environment space adaptability mechanism enables the agent to handle novel states encountered across multiple experimental batches.

Result: RL²C achieved up to 12.5% reduction in optimization steps and up to 81.8% reduction in processing time compared to other RL-based optimization methods, while also reducing taper size and film wastage.

Conclusion: RL²C demonstrates strong potential for industrial laser-cutting applications by improving cut quality, reducing time and material waste, and minimizing the need for manual parameter tuning interventions.

Abstract: Achieving high accuracy in laser-based cutting of optical films requires careful tuning of parameters such as focal length and laser power beam, adjusted according to the specific properties of each film type. Trial-and-error based traditional methods are used to find the most suitable cutting parameters for various films, but they are slow and inaccurate. To address this issue, this paper presents the Reinforcement Learning for Laser Cutting (RL$^{2}$C) algorithm, which uses Q-learning with an epsilon-greedy policy to dynamically optimize cutting parameters, significantly reducing taper size and film wastage. Additionally, RL$^{2}$C incorporates a dynamic environment space adaptability mechanism to allow it to adapt to new states encountered during the learning process over multiple batches of experiments. Experimental results demonstrate that RL$^{2}$C requires fewer steps and less time to find optimal cutting parameters compared to various RL-based optimization methods. Specifically, RL$^{2}$C reduces the number of optimization steps by up to 12.5\% and processing time by up to 81.8\% compared to existing methods. This study demonstrates the potential of RL in industrial laser-cutting processes by improving cut quality, reducing time and film wastage, and minimizing manual interventions.

</details>


### [159] [DashArena: Benchmarking LLMs on Interactive Analytic Dashboard Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10567)
*Xiaotong Wang,Dazhen Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DashArena introduces the first benchmark for task-grounded, open-ended interactive dashboard generation, evaluating systems on both dashboard output and replayable interaction trajectories. A browser executor replays trajectories to produce reproducible evidence, judged by a VLM via Bradley–Terry aggregation. The distilled DashJudge-8B aligns well with human judgments, and experiments reveal persistent failures in rendering, analytics, and interaction that static or execution-only evaluations miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dashboard generation models are evaluated primarily on static appearance or execution correctness, neither of which captures analytical support quality or interaction fidelity. Dashboard generation is inherently open-ended, and no benchmark exists that evaluates systems based on realistic, task-driven interactive workflows.

Method: DashArena requires systems to produce both a dashboard and a replayable interaction trajectory. A browser-based executor replays the trajectory to generate reproducible visual and execution evidence. A VLM judge compares candidate dashboards using this evidence, and Bradley–Terry aggregation ranks systems. The judge is further distilled into the open-weight DashJudge-8B model.

Result: Human evaluations confirm DashJudge-8B effectively reproduces human judgments. Ablation studies demonstrate that interaction evidence improves judge agreement with humans. Experiments with frontier models expose persistent failures in rendering, analytical reasoning, and interaction handling that static or execution-only checks fail to detect.

Conclusion: Realistic dashboard generation remains a challenging open problem. Interaction-aware evaluation — capturing replayable analytical workflows — is essential for surfacing failures that conventional static or execution-only metrics overlook. DashArena and DashJudge-8B provide a robust foundation for future progress in this area.

Abstract: Analytic dashboards combine coordinated views and interactions for data exploration and decision-making. Recent models can generate them from data and natural-language goals, but evaluating their usefulness remains difficult. Dashboard generation is open-ended, and neither static appearance nor successful execution alone captures analytical support and interaction quality. We introduce DashArena, to our knowledge the first benchmark for open-ended, task-grounded generation of interactive analytic dashboards. Its key innovation is to require each system to generate both a dashboard and a replayable interaction trajectory. A browser executor replays the trajectory and turns the system's intended analytical workflow into reproducible visual and execution evidence. A VLM judge compares candidates using this evidence, and Bradley--Terry aggregation produces the leaderboard. We further distill the judge into the open-weight DashJudge-8B. Human evaluations show that DashJudge-8B effectively reproduces human judgments and ablations show that interaction evidence improves judge agreement. Experiments with frontier models reveal persistent rendering, analytical, and interaction failures. Together, these results show that realistic dashboard generation remains challenging and that interaction-aware evaluation captures failures missed by static or execution-only checks.

</details>


### [160] [Agentic Instruction Data Selection: Let DataMaster Interpret Your Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10579)
*Fanqi Zhou,Qiaosheng Chen,Zixian Huang,Gong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DataMaster is an automated agent that interprets natural language descriptions of data needs and autonomously composes optimal instruction data selection strategies, outperforming static baselines and even full-pool training across math, medical, and code domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instruction data selection methods rely on individual metrics that cannot generalize across diverse real-world datasets, forcing developers into manual, heuristic-driven, error-prone data curation. The paper aims to replace this manual configuration paradigm with automated orchestration.

Method: The authors propose DataMaster, an Instruction Data Selection Agent that takes natural language descriptions of user intent and autonomously composes optimal selection strategies by orchestrating multiple metrics and heuristics without manual intervention.

Result: Extensive experiments across math, medical, and code domains demonstrate that DataMaster outperforms static selection baselines in most settings and surpasses full-pool training performance in a substantial number of cases.

Conclusion: Automated orchestration of data selection via a language-interpretive agent (DataMaster) is not only feasible but superior to both manual heuristic design and full-data training, offering a practical, scalable solution for data curation. Code is publicly released.

Abstract: Although existing instruction data selection methods have introduced various metrics, the inherent complexity of real-world datasets makes it impractical for any single metric to generalize across all scenarios. Developers are thus often forced to manually inspect data and craft heuristic rules for each new application---a tedious and error-prone process. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift from manual configuration to automated orchestration via the Instruction Data Selection Agent (DataMaster), which interprets user intent and autonomously composes optimal selection strategies. By allowing users to specify data needs through natural language descriptions, DataMaster simplifies data curation and removes the burden of manual strategy design. Extensive experiments across the math, medical, and code domains show that DataMaster outperforms static baselines in most settings and surpasses full-pool training in a substantial number of cases. The implementation of DataMaster and the scripts needed to reproduce the reported pipeline are publicly available at https://github.com/nju-websoft/DataMaster.

</details>


### [161] [HexEval: An Evidence-Driven Hexagonal Framework for Multidimensional Scholar Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10584)
*Xiaokang Qu,Yiting Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HexEval proposes an evidence-driven hexagonal framework for multidimensional scholar assessment that combines intrinsic research quality (rigor, innovation, contribution) with external scholarly behavior (knowledge translation, coherence, impact) using heterogeneous public data sources, producing interpretable, auditable profiles rather than opaque scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scholar assessment methods rely on bibliometric indicators and reputation proxies, while LLM-based approaches focus narrowly on individual papers rather than comprehensive scholar evaluation. The authors argue scholar assessment should be an evidence-driven reasoning problem integrating intrinsic quality and verifiable external behavior.

Method: HexEval, a hexagonal framework with two evidence layers: (1) an intrinsic layer evaluating anonymized representative works on research rigor, methodological innovation, and scientific contribution; (2) an external layer characterizing scholars via knowledge translation, research coherence, and academic impact using evidence from GitHub, Lens, OpenAlex, and other public sources. The framework preserves intermediate evidence, dimension-specific rationales, and verification signals for interpretability.

Result: Experiments across all six dimensions show dimension-dependent agreement with human or external reference criteria. Structured calibration improves absolute agreement for intrinsic quality dimensions, while external modules recover broad trajectory and ordinal impact signals.

Conclusion: Evidence-driven reasoning over heterogeneous scholarly evidence is a promising paradigm for auditable AI-assisted scholar assessment, though coverage and attribution limitations in public scholarly data remain challenges.

Abstract: Scholar assessment plays a fundamental role in faculty recruitment, funding allocation, academic promotion, and talent discovery. Existing scholar assessment methods predominantly rely on bibliometric indicators and reputation proxies, while recent large language model (LLM)-based approaches mainly focus on evaluating individual research papers rather than comprehensively assessing scholars. We argue that scholar assessment should be formulated as an evidence-driven reasoning problem that jointly considers intrinsic research quality and externally verifiable scholarly behavior. To this end, we propose HexEval, an evidence-driven hexagonal framework for multidimensional scholar assessment. HexEval explicitly organizes scholar assessment into two complementary evidence layers. The intrinsic layer evaluates anonymized representative works along three dimensions, namely research rigor, methodological innovation, and scientific contribution, whereas the external layer characterizes scholars through knowledge translation, research coherence, and academic impact using heterogeneous evidence collected from GitHub, Lens, OpenAlex, and other publicly verifiable sources. Instead of producing opaque aggregate scores, HexEval preserves intermediate evidence, dimension-specific rationales, and verification signals throughout the evaluation process, enabling interpretable and auditable scholar profiles. Experiments across all six dimensions show dimension-dependent agreement with human or external reference criteria: structured calibration improves absolute agreement for intrinsic quality, while the external modules recover broad trajectory and ordinal impact signals. These results support evidence-driven reasoning over heterogeneous scholarly evidence as a promising paradigm for auditable AI-assisted scholar assessment, while exposing the coverage and attribution limitations of public scholarly data.

</details>


### [162] [Curate Before You Connect: Identity and Ontology Tagging in a Production Knowledge Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10644)
*Vaibhav Dangaich,Kevin Lewis,Kundeshwar Pundalik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Describes a production pipeline for ingesting extracted entities/relations into a knowledge graph, focusing on identity resolution via a "record-identity ladder" (not name similarity), a conservative merge policy using canonical-name keys, and multi-class ontology tagging with anchored evidence to prevent spurious classifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Entity resolution decisions are destructive and irreversible — merged records cannot be separated post-hoc, unlike type errors. The authors argue that automation should be conservative (flagging candidates, not auto-merging), motivated by a real incident where an over-merge corrupted a correct record and deleted eight entities. They also address the problem of ontology tagging creating false classifications when treating entity names as type assertions.

Method: A "record-identity ladder" determines sameness using identifier columns, name columns, display names, and type-scoped position — deliberately avoiding name similarity. De-duplication within parsed tables uses this ladder. Graph writing applies a coarser canonical-name key for exact-match auto-merging. Multi-class ontology tagging requires "anchored evidence," matching name fragments only when tied to explicit structural evidence, dramatically reducing false role assignments. A curation queue manages pending proposals against human decisions.

Result: The pipeline produced a knowledge graph of 537,157 entities and 2,198,567 relationships from 98,795 government documents. Requiring anchored evidence reduced role assignments on an enriched sample from 36 to 4, all confirmed correct. The curation queue grew to 48,403 pending proposals against only 775 human decisions. Conformance debt is quantified, with secondary classifications compensating for a mis-parented primary class.

Conclusion: No identity benchmark is reported because over-merges from the canonical-name key are undetectable by construction — the authors argue this is the correct automation boundary. Entity resolution should only flag candidates for human review. Anchored evidence is essential for trustworthy ontology tagging.

Abstract: Extraction produces candidate entities and relationships; writing them into a graph is where identity is decided, and identity decisions are destructive in a way extraction errors are not. A wrong type can be corrected later, but two records merged under one identity cannot be separated once their properties have been combined, and the merge leaves no error behind. This paper describes the ingestion and ontology-tagging layer that turns a validated extraction stream into a knowledge graph of 537,157 entities and 2,198,567 relationships drawn from 98,795 government documents. We describe a record-identity ladder that decides sameness from identifier columns, name columns, display names and type-scoped position rather than from name similarity. The ladder governs de-duplication within parsed tables, while the graph write applies a coarser canonical-name key, so records sharing a canonical name merge automatically on exact equality. We argue rather than demonstrate that this is where the automation line belongs: no identity benchmark is reported, and the over-merges the key permits are undetectable by construction. That policy, under which entity resolution only ever flags candidates, followed an incident in which two surface forms of one name were merged, corrupting a correct record and deleting eight entities from an unrelated document. We then describe multi-class ontology tagging and an evidence asymmetry we did not anticipate: an entity name is an instance label rather than a type assertion, so matching name fragments against a class index invents classifications. Requiring anchored evidence cut role assignments on an enriched sample from 36 to 4, all confirmed correct. We quantify the graph's conformance debt, show secondary classifications compensating for a mis-parented primary class, and describe a curation queue grown to 48,403 pending proposals against 775 human decisions.

</details>


### [163] [Decision-Aware Approximation of Belief Functions for Evidential Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10650)
*Sohaib Afifi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a decision-aware approximation for reducing focal elements in mass functions, prioritizing decision quality over representational closeness. It targets the regret of decisions made with cheaper approximations evaluated under true mass functions, demonstrating that decision-aware merging preserves optimal decisions more reliably than distance-based methods, both theoretically (via a one-point bound and dynamic programming) and experimentally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional focal element reduction uses intrinsic distances (e.g., Jaccard, Jousselme) to keep the approximation close to the original mass function. However, when the mass function feeds a linear combinatorial optimization problem with evidential costs, what matters is not representational closeness but the quality of the resulting decision. The authors aim to develop an approximation method that minimizes decision regret rather than representation error.

Method: The authors introduce a decision-aware approximation framework targeting the regret criterion: one decides using the cheaper approximation and is evaluated under the true mass function. They prove a one-point bound that localizes regret at the true optimum, convert this into an exact dynamic program for the scalar case, and extend it to an online version that prunes focal elements before the final cost is known. Experiments compare decision-aware compression against representation-aware (distance-based) compression on minimal shortest path problems and a non-linear proxy read-out.

Result: On minimal shortest path problems, distance-optimal approximation flips the decision while decision-aware merging preserves it, occurring on a non-negligible fraction of random instances. The decision-aware compressor flips the decision less often than representation-aware compression for both linear criteria and non-linear proxy read-outs.

Conclusion: When mass functions are used to feed decision-making problems, approximation should be driven by decision quality rather than representational fidelity. The proposed decision-aware approach, grounded in regret minimization and supported by theoretical guarantees (one-point bound, dynamic programming), consistently outperforms distance-based methods in preserving optimal decisions.

Abstract: Reducing the number of focal elements of a mass function is classically driven by an intrinsic distance, such as Jaccard or Jousselme, that keeps the approximation close to the original as a body of evidence. We consider instead the case where the mass function feeds a linear combinatorial optimisation problem with evidential costs. What should then be preserved is not the closeness of the two mass functions, but the quality of the decision they induce. We introduce a decision-aware approximation that targets the regret of the decision: one decides with the cheaper approximation and is evaluated under the true mass function. On a minimal shortest path, the distance-optimal approximation flips the decision while a decision-aware merge preserves it, and this occurs on a non-negligible fraction of random instances. We prove a one-point bound that localises the regret at the true optimum, turn it into an exact dynamic program for the scalar case, and extend it to an online version that prunes focal elements before the final cost is known. In experiments the decision-aware compressor flips the decision less often than representation-aware compression, for both the linear criterion and a non-linear proxy read-out.

</details>


### [164] [Operationalising Relative Causal Knowledge: Backbone Identifiability from Private Reports on a Shared Outcome](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10664)
*Fabrizio Russo,Mark Somers*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines when agents' private causal knowledge determines a shared interventionally consistent abstraction (backbone). It shows that in the two-agent common-effect case, local causal marginals do not uniquely identify a backbone due to hidden interaction degrees of freedom. Identification becomes possible under additive separability and when agents communicate causally identified response functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Relativity of Causal Knowledge (RCK) framework presupposes that a shared backbone can be identified from agents' private causal models. This paper asks the foundational prior identification question: under what conditions do agents' private causal knowledge uniquely determine that backbone? Without answering this, the entire transport mechanism of RCK lacks a rigorous footing.

Method: The authors work within the basic two-agent common-effect setting: two private causes influence one shared outcome, and each agent identifies only the single-cause causal marginal relevant to its own perspective. They impose standard compatibility, non-degeneracy, and local overlap assumptions, then analyze whether local causal marginals uniquely pin down a joint intervention kernel. They examine the role of additive separability and response-function communication in restoring identifiability.

Result: Local causal marginals do not identify a unique backbone: infinitely many joint intervention kernels induce identical private reports while disagreeing on joint interventions. Additive separability eliminates the hidden interaction degree of freedom, but observational residual summaries alone remain insufficient. Full identification requires agents to communicate causally identified response functions.

Conclusion: The problem of backbone identification is first a communication problem — agents must share causally identified response functions — and only then a policy-composition problem. An education value-added example illustrates this point concretely.

Abstract: The Relativity of Causal Knowledge (RCK) explains how a network of agents with different structural causal models can exchange causal knowledge through a shared interventionally consistent abstraction, or backbone. We ask the prior identification question that this transport mechanism presupposes: when is that backbone determined by the agents' private causal knowledge? In the basic two-agent common-effect case, two private causes influence one shared outcome and each agent identifies only the single-cause causal marginal relevant to its own perspective. We show that, under standard compatibility, non-degeneracy, and local overlap assumptions, those local causal marginals do not identify a unique backbone. Infinitely many joint intervention kernels can induce exactly the same private reports while disagreeing on joint interventions. We then give a conditional recovery result. Additive separability removes the hidden interaction degree of freedom, but observational residual summaries remain insufficient. Identification becomes possible when agents communicate causally identified response functions. An education value-added example illustrates why this is first a communication problem, and only then a policy-composition problem.

</details>


### [165] [VERDICT: Training-Free Step-Wise Verification of Multimodal Reasoning via Disagreement-Aware Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10665)
*Rohit Sinha,Kunal Tilaganji,Tanuja Ganu,Nagarajan Natarajan,Amit Sharma,Vineeth Balasubramanian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VERDICT is a training-free, domain-agnostic step-wise verification method for multimodal LLMs that treats cross-modal disagreement among frozen verifiers as a coordination game, using a closed-form equilibrium solution to filter erroneous reasoning steps and improve answer accuracy by up to +5.95% across six benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current verification approaches for multimodal LLM reasoning chains either require expensive labeled supervision with inconsistent cross-task performance, or naively aggregate scores from multiple verifiers without exploiting the informational value of their disagreements. The key insight is that disagreement itself signals reasoning-step validity.

Method: VERDICT formalizes step-wise verification as a coupled scoring problem among disparate frozen verifiers, modeled as a coordination game with a unique closed-form equilibrium. Agreement among verifiers signals valid steps, while disagreement reveals instability. It computes consensus scores via this closed-form solution, enabling disagreement-aware filtering and stability-conscious ranking of reasoning steps — all without any training or task-specific adaptation.

Result: Evaluated across six benchmarks, VERDICT consistently improves over the base model by up to +5.95% and performs competitively with domain-specific critics that require extensive supervision.

Conclusion: Cross-modal agreement provides a robust, training-free verification signal. Making the structure of cross-modal disagreement explicit and actionable is both feasible and effective, matching or approaching the performance of fully supervised domain-specific verifiers.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models often generate reasoning chains containing subtle errors that lead to incorrect answers. Current verification approaches have notable limitations. Existing approaches either require expensive labelled supervision with inconsistent cross-task performance or aggregate scores from multiple sources by simple aggregations, missing a key insight: when these scores disagree, that disagreement itself carries important information about whether a reasoning step is truly valid or not. We formalise this as a coupled scoring problem among disparate, frozen verifiers, interpretable as a coordination game with a unique closed-form equilibrium where agreement signals valid steps while disagreement reveals instability. Towards this end, we propose a training-free domain-agnostic step-wise verification approach we call VERDICT: VERification via Disagreement-Informed Coupled Thresholding. To our knowledge, VERDICT is the first training-free verifier that makes the structure of cross-modal disagreement explicit and actionable. It computes consensus scores through a closed-form solution, enabling both disagreement-aware filtering and stability-conscious ranking of reasoning steps. Evaluated across six benchmarks, \method consistently improves over the base model by up to +5.95%, and performs competitively with domain-specific critics that demand extensive supervision, demonstrating that cross-modal agreement provides robust verification signals without task-specific adaptation and Training-Free Verification

</details>


### [166] [FITTER: Vocabulary-Agnostic Cross-Domain Inference on Temporal Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10668)
*Jiaxin Pan,Mojtaba Nayyeri,Osama Mohammed,Daniel Hernandez,Rongchuan Zhang,Cheng Cheng,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FITTER is a fully-inductive temporal knowledge graph completion model that enables cross-domain transfer using vocabulary-agnostic, structure-based embeddings with time-shift invariant relative temporal encoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal knowledge graph completion methods assume all entities, relation names, and timestamps are known at training time, locking each model to a single graph and vocabulary. This prevents generalization across the heterogeneous knowledge graphs of the Semantic Web. FITTER addresses the need for a model that can perform link prediction on entirely unseen entities, relation names, and timestamps from different domains without retraining.

Method: FITTER represents each predicate through interaction patterns with others and time, using relative rather than absolute ordering encodings. A message-passing mechanism fuses local and global temporal context to produce vocabulary-agnostic embeddings. The temporal encoding is formally proven to be time-shift invariant, ensuring robustness to absolute timestamp values.

Result: Evaluated on six temporal knowledge graph benchmarks spanning diverse domains, granularities, and time spans, FITTER consistently outperforms inductive baselines in cross-domain, cross-graph transfer settings without any retraining.

Conclusion: Vocabulary-agnostic structural learning is a viable and effective foundation for inference over the heterogeneous knowledge graphs of the Semantic Web, enabling models to generalize beyond their training vocabulary and domain.

Abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs are central to many uses of the Semantic Web, but existing completion methods assume the entities, relation names, and timestamps to be reasoned about are already known at training time, restricting each model to a single graph and vocabulary. We propose FITTER, the first fully-inductive structural model for temporal knowledge graph link prediction that supports cross-domain transfer: the inference graph may contain entirely unseen entities, relation names, and timestamps drawn from a different domain. FITTER represents each predicate by its interaction patterns with others and time through encodings of relative rather than absolute ordering; message-passing fuses local and global temporal context to produce vocabulary-agnostic embeddings. We prove the temporal encoding is time-shift invariant and evaluate FITTER on cross-domain, cross-graph transfer over six temporal knowledge graph benchmarks of diverse domains, granularities, and time spans. FITTER consistently outperforms inductive baselines without retraining, indicating that vocabulary-agnostic structural learning is a viable foundation for inference over the heterogeneous knowledge graphs of the Semantic Web.

</details>


### [167] [REDAgentBench: Executable Red Teaming and Faithful Measurement of LLM Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10669)
*Zixing Chen,Xingyuan Liu,Jie Zhu,Huaixia Dou,Shuo Jiang,Junhui Li,Lifan Guo,Feng Chen,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: REDAgentBench is an executable red-teaming framework for LLM agents that measures safety violations using service receipts and state changes rather than surface-level attack success rates. Across 1,661 cases, six models, and three harnesses, it finds a 65.69% macro-average ASR, reveals a Recognition–Execution Gap where agents violate policies after stating relevant constraints, and shows a training-free policy reminder can reduce violations by >70 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent safety evaluations collapse exposure, execution, observation, and adjudication into a single attack success rate (ASR), conflating actual violations with evidence visibility. This makes it hard to faithfully measure safety, pinpoint where failures occur, and design effective interventions.

Method: REDAgentBench derives attacks from explicit safety constraints and agent-system vulnerabilities, executes them in isolated service sandboxes, and verifies harmful effects from service receipts and final-state changes. The benchmark includes 1,661 cases across five service surfaces, tested on six models with three agent harnesses. A training-free policy reminder intervention is evaluated through matched replay.

Result: Macro-average ASR is 65.69%, with variation across harnesses and evidence views. Evaluation-context disclosure alters execution behavior. In a state-grounded diagnostic cohort, ~20% of confirmed violations occur after the agent states the relevant constraint or risk (Recognition–Execution Gap). A training-free policy reminder reduces confirmed violations by >70 percentage points.

Conclusion: Executable evaluation grounded in state changes and service receipts yields more faithful safety measurement than surface-level ASR. The Recognition–Execution Gap and the effectiveness of policy reminders point to actionable intervention points for improving LLM agent safety.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents combine language-based reasoning with external tools to perform complex tasks. Adversarial inputs can exploit interactions between the agent and its environment, causing the agent to violate safety policies during execution. Yet existing evaluations often reduce agent safety to a single attack success rate (ASR), collapsing exposure, execution, observation, and adjudication and potentially conflating actual violations with evidence visibility. We introduce REDAgentBench, an executable framework for autonomous red-teaming and faithful measurement. It derives attacks from explicit safety constraints and associated agent-system vulnerabilities, runs them in isolated service sandboxes, and verifies harmful effects from service receipts and final-state changes. The benchmark contains 1,661 cases across five service surfaces. Across six models and three agent harnesses, macro-average ASR is 65.69%; reported ASR varies with harness and evidence view, while evaluation-context disclosure changes execution behavior. In a state-grounded diagnostic cohort, almost one in five confirmed violations with resolved action anchors occurs after the agent states the relevant constraint or risk, revealing a Recognition--Execution Gap. Finally, a training-free policy reminder reduces confirmed violations by more than 70 percentage points in matched replay. These findings show that executable evaluation can improve safety measurement and identify actionable intervention points.

</details>


### [168] [Divergent Response Modes in Frontier Language Models Under Steering Pressure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06578)
*Ali Jalal-Kamali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Six frontier LLMs exhibit measurably distinct behavioral steerability under explicit pressure, differing not only in shift magnitude but in qualitative response modes. GPT-5 uniquely deflects reasoning disclosure, while Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist suppression differently. A linear probe on Llama decodes and causally drives the behavior with high accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier language models are developed with different data, objectives, and safety pipelines, yet whether these divergences yield measurably different behaviors under explicit steering pressure remains underexplored. The study aims to systematically characterize inter-model differences in steerability.

Method: Six frontier models from six developers are evaluated using 300 paired base-vs-steered items across three categories: values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, and reasoning-suppression (plus 40 validation items). All six models serve as blind peer judges, classifying responses against fixed behavioral rubrics. The 24,480 resulting judgments are scored via leave-one-out consensus. For Llama (the open-weight model), a linear probe is trained to decode behavior from the residual stream, and a causal intervention sweep injects the decoded direction during generation.

Result: Models diverge in both steerability magnitude and qualitative response modes, with some modes appearing in only one or two models. GPT-5 deflects reasoning-disclosure requests while preserving answers (99% vs. 0% for others). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist explicit suppression via distinct strategies. The linear probe on Llama decodes behavior at 0.87 held-out accuracy; injecting the direction during generation shifts behavior from 0% to 86%. All findings are robust under token-budget remediation and a hypothesis-blind control experiment.

Conclusion: Frontier models exhibit distinct behavioral signatures under steering pressure, reflecting their divergent training pipelines. These differences have implications for interpretability, safety, and model selection in deployment contexts where steerability matters.

Abstract: Frontier language models are trained using distinct data, objectives, and safety pipelines. Whether these differences produce measurably different behaviors under explicit steering pressure remains underexplored. This study evaluates behavioral steerability across six frontier models from six developers using 300 paired base and steered items over three categories: values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, and reasoning-suppression (plus 40 validation items). All six models act as blind peer judges and classify every response based on fixed behavioral rubrics. The resulting 24,480 judgments are scored by leave-one-out consensus. We find that models differ not just in how much steering shifts their behavior but in what kind (mode) of response they give, and some response modes appear in only one or two of them. GPT-5 deflects requests to disclose its reasoning while leaving its answer intact (99% vs. 0% for all other models). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist explicit suppression instructions and in different ways. Using Llama as the open-weight model, we trace the largest behavioral split to its internals. A linear probe decodes the behavior from the residual stream at 0.87 held-out accuracy while injecting that direction during generation drives the behavior from 0% to 86% across an intervention sweep. Every finding holds under both a token-budget remediation and a control experiment with a hypothesis-blind judgment prompt.

</details>


### [169] [Self-Correcting Long-Horizon Search Agents via Tree-Structured Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10676)
*Aijun Yang,Qianxue Guo,Ziyi Huang,Yuxuan Chen,Shiyou Qian,Jian Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReTree is a self-correcting, tree-structured memory mechanism for LLM-based search agents that bounds per-step context, preserves evidence provenance, and automatically revises contradictory claims by tracing, replacing, and pruning affected reasoning branches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based search agents suffer from unbounded context growth and noise when full execution trajectories are provided. Current compression methods sacrifice important details and often replace erroneous facts without repairing downstream reasoning derived from them, leaving conclusions unreliable.

Method: ReTree models search as an evidence tree where nodes store bounded summaries, evidence, and revision histories. When newly retrieved evidence contradicts an earlier claim, ReTree traces back to the originating node, replaces outdated evidence, regenerates summaries, prunes affected branches, and resumes search. Source-grounded evidence provenance enables reliable conflict localization.

Result: On four public QA and search benchmarks, ReTree consistently outperforms Full-Trajectory ReAct, improving answer accuracy by up to 25.6 percentage points. The average maximum per-step reasoning context of Full-Trajectory ReAct is 1.27–1.51× that of ReTree.

Conclusion: ReTree establishes an effective self-correcting memory abstraction for long-horizon search, combining bounded context, evidence traceability, and automatic repair of contradictory reasoning chains.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based search agents answer questions through multi-step interactions with external environments. However, providing complete execution trajectories to the LLM causes unbounded context growth and introduces noise. Existing compression methods reduce context at the cost of important details and often replace erroneous facts without repairing downstream reasoning derived from them. To address this problem, we propose ReTree, a self-correcting tree-structured memory mechanism for search agents. ReTree constructs a bounded per-step reasoning context while preserving source-linked evidence. It models search as an evidence tree whose nodes store bounded summaries, evidence, and revision histories. When newly retrieved evidence contradicts an earlier claim, ReTree traces back to the node where the claim was introduced, replaces outdated evidence, regenerates summaries, prunes affected branches, and resumes search. Source-grounded evidence provenance supports reliable conflict localization and keeps final claims traceable to retrieved passages. Experiments on four public question-answering and search benchmarks show that ReTree consistently outperforms Full-Trajectory ReAct, improving answer accuracy by up to 25.6 percentage points (pp); the average maximum per-step reasoning context of Full-Trajectory ReAct is $1.27$--$1.51\times$ that of ReTree. These results establish ReTree as an effective self-correcting memory abstraction for long-horizon search.

</details>


### [170] [Ex-Omni-2D: Expressive Omni-Modal Dialogue Models with Native Visual Presence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10720)
*Haoyu Zhang,Zhipeng Li,Xiaoying Tang,Tianshu Yu,Yiwen Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Ex-Omni-2D introduces an omni-modal dialogue framework that generates synchronized text, personalized speech, and reference-conditioned avatar video. It uses a Visual Thought Plan and shared acoustic-temporal interface to avoid large-scale paired supervision, with a teacher-student distillation strategy enabling efficient streaming video generation at practical real-time factors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current omni-modal dialogue models can process multimodal inputs and produce spoken responses, but their outputs lack visual embodiment (avatar video). The authors aim to close this gap by enabling coordinated generation of text, speech, and video responses without requiring prohibitively expensive large-scale paired query-text-speech-video datasets.

Method: The framework predicts a Visual Thought Plan (VTP) capturing scene, emotion, and motion, then generates response text and native multi-codebook speech units. These units serve as a shared acoustic-temporal interface: decoded into speech and temporally aligned with video frames during online generation. This decoupling allows heterogeneous data sources for training. A full-sequence Video Generator acts as Teacher; a block-causal Streaming Student is distilled from it using a Prefix Streaming mechanism that carries a clean latent across chunks to mitigate cumulative late-chunk degradation, enabling efficient few-step (4-step) incremental generation.

Result: With four-step inference, the complete four-GPU pipeline achieves an end-to-end real-time factor (RTF) of 1.293 at 400×720 / 720×400 resolution, representing a practical quality-efficiency operating point for real-time omni-modal dialogue with avatar video.

Conclusion: Ex-Omni-2D demonstrates that coordinated text-speech-video generation for embodied dialogue agents is feasible without large-scale paired supervision, and that teacher-student distillation with prefix streaming enables practical real-time inference.

Abstract: Omni-modal dialogue models can understand multimodal inputs and synthesize spoken replies, yet their responses remain visually disembodied. We introduce \textbf{Ex-Omni-2D}, an omni-modal dialogue framework that generates a coordinated response comprising text, personalized speech, and reference-conditioned video. Given a multimodal query, reference image, and reference audio, the model predicts a structured \textit{Visual Thought Plan} (VTP) describing scene, emotion, and motion, followed by response text and native multi-codebook speech units. These units form a shared acoustic-temporal interface: they are decoded into speech and aligned online with video frames. This interface enables the response and avatar pathways to be learned from heterogeneous speech, dialogue, and avatar-video data, avoiding the need for large-scale query--text--speech--video supervision. A full-sequence Video Generator serves as the primary Teacher. For efficient incremental generation, we further distill it into a few-step block-causal \emph{Streaming Student} whose Prefix Streaming mechanism carries a clean latent across consecutive chunks to reduce cumulative late-chunk degradation. With four-step inference, the complete four-GPU pipeline achieves an end-to-end RTF of 1.293 at $400\times720$/$720\times400$, providing a practical quality--efficiency operating point.

</details>


### [171] [Tree-of-Ideas: Automated Research Ideation via Cross-Trajectory Reasoning over Scholarly Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10740)
*Xun Li,Yiying Yang,Pengtao Li,Xiao Yao,Suyu Liu,Xiaoyang Ye,Ziyu Lu,Yuan Yao,Yangning Li,Yinghui Li,Wenhao Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Tree-of-Ideas (ToI) is a two-stage framework that reconstructs branching scholarly trajectories from citations and reasons across them to generate grounded research ideas, outperforming baselines and approaching human-level quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research ideation methods treat papers as unstructured context or model scholarly evolution as isolated citation chains, failing to capture how research problems and solutions co-evolve through interacting trajectories. The authors aim to address this gap by modeling cross-path evolutionary reasoning across the literature.

Method: Tree-of-Ideas (ToI) is a two-stage framework: (1) EvoTrace reconstructs branching scholarly trajectories from citation networks, tracking evolving methods, resolved problems, and remaining gaps; (2) EvoAgent reasons across these trajectories to identify convergent problems and complementary solutions, then synthesizes grounded research ideas.

Result: Evaluated across six AI research topics, ToI achieved the highest automatic score of 6.27/10 (vs. 5.36 for the strongest baseline), with Novelty at 6.36 and Groundedness at 7.00. Its score closely approaches that of human-paper references (6.29).

Conclusion: Cross-path evolutionary reasoning across branching scholarly trajectories significantly improves both the novelty and groundedness of automatically generated research ideas, demonstrating that modeling the co-evolution of problems and solutions is crucial for effective research ideation.

Abstract: Effective research ideation requires moving beyond a static understanding of prior work to trace how research problems and solutions evolve across the literature. Existing methods either treat papers as unstructured context or model scholarly evolution as isolated citation chains, overlooking interactions among research trajectories. We propose Tree-of-Ideas (ToI), a two-stage framework. EvoTrace reconstructs branching scholarly trajectories from citations, tracking evolving methods, resolved problems, and gaps. EvoAgent then reasons across trajectories to identify convergent problems and complementary solutions, generating grounded research ideas. Across six AI research topics, ToI achieves the highest score among automatic methods (6.27 vs. 5.36 for the strongest baseline on a 10-point scale), with strong Novelty (6.36) and Groundedness (7.00). Also, its score approaches that of human-paper references (6.29), demonstrating the value of cross-path evolutionary reasoning.

</details>


### [172] [Compositional Benchmark Synthesis for Hierarchical Human Action Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10765)
*Farnaz Soleimani,Abdelghani Chibani,Yacine Amirat,Ghazaleh Khodabandelou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a framework to synthesize a four-level hierarchical-intention benchmark from flat action-labeled datasets, with built-in safeguards against circular supervision. Four baselines reveal a persistent 0.13–0.17 macro-F1 held-out gap, indicating a structural reasoning challenge rather than a model artifact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video datasets either provide isolated atomic action labels without temporal composition or offer shallow, domain-narrow, fixed hierarchies for composite activities. No benchmark exists that spans a deep semantic hierarchy—actions, activities, low-level intentions (LLIs), and high-level intentions (HLIs)—while retaining real visual features and avoiding circular-supervision pitfalls.

Method: A benchmark-generation framework synthesizes a four-level hierarchy from a flat single-label action corpus. Episodes are constructed using a transition model with subject-consistency constraints, and a coverage-aware sampler reduces subject-usage imbalance (Gini from 0.566 to 0.248). Circular supervision is mitigated by keeping the sequence-generation rules disjoint from the first-order-logic rules used at evaluation. The instantiation produces 15,002 episodes. Four reference baselines (including a graph-aware model) are evaluated, with controls for generator consistency (order-destroying baseline) and logic-free violation checks.

Result: All baselines exhibit a compositional held-out gap of 0.13–0.17 macro-F1; even the best-performing graph-aware model fails to close this gap. A logic-free baseline still violates held-out semantic rules above the intrinsic data rate, confirming the gap is not merely a model artifact. The order-destroying control changes macro-F1 only within seed variation, supporting generator consistency.

Conclusion: The persistent held-out gap across diverse model families indicates a fundamental structural property of hierarchical intention recognition, not a weakness of specific architectures. The framework and released ontology, transition model, and generator enable reproducible benchmark regeneration and extension.

Abstract: Recognizing human behavior across levels of abstraction, from atomic actions to long-horizon intentions, requires data annotated along a semantic hierarchy. Large corpora provide isolated, atomically labeled clips without temporal composition, whereas recorded composite-activity corpora offer shallow, domain-narrow, fixedhierarchies. A benchmark-generation and evaluation frameworkis proposed that synthesizes a four-level hierarchical-intention benchmark, spanning actions, activities, low-level intentions (LLIs), and high-level intentions (HLIs), from a flat single-label action corpus while retaining real pre-extracted features at the action level. Episodes are assembled by a transition model under a subject-consistency constraint, and a coverage-aware sampler reduces the subject usage Gini from 0.566 to 0.248. Synthesizing such a benchmark raises a circular-supervision risk that recorded datasets avoid: if the rules generating the episodes also govern the evaluation, models can succeed by recovering the generator rather than through genuine reasoning. Validity is addressed by design, holding sequence-generation rules disjoint from the first-order-logic rules used at evaluation. The instantiation yields 15,002 episodes. Four reference baselines from different model families characterize difficulty, not as recognition methods. A compositional held-out gap of 0.13 to 0.17 macro-F1 appears across all baselines, including a graph-aware model that recognizes best yet does not close the gap, indicating a structural property of the benchmark rather than a model artifact. A logic-free baseline still violates the held-out semantic rules above their intrinsic data rate, and the order-destroying control changes macro-F1 within seed variation, serving as a generator-consistency check. Theontology, transition model, and generator are released so the benchmark can beregenerated and extended.

</details>


### [173] [Rule of Thumb: Explaining Artificial Intelligence Systems using Partial Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10766)
*Kaivalya Rawal,Daria Onitiu,Brent Mittelstadt,Sandra Wachter,Chris Russell*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Rule of Thumb (RoT) is a model-agnostic XAI method that identifies the most relevant features driving an AI system's decision for a specific datapoint, enabling fast, regulation-compliant explanations for LLM classification, opaque system auditing, and scientific discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing XAI methods face challenges in speed, model access requirements, and compatibility with emerging AI regulations. There is a need for a fast, model-agnostic explanation approach that works without internal model access, supports modern systems like LLMs, and satisfies regulatory requirements for explainability.

Method: The authors formulate RoT as identifying the most relevant features that predict an AI system's behavior for a given datapoint, using a partial information framework. The approach determines which subset of input features, when revealed, best approximates the model's output decision, providing a "rule of thumb" style explanation that is both intuitive and computationally efficient.

Result: RoT is demonstrated to be effective across three distinct use cases: (1) zero-shot classification with LLMs, (2) auditing opaque AI systems without requiring model access, and (3) facilitating scientific discovery through AI. It is substantially faster than alternatives, meets key AI regulatory requirements, and provides familiar visualizations for practitioners.

Conclusion: RoT offers a practical, fast, and model-agnostic XAI solution that bridges the gap between technical explainability and regulatory compliance, with broad applicability from LLMs to scientific research.

Abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) seeks to explain how an Artificial Intelligence (AI) system arrived at a particular decision. We propose ''Rule of Thumb'' (RoT) explanations, a new approach to XAI based upon a novel formulation that identifies the most relevant features for predicting the behaviour of an AI system, for a particular datapoint. We show how RoT is well-suited to enable XAI in: (a) zero-shot classification using large language models (LLMs), (b) auditing of opaque AI systems without model access, and (c) the use of AI in scientific discovery. Additionally, RoT meets specific requirements from leading AI regulations, provides a familiar interface and visualisations for XAI practitioners, is model-agnostic, and is substantially faster than alternatives.
  Code available at: https://github.com/KaiRawal/Rule-of-Thumb-Explaining-Artificial-Intelligence-Systems-using-Partial-Information

</details>


### [174] [SkillLens: Visual Skill Cards for Retrieval-Augmented GUI Action Prediction and On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10775)
*Zhou Liu,Ligang Huang,Zeli Su,Zewei Pan,Zhaoyang Han,Xing Chen,Yuanfeng Song,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillLens introduces Visual Skill Cards (VSCs), a state-conditioned memory representation that encodes reusable GUI workflows with visual applicability cues and verification signals, enabling frozen VLM-based agents to act more accurately. CardDistill further distills this privileged knowledge into a lightweight student model, yielding significant gains on Multimodal-Mind2Web and WebLINX-BrowserGym.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-using agents can perceive individual GUI controls but lack visual procedural memory — they fail to recognize which familiar workflow is active, which control matters next, or what evidence confirms progress. Raw interaction traces are too long and noisy to condition on, while text-only skill descriptions omit the visual state that makes a procedure applicable.

Method: The authors propose Visual Skill Cards (VSCs), a state-conditioned memory binding reusable procedures with applicability cues, visual evidence, and verification signals. The SkillLens framework constructs VSCs from heterogeneous interaction traces via a Trace-to-Visual-Skill-Card process. At inference, it retrieves relevant cards and selectively expands only the evidence needed by a frozen VLM executor for grounded GUI action prediction. CardDistill uses VSC evidence as privileged teacher context to train a student model that acts without runtime card retrieval.

Result: On Multimodal-Mind2Web, SkillLens improves a frozen GPT-5.4-mini executor by +11.6 points in Step Success Rate. On WebLINX-BrowserGym, it yields +2.9 points in Overall. CardDistill further improves the student Qwen3-VL-2B by +12.0 and +3.2 points on these respective benchmarks.

Conclusion: VSCs provide an effective form of visual procedural memory for GUI agents, bridging the gap between raw trace conditioning and text-only skill representations. The representation supports both runtime retrieval-augmented execution and distillation into compact student models, demonstrating strong empirical improvements across benchmarks.

Abstract: Computer-using agents can perceive rich software interfaces, yet their decisions often lack visual procedural memory: they may recognize individual controls without identifying which familiar workflow is active, which control matters next, or what evidence would confirm progress. Raw interaction traces preserve such information but are long and noisy to condition on, whereas text-only skills often omit the visual state that makes a procedure applicable. We introduce Visual Skill Cards (VSCs), a state-conditioned memory representation that binds reusable procedures with applicability cues, visual evidence, and verification signals. SkillLens constructs VSCs from heterogeneous interaction experience through Trace-to-Visual-Skill-Card and, at inference time, retrieves relevant cards and selectively expands only the evidence needed by a fixed visual-language model executor for grounded GUI action prediction. The same representation also supports CardDistill, which uses VSC evidence as privileged teacher context to train a student that acts without runtime card retrieval. Across Multimodal-Mind2Web and WebLINX-BrowserGym, SkillLens improves the frozen GPT-5.4-mini executor by +11.6 points in Step SR and +2.9 points in Overall, respectively; CardDistill further improves the corresponding student-only Qwen3-VL-2B metrics by +12.0 and +3.2 points.

</details>


### [175] [ChemWorld: Programmable Chemical Worlds for Controlled and Replayable Agent Experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10792)
*Jiangjie Qiu,Yijun Li,Xiaonan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ChemWorld is a programmable chemical environment that decouples the public experimental interface from private chemical laws, enabling controlled, replayable, and systematically varied experimentation across different chemical worlds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physical labs are costly and hard to replicate for controlled interventions, while existing digital environments fix the underlying experimental world. There is a need for a substrate that allows systematic variation of chemical laws while holding the agent-facing interface constant, to study autonomous experimentation rigorously.

Method: ChemWorld compiles reusable process and observation components into executable worlds, separating the public experimental contract (what agents see) from evaluator-owned chemical/material laws. It records transactional execution traces (operations, failures, resource changes, state transitions) enabling exact replay. The system supports world forking, where a single private law can be changed while keeping public conditions fixed. Validation included full-census qualification tests, deterministic case studies, and fork-pair experiments.

Result: Full-census qualification covered the reference registry, 52 generated compositions, and module/interface/compilation/invalid-action tests. Eight deterministic cases demonstrated shared lifecycle semantics, failure recovery, and exact replay. Six parent-child fork pairs successfully isolated the effects of single private-law changes. An independent agent completed a full lifecycle in a non-reference world through the same public interface.

Conclusion: Within its declared component and model domain, ChemWorld provides a controlled, replayable substrate for studying experimentation across systematically varied chemical worlds, serving as a complement to physical-laboratory evidence and calibration.

Abstract: Autonomous chemistry increasingly depends on environments in which agents can repeatedly act, observe, and adapt.Physical laboratories provide essential real-material evidence but are costly to repeat and difficult to use for tightly matched interventions, whereas most digital environments keep the underlying experimental world largely fixed. We introduce ChemWorld, a programmable chemical environment in which reusable process and observation components are compiled into executable worlds. ChemWorld separates the public experimental contract available to an agent from evaluator-owned chemical and material laws. Researchers can therefore vary world composition and operating conditions, or change a single hidden law while holding the public task and interaction conditions fixed. Transactional execution records operations, failures, resource changes, and state transitions, allowing complete environment-action trajectories to be replayed exactly and audited. Full-census qualification covered the reference registry, 52 generated compositions, and module, interface, compilation, and invalid-action tests. Eight deterministic experimental cases demonstrated shared lifecycle semantics, failure recovery, and exact replay, while six parent-child world-fork pairs isolated the effects of single private-law interventions under matched public conditions. An independent agent also completed a full lifecycle in a non-reference world through the same public interface. Within the declared component and model domain, ChemWorld provides a controlled and replayable substrate for studying experimentation across systematically varied chemical worlds, complementary to physical-laboratory evidence and calibration.

</details>


### [176] [EvoMem: Memory-Augmented Evolution for Code Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10795)
*Viktor Volkov,Valentin Khrulkov,Andrey V. Galichin,Danil Sivtsov,Nikita Glazkov,Olga Volkova,Konstantin Pchelin,Iaroslav Bespalov,Dmitry V. Dylov,Petr Anokhin,Ivan Oseledets*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoMem introduces a persistent memory architecture for LLM-driven evolutionary program search that captures successful mutation strategies across runs and tasks, reducing redundant exploration and improving cross-run knowledge reuse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-driven evolutionary frameworks discard potentially reusable mutation knowledge after each run, forcing repeated rediscovery of similar strategies and missing opportunities for cross-task transfer learning.

Method: EvoMem operates in two phases: (1) a post-run extraction phase that converts successful mutation events into structured, task-aware advice with provenance tracking, and (2) an in-evolution retrieval phase that selects a small set of contextually relevant instructions based on the current task and program context to guide mutation operators.

Result: Across geometric optimization, multi-hop QA, GPU kernel optimization, and related benchmarks, EvoMem shows positive average improvements in target metrics or search speed for most evaluated settings, though variability across tasks is observed.
