Conclusion: Persistent memory can reduce redundant exploration and improve the reuse and adaptation of successful strategies in LLM-driven evolutionary search, demonstrating the value of retaining and transferring mutation knowledge beyond single runs.

Abstract: Successful mutation strategies in evolutionary code search may contain reusable knowledge that is useful beyond a single run, and in some cases may transfer across related tasks and domains. However, existing LLM-driven evolutionary frameworks largely discard such knowledge, repeatedly rediscovering similar ideas and limiting opportunities for cross-run and cross-task learning. We introduce EvoMem, a persistent memory architecture for LLM-based evolutionary program search that captures and reuses candidate mutation knowledge. EvoMem converts successful mutation events into structured, task-aware advice for future runs. It operates in two phases: after each run, it extracts and stores promising ideas with provenance, and during subsequent evolution, it retrieves a small set of relevant instructions based on the current task and program context to guide mutation. Across geometric optimization, multi-hop question answering, GPU kernel optimization, and related benchmarks, our experiments show positive average improvements in target metrics or search speed for most evaluated settings, while also revealing variability across tasks. Overall, EvoMem provides evidence that persistent memory can reduce some redundant exploration and improve the reuse and adaptation of successful strategies in LLM-driven evolutionary search.

</details>


### [177] [Hypothesis Frontier: Verifier Guided LLM and Symbolic Search for First-Order Induction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10843)
*Serafim Batzoglou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hypothesis Frontier is a neurosymbolic framework that iteratively refines LLM-generated first-order logic formulas using a verifier: the best verified hypothesis is retained, its errors guide subsequent LLM generation, and symbolic processing repairs invalid formulas while simplifying correct ones without altering training predictions, solving more induction problems than repeated prompting under matched budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: First-order concept synthesis requires classifying labeled objects across finite relational structures. While LLMs produce semantically promising formulas, they are often not fully correct, and the search space of quantified first-order formulas is vast. Exact evaluation is possible, but purely generative approaches waste budget regenerating from scratch. The authors seek a framework that leverages verification feedback and symbolic repair/simplification to improve solve rates and formula compressibility.

Method: The Hypothesis Frontier framework operates in rounds: an LLM generates candidate first-order formulas; a verifier evaluates each on all training objects. The strongest verified hypothesis is retained and its error instances are fed back to guide the next round of LLM generation. Symbolic processing performs two functions: (1) repairing syntactically or semantically invalid formulas while staying anchored to the LLM's intended hypothesis, and (2) simplifying train-valid formulas exactly—preserving all training predictions while shortening them. The process iterates under a fixed LLM-round budget.

Result: Under controlled conditions—matched models, problem sets, and LLM-round budgets—Hypothesis Frontier solves substantially more first-order concept synthesis problems than repeated original-prompt generation. Additionally, exact symbolic simplification successfully shortens many train-valid formulas while preserving every training prediction.

Conclusion: Exact symbolic reasoning, when tightly integrated with LLM generation in a verifier-guided loop, both increases the number of solved induction problems and compresses the resulting formulas without loss of training accuracy.

Abstract: First-order concept synthesis asks a system to infer one formula that classifies labeled objects consistently across several finite relational structures. Every candidate can be evaluated exactly, but quantified first-order formulas form a vast search space, and LLM outputs are often semantically promising without being fully correct. We introduce Hypothesis Frontier, a verifier-guided neurosymbolic framework that evaluates each LLM formula on every training object, retains the strongest verified hypothesis across rounds, and uses its remaining errors to guide subsequent generation. Symbolic processing repairs invalid formulas while remaining anchored to the LLM-generated hypothesis, and simplifies train-valid formulas without changing any training prediction. Under matched models, problem sets, and LLM-round budgets, Hypothesis Frontier solves substantially more problems than repeated original-prompt generation. After the final formulas are selected, exact simplification shortens many train-valid formulas while preserving every training prediction. Exact symbolic reasoning therefore helps both to solve more induction problems and to compress many of the resulting formulas.

</details>


### [178] [Enhanced Filtering Algorithms for the Euclidean Traveling Salesperson Problem and its variants in Constraint Logic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10881)
*Alessandro Bertagnon,Marco Gavanelli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces new filtering algorithms for Constraint Logic Programming that exploit geometric information from point coordinates to achieve stronger constraint propagation for the Euclidean Traveling Salesperson Problem and its Generalized variant, outperforming traditional distance-matrix-based CP approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CP approaches to the Euclidean TSP discard valuable geometric information by precomputing a full distance matrix and treating the problem as a general TSP. This ignores the structure inherent in the points' spatial coordinates, limiting the effectiveness of constraint propagation.

Method: The authors propose novel filtering algorithms within a Constraint Logic Programming (CLP) framework that directly exploit the Euclidean coordinates of nodes. These algorithms leverage geometric properties (e.g., triangle inequality, spatial proximity) to prune the search space more aggressively. The methodology is also extended to the Euclidean Generalized Traveling Salesperson Problem (EGTSP).

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that the geometry-aware filtering yields significant computational advantages over standard distance-matrix-based CP methods for Euclidean TSP variants.

Conclusion: Exploiting geometric information directly within CP/CLP filtering algorithms enables stronger constraint propagation and improved solving performance for Euclidean routing problems compared to treating them as general TSP instances.

Abstract: The Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) is one of the best-known problems in computer science and arises in many engineering applications, such as smart vehicles and intelligent transportation systems. In the "Euclidean" case, each node is defined by its coordinates in the plane and distances are computed using the Euclidean metric. In the Constraint Programming (CP) literature, the Euclidean TSP is typically addressed by computing the full distance matrix and treating it as a general case; however this approach ignores the geometric information carried by the points' coordinates. In this work, we propose new filtering algorithms, implemented in Constraint Logic Programming (CLP), that exploit such geometric information to achieve stronger constraint propagation than existing approaches. Moreover, we show how this methodology can be extended to other Euclidean variants of the TSP, including the Euclidean Generalized Traveling Salesperson Problem (EGTSP), which is relevant in practical routing and logistics applications. Experimental results demonstrate the computational advantages of the proposed approach.

</details>


### [179] [ComBodied Agents: a New Paradigm of Human-Centric Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10915)
*Qianggang Ding,Xingyao Wang,Rui Feng,Zhibin Wang,Feixiang Wang,Kelong Mao,Hao Sun,Zhiyao Luo,Jiankai Tang,Lei Li,Jiadong Guo,Minheng Ni,Weicong Lin,Chenxi Yang,Hongxiang Gao,Zhenghua Chen,Yang Bai,Min Wu,Jun Cheng,Huazhu Fu,Dacheng Tao,Bang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces "Combodied Agents," a human-centered AI paradigm that models and supports individual human-state trajectories over time, bridging the gap between digital agents (software-state focused) and embodied agents (physical-state focused). It proposes a closed-loop architecture integrating multimodal perception, longitudinal memory, personal world models, and admissible intervention policies to deliver sustained, proportionate, and consent-aware support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Agentic AI exhibits a structural gap: digital agents transform software states and embodied agents transform physical states, but neither treats a person's evolving internal state and agency as the primary object of modeling and intervention. The medication adherence example illustrates this—existing agents can remind or deliver medication but cannot determine whether the person forgot, is confused, has side effects, or deliberately refused, nor can they select appropriate support accordingly.

Method: The Combodied Agent framework operates as a closed loop: (1) event-based multimodal perception reconstructs meaningful personal events from sensors, wearables, and software; (2) longitudinal, correctable memory provides temporal context; (3) Personal World Models estimate future personal states and outcomes under alternative decisions/interventions; (4) an admissible intervention policy selects proportionate support under constraints of consent, uncertainty, safety, reversibility, and user control. Feedback from the person and environment continuously updates the loop. Representations are purpose-bounded, uncertainty-aware, and user-correctable rather than exhaustive Human Digital Twins.

Result: The paper organizes a design space along human-state targets, relational contexts, and agent roles. It proposes scenario-centered evaluation, agency-preservation metrics, benchmark requirements, edge-native personal models, and governance directions. The framework unifies fragmented capabilities from personal assistants, health agents, AI companions, and adaptive human-AI systems.

Conclusion: Combodied Agents shift Agentic AI from external task completion toward sustained human benefit by making the person's evolving state and agency the central object of modeling and intervention, thereby closing the structural gap left by purely digital or embodied approaches.

Abstract: After an older adult misses a medication dose, a software agent can send another reminder and an embodied agent can bring the medication. Yet neither explains whether the person forgot, is confused, has side effects, or deliberately refused, nor what support is appropriate. This reveals a structural gap in Agentic AI: Digital Agents primarily transform software states, while Embodied Agents transform physical states; neither makes a person's evolving state and agency the primary object of modeling, intervention, and evaluation. We introduce Combodied Agents, a human-centered paradigm that perceives, models, predicts, and supports individual human-state trajectories over time, using software tools, sensors, wearables, robots, and human services as action channels rather than end goals. We unify fragmented capabilities across personal assistants, health agents, AI companions, and adaptive human--AI systems into a closed loop: event-based multimodal perception reconstructs meaningful personal events; longitudinal, correctable memory provides temporal context; Personal World Models estimate future personal states and outcomes under alternative decisions and interventions; and an admissible intervention policy selects proportionate support under consent, uncertainty, safety, reversibility, and user control. Feedback from the person and environment updates the loop. Rather than requiring an exhaustive Human Digital Twin, the framework uses purpose-bounded, uncertainty-aware, user-correctable representations. We organize the design space by human-state targets, relational contexts, and agent roles, and propose scenario-centered evaluation, agency-preservation metrics, benchmark requirements, edge-native personal models, and governance directions. Combodied Agents shift Agentic AI from external task completion toward sustained human benefit.

</details>


### [180] [IO Factory: Simulating AI-Enabled Influence Campaigns at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10920)
*Lukasz Olejnik,Wenchao Dong,Jonas R. Kunst,Signe Riemer-Sørensen,Tobias Herb,Meeyoung Cha,Daniel Thilo Schroeder*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IO Factory is an AI-driven framework that simulates coordinated information/influence campaigns as traceable, end-to-end processes within a controlled platform, supporting up to 100,000 agents and enabling reproducible research on AI swarm-based manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Digital manipulation has evolved from isolated persuasive text to AI swarms—coordinated, persistent agent groups that adapt to platform feedback and disguise campaigns as ordinary social interaction. Such campaigns cannot be detected from individual messages alone and require analysis across a continuous spectrum: planning, action, exposure, interpretation, measurement, and adaptation. Existing approaches lack integrated, traceable frameworks for studying this full lifecycle.

Method: IO Factory implements a controlled simulated platform that captures the entire campaign pipeline: actor roles, platform actions, exposure records, structured model-based evaluations, and configurable population changes. The architecture links these components into a unified, inspectable process where every campaign step—from objectives and action constraints to exposure paths and measurement rules—is recorded for reproducibility.

Result: IO Factory successfully executes campaign timelines at scale across configurations with up to 100,000 agents, producing inspectable evidence of exposure and measurable shifts in configured belief variables.

Conclusion: By recording all campaign elements (actors, objectives, constraints, exposure paths, measurement rules), IO Factory enables reproducible research and red-team analysis of coordinated influence operations, addressing the growing threat of AI swarm-based digital manipulation.

Abstract: We introduce IO Factory, an AI-driven framework for simulating information and influence campaigns as fully integrated, traceable processes. The threat of digital manipulation now extends beyond persuasive text from individual language models to AI swarms, i.e., persistent groups of coordinated agents that adapt to platform feedback and disguise organized campaigns as ordinary social interaction. Because such campaigns cannot be identified from isolated messages alone, they must be analyzed across a continuous spectrum of planning, platform action, exposure, interpretation, measurement, and adaptation. IO Factory represents this process inside a controlled simulated platform, linking actor roles, platform actions, exposure records, structured model-based evaluations, and configured changes in the simulated population. We implement the architecture and evaluate it across configurations of up to 100,000 agents. The results show that IO Factory executes campaign timelines at scale and produces inspectable evidence of exposure and measured movement in configured belief variables. By recording the actors, objectives, action constraints, exposure paths, and measurement rules used in each run, IO Factory supports reproducible research and red-team analysis of coordinated influence.

</details>


### [181] [ThinkRetrieve: Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning Traces for Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10928)
*Vaibhav Singh,Soumya Suvra Ghosal,Sarvesh Gharat,Soumyabrata Pal,Ramasuri Narayanam,Dinesh Manocha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ThinkRetrieve is a test-time scaling framework that dynamically retrieves step-by-step solved examples and injects them into the reasoning traces of Large Reasoning Models, improving accuracy over standard sequential scaling—achieving up to 60% relative gains on AIME 2025.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard test-time scaling for LRMs by generating longer chain-of-thought traces often yields diminishing or negative returns due to increased uncertainty, error compounding, and drift from the original problem. The authors aim to address this by providing procedural guidance rather than just factual retrieval.

Method: ThinkRetrieve augments LRM reasoning by maintaining an external corpus of problem-solution pairs. At each intermediate reasoning step, the framework retrieves relevant exemplars and injects them directly into the model's thinking trace, guiding the model on *how* to reason rather than *what* facts are relevant.

Result: Experiments on five reasoning models (1.5B–8B parameters) across GSM-8K, MATH-500, AIME 2025, and SciQ show consistent accuracy improvements over standard test-time scaling, with relative gains of up to 60% on AIME 2025.

Conclusion: Retrieving and injecting step-wise reasoning exemplars during test-time scaling effectively mitigates the drawbacks of longer reasoning traces, offering a more reliable approach to scaling inference-time compute in LRMs.

Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) improve performance by allocating additional inference-time compute to generate extended chain-of-thought reasoning. However, recent studies reveal that sequential test-time scaling often yields diminishing or even negative returns, as longer traces exhibit increased uncertainty, error compounding, and drift from the original problem. We propose ThinkRetrieve, a test-time scaling framework that augments the reasoning traces of LRMs with dynamically retrieved solved examples at each reasoning step. Given an external corpus of problems paired with step-by-step solutions, ThinkRetrieve retrieves relevant exemplars at each intermediate step and injects them directly into the thinking trace, providing the model with guidance on how to reason rather than merely what facts are relevant. Experiments across five reasoning models (1.5B--8B parameters) on GSM-8K, MATH-500, AIME 2025, and SciQ demonstrate that ThinkRetrieve consistently improves accuracy over standard test-time scaling, with relative gains of up to $60\%$ on AIME 2025.

</details>


### [182] [FedCGR: Federated Cross-Domain Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10929)
*Zhuodong Liu,Hugen Lv,Xiangyu Li,Bohan Guo,Peiyu Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedCGR proposes a federated cross-domain recommendation framework that uses discrete semantic IDs from public metadata to align item spaces across clients without sharing private interactions, employing a reliability-aware semantic interface and prototype-personalized generator to overcome semantic-only bottlenecks and domain heterogeneity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated cross-domain recommendation faces a fundamental tension: cross-domain alignment typically requires behavioral anchors (overlapping users, shared interactions) that are sparse, unavailable, or privacy-sensitive in federated settings. The authors aim to resolve this by aligning items through a shared semantic token vocabulary derived from public metadata, but this introduces new challenges — fixed tokenizers create a semantic-only bottleneck (no global CF signal sharing), and standard federated averaging causes negative transfer under domain heterogeneity.

Method: FedCGR operates on two key components: (1) A reliability-aware semantic interface that injects local collaborative filtering signals by weighting semantic ID predictions based on their reliability, bridging the gap between purely semantic representations and local interaction patterns. (2) A prototype-personalized generator that selectively aggregates shared parameters according to domain relatedness — clustering client domains into prototypes and aggregating within similar prototypes while keeping domain-specific parameters local, thus mitigating negative transfer from heterogeneous domains.

Result: Experiments on six Amazon cross-domain scenarios demonstrate that FedCGR consistently outperforms federated generative baselines and achieves competitive performance against strong sequential and federated CDR methods under both full-ranking and sampled evaluation protocols.

Conclusion: Keeping the item language stable via discrete semantic IDs while making adaptation explicit through reliability-aware interfaces and prototype-based personalization enables effective federated CDR without requiring private interaction exchange across clients.

Abstract: Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) transfers preference knowledge across related domains, but federated deployment makes cross-domain alignment difficult because the behavioral anchors that align item spaces, such as overlapping users and shared interaction signals, are often sparse, unavailable, or privacy-sensitive across clients. To address this tension, we revisit federated CDR as generation over a stable semantic item language. By representing items as discrete semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from public item-side metadata, cross-domain item alignment is induced by a shared vocabulary rather than by exchanging private interactions or aligning domain-specific embeddings. Directly federating SID-based generators, however, introduces two design constraints: the SID tokenizer must remain fixed to preserve cross-client token consistency, which creates a semantic-only bottleneck because local collaborative filtering (CF) signals cannot be globally shared or aligned; meanwhile, standard federated averaging can cause negative transfer under domain heterogeneity. To overcome these constraints, we propose FedCGR, a federated generative CDR framework that keeps the item language stable and makes adaptation explicit. FedCGR injects local CF evidence through a reliability-aware semantic interface and trains a prototype-personalized generator that selectively aggregates shared parameters according to domain relatedness while keeping domain-specific quantities local. Experiments on six Amazon cross-domain scenarios show that FedCGR consistently outperforms federated generative baselines and achieves competitive performance against strong sequential and federated CDR methods under both full-ranking and sampled evaluation protocols.

</details>


### [183] [XCoT-VLA: Executable Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language-Action Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10976)
*Foundation Model Team,XPeng Inc*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: XCoT-VLA replaces verbose natural-language Chain-of-Thought reasoning in autonomous driving VLAs with compact (2–6) executable tokens, learned from Reason-Action supervision, significantly reducing trajectory prediction error while staying within real-time planning budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Chain-of-Thought reasoning in VLA models is ill-suited for real-time autonomous driving control due to its open-ended, costly decoding and difficulty in optimization as an action-facing representation.

Method: XCoT-VLA introduces compact, executable CoT tokens supervised by automatically constructed Reason-Action pairs from logged trajectories and scene context. These tokens condition fixed trajectory queries via shared multimodal self-attention. A deterministic token-function routing mechanism applies separate FFNs: Reason FFN for XCoT tokens and Control FFN for flow-matching trajectory generation. An optional refinement extension, XCoT Policy Optimization (XCPO), operates in the same token space.

Result: XCoT-VLA reduces longitudinal Average Displacement Error (ADE) from 1.645 to 1.323 on general-distribution sets, and lateral Final Displacement Error (FDE) from 1.616 to 0.648 in lane-change scenarios, using only 2–6 tokens.

Conclusion: Driving-oriented reasoning can be made compact, executable, and directly connected to trajectory generation, enabling efficient real-time autonomous driving planning without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can connect scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and trajectory generation for autonomous driving. However, verbose natural-language Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is poorly suited to real-time control because it is open-ended, costly to decode, and difficult to optimize as an action-facing representation. We propose XCoT-VLA, which replaces descriptive rationales with compact executable CoT tokens learned from automatically constructed Reason-Action supervision. Logged trajectories provide action evidence, while scene context supplies causal semantics. The predicted XCoT sequence remains in context and conditions fixed trajectory queries through shared multimodal self-attention. Deterministic token-function routing applies the Reason FFN to XCoT tokens and the Control FFN to trajectory queries for flow-matching trajectory generation. We further introduce XCoT Policy Optimization (XCPO) as an optional refinement extension in the same executable token space. XCoT-VLA reduces longitudinal ADE from 1.645 to 1.323 on a general-distribution set and lateral FDE from 1.616 to 0.648 in lane-change scenarios. By representing driving-oriented reasoning with only 2-6 executable XCoT tokens, our method substantially reduces autoregressive reasoning overhead and remains within the real-time planning budget. These results demonstrate that driving-oriented reasoning can be compact, executable, and directly connected to trajectory generation.

</details>


### [184] [V-FiLLM: Verified Financial LLM Reasoning Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11047)
*Alicia Larsen,Victoire Laurent,Aulia Kharis Rakhamsari,Lara Turgut,Nino Antulov-Fantulin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: V-FiLLM is a framework for generating scalable, verified financial reasoning benchmarks from executable computation trees over real tables, exposing four controllable difficulty axes and revealing significant LLM performance degradation under increased depth and adversarial perturbations, while demonstrating that lightweight LoRA fine-tuning meaningfully improves compositional financial QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately evaluate LLMs on financial reasoning over structured (tabular) data. Current approaches often rely on model-generated labels, introducing error and limiting scalability. A method is needed to produce large-scale, verified benchmarks without annotation cost or generator bias.

Method: V-FiLLM generates benchmarks by constructing executable computation trees grounded in real financial tables. Trees are evaluated symbolically to produce ground-truth answers, then rendered into natural-language questions via templates. This removes any model from the labeling loop, enabling arbitrary-scale generation with answers correct by construction. The framework exposes four independently controllable difficulty axes: computation depth, expression breadth, financial concept complexity, and context size.

Result: Open-source LLM accuracy drops up to 51% as reasoning depth increases and up to 47 percentage points under adversarial numerical perturbations. Lightweight LoRA fine-tuning on verified chain-of-thought traces improves accuracy from 81.1% to 85.6% on held-out problems and outperforms the base model by 5 percentage points on the FinQA benchmark.

Conclusion: Robust financial reasoning over structured data remains challenging for LLMs, particularly under increased depth and adversarial perturbations. Targeted, low-cost adaptation via LoRA fine-tuning on verified reasoning traces is a promising direction for improving compositional reasoning in financial QA.

Abstract: While existing benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating LLMs across STEM domains, financial reasoning over structured data remains comparatively less explored. We introduce V-FiLLM, a framework that generates financial reasoning benchmarks from executable computation trees grounded in real tables, yielding items whose answers are correct by construction. Trees are evaluated symbolically to obtain ground truth and rendered into natural-language questions, removing any model from the labeling loop, so items can be generated at arbitrary scale without annotation cost and without inheriting a generator's error rate. V-FiLLM exposes four independently controllable axes of difficulty including computation depth, expression breadth, financial concept complexity, and context size. By evaluating on open-source models, we find that accuracy falls up to 51% as reasoning depth increases, and up to 47% points under adversarial numerical perturbations, highlighting remaining challenges in robust financial reasoning over tables. We further show that lightweight LoRA fine-tuning on verified chain-of-thought traces improves accuracy from 81.1% to 85.6% on held-out problems and outperforms the base model by 5% points on FinQA (Chen et al., 2022a), s), suggesting that targeted, low-cost adaptation is a promising direction for compositional reasoning in financial QA.

</details>


### [185] [SkillZip: Evaluation-Free Skill Compression for Self-Evolving Agents by Discovering Reusable Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11079)
*Xiaofan Bai,Hongqiang Lin,Chao Liu,Yantao Zhang,Xuan Jin,Xipeng Cao,Yuhong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillZip is an evaluation-free method for compressing self-evolving agent skills by finding the shortest faithful structural explanation, using a typed minimum description-length objective with hard coverage constraints. It operates in one-shot or continual Zip-on-Write modes and outperforms baselines in compression, generalizability, and cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-evolving agents accumulate skills with significant redundancy—common action sequences are copied rather than reused, and rules are restated across branches. Generic prompt compression fails because skills have structured components (name, description, workflow, tool contracts, exceptions) that flat compression cannot preserve. Evaluation-guided compression introduces rollout costs and evaluation-set dependence. An evaluation-free, structure-aware compression method is needed.

Method: SkillZip formalizes compression as a typed minimum description-length objective over a skill contract and a residual, with hard coverage constraints for every extracted trigger, workflow edge, tool requirement, obligation, and output field. The approach follows "explain once, reference many": repeated rules are stated once at the applicable scope, repeated action sequences are factored into shared procedures, and differences are kept as explicit exceptions. It provides simple sharing thresholds, preserves unique rare rules, and supports efficient local updates. Two modes are offered: a one-shot mode using one structured extraction call with deterministic optimization, and a continual Zip-on-Write mode that integrates self-evolution patches without replaying tasks or reparsing history.

Result: Comprehensive experimental evaluations demonstrate SkillZip's effectiveness and superiority over baselines in compression performance, generalizability, and cost overhead.

Conclusion: SkillZip provides a principled, structure-aware approach to skill compression for self-evolving agents that avoids the pitfalls of both generic prompt compression and evaluation-guided methods. Its formal MDL-based objective with hard coverage constraints ensures faithfulness while eliminating redundancy.

Abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate reusable skills by appending successful procedures and failure fixes. Over time, the same requirement is often restated in several branches, examples, and warnings, while common action sequences are copied rather than reused. The resulting skill becomes expensive to inject and difficult to maintain. Generic prompt compression is ill-suited to this setting because a skill is not a flat passage: its name and description define when it applies, its workflow controls execution, its tool and output contracts constrain validity, and rare exceptions may remain essential even when no sampled task activates them. Evaluation-guided compression can test these behaviors, but it introduces rollouts, cost, and dependence on the compression-time evaluation set. We present SkillZip, an evaluation-free method that compresses a skill by finding its shortest faithful structural explanation. The intuition is explain once, reference many: state a repeated rule once at the scope where it applies, factor a repeated action sequence into a shared procedure, and keep only the differences as explicit exceptions. We formalize this intuition as a typed minimum description-length objective over a skill contract and a residual, subject to a hard coverage constraint for every extracted trigger, workflow edge, tool requirement, obligation, and output field. The formulation provides simple sharing thresholds, preserves unique rare rules by construction, and supports efficient local updates. SkillZip has a one-shot mode with one structured extraction call and deterministic optimization, and a continual Zip-on-Write mode that integrates each self-evolution patch without replaying tasks or reparsing the full history. Through comprehensive experimental evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of SkillZip in compression performance, generalizability, and cost overhead.

</details>


### [186] [RTSKG: Building a Rail Transit Station Knowledge Graph Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11080)
*Shutong Zhu,Tianxing Wu,Runfeng Liu,Yuang Gu,Xuan He,Yuan Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RTSKG, a Rail Transit Station Knowledge Graph dataset that explicitly models spatial and semantic interactions among heterogeneous urban entities (stations, roads, POIs) using a unified schema, and demonstrates its effectiveness on store recommendation and knowledge-enhanced ridership prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current city-level rail transit station studies (e.g., ridership prediction) rely on large-scale urban data but neglect complex interactions among diverse urban entities in their data organization, limiting analytical effectiveness.

Method: The authors construct RTSKG by integrating heterogeneous urban entities—rail transit stations, road segments, and points of interest—under a specially designed unified schema that explicitly captures spatial and semantic interactions. The dataset is published as Linked Data for accessibility and interoperability.

Result: Evaluations on two downstream tasks—station-area store recommendation and knowledge-enhanced ridership prediction—demonstrate the effectiveness of RTSKG, validating its practical utility for urban computing applications.

Conclusion: RTSKG fills a gap in structured urban data organization by explicitly modeling inter-entity interactions, and shows strong potential to support and enhance a range of city-level rail transit station analyses.

Abstract: Rail transit systems play a vital role in urban mobility and economic development. As key components of such systems, rail transit stations function as critical transport hubs that enhance urban accessibility and stimulate development in surrounding areas. City-level rail transit station related tasks (e.g., ridership prediction) require large-scale urban data, but current studies often neglect complex interactions among various urban entities in terms of data organization. In this paper, to address the above issue, we build a Rail Transit Station Knowledge Graph (RTSKG) dataset which explicitly models the spatial and semantic interactions among different kinds of urban entities, to benefit city-level rail transit station related tasks. RTSKG integrates heterogeneous urban entities, such as rail transit stations, road segments, and points of interest, with a specially designed unified schema, and is accessible as Linked Data at https://w3id.org/rtskg/. Evaluations on station-area store recommendation and knowledge-enhanced ridership prediction demonstrate the effectiveness of RTSKG, highlighting its potential to support city-level rail transit station analysis.

</details>


### [187] [sLTN: Structural Logic Tensor Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11136)
*Davide Rinaldi,Luciano Serafini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: sLTN extends Logic Tensor Networks by introducing structural dimensions as first-class elements, enabling explicit representation of temporal, sequential, and relational organization within the neurosymbolic framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Original LTN treats data as flat collections of individuals and lacks native support for structural organization such as temporal order, sequence position, or graph connectivity, limiting its applicability to structured domains.

Method: Introduce structural dimensions as named tensor axes representing domain-specific organization (time steps, sequence positions, graph nodes). These can be quantified, related through structural relations, and used to express constraints at the logical level. Formalize syntax and fuzzy tensor semantics, with a PyTorch implementation using declarative signatures, formula parsing, and tensorial interpretation.

Result: Without structural dimensions, sLTN recovers original LTN semantics as a special case. The framework is demonstrated on temporal and sequential reasoning examples.

Conclusion: sLTN successfully extends LTN to handle structured data, bridging the gap between logical constraints and structured deep learning. The paper accompanies the open-source sltn library.

Abstract: Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) provide a neurosymbolic framework in which first-order logic is interpreted through tensor operations, enabling logical constraints to be integrated with differentiable learning. However, the original formulation of LTN is primarily suited to data represented as flat collections of individuals, and does not explicitly capture structural organization such as temporal order, sequential position, or graph connectivity. We introduce sLTN, an extension of LTN that makes structural dimensions first-class elements of the language. Structural dimensions represent named tensor axes associated with domain-specific organization, such as time steps, sequence positions, or graph nodes. They can be quantified explicitly, related through structural relations, and used to express temporal, sequential, and relational constraints directly at the logical level. We formalize the syntax and fuzzy tensor semantics of sLTN and show that, in the absence of structural dimensions, the framework recovers the original LTN semantics as a special case. We further describe a PyTorch implementation based on a declarative signature, formula parsing, and tensorial interpretation. The framework is illustrated on representative temporal and sequential reasoning examples. This paper serves as a companion to the sltn library, available at https://github.com/logictensornetworks/sltn.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [188] [Transformer Geometry Observatory TGO-IV: Developmental Topology Observatory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09997)
*Kaustubh Kapil,Kishor P. Upla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TGO-IV introduces a topological framework using Persistent Homology (Vietoris–Rips complexes, persistence diagrams, Betti curves, etc.) to track how token-level representation point clouds evolve globally across Transformer layers, revealing the developmental trajectory from raw input to task-relevant features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Transformer interpretability studies focus on isolated layers or holistic network analysis, neglecting how individual representations and their global manifold structure develop progressively across layers. The work aims to isolate when and how raw representations transform into task-relevant features by tracking this evolution.

Method: Construct Vietoris–Rips simplicial complexes from token-level representation point clouds at each Transformer layer; compute persistent topological signatures using a suite of tools: Persistence Diagrams, Barcode Diagrams, Betti Curves, Persistence Landscapes, Bottleneck Distance, and Wasserstein Distance. This enables comparative analysis of global topology across layers.

Result: The framework provides a comprehensive multi-faceted topological observatory for analyzing representation evolution. (The abstract describes the framework and its capabilities but does not report specific empirical findings.)

Conclusion: Persistent Homology offers a principled lens for understanding the global topological development of Transformer representations across layers, moving beyond local geometric analyses toward a developmental account of representation learning.

Abstract: Transformers have had a profound impact on the world of language processing and computer vision. As efforts to answer the million-dollar question of ``How does a Transformer learn?" have been increasing, existing interpretability studies primarily analyze representations at isolated layers or the network as a whole, while the developmental evolution of individual representations and its manifolds across transformer layers remains underexplored. With this work, we aim at providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolution of representations as the representation point cloud transforms across the layers; thereby attempting to isolate layers or establish a trend which comes closer to justifying how and when raw input representations evolve into task-relevant feature representations. Thus, Transformer Geometry Observatory-TGO-IV introduces a topological framework for analysing the evolution of Transformer representations through the lens of Persistent Homology. Rather than studying local geometric properties alone, TGO-IV constructs Vietoris--Rips simplicial complexes from token-level representation point clouds and investigates the evolution of their persistent topological signatures across Transformer layers. The proposed framework comprises complementary topological observatories including Persistence Diagrams, Barcode Diagrams, Betti Curves, Persistence Landscapes, Bottleneck Distance, and Wasserstein Distance, enabling a comprehensive analysis of how the global topology of representation point clouds develops throughout the forward pass.

</details>


### [189] [Uncertainty-Aware Ensemble Deep Randomized Neural Networks for Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10007)
*M. Sajid,A. Quadir,A. Rahaman,P. N. Suganthan,M. Tanveer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes intuitionistic fuzzy extensions of deep RVFL and ensemble deep RVFL (IF-dRVFL and IF-edRVFL) that assign adaptive sample weights using membership (distance to class centroid) and non-membership (local neighborhood heterogeneity) degrees in kernel space, achieving superior robustness to noise and outliers on UCI/KEEL benchmarks compared to SOTA fuzzy and non-fuzzy methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SOTA deep randomized neural networks (dRVFL, edRVFL) treat all training samples uniformly, making them vulnerable to noise and outliers. Contaminated features also propagate across hidden layers, degrading decision-making. The authors aim to introduce sample-wise adaptive weighting to mitigate these issues.

Method: The authors propose IF-dRVFL and IF-edRVFL, which integrate intuitionistic fuzzy theory into deep randomized networks. In kernel space, each sample receives a membership degree (based on distance to its class centroid) and a non-membership degree (quantifying heterogeneity within its local neighborhood). These two measures jointly produce adaptive weights that distinguish clean, noisy, and outlier samples, preventing contaminated features from propagating through hidden layers.

Result: Extensive experiments on UCI and KEEL benchmark datasets (with and without Gaussian noise) show that IF-dRVFL and IF-edRVFL outperform existing state-of-the-art fuzzy and non-fuzzy approaches in terms of robustness and classification performance.

Conclusion: Incorporating intuitionistic fuzzy sample weighting significantly enhances the robustness of deep randomized neural networks against noise and outliers. The proposed IF-dRVFL and IF-edRVFL frameworks provide an effective, publicly available solution for real-world noisy datasets.

Abstract: The current state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep randomized neural networks, such as deep Random Vector Functional Link (dRVFL) and ensemble deep RVFL (edRVFL), treat all training samples uniformly, which limits their robustness and effectiveness when applied to real-world datasets containing noise and outliers. Furthermore, the propagation of contaminated features across hidden layers negatively influences the decision-making capability of these models. To overcome these limitations, we propose intuitionistic fuzzy dRVFL (IF-dRVFL) and intuitionistic fuzzy edRVFL (IF-edRVFL) frameworks that enhance model robustness. The proposed models unify intuitionistic fuzzy theory to exploit sample neighborhood information in the kernel space by jointly considering membership and non-membership degrees for each sample. Membership degrees are computed based on the distance of samples from their respective class centroids, while non-membership degrees quantify sample heterogeneity within local neighborhoods. These measures are employed to assign adaptive weights to training samples, enabling effective discrimination among clean, noisy, and outlier data points. Extensive experiments conducted on UCI and KEEL benchmark datasets, with and without the presence of Gaussian noise, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed IF-dRVFL and IF-edRVFL models over existing SOTA fuzzy and non-fuzzy approaches. The source code is available at https://github.com/mtanveer1/IF-edRVFL.

</details>


### [190] [CurveFP: Rational-Radix Logarithmic Datatypes with Closed Products for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10010)
*Ye Qiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CurveFP introduces a closed-product codebook for low-precision floating-point arithmetic where every nonzero product maps to another valid codepoint, simplifying multiplication to sign XOR and integer-index addition. The E4C3/E5C2 (8-bit) and E3C3 (7-bit) formats match or surpass FP8 perplexity in LLM training/inference with fewer bits and simpler hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing low-precision formats (e.g., FP8) optimize scalar fidelity but leave product arithmetic unchanged, meaning hardware multipliers still operate on complex floating-point representations. The authors aim to co-design the codebook so that the product of any two codepoints is itself a codepoint (algebraic closure under multiplication), drastically simplifying multiply-accumulate hardware.

Method: CurveFP distributes quantized magnitudes across interleaved logarithmic curves with compact block scales. A rational radix balances dynamic range and local resolution. Uniform curve indices guarantee that every nonzero product is algebraically closed: multiplication reduces to sign XOR and integer-index addition. A derived finite phase count determines the accumulation schedule. Instantiations include CurveFP8 (E4C3/E5C2) for training and CurveFP7 (E3C3) for deployment.

Result: CurveFP7 beats tensor-wise FP8 perplexity on four 7B–9B models with one fewer bit, staying within 1.32% of native quality. CurveFP8 lowers operand NMSE in all 36 paired forward/backward GEMM comparisons. Across three matched 128.3M-parameter triplets completing 3B-token pretraining, CurveFP8 achieves mean BF16-inference perplexity of 22.5366 vs. 22.5407 for FP8, with lower format-induced penalty in all three seeds. On a 36-cell downstream matrix, CurveFP8 checkpoints yield lower WikiText-103 perplexity in all 12 seed-format comparisons.

Conclusion: CurveFP demonstrates that arithmetic-codebook co-design yields FP8-class numerical behavior with seven-bit inference and a substantially simpler product datapath, making it a compelling alternative for both training and compact deployment of large language models.

Abstract: Low-precision datatypes reduce language-model cost, but most formats optimize scalar fidelity while leaving the arithmetic induced by their products unchanged. We introduce CurveFP, a closed-product codebook family that distributes quantized magnitudes across interleaved logarithmic curves under compact block scales. A rational radix tunes dynamic range against local resolution, while uniform curve indices make every nonzero product algebraically closed. Product formation becomes an exact sign XOR and integer-index update, and a derived finite phase count determines the accumulation schedule. We instantiate this algebra as CurveFP eight E4C3/E5C2 for training and CurveFP seven E3C3 for compact deployment. In evaluation, CurveFP seven beats tensor-wise FP8 perplexity on four 7B--9B models with one fewer element bit and stays within 1.32\% of native quality. CurveFP eight lowers operand NMSE in all 36 paired forward and backward GEMM comparisons. Across three matched 128.3M-parameter triplets, every mode completes 3B-token pretraining per seed; CurveFP eight reaches mean BF16-inference perplexity 22.5366 versus 22.5407 for FP8 and incurs a lower format-induced penalty in all three seeds. A 36-cell downstream matrix finds lower WikiText-103 perplexity for the CurveFP eight-trained checkpoints in all 12 seed-format comparisons, with mixed PG-19 and task deltas. Together, these results establish CurveFP as an arithmetic co-design that combines FP8-class numerical behavior, seven-bit inference, and a substantially simpler product path.

</details>


### [191] [Sheaf-Based Federated Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10016)
*Gabriele D'Acunto,Enrico Grimaldi,Valeria Avino,Mario Edoardo Pandolfo,Leonardo Di Nino,Sergio Barbarossa,Paolo Di Lorenzo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SFRL introduces sheaf theory to federated representation learning, using learnable restriction maps and a sheaf Laplacian regularizer to align heterogeneous latent spaces without requiring a shared global latent space. The method uses shared pilot samples, Procrustes-based updates, and is shown to converge to first-order stationary points, outperforming baselines in semantic communication tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Heterogeneous federated systems face fundamental challenges: agents differ in data distributions, sensing modalities, model architectures, latent dimensionalities, and local objectives. Existing federated representation learning methods typically assume a shared global latent space, which is unrealistic under such heterogeneity. A framework is needed that enables alignment without this assumption.

Method: SFRL jointly optimizes local objectives with a manifold-constrained geometric alignment regularizer based on learnable sheaf restriction maps. Global consistency emerges from aligning neighboring latent representations via orthogonal transformations and isometric embeddings, enforced by a quadratic gluing regularizer from the sheaf Laplacian. The penalty uses a small set of shared pilot samples for scalability. The decentralized Sheaf-FRL algorithm alternates between local gradient updates and closed-form Procrustes updates of edge-wise restriction maps.

Result: Sheaf-FRL converges to first-order stationary points in both deterministic and stochastic settings. In cooperative classification under semantic communication with model and data heterogeneity, Sheaf-FRL outperforms baselines in local and post-communication classification accuracy across different levels of local distribution shift and shows greater robustness to latent-space dimensionality compression.

Conclusion: SFRL provides a principled geometric framework for federated representation learning under severe heterogeneity, eliminating the need for a shared latent space. The sheaf-theoretic approach with learnable restriction maps and Procrustes alignment proves both theoretically sound (with convergence guarantees) and empirically effective, particularly in semantic communication scenarios.

Abstract: Heterogeneous federated systems require agents to learn and exchange informative representations despite differences in data distributions, sensing modalities, model architectures, latent dimensionalities, and local learning objectives. To address this challenge, we propose Sheaf-based Federated Representation Learning (SFRL), a general framework that jointly optimizes local objectives with a manifold-constrained geometric alignment regularizer based on learnable sheaf restriction maps. Unlike most existing approaches, SFRL does not assume a shared global latent space. Instead, global consistency emerges from the alignment of neighboring latent representations through orthogonal transformations and isometric embeddings. This alignment is enforced by a quadratic gluing regularizer induced by the sheaf Laplacian, whose learnable restriction maps adapt the geometry to the observed data. The penalty is evaluated on a small set of shared pilot samples, ensuring scalability and communication efficiency. We develop a decentralized algorithm for solving SFRL, termed Sheaf-FRL, which alternates between gradient updates of the local models and closed-form Procrustes updates of the edge-wise restriction maps. We further establish convergence of Sheaf-FRL to first-order stationary points in both deterministic and stochastic settings. As an application, we consider a cooperative classification task in the context of semantic communication, under model and data heterogeneity. Our results show that Sheaf-FRL outperforms baseline approaches in terms of local and post-communication classification accuracy across different levels of local distribution shift and exhibits greater robustness to latent-space dimensionality compression.

</details>


### [192] [DOCSCHISEL: Adaptive Tool Documentation Optimization Framework for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10037)
*You Lu,Kun Zhang,Bihuan Chen,Xin Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tool documentation significantly impacts LLM agent performance, but its effectiveness varies by domain, model, and agent paradigm. The authors propose DocsChisel, an adaptive framework that iteratively optimizes tool documentation by analyzing failure traces, achieving 95.89% improvement over original docs and 75.15% over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research treats tool documentation as fixed input, focusing only on improving LLM tool-use capabilities. Little is known about how tool documentation content affects agent performance across different settings. The authors aim to understand this relationship and develop adaptive optimization methods.

Method: First, a large-scale empirical study on how information fields in tool documentation affect agent performance across different task domains, LLM backbones, and agent paradigms. Then, DocsChisel is proposed: it analyzes failed execution traces to identify documentation issues and iteratively optimizes documentation by adding, removing, and refining information fields per tool.

Result: The empirical study reveals substantial heterogeneity in documentation information fields, with effectiveness highly dependent on domain, model, and paradigm. DocsChisel improves task success rate by 95.89% over original documentation and by 75.15% on average over EasyTool and DRAFT baselines, with limited optimization time and token overhead.

Conclusion: No fixed tool documentation generalizes across diverse agent settings. Adaptive, failure-driven optimization like DocsChisel is both effective and efficient for tailoring tool documentation to specific LLM agents.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on external tools to accomplish complex real-world tasks, making tool documentation a critical grounding resource for LLM agents. Existing studies mainly focus on improving the tool-use capabilities of LLM agents, while largely treating tool documentation as a fixed input. Although several recent works attempt to optimize tool documentation through rewriting or compression, little is known about how the information contained in tool documentation affects agent performance across different settings.
  To bridge this gap, we conduct a large-scale empirical study on tool documentation for LLM agents. Our study reveals substantial heterogeneity in the information fields provided by existing tool documentation. Moreover, the effectiveness of different information fields is highly dependent on the task domain, LLM backbone, and agent paradigm, indicating that no fixed tool documentation can consistently generalize across diverse agent settings.
  Motivated by these findings, we propose DocsChisel, an adaptive tool documentation optimization framework for LLM agents. DocsChisel analyzes failed execution traces of a target LLM agent to identify documentation-related issues, and iteratively optimizes tool documentation by adding, removing, and refining information fields for each tool. We evaluate DocsChisel against two state-of-the-art baselines, i.e., EasyTool and DRAFT. Experimental results show that DocsChisel improves the task success rate of LLM agents by 95.89% over the original tool documentation and by 75.15%, on average, over existing baselines, while incurring limited optimization time and token overhead

</details>


### [193] [FlowScout: From Execution Feedback to Reliable Tool-Using Agent Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10039)
*Shuo Hao,You Lu,Bihuan Chen,Xin Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlowScout is an execution-guided framework that automatically generates tool-integrated agentic workflows from historical task-solving records, using graph-based workflow representation with Monte Carlo tree search refinement, achieving significant improvements in tool invocation correctness and execution quality over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual construction of high-quality agentic workflows requires substantial domain expertise. Existing automatic generation methods produce LLM-centric workflows where real tool executions are abstracted/simulated by LLM nodes, limiting usability and stability. A method that generates workflows with real tool integrations is needed.

Method: FlowScout represents agentic workflows as directed graphs with LLM nodes, tool-calling nodes, and dependency edges. It operates in two phases: (1) mining a common tool coordination skeleton from historical task-solving records to construct an initial workflow, and (2) refining the workflow topology via Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) guided by execution feedback.

Result: Evaluated on four task domains against PM4Py, ReAct, and AFlow baselines, FlowScout improved tool invocation correctness by at least 92.69% and execution quality by at least 17.66%, with lower performance variation across repeated runs.

Conclusion: FlowScout effectively addresses the limitations of LLM-centric workflow generation by producing tool-integrated agentic workflows, yielding substantial gains in correctness, quality, and stability over existing approaches.

Abstract: Agentic workflows have become an important abstraction for building reliable LLM-based automation systems by organizing large language models (LLMs), tools, and control logic into explicit execution structures. However, constructing high-quality agentic workflows remains largely manual and requires substantial domain expertise. Recent studies have explored automatic agentic workflow generation from historical task-solving records, but they mainly produce LLM-centric workflows, where real tool executions are abstracted and simulated by LLM nodes, limiting the usability and stability of generated workflows. To address these limitations, we propose FlowScout, an execution-guided framework for generating tool-integrated agentic workflows from historical task-solving records. Specifically, FlowScout represents an agentic workflow as a directed graph composed of LLM nodes, tool-calling nodes, and dependency edges. It first mines a common tool coordination skeleton from historical records to construct an initial workflow, and then refines the workflow topology through Monte Carlo tree search guided by execution feedback. We evaluate FlowScout on four representative task domains and compare it with three baselines, i.e., PM4Py, ReAct and AFlow. Experimental results show that agentic workflows generated by FlowScout improve tool invocation correctness by at least 92.69% and execution quality by at least 17.66% over the baselines, while achieving lower performance variation across repeated runs.

</details>


### [194] [UserToolBench: A User-Profile-Hidden Benchmark for Personalized Decision Making in Tool-Use LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10042)
*Xuexiong Yin,Zechuan Chen,Yongsen Zheng,Yuxiang Zhang,Jingyuan Yang,Bin Wang,Yubin Wang,Keze Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UserToolBench is a benchmark for evaluating personalized decision-making in tool-use LLMs, testing whether models can infer latent user preferences from interaction history, recognize when clarification is needed, and produce user-aligned tool-call trajectories. Experiments reveal that current models struggle with multi-tool coordination, missing-constraint inference, and long-horizon behavioral consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-use LLM benchmarks focus on profile recall, style imitation, generic tool use, or response-level personalization — none adequately test whether LLMs can make correct personalized decisions on behalf of users. There is a gap in evaluating true decision-level personalization where models must infer latent preferences under incomplete information and produce user-aligned action trajectories.

Method: The authors construct UserToolBench from privacy-sanitized real interaction traces. It comprises 10 structured user persona profiles, 36 public API-style tool ecosystems, and 1,065 multi-turn dialogue turns across 170 unique tools. Task types are designed around three evaluation-relevant scenarios: lack-of-information (requiring clarification), single-tool, and multi-tool settings. Strong tool-use LLMs are then evaluated on their ability to generate user-aligned tool-call trajectories.

Result: Current strong tool-use LLMs exhibit significant difficulty with personalized delegation. Three major bottlenecks are identified: multi-tool coordination, inference of missing constraints from latent preferences, and maintaining behavioral consistency over long-horizon interactions.

Conclusion: Personalization evaluation for LLMs should shift from assessing whether outputs sound user-specific (surface-level) to assessing whether models make correct decisions for the users they represent (decision-level). UserToolBench provides a framework for this more rigorous evaluation paradigm.

Abstract: Tool-use LLMs are increasingly asked to act on users' behalf, but existing benchmarks usually focus on profile recall, style imitation, generic tool use, or response-level personalization. We introduce UserToolBench , a benchmark for personalized decision making in tool-use LLMs. UserToolBench tests whether a model can infer latent user preferences from interaction history, recognize when clarification is needed, and produce user-aligned tool-call trajectories under incomplete information. The benchmark is built from privacy-sanitized real interaction traces and combines structured persona profiles, public API-style tool ecosystems, and long-horizon multi-turn trajectories. It includes 10 user profiles, 36 tool sets, 1,065 turns, 170 unique tools, and evaluation-focused task types covering lack-of-information, single-tool, and multi-tool settings. Experiments with strong tool-use LLMs show that current models still have difficulty with personalized delegation. Multi-tool coordination, missing-constraint inference, and long-horizon behavioral consistency remain major bottlenecks. These results suggest that personalization evaluation should move beyond asking whether outputs sound user-specific and instead ask whether LLMs make correct decisions for the users they represent.

</details>


### [195] [Finding the Signal in the Spam: Jointly Learning Rewards and Worker Reliability from Pairwise Comparisons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10045)
*Kaustubh Shivshankar Shejole,Tanish Agarwal,Arpit Agarwal,Avishek Ghosh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an EM-based algorithm for jointly learning item rewards and worker competencies from pairwise comparisons under a Boltzmann-rational (BoRa) model. Using Pólya-Gamma latent variables, the authors transform the non-conjugate logistic likelihood into a conditionally Gaussian form, reducing the problem to matrix sensing with theoretical convergence guarantees. Experiments show strong robustness to spammers and adversarial workers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crowdworkers on platforms like MTurk are often unreliable due to limited knowledge or spamming behavior. Existing pairwise comparison models (e.g., Bradley-Terry-Luce) typically assume homogeneous, perfect workers. The authors aim to jointly learn item rewards and worker competencies to improve robustness against unreliable annotators in crowdsourcing and reward-learning settings.

Method: The paper adopts the Boltzmann-rational (BoRa) model, which extends BTL by incorporating per-worker competency parameters. To handle the non-conjugate logistic likelihood, the authors introduce Pólya-Gamma latent variables, transforming the likelihood into a conditionally Gaussian form. This enables a tractable EM algorithm where the E-step has a simplified Q-function and the M-step reduces to a matrix sensing problem. Theoretical convergence guarantees are established via this matrix sensing formulation.

Result: Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms several baselines. The method exhibits strong robustness to spammers and adversarial workers, confirming its practical effectiveness in realistic crowdsourcing and reward-learning scenarios.

Conclusion: Joint learning of worker competencies and item rewards is both feasible and beneficial. The EM algorithm with Pólya-Gamma augmentation provides a tractable, theoretically grounded solution that is robust to unreliable annotators, with practical utility demonstrated through extensive empirical validation.

Abstract: The problem of learning from pairwise comparisons has been widely studied across many domains such as recommendation systems, social choice, and more recently, fine-tuning large language models. In this problem, the goal is to learn item rewards based on pairwise comparisons between them. In many scenarios, these comparisons are elicited from crowdworkers using platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk, Scale AI, etc. However, crowdworkers are often unreliable due to limited domain knowledge or revenue-maximizing (spamming) behavior. In this work, our goal is to understand whether worker reliability (competency) can be learned jointly with item rewards. To this end, we adopt the Boltzmann-rational model for pairwise comparisons, which extends the Bradley-Terry-Luce model by incorporating worker competencies. We derive an EM-based algorithm for learning under this model by introducing Polya-Gamma latent variables to transform the logistic likelihood into a conditionally Gaussian form, enabling tractable optimization and leading to a simplified $Q$ function in the E-step of the algorithm. This technique allows us to reduce our formulation to a matrix sensing problem, using which we establish theoretical convergence guarantees for our algorithm. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets. These experiments demonstrate the advantages of using our algorithm over several baselines and confirm its strong robustness to both spammers and adversarial workers, highlighting its practical effectiveness in realistic crowdsourcing and reward learning settings. The code and data is publicly available at https://github.com/KaustubhShejole/BoRa_EM.

</details>


### [196] [Detecting Soft Skills in ML Engineering Roles CVs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10046)
*Aidin Azamnouri,Nouran Ayad,Justus Bogner,Stefan Wagner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper examines how ML engineers, data scientists, and software engineers articulate soft skills in their CVs using an LLM-based pipeline that distinguishes explicitly listed from implicitly narrated competencies. Testing 13 demand-side hypotheses against candidate-side data, the study finds candidates overwhelmingly use narrative (3:1 ratio) to disclose soft skills, seniority strongly predicts leadership articulation, and keyword-based screening systematically misses these competencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on soft skills in ML-enabled systems relies exclusively on demand-side data (job ads, surveys, hiring manager interviews). Existing CV-mining approaches are keyword-based—unable to capture skills conveyed through narrative—and merely descriptive, reporting frequency rankings without statistically testing whether group differences are meaningful. The authors aim to close both gaps by bringing candidate-side evidence to bear on demand-side claims.

Method: The authors construct a balanced corpus of 300 curated CVs across three roles (ML engineers, data scientists, software engineers). They develop an LLM-based extraction pipeline validated against human-annotated ground truth that distinguishes explicitly listed soft skills from those implicitly narrated. They then translate demand-side literature claims into 13 falsifiable hypotheses about role signatures, seniority progression, and disclosure style, testing them with effect sizes under family-wise error control.

Result: Eleven of 13 hypotheses are supported, one partially, and one refuted. Candidates disclose soft skills through narrative rather than keyword lists at roughly a 3:1 ratio, with the highest narrative rates for leadership, coordination, and mentoring (88–96%). Seniority nearly triples the odds of articulating leadership. Software engineers articulate leadership at half the rate of their peers, contradicting the assumption that this competency is universal. Keyword-based screening systematically misses soft skills that candidates do articulate.

Conclusion: Technical candidates do articulate soft skills in their CVs, but predominantly through narrative rather than explicit keyword lists. This renders keyword-based screening methods systematically ineffective. The candidate-side data largely corroborates demand-side accounts but reveals important nuances—particularly that leadership articulation is not universal across roles. Methodologically, distinguishing explicit from implicit disclosure is essential for accurate soft-skill extraction from CVs.

Abstract: Soft skills shape collaboration among ML engineers, data scientists, and software engineers building ML-enabled systems, yet what we know about them comes almost entirely from the demand side. Job advertisements, surveys, and hiring manager interviews capture what employers ask for. How candidates themselves articulate these competencies has not been studied, and existing CV-mining work is both keyword-based, so it cannot see skills conveyed through narrative, and descriptive, reporting frequency rankings without testing whether group differences exceed sampling variation. We close both gaps. Using a balanced corpus of 300 curated CVs spanning the three roles, we extract explicitly listed and implicitly narrated soft skills with an LLM-based pipeline validated against a human-annotated ground truth, a distinction that existing extractors were not designed to make. We then convert the demand-side literature's claims into 13 falsifiable hypotheses about role signatures, seniority progression, and disclosure style, and test them with effect sizes under family-wise error control, so that candidate-side data can corroborate or contradict the demand-side account rather than merely illustrate it. Eleven hypotheses are supported, one partially, and one refuted. Candidates disclose soft skills through narrative rather than keyword lists by roughly three to one, and most so for the competencies employers value most: leadership, coordination, and mentoring (88-96% narrative). Seniority nearly triples the odds of articulating leadership. That competency, assumed universal in prior work, is articulated by software engineers at half the rate of their peers. Technical candidates do articulate soft skills, but a keyword-based screening systematically misses them.

</details>


### [197] [Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Prognostics and Health Management: A Systematic Literature Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10047)
*Christopher Braun,Julian Raible,Marco F. Huber*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This systematic review of 212 studies examines Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). It proposes a four-class taxonomy (observational, inductive, learning bias, and hybrid) and finds consistent predictive improvements over data-driven baselines, though the literature is skewed toward batteries/bearings and lacks evidence for claims about interpretability and causal reasoning. Future work should target transferable design patterns, benchmarked integration strategies, and lightweight uncertainty-aware models for real-time deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Purely data-driven ML models for PHM suffer from poor generalization, inability to infer causal relationships, and lack of interpretability. PIML promises to mitigate these limitations by embedding physical knowledge into ML pipelines, yet the breadth, maturity, and actual benefits of PIML in PHM remain unclear. A systematic review is needed to map the landscape, assess claimed advantages, and identify gaps.

Method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review of 212 studies on PIML applied to PHM. They developed a four-class classification scheme: (1) observational bias (physics-informed data preprocessing/augmentation), (2) inductive bias (physics-constrained model architectures), (3) learning bias (physics-guided loss functions or regularization), and (4) hybrid approaches (combinations of the above). Studies were further categorized by PHM task (diagnostics, prognostics, health state estimation).

Result: All four PIML classes consistently demonstrate improved predictive performance over conventional data-driven baselines across diverse asset types. The literature is heavily skewed toward lithium-ion batteries and bearings, with predominantly problem-specific solutions. While tangible performance benefits are well-supported, claims regarding improved interpretability, generalization, and causal inference lack sufficient empirical evidence.

Conclusion: PIML delivers measurable predictive gains in PHM but the field remains fragmented and narrow in scope. Future research should emphasize transferable design patterns, systematic benchmarks comparing integration strategies, and lightweight, uncertainty-aware models suitable for online, real-world deployment.

Abstract: In modern industry, keeping complex systems reliable, safe, and efficient hinges on Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). Machine Learning (ML) has largely driven advancements in diagnostics and prognostics, yet purely data-driven models face inherent limitations, such as poor generalization, an inability to infer causal relationships, and a lack of interpretability. Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) helps mitigate these limitations by incorporating prior physical knowledge directly into the ML pipeline, thereby fostering growing interest in its application to PHM. This work investigates how PIML is being leveraged in the context of PHM through a systematic literature review of 212 studies. The review introduces a four-class classification scheme, consisting of observational bias, inductive bias, learning bias, and hybrid approaches, and further categorizes studies by PHM task. Across all four classes, the reviewed studies consistently demonstrate improved predictive performance over conventional baselines across a broad range of assets, although the literature is heavily skewed toward lithium-ion batteries and bearings, and dominated by problem-specific solutions. Overall, the review indicates that physics-informed approaches already provide tangible benefits, whereas claims of improvements concerning some of the aforementioned limitations lack sufficient supporting evidence. Future research should prioritize transferable design patterns, benchmarks comparing integration strategies, and uncertainty-aware models that are lightweight and robust enough for online deployment in real-world settings.

</details>


### [198] [Observational Policy Ranking for SMB Financial Guidance from Multi-Action Accounting Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10050)
*Shrutendra Harsola,Vignesh Subrahmaniam,Vikas Raturi,Kamalika Das,Xiang Gao,Kratika Gupta,Ruocheng Guo,Padmaja Jonnalagedda,Ananya Pramod,Sricharan Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces CAR-PL, a covariate-adjusted residual policy learning method for ranking business-change recommendations from observational accounting logs, evaluating it against several baselines on 85,078 company-month observations from 7,505 SMBs across 34 action categories and multiple financial KPIs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) need timely financial guidance, but historical accounting logs contain self-selected, co-occurring business changes rather than randomized recommendations. This creates a need for observational policy learning methods that can rank actions (business-change categories) to optimize target financial KPIs from purely observational data.

Method: The authors propose Covariate-Adjusted Residual Policy Learning (CAR-PL), an action-wise R-learner designed for multi-hot logged actions. It operates directly on multi-hot representations, regularizes selection by observational support, and ranks 34 ledger-derived business-change categories from pre-decision financial information. CAR-PL is compared against an uplift T-Learner, a conservative contextual value model, a zero-shot LLM, and non-personalized references. Evaluation uses company-disjoint held-out firms under a shared model-assisted scoring rule with matched company-clustered comparisons.

Result: CAR-PL achieves the highest Gross Profit point estimate (0.084); the T-Learner leads on Revenue (0.085); and the contextual value model leads on Quick Ratio (0.062).
