CAR-PL and the T-Learner are not statistically separable on either growth KPI. CAR-PL selects 33-34 of 34 categories and yields less concentrated selections. Outcome-model-only scoring preserves the same KPI-level leader or top pair, and category rankings remain stable when replacing the all-zero reference with the most common co-action pattern.

Conclusion: The findings support objective-specific ranking of SMB financial guidance from multi-action accounting logs, demonstrating that observational policy learning can provide actionable, personalized business-change recommendations without requiring randomized experiments.

Abstract: Small and medium-sized businesses need timely financial guidance, yet historical accounting logs record self-selected and often co-occurring business changes rather than randomized recommendations. We formulate this setting as observational policy ranking: from pre-decision financial information, a policy selects one of 34 ledger-derived business-change categories for a target financial KPI. Using 85,078 company-month observations from 7,505 firms, we introduce Covariate-Adjusted Residual Policy Learning (CAR-PL), an action-wise R-learner that operates directly on multi-hot logs and regularizes selection by observational support. We compare CAR-PL with an uplift T-Learner, a conservative contextual value model, a zero-shot LLM, and non-personalized references on company-disjoint held-out firms under a shared model-assisted scoring rule. CAR-PL has the highest Gross Profit point estimate (0.084), the T-Learner has the highest Revenue point estimate (0.085), and the contextual value model has the highest Quick Ratio point estimate (0.062). CAR-PL and the T-Learner are not statistically separated on either growth KPI in matched company-clustered comparisons, while CAR-PL selects 33-34 categories and produces less concentrated selections across the catalog. Outcome-model-only scoring retains the same KPI-level point-estimate leader or top pair, and category rankings remain similar when the all-zero treatment reference is replaced by the most common training co-action pattern. These findings support objective-specific ranking of SMB financial guidance from multi-action accounting logs.

</details>


### [199] [ChronoSSM: Training for Temporally Aware Representations in Autoregressive State Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10120)
*Adrien Schoen,Nachiketa Ratnakar Patil,Arjun Bhagoji,Francesco Bronzino*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ChronoSSM introduces a jointly trained autoregressive State Space Model that models events and timestamps together, showing that joint temporal supervision yields more temporally informative representations without degrading content-generation quality compared to two-stage approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern sequence models (Transformers, SSMs) prioritize event prediction while treating timing as secondary. In data-mining contexts with explicit timestamps, this separation impairs temporal reasoning, anomaly detection, and event chronology reconstruction. The common two-stage approach—training a separate timing model on frozen event representations—assumes event-optimized representations already encode sufficient temporal structure, an assumption that may not hold.

Method: The authors propose ChronoSSM, an autoregressive State Space Model with a shared backbone trained jointly on combined token prediction and temporal generation objectives. They compare the joint regime (temporal supervision updates the backbone) against the two-stage regime (timing learned from frozen event representations) across four domains with varying timestamp supervision density.

Result: Joint training consistently makes inter-arrival information more recoverable from frozen representations across all four domains and supervision levels (dense and partial), with no systematic degradation in content-generation quality overall.

Conclusion: Temporal supervision can be integrated into the backbone training of autoregressive SSMs to produce more temporally informative representations without materially degrading autoregressive event modeling performance, challenging the prevailing two-stage paradigm.

Abstract: Modern sequence models, from Transformers to State Space Models, have enabled powerful generative modeling across diverse domains, yet they are typically trained to predict what happens while treating when it happens as a secondary concern. In data-mining settings where events are associated with explicit timing information, this separation can limit temporal reasoning, anomaly detection, and faithful reconstruction of event chronology. A common strategy is to treat timing as an auxiliary signal, training a separate timing model using representations learned solely for event prediction. However, this two-stage approach implicitly assumes that representations optimized for event prediction already contain sufficient temporal structure.
  We introduce ChronoSSM, an autoregressive State Space Model (SSM) that jointly models events and timestamps with a shared backbone trained using combined token and temporal generation objectives. We compare the joint regime, where temporal supervision updates the backbone, with the two-stage regime, where timing is learned only using the frozen event representations. Across four domains spanning dense and partial timestamp supervision, joint training consistently makes inter-arrival information more recoverable from frozen representations without any systematic degradation in content-generation quality overall. Our results show that temporal supervision can produce more temporally informative representations without materially degrading autoregressive event modeling.

</details>


### [200] [Procedural Fairness Failures in RLHF from Preference Averaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10126)
*M P V S Gopinadh,Karthik Kamuju,Kummari Avinash,John Joshua,Srinivasa Raju Rudraraju*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard RLHF averages heterogeneous human preferences into a single reward model, causing majority groups to dominate and minority groups to be underrepresented. The authors propose PA-RLHF, which preserves distinct preference signals during reward learning, improving alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reducing the fairness gap from 15.9 to 9.6 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RLHF assumes preference homogeneity when aggregating human feedback, but real-world preferences are heterogeneous. This aggregation leads to a procedural fairness failure: majority preferences dominate the learned reward model while minority preferences are systematically under-represented, producing inequitable alignment outcomes.

Method: The authors propose Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF), which separates optimization across distinct preference modes at the reward learning stage rather than averaging preferences into a single reward model. This preserves distinct preference signals during the reward modeling process.

Result: In controlled experiments, PA-RLHF improved overall alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reduced the fairness gap between the best- and worst-aligned groups from 15.9 to 9.6 percentage points.

Conclusion: Procedural fairness failures in alignment stem from structural design choices in reward learning, even in controlled, noise-free settings. This has direct implications for LLMs and agentic systems, where biased reward models can compound inequities across sequential decisions.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) aggregates heterogeneous preferences into a single reward model, assuming preference homogeneity. When preferences are heterogeneous, this aggregation induces a procedural fairness failure where majority preference groups dominate reward learning while minority preferences are systematically under-represented. This work defines procedural fairness in alignment as preserving distinct preference signals during reward modeling and shows that standard RLHF violates this via preference averaging. Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF) is introduced, separating optimization across preference modes at the reward learning stage. In a controlled setting, PA-RLHF improves overall alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reduces the fairness gap between best and worst aligned groups from 15.9 to 9.6 percentage points. These results show that procedural fairness failures in alignment can arise from structural design choices in reward learning, even in controlled, noise-free settings, with direct implications for large language models and agentic systems, where biased reward models can compound inequities across sequential decisions.

</details>


### [201] [SeFoRA: Sketch-Aggregated Federated Low-Rank Adaptation with Heterogeneous Client Ranks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10144)
*Yue Xia,Tayyebeh Jahani-Nezhad,Mayank Bakshi,Rawad Bitar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SeFoRA is a federated LoRA fine-tuning algorithm where clients transmit linear sketches of their updates, enabling aggregation across heterogeneous ranks and addressing the bilinear mismatch problem, with proven convergence and strong empirical results on GLUE benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with LoRA presents two key challenges: (1) clients may use different LoRA ranks, making factor matrices dimensionally incompatible for aggregation, and (2) naive factor-wise averaging suffers from a bilinear mismatch. Existing methods fail to simultaneously address both issues.

Method: SeFoRA (Sketch-aggregated Federated LoRA) has each client transmit a linear sketch of its local LoRA updates to the federator, enabling direct aggregation in a small subspace. A rank-homogeneous variant, SeFoRA-Ho, supports direct adapter aggregation when all clients use the same rank. Convergence is proved at rate O(1/T) to a neighborhood of a first-order stationary point.

Result: SeFoRA outperforms state-of-the-art federated LoRA methods on fine-tuning RoBERTa-Large across GLUE benchmark datasets. Theoretically, the homogeneous variant converges at rate O(1/T).

Conclusion: SeFoRA effectively resolves both the dimension incompatibility and bilinear mismatch challenges in federated LoRA, offering a principled sketch-based aggregation framework with strong theoretical guarantees and superior empirical performance.

Abstract: We consider federated parameter efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks with low-rank adaptation (LoRA,~Hu et al.\ 2022). Combining LoRA with federated PEFT introduces challenges absent from either setting alone: clients may use different LoRA ranks, making their factor matrices dimension-incompatible, and factor-wise averaging suffers from a bilinear mismatch. We propose SeFoRA, a sketch-aggregated federated LoRA algorithm in which each client transmits a linear sketch of its local updates, enabling direct aggregation at the federator. As a result, SeFoRA alleviates the bilinear mismatch, and allows for aggregation in a small subspace of the full model. We introduce a rank-homogeneous version called SeFoRA-Ho which allows for direct adapter aggregation in this setting. We prove convergence to a neighborhood of the first-order stationary point at rate $\cO(1/T)$ for the rank-homogeneous setting. Numerical experiments on fine-tuning RoBERTa-Large on GLUE datasets show how our algorithms outperform the state-of-the-art.

</details>


### [202] [The Evaluation Protocol Determines the Result: An Independent Reproduction of LeWorldModel on TwoRoom](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10145)
*Joyjeet Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An independent reproduction of LeWorldModel reveals that reported results depend on four undocumented implementation conventions. The evaluation protocol is internally contested by the paper's own materials. Two general findings emerge: one-step prediction accuracy does not predict long-horizon planning success, and a batch normalisation layer inflated validation loss up to 300×, concealing flat training loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: This is a reproducibility study aiming to independently verify the claims of LeWorldModel, a latent world model trained with prediction loss and anti-collapse regularisation on the TwoRoom environment. The authors seek to determine whether the reported ~87% goal-reaching rate can be replicated and to identify any hidden implementation details that may be critical to success.

Method: Independent reimplementation on approximately $25 of rented GPU compute, with all evaluation conducted on a single laptop CPU. The reproducer systematically tested the released code, configuration files, and author-provided checkpoint against identical episodes. Position probing (Pearson r) was used to verify representation quality. Multiple evaluation protocols were compared using the paper's appendix versus the repository's configuration specifications, with varying goal offsets and step budgets.

Result: The reproduction achieved 94.0% goals reached versus 84.0% for the authors' released checkpoint under identical protocol. Position probe Pearson r = 0.9988 (reported: 0.996). Four undocumented conventions proved critical: dense action gathering across frameskip, programmatic action-encoder width, ImageNet pixel normalisation, and action z-scoring. Without these, the predictor fails to converge. The evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent: paper appendix and repository config specify different parameters yielding 14.0% vs 84.0% on the same weights. Changing only goal construction dropped performance from 84.0% to 8.0%. One-step prediction error fails to order long-horizon planning success across three checkpoints. A batch normalisation layer inflated validation loss up to 300×, masking flat training loss throughout.

Conclusion: The LeWorldModel results are reproducible but only when employing undocumented implementation conventions absent from released configurations. The paper's own materials contain conflicting evaluation protocols. The findings cast doubt on using one-step prediction accuracy as a proxy for planning capability and highlight how batch normalisation can obscure training dynamics, raising broader concerns about evaluation rigor in model-based reinforcement learning research.

Abstract: LeWorldModel trains a latent world model with a prediction loss and a single anti-collapse regulariser, and reports approximately 87% of goals reached on TwoRoom, its simplest diagnostic environment. We reproduce that result by independent reimplementation on roughly $25 of rented compute, with all evaluation on one laptop CPU.
  We reach 94.0% at the repository's evaluation goal offset, against 84.0% for the authors' own released checkpoint measured under our protocol on identical episodes, and we reproduce the reported representation result directly (position probe Pearson r = 0.9988 against a reported 0.996). Reaching that point required four conventions that determine the outcome and appear in no released configuration file: dense action gathering across a frameskip block, a programmatically-set action-encoder width, ImageNet pixel normalisation, and action z-scoring. A reproducer following the released configurations alone obtains a model whose predictor cannot converge.
  The evaluation protocol is itself contested by the released material. The paper's appendix and the repository's configuration specify different goal offsets and step budgets; on the authors' own weights these yield 14.0% and 84.0%, and only the configuration's values reproduce the reported figure. On fifty identical episodes, changing nothing but how the goal is constructed moves that checkpoint from 84.0% to 8.0%.
  Two findings generalise. One-step prediction accuracy does not predict long-horizon planning success: across three checkpoints spanning a sevenfold range in prediction error, including the authors' own, it orders short-horizon success monotonically and fails to order long-horizon success at all. And a batch normalisation layer inflated our reported validation loss by up to a factor of 300, concealing a training loss that was flat throughout.

</details>


### [203] [REATS: LLM Reasoning-based Ensemble Learning for Adaptive Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10149)
*Xu Zhang,Chang Xu,Hui Sun,Nan Ma,Zijian Zhang,Peng Wang,Wei Wang,Li Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REATS proposes an LLM-based ensemble router for time series forecasting that combines textual descriptions of temporal patterns with numerical features via chain-of-thought reasoning to produce interpretable, sample-adaptive ensemble weights, outperforming baselines while offering natural language explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No single forecasting model dominates all time series due to real-world diversity. Existing ensemble methods use fixed rules or black-box models on numerical inputs, failing to leverage LLM reasoning for interpretable, adaptive weight decisions.

Method: REATS uses: (i) a structured hybrid textual-numerical input pipeline with fixed token cost and retrieved similar-sample priors; (ii) diverse multi-row weight supervision with a token-efficient percentage-table format to reduce hallucinations; and (iii) a two-stage SFT+GRPO fine-tuning framework with a reciprocal reward mapping that addresses uniform sensitivity and outlier-dominated advantage compression in naive regression-based GRPO.

Result: REATS outperforms competitive ensemble baselines across eight benchmarks, demonstrates strong transfer learning, and generalizes out-of-domain to unseen candidate models, while providing natural language explanations for its weighting decisions.

Conclusion: LLM reasoning can serve as an effective, interpretable ensemble router for time series forecasting when paired with carefully designed input representations, supervision schemes, and reward structures for fine-tuning.

Abstract: Due to the diversity of real-world time series, no single forecasting model consistently dominates across all samples. Ensemble learning addresses this by combining complementary model strengths, yet existing methods rely on fixed rules or black-box models based solely on numerical inputs, failing to leverage LLM reasoning for interpretable weighting decisions. We propose REATS, which leverages LLM reasoning capabilities as an intelligent ensemble router that jointly processes textual temporal pattern descriptions and numerical features to produce interpretable, sample-adaptive ensemble weights through chain-of-thought reasoning. To enable effective LLM-based ensembling, we study its key design choices and propose: (i) a structured input pipeline that transforms raw time series into hybrid textual--numerical representations with fixed token cost, enabling rule-based chain-of-thought construction without API dependency, augmented with retrieved similar-sample priors; (ii) a diverse multi-row weight supervision scheme coupled with a token-efficient percentage-table format that reduces numerical complexity and mitigates LLM hallucinations; and (iii) a two-stage fine-tuning framework combining SFT with GRPO, where a reciprocal reward mapping transforms the continuous unbounded MSE gap into bounded signals with amplified near-oracle sensitivity, addressing the uniform sensitivity and outlier-dominated advantage compression inherent in naive reward designs for regression-based GRPO. Experiments on eight benchmarks demonstrate that REATS outperforms competitive ensemble baselines while providing natural language explanations and demonstrating strong transfer learning and out-of-domain generalization to unseen candidate models.

</details>


### [204] [Intrinsic Structure: Spectral Identifiability for Mechanistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10172)
*Ashim Dhor,Pin-Yu Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper establishes identifiability guarantees for dictionary learning in mechanistic interpretability by applying Koopman operator theory. The spectrum of the lifted linear dynamics is proven recoverable at rate M^{-1/2}, with matching lower bounds and a dissociation theorem showing that variance-carrying and information-carrying directions diverge under non-normality. Empirical validation on GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2-2B, and Qwen3-8B-Base confirms the theoretical predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mechanistic interpretability lacks a principled way to distinguish whether discovered circuits are genuine model properties or artifacts of the discovery method. Sparse autoencoders exemplify this: different random seeds and widths recover materially different features from identical activations, yet no theory addresses whether this variability is incidental or structural. The paper aims to put dictionary learning for interpretability on a rigorous identifiability footing.

Method: The forward pass is treated as a controlled dynamical system with depth as the time variable and lifted via the Koopman operator into a finite linear realisation. The spectrum of this operator becomes the coordinate-free, model-intrinsic object of study. The authors prove that this spectrum is recoverable from M calibration samples at a rate of M^{-1/2} (up to permutation), provide a matching minimax lower bound, a median-of-means variant for heavy-tailed activations, and a dissociation theorem stating that under non-normality, variance-carrying directions and information-carrying directions across depth cannot coincide.

Result: On GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2-2B, and Qwen3-8B-Base, the Koopman spectrum converges everywhere and attains the predicted M^{-1/2} exponent on Qwen3-8B-Base (0.506 ± 0.031). Shortfalls collapse onto a single curve when plotted against each cell's sample threshold. Koopman modes outperform random directions but underperform principal components on indirect-object identification, with the gap decaying by a factor of 4.1× in depth-distance, consistent with the dissociation theorem.

Conclusion: The Koopman spectrum is an identifiable, model-intrinsic fingerprint with a stated error bar — not a legible decomposition. A fundamental tension exists: the identifiable object and the legible object are not the same. This provides the first identifiability theorem for a mechanistic-interpretability primitive.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability explains models by identifying circuits inside them, but has no way to tell whether a circuit is a property of the model or an artifact of the method that found it. Sparse autoencoders illustrate the problem: different seeds and widths recover materially different features from the same activations, and no theory says whether that variability is incidental or structural. We put dictionary learning for interpretability on an identifiability footing. Treating the forward pass as a controlled dynamical system with depth as time and lifting it with the Koopman operator yields a finite linear realisation whose \emph{spectrum} is a coordinate-free property of the model. We prove the spectrum is recoverable from $M$ calibration samples at rate $M^{-1/2}$ up to permutation - to our knowledge the first identifiability theorem for a mechanistic-interpretability primitive, with a matching minimax lower bound, a median-of-means variant for heavy-tailed activations, and a dissociation theorem: whenever the realisation is non-normal, the directions carrying activation variance and the directions carrying information across depth cannot coincide. The identifiable object and the legible object are not the same object. On GPT-2 small, Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-8B-Base the spectrum converges everywhere and attains the predicted exponent on Qwen3-8B-Base ($0.506 \pm 0.031$); shortfalls collapse onto one curve against each cell's sample threshold. Koopman modes beat random directions but lose to principal components on indirect-object identification, with the gap decaying $4.1\times$ in depth-distance, as the theorem predicts. The Koopman spectrum is an identifiable, model-intrinsic fingerprint with a stated error bar, not a legible decomposition.

</details>


### [205] [From Prediction to Incrementality: Causal Optimization for Large-Scale Targeting and Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10182)
*Changshuai Wei,John Bencina,Phuc Nguyen,Andre Assuncao Silva T Ribeiro,Benjamin Zelditch*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a decision-centric framework that replaces heuristic allocation with causal optimization under global constraints, using a Transformer-based causal network, Bayesian bandit exploration, and dual linear programming for constrained allocation, achieving +7.20% lift in a LinkedIn A/B test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional recommendation systems rely on predictive scores that misallocate resources toward users who would convert independently, undermining incremental business impact. There is a need for a unified framework that directly optimizes treatment effects under real-world business constraints.

Method: The framework integrates three components under a single objective: (1) a causal neural network with a Transformer backbone for individual treatment-effect estimation, supporting sequential context and multi-outcome scoring via outcome embeddings; (2) a Bayesian neural-bandit layer for uncertainty-aware exploration; and (3) a dual-based large-scale linear-programming layer for globally constrained allocation. Causal training-data construction and cost/delivery control are also addressed as production necessities.

Result: Offline simulations on a public bandit dataset, targeted architectural ablations, and an online A/B test on LinkedIn Feed marketing traffic demonstrated a statistically significant +7.20% lift in the primary long-term-value metric.

Conclusion: The end-to-end causal optimization policy is feasible at production scale, delivering meaningful incremental impact under business constraints while providing practical lessons on data construction and operational control.

Abstract: Large-scale targeting and recommendation systems are typically built around predictive scores fed into heuristic or local allocation. When the business goal is incremental impact, as in marketing campaigns, incentives, and notifications, this paradigm systematically misallocates resources toward users who would have acted anyway. We present a decision-centric framework that instead optimizes causal effects under global constraints, aligning three components under a single objective: a causal neural network with a Transformer backbone for individual treatment-effect estimation, a Bayesian neural-bandit layer for uncertainty-aware exploration, and a dual-based large-scale linear-programming layer for constrained allocation. The framework also supports sequential context and multi-outcome, attribute-conditioned scoring through a Transformer encoder and outcome embeddings. We evaluate it with offline simulations on a public bandit dataset, targeted architectural ablations, and an online A/B test on LinkedIn Feed marketing traffic. We also distill production lessons on causal training-data construction and cost and delivery control, which were critical to successful deployment. The end-to-end treatment policy delivered a statistically significant $+7.20\%$ lift in the primary long-term-value metric, demonstrating the feasibility of production-scale causal optimization under business constraints.

</details>


### [206] [ELMER: Evolutionary Language Model that Explores and Refines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10196)
*Matthew Siper,Ahmed Khalifa,Julian Togelius*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces an Evolutionary Language Model that searches over natural-language policy descriptions, compiles them into executable programs, and uses conditional semantic mutation with oDPO to achieve steerable, efficient evolutionary search in program space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Syntactic edit size in program evolution is an unreliable proxy for behavioral change — small code changes can drastically alter behavior, while large rewrites may preserve identical execution traces. The authors seek a representation where mutation magnitude correlates with behavioral displacement, enabling controlled exploration in evolutionary search.

Method: A Qwen3-8B model is fully fine-tuned for three task-conditioned operations: (1) conditional semantic mutation with tunable strength (low, medium, high), (2) natural language to domain-specific language (GPTL) compilation, and (3) GPTL to natural language translation. Training uses Direct Preference Optimization (oDPO) with conditional input on mutation strength. Evaluation spans 252 fixed-budget evolutionary searches.

Result: oDPO improves both behavioral calibration and finite-budget search efficiency. Natural-language representation attains the highest observed held-out fitness. The mutation-strength condition input systematically changes semantic edit composition, and language mutations preserve more parent fitness at matched small-to-moderate behavioral displacement compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Natural language can serve as a steerable, execution-grounded search representation over executable program space, enabling controlled mutation magnitudes that better preserve parent fitness while systematically exploring behavioral variation.

Abstract: Program evolution can measure whether a mutation helped, but it rarely controls how far the mutation moves in behavior space. Syntactic edit size is an unreliable proxy: a small code change can alter nearly every action, while a larger rewrite can preserve the same execution trace. We introduce an Evolutionary Language Model that searches over natural-language policy descriptions and compiles typed programs for execution. A fully fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model learns three task-conditioned operations: conditional semantic mutation, natural language to domain-specific language (GPTL) compilation, and GPTL to natural language translation. The model is fine-tuned with conditional input on the mutation strength (low, medium, high) using Direct Preference Optimization (oDPO). Across 252 fixed-budget evolutionary searches, oDPO improves both behavioral calibration and finite-budget search efficiency. Natural-language attains the highest observed held-out fitness. Our analysis shows that the condition input (mutation strength) systematically changes semantic edit composition and that language mutations preserve more parent fitness at matched small-to-moderate behavioral displacement. These results show that language can serve as a steerable, execution-grounded search representation over executable program space.

</details>


### [207] [Detecting an Effect Is Not Learning to Act on It: A Reward-SNR Floor for LLM Acquisition Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10441)
*Ying Yuan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that learning a per-instance policy for when to acquire costly auxiliary signals (e.g., LLM reasoning) is fundamentally bounded by a reward signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) floor. Below this floor (~2.8/√N), apparent oracle gains are illusory — driven by noise order statistics — and learned routing never beats random. The authors introduce Structured Hypothesis Embeddings (SHE) as a concrete instantiation and show across three public datasets that per-instance acquisition policies fail, advocating instead for design-time regime gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many ML pipelines can optionally acquire costly per-example auxiliary signals (LLM reasoning, oracle labels, expensive measurements). Practitioners often observe that using these signals helps "on average," but this paper identifies a critical, overlooked distinction: detecting a mean benefit does not imply that a deployable policy can learn *when* to acquire the signal on a per-instance basis. The motivation is to formalize and empirically demonstrate the conditions under which per-instance acquisition routing is fundamentally impossible due to insufficient reward SNR.

Method: (1) Theoretical framing: Derivation of a reward-SNR detectability floor ρ*(N) ≈ 2.8/√N that must be cleared for offline estimable routing. (2) Matched-moment noise placebo: A synthetic signal with identical moments but no true structure is shown to reproduce ≥100% of the oracle's apparent gain, proving apparent gains are artifacts of order statistics. (3) Empirical instantiation (SHE): A frozen LLM generates ranked, confidence-scored, evidence-grounded intent hypotheses from user history, fused into a recommender. (4) Multi-granularity routing evaluation: Learned routing policies tested at per-impression, cluster, regime, and uplift-tree levels across three public datasets (MIND, REES46, Amazon-Beauty). (5) Positive control confirming the failure is due to low SNR, not a broken pipeline.

Result: SHE is faithful and calibratable, yielding significant gains over an ordered GRU (+0.0114, 95% CI [+0.0030, +0.0209]), but this is backbone- and regime-conditional, with a global redundancy gap indistinguishable from zero. Learned acquisition policies fail at every granularity on all three datasets because they all sit below the SNR floor. The matched-moment noise placebo reproduces ≥100% of the oracle's apparent gain. The positive control confirms a true low-SNR limit.

Conclusion: The realizable unit for leveraging costly auxiliary signals is not a per-instance acquisition policy but a design-time regime gate — a static decision about when the signal is worth using based on global conditions. The reward-SNR floor provides a practical diagnostic: if ρ does not clear ~2.8/√N, practitioners should not attempt learned per-instance routing, as any apparent oracle gain is likely noise.

Abstract: Many pipelines can pay a per-example cost to acquire an auxiliary, model-derived observation -- an LLM's structured reasoning, a slow oracle, an expensive measurement -- and then must decide when the acquired signal is worth using. Our thesis is a distinction that is easy to miss: detecting that such a signal helps on average is not the same as learning to act on it per instance, and a reward-SNR floor governs when the second is even possible. Even when the signal is faithful and an in-sample oracle picking the top-b examples by realized reward shows a sizable apparent gain, no deployable policy can learn when to acquire it: across per-impression, cluster, regime, and uplift-tree granularities, learned routing never beats random, and a matched-moment noise placebo reproduces >=100% of the oracle's apparent gain -- the apparent "learnable structure" is order statistics of noise. We explain this with one distinction, detecting a mean effect vs. learning a per-instance acquisition policy, and a reward-SNR detectability floor: routing is estimable offline only if the reward SNR rho clears rho*(N) ~= 2.8/sqrt(N), with a positive control confirming a true low-SNR limit rather than a broken pipeline. As a concrete instantiation we introduce Structured Hypothesis Embeddings (SHE): a frozen LLM turns a user history into ranked, confidence-scored, evidence-grounded intent hypotheses, fused into a recommender. On three public datasets (MIND, REES46, Amazon-Beauty), SHE is faithful and calibratable, yet its value is backbone- and regime-conditional (significant over an ordered GRU, +0.0114, 95% CI [+0.0030, +0.0209], but a global redundancy gap indistinguishable from zero), and learned acquisition collapses at every granularity because all three datasets sit below the floor. The realizable unit is a design-time regime gate, not a per-instance policy. We release code and a one-command reproduction.

</details>


### [208] [Boundary-Seeking Policy Gradient for Safe Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10204)
*Chenhua Fan,Jiahui Zhu,Yuhang Zhang,Honghao Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BSPG is a first-order policy gradient method for safe RL that explicitly drives the policy toward the active constraint boundary, combining a reward-improving tangential component with a residual-driven normal component, achieving O(1/√T) convergence of the constraint residual without a learned dual variable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard gradient-based methods for constrained MDPs often settle in the feasible interior rather than on the constraint boundary where the optimal policy lies under active constraints. Existing analyses certify feasibility but fail to characterize the constraint value at convergence. The authors aim to exploit the boundary-seeking structure inherent in the occupancy-measure LP formulation.

Method: BSPG decomposes the update into two components: (1) a tangential component that follows the reward gradient projected onto the constraint's tangent space, preserving cost to first order, and (2) a signed, residual-driven normal component that pushes the policy toward the active constraint boundary from either side. The combined direction admits an algebraic Lagrangian form with an induced coefficient, eliminating the need for a learned dual variable.

Result: Under exact gradients and regularity conditions, the constraint residual converges to zero with a finite-horizon O(1/√T) bound. The tangential component ensures reward ascent along the boundary. Any convergent parameter sequence is stationary on the active constraint set, satisfying KKT conditions when the limit is a local maximizer. On Safety-Gymnasium, BSPG achieves higher reward and tighter boundary tracking than baselines.

Conclusion: BSPG provides a principled, boundary-seeking alternative to standard safe RL methods, offering finite-horizon convergence guarantees for both residual reduction and KKT stationarity, along with empirical improvements in reward and constraint satisfaction over existing approaches.

Abstract: Safe reinforcement learning maximizes reward subject to safety constraints. For Constrained Markov Decision Processes, the linear-programming view over occupancy measures implies that whenever the constraint is active at optimality, the optimal policy lies exactly on the constraint boundary, yet standard gradient-based methods do not exploit this structure and often settle in the feasible interior. We introduce Boundary-Seeking Policy Gradient (BSPG), a first-order method whose update combines a tangential component that improves reward while preserving cost to first order with a signed, residual-driven normal component that regulates the policy toward the active boundary from either side; the combined direction admits an algebraic Lagrangian form with an induced coefficient and no learned dual variable. Under exact gradients and stated regularity conditions, the constraint residual converges to zero from either side with a finite-horizon $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ bound, the tangential component is a reward-ascent direction on the boundary, and any convergent parameter sequence is stationary on the active constraint set, satisfying the KKT conditions when the limit is also a local maximizer over the feasible set. This complements existing analyses, which certify feasibility but do not characterize the constraint value at convergence. On a standard Safety-Gymnasium navigation task, BSPG attains higher reward while tracking the boundary more tightly than the compared baselines.

</details>


### [209] [A matched-integrator evaluation of Hamiltonian neural networks on pendulum and Kepler dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10235)
*Lenick Kemunto Nyabuto,Yae Ulrich Gaba,Birahim Tewe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled experimental study comparing Hamiltonian Neural Networks against parameter-matched feedforward baselines on two conservative systems (nonlinear pendulum and Kepler two-body problem), finding HNNs reduce energy drift by 42-fold and trajectory MSE by 15.8-fold on the pendulum, with benefits amplified in nonlinear phase-space regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously isolate and quantify the benefit of the Hamiltonian architectural prior (conservation of a scalar Hamiltonian) versus generic vector-field neural networks, under a strictly controlled protocol that matches parameters, training data, derivative targets, optimization, and inference integrators.

Method: An HNN and a parameter-matched feedforward baseline are both trained on identical RK4-generated trajectories using central-difference derivative targets and identical optimization settings, then integrated at inference with the same RK4 scheme. Five independent training seeds are used. Additionally, a Störmer-Verlet-style rollout of the learned HNN is examined. The protocol is applied to both a nonlinear pendulum and the 3D Kepler two-body problem.

Result: On the nonlinear pendulum at T=100 (~16 periods), the HNN achieves 42-fold lower mean energy drift and 15.8-fold lower mean trajectory MSE. Energy drift remains bounded with lower seed-to-seed variability. Energy-stratified analysis shows larger gains in more nonlinear phase-space regions. On the Kepler problem, the HNN similarly exhibits lower trajectory, energy, and angular-momentum drift. The Störmer-Verlet analysis notes that standard symplecticity guarantees do not directly apply since the learned Hamiltonian is not constrained to separable form T(p)+V(q).

Conclusion: The Hamiltonian architectural prior provides substantial, quantifiable advantages for long-horizon prediction and physical consistency in conservative dynamical systems, with benefits that grow as trajectories explore more nonlinear regimes. The controlled matching protocol strengthens confidence that these gains stem from the inductive bias itself rather than confounding factors.

Abstract: Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) parameterize conservative dynamics through a learned scalar Hamiltonian, providing an architectural prior that is absent from generic vector-field neural networks. We evaluate this prior under a controlled protocol in which an HNN and a parameter-matched feedforward baseline are trained on the same RK4-generated trajectories, use the same central-difference derivative targets and optimization settings, and are integrated at inference with the same RK4 scheme. Results are reported over five independent training seeds.
  On the nonlinear pendulum, the HNN reduces mean energy drift by 42-fold and mean trajectory MSE by 15.8-fold at T = 100, approximately 16 pendulum periods. Its energy drift also remains bounded and exhibits substantially lower seed-to-seed variability than the standard-network baseline. An energy-stratified analysis shows that the difference becomes more pronounced as trajectories explore more nonlinear regions of phase space.
  As an additional diagnostic, we examine an explicit Störmer--Verlet-style rollout of the learned HNN. Because the learned Hamiltonian is not constrained to the separable form H(q,p) = T(p) + V(q), the standard symplecticity guarantee of velocity Verlet does not directly apply.
  We further apply the same matched-integrator protocol to the three-dimensional Kepler two-body problem. The HNN again exhibits lower trajectory, energy, and angular-momentum drift than the parameter-matched baseline. These experiments provide a controlled study of how Hamiltonian parameterization affects long-horizon prediction and physical consistency across two conservative dynamical systems.

</details>


### [210] [STCAD: Scalable Trajectory Clustering and Anomaly Detection on Terabyte-Scale AIS Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10249)
*Bertram Hage,Alexander Schiøtz,Felix Thomsen,Christian Rand,Peder Heiselberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A BERT-based trajectory encoding framework with CURE hierarchical clustering is proposed for unsupervised clustering of massive AIS vessel data, achieving interpretable trajectory groups and anomaly detection without predefined cluster counts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for maritime trajectory analysis struggle with the scale (terabyte-level), variable-length trajectories, and the need to pre-specify cluster numbers. There is a need for an unsupervised, scalable framework that produces physically meaningful trajectory clusters and can detect anomalous vessel behavior without manual labeling.

Method: The framework consists of three components: (1) a custom BERT-based encoder trained via masked token modeling to embed variable-length AIS trajectories into fixed-length representations; (2) CURE (Clustering Using Representatives) hierarchical clustering to group encoded trajectories without requiring a predefined number of clusters; and (3) an intrinsic unsupervised anomaly detection mechanism that combines reconstruction loss from the BERT model with clustering noise assignment to flag irregular navigation patterns.

Result: Demonstrated on a national-scale AIS dataset with billions of messages over one year, the framework produced stable trajectory clusters and achieved clear separation between nominal and anomalous vessel behaviors.

Conclusion: The proposed BERT+CURE pipeline offers a scalable, fully unsupervised solution for maritime traffic pattern discovery and anomaly detection from massive AIS archives, overcoming limitations of prior approaches that require fixed cluster counts or struggle with data volume.

Abstract: We present a scalable framework for unsupervised clustering of maritime trajectories derived from terabyte-scale Automatic Identification System (AIS) archives. Variable-length trajectories are encoded with a custom BERT-based model trained via masked token modeling and clustered using CURE hierarchical clustering, producing physically interpretable trajectory groups without requiring a predefined number of clusters. An intrinsic unsupervised anomaly detection method based on reconstruction loss and clustering noise assignment identifies irregular navigation patterns. The framework is demonstrated on a national-scale AIS dataset comprising billions of messages spanning one year, yielding stable trajectory clusters and a clear separation between nominal and anomalous vessel behavior.

</details>


### [211] [CRHT: A Continuous Regression Hybrid Transformer for Vessel Trajectory Prediction with Online Cluster Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10256)
*Alexander Schiøtz,Bertram Hage,Christian Rand,Felix Thomsen,Peder Heiselberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRHT is a hybrid deep learning framework that combines 1D CNNs with multi-head attention for vessel trajectory prediction, using online K-means cluster sampling to address geographic bias in AIS data, achieving optimal short-term forecasting precision for real-time maritime surveillance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vessel trajectory prediction models suffer from geographic bias (spatial data imbalance) and lack navigational realism, limiting their effectiveness for maritime safety and anomaly detection. There is a need for a model that balances precision with realistic maneuver tracking.

Method: The authors propose CRHT, which employs: (1) an online K-means cluster sampling strategy to ensure diverse exposure to rare maneuvers during training, mitigating spatial data imbalance; (2) a hybrid architecture integrating 1D convolutional layers for local kinematic feature extraction with multi-head attention for capturing global temporal context from AIS data.

Result: CRHT achieves the lowest prediction errors at the 1-hour short-term forecasting horizon. Compared to discrete models that offer high navigational stability over long horizons, CRHT provides a superior balance of precision and maneuver tracking suitable for real-time maritime surveillance.

Conclusion: CRHT offers an optimal trade-off between forecasting precision and navigational realism for short-term vessel trajectory prediction, making it well-suited for real-time maritime surveillance applications, while discrete models remain preferable for long-horizon stability.

Abstract: Accurate vessel trajectory prediction is critical for maritime safety and anomaly detection, yet existing models often struggle with geographic bias and navigational realism. We propose the Continuous Regression Hybrid Transformer (CRHT), a deep learning framework designed to forecast vessel motion using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. To mitigate spatial data imbalance, we introduce an online K-means cluster sampling strategy that ensures diverse exposure to rare maneuvers during training. Our hybrid architecture integrates 1D convolutional layers for local kinematic feature extraction with a multi-head attention mechanism for global temporal context. CRHT demonstrates superior performance in short-term forecasting, achieving the lowest errors at the 1-hour horizon. The results demonstrate that while discrete models provide high navigational stability over long horizons, CRHT offers an optimal balance of precision and maneuver tracking for real-time maritime surveillance.

</details>


### [212] [Toward Human Rights Benchmarking for LLMs: A Pilot Methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10268)
*Savannah Thais,Wm. Matthew Kennedy,Abhigyan Acherjee,Matilda Wysocki,Malcolm Langford,Caitlin Kraft Buchman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HumRightsBench is the first expert-validated, scenario-based benchmark for evaluating how well LLMs reason about international human rights law, adapting the IRAC legal framework to IRAP (Issue, Rule, Application, Proposing remedies) and revealing significant performance variability across models and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in legal determinations affecting human rights, yet no evaluation benchmark exists to assess their reasoning competence in international human rights law. The authors address this gap by creating a dedicated, expert-validated benchmark.

Method: The authors adapt the standard IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion) legal reasoning framework to IRAP (replacing "Conclusion" with "Proposing remedies") to better capture human rights reasoning patterns. They construct a pilot series of authentic scenarios implicating multidimensional real-world human rights issues, annotated by human rights lawyers and professionals worldwide.

Result: Model accuracy spans a wide range across legal reasoning tasks: overall model performance ranges from 0.339 to 0.577, with task-level scores varying from 0.025 to 0.774. This variability indicates the benchmark's capacity to discriminate model capabilities.

Conclusion: HumRightsBench is a capable and timely instrument for advancing the emerging subfield of AI evaluations focused on human rights law, arriving at a critical juncture in the field's evolution.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate legal determinations over what human rights are realized, and how. Yet, no evaluation benchmark exists to assess whether they can reason correctly about human rights law. To this end, we report our efforts to develop a robust and scalable methodology for creating HumRightsBench: the first expert-validated, scenario-based benchmark for evaluating reasoning grounded in the obligation structure of international human rights law. We adapt the IRAC framework for legal reasoning to better suit the unique reasoning patterns of human rights work (substituting P, "proposing remedies," for C, "legal conclusion," yielding IRAP) to structure our evaluation heuristics. We also produce a pilot series of authentic scenarios designed to implicate the many dimensions of real-world human rights issues and annotated by human rights lawyers and professionals across the world. Ultimately, we find that model accuracy scores range considerably across legal reasoning tasks (overall model performance ranges from 0.339 to 0.577, task min-max ranges from 0.025 to 0.774), which strongly implies that HumRightsBench is a capable instrument for advancing this emerging subfield of AI evaluations science at a critical moment in its evolution.

</details>


### [213] [Power law graph attention: exact generalization of scaled dot-product attention, empirical collapse at inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10288)
*Burc Gokden*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PLDR-LLM replaces standard scaled dot-product attention with a learned power-law bilinear operator (PLGA), featuring Perron-Frobenius structure, a DAG regularizer, and a commutant criterion for relative-position dependence. An inference-collapse theorem shows exact input invariance reduces to constant-operator SDPA. Empirical measurements confirm near-invariance (~10⁻⁶), a three-stage mechanism, block/sequential scoring agreement, and self-organized criticality framing. Selected proofs are machine-checked in Lean 4.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To generalize the fixed bilinear form of scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) into a learned, input-dependent operator with richer algebraic structure, enabling formal analysis of attention mechanisms, inference behavior, and emergent properties such as self-organized criticality in large language models.

Method: The PLDR-LLM architecture replaces SDPA with Power Law Graph Attention (PLGA), using a learned operator G_LM built from a strictly positive tensor A_LM via elementwise power laws. The paper introduces a taxonomy of claims (theorem, conditional theorem, measurement, conjecture), a DAG regularizer based on NOTEARS walk-counting, a commutant criterion for rotary-position sensitivity, an inference-collapse theorem, perturbation bounds, a three-stage mechanism (rotary twirl, concentration, row-map contraction), blockwise training/scoring under a global Gram, and a self-organized criticality framework with an intrinsic order parameter. Proof cores are verified in Lean 4.

Result: PLGA contains SDPA as the special case G_LM=I. A_LM has Perron-Frobenius structure. The DAG regularizer's positivity obstructs exact acyclicity. Under nonresonance (standard rotary frequencies), a commutant criterion identifies relative-position-preserving operators. The inference-collapse theorem proves that exact input invariance of deductive outputs collapses inference to generalized SDPA with a constant operator. Measured invariance shows relative fluctuations ≤10⁻⁶. Perturbation bounds quantify but do not certify cached inference. The proxy misses the decoding margin. The three-stage mechanism is measured on a released checkpoint. Block and sequential scoring agree on TruthfulQA within 5×10⁻⁵ per item.

Conclusion: PLDR-LLM provides a principled generalization of SDPA with formal guarantees and measurable structure. The framework connects attention design to algebraic properties (Perron-Frobenius, commutants), training dynamics (three-stage mechanism), inference behavior (collapse theorem), and phenomenological models (self-organized criticality), while maintaining empirical compatibility with existing architectures and offering machine-checked proofs for key results.

Abstract: The Large Language Model from Power Law Decoder Representations (PLDR-LLM) and its attention, Power Law Graph Attention (PLGA), replace the fixed bilinear form of scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) with a learned, input-generated bilinear operator $G_{LM}$, built from a positive tensor $A_{LM}$ by elementwise power laws. The architecture is fully specified, verified against pinned reference releases; claims are labeled theorem, conditional theorem, measurement, or conjecture. Unconditionally: PLGA contains SDPA exactly at $G_{LM}=I$; $A_{LM}$ and $A_P$ are strictly entrywise positive, with Perron-Frobenius structure on $A_{LM}$; the DAG regularizer has the NOTEARS walk-counting form and positivity obstructs exact acyclicity; and, under nonresonance (satisfied by standard rotary frequencies), a commutant criterion identifies which operators preserve relative-position dependence. An inference-collapse theorem: exact input invariance of deductive outputs collapses inference to generalized SDPA with a constant operator. Measured invariance: relative fluctuations of $10^{-6}$ and below; perturbation bounds quantify but do not certify cached inference; the assembled proxy misses the decoding margin. A conditional three-stage mechanism (rotary twirl, concentration, row-map contraction) is measured on a released checkpoint. Blockwise training and scoring under the global Gram are stated with explicit target exposure; on tested samples, block and sequential scoring select identical answers and agree on the published TruthfulQA probability-mass metric within $5\times 10^{-5}$ per item. Self-organized criticality enters as a phenomenological framework with an intrinsic order parameter; open claims become falsifiable conjectures. Selected proof cores are machine-checked in Lean 4.

</details>


### [214] [MERA: Model Evolution and Routing with Skill Adaptation for Agentic Systems at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10333)
*Yuhang Yao,Zeyu Wang,Wanyi Chen,Tongyun Yang,Yuhang Han,Jie Xiao,Chengke Bao,Tianyi Zhao,Lynn Ai,Eric Yang,Tianyu Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MERA introduces a multi-cycle adaptation framework that improves a small LLM's own capabilities (not just routing around it), using execution-verified teacher demonstrations, a distilled SkillBook, and LoRA fine-tuning, achieving significant gains on coding benchmarks while maintaining cost efficiency through verifier-backed routing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior routing methods reduce inference cost by assigning easy tasks to small models and hard tasks to large models, but they leave the small model's capability unchanged, capping potential savings at what the student can already solve. MERA addresses this limitation by actively improving the small model itself.

Method: MERA uses a single model invocation as the unit of adaptation. Each cycle: (1) replays failed student invocations to obtain execution-verified teacher demonstrations, (2) distills recurring procedures into an iteratively updated SkillBook, (3) fine-tunes a student LoRA adapter via supervised learning and optional GRPO. For deployment, the improved student is served behind a cost-calibrated router with verifier-backed fallback. A candidate SkillBook, adapter, or router is admitted only when joint replay preserves task quality.

Result: Four-cycle adaptation raises Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B from 28.7% to 49.7% pass on held-out HumanEval+MBPP. Under verifier-backed fallback, the deployed policy retains 88.3% pass at 60.8% of always-Luna cost. On TAU-2, fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B improves from 14/35 to 18/35, matching an unadapted 4B model.

Conclusion: Verifier-backed multi-cycle adaptation can increase small-model capability, rather than only routing around a fixed student, demonstrating that combining iterative self-improvement with cost-calibrated routing yields both higher task performance and lower inference cost.

Abstract: LLM agents execute heterogeneous sequences of model calls within a single task: some invocations require careful reasoning, while others are structured steps such as formatting or tool-argument construction. Prior routing methods exploit this asymmetry by assigning easy invocations to a cheaper small model and difficult ones to a large model. Such policies reduce inference cost, but they leave the small model's capability unchanged, so attainable savings remain bounded by the work the student can already solve. MERA instead improves the small model itself, using a single model invocation as the unit of adaptation. In each cycle, MERA replays failed student invocations to obtain execution-verified teacher demonstrations, distills recurring procedures into an iteratively updated SkillBook, and fine-tunes a student LoRA adapter via supervised learning and optional GRPO. Routing serves as supporting machinery for deployment: the improved student is served behind a cost-calibrated router with verifier-backed fallback, and a candidate SkillBook, adapter, or router is admitted only when joint replay preserves task quality. Empirically, four-cycle adaptation raises Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B from 28.7% to 49.7% pass on held-out HumanEval+MBPP. Under verifier-backed fallback, the deployed policy retains 88.3% pass at 60.8% of always-Luna cost. On TAU-2, a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B improves from 14/35 to 18/35 and matches an unadapted 4B model. These results indicate that verifier-backed multi-cycle adaptation can increase small-model capability, rather than only routing around a fixed student.

</details>


### [215] [Accelerated Learning of High Dimensional Functions with a Tensor-Featured Training Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10351)
*Karl Pierce,Yuehaw Khoo,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A method to accelerate high-dimensional function optimization using DNNs by alternating between gradient descent on network parameters and updates to a contextually-aware feature layer. Features include fast rank-1 functions and tensor-network-decomposed features distilled from pretrained DNNs, with randomized tensor decomposition reducing storage costs by 8+ orders of magnitude, enabling training in 5–40 dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimizing high-dimensional functions with DNNs is computationally expensive. The authors seek to accelerate this process by introducing adaptive contextual features and leveraging tensor network decompositions to efficiently represent complex, high-dimensional feature representations distilled from pretrained models.

Method: The method alternates between two phases: (1) optimizing DNN parameters via standard gradient descent with a fixed input-feature basis, and (2) updating the feature layer itself. Features are of two types: matrix-free rank-1 features (fast evaluation) and tensor features requiring TN decomposition. Pretrained DNNs are distilled into tensor networks using a "discretize and decompose" strategy, with randomized tensor decomposition employed to drastically reduce storage costs when decomposing high-dimensional discretized functions.

Result: Randomized tensor decomposition reduces storage costs for high-dimensional function decomposition by at least 8 orders of magnitude. The approach successfully trains models in dimensions ranging from 5 to 40.

Conclusion: The proposed alternating optimization framework, combining contextual features with tensor-network-decomposed representations distilled from pretrained DNNs, enables efficient and scalable training of high-dimensional function approximators, overcoming significant storage and computational barriers.

Abstract: In this work we present a method to accelerate the optimization of learning high dimensional functions using deep neural network (DNN). This optimization procedure introduces contextual features into the first layer of a DNN. The parameters of DNN are optimized via standard gradient descent while keeping the input-feature basis fixed. After optimization of the DNN parameters, the feature layer is provided a chance to update and change before DNN optimization resumes. The feature layer has two types of functions: those that can be evaluated quickly in a matrix-free way on the domain (i.e. rank-1 features) and more complex features that must first be decomposed using tensor network (TN) decomposition strategies (tensor features). In particular, we study the effect of adding features which distill pretrained DNN into TNs using a discretize and decompose strategy. To efficiently decompose high-dimensional functions constructed from discretized DNN, we leverage a randomized tensor decomposition strategy. Using randomization, we are able to reduce the storage cost of decomposing high dimensional functions by at least 8 orders of magnitude. Using this approach, we are able to efficiently train models between 5 and 40 dimensions.

</details>


### [216] [Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agentic Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10357)
*Zelei Cheng,Amritansh Mishra,Sambit Sahu,William Campbell*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SINKFLEX-RL is a modular RL training system for long-horizon tool-using agents that combines a Gymnasium environment wrapper, VERL-style dataflow, group-relative policy optimization, and a sink-aware FlexAttention mechanism, achieving improved validation rewards and up to 19.7% VRAM reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training long-horizon tool-using agents via RL is challenging due to long multi-turn contexts, model-specific attention masks, and memory constraints. Existing approaches struggle with the interplay between environment interaction, policy optimization, and attention-kernel efficiency.

Method: SINKFLEX-RL integrates four components: (1) a Gymnasium-compatible environment wrapper for dual-control tool-use settings, (2) a VERL-style rollout dataflow for managing on-policy trajectories, (3) group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) that eliminates the need for a separate value model, and (4) a sink-aware FlexAttention path that preserves model-specific sink token scaling under causal and sliding-window masks.

Result: On Tau2Bench retail tasks, validation reward (mean@1) improved from 0.25 to 0.44 during training. In a memory benchmark at 4096 tokens, peak VRAM dropped from 28.06GB to 22.52GB (19.7% reduction). At 8192 tokens, the optimized path used 25.53GB while the eager baseline ran out of memory.

Conclusion: Integrating environment interfaces, RL dataflow, and attention-kernel design is critical for memory-feasible long-horizon agent training. SINKFLEX-RL demonstrates both improved reward outcomes and substantial memory efficiency gains.

Abstract: Long-horizon tool-using agents must reason over user goals, domain policies, tool calls, simulator state, and delayed verifiable rewards. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural fit for this setting, but multi-turn on-policy rollouts create long contexts, while model-specific attention layers may require custom masks and learned sink normalization. We present SINKFLEX-RL, a modular training system for RL in dual-control tool-use environments. The system combines a Gymnasium-compatible environment wrapper, a VERL-style rollout dataflow, group-relative policy optimization without a separate value model, and a sink-aware FlexAttention path designed to preserve model-specific sink scaling under causal and sliding-window masks. In a preliminary Tau2Bench retail run, validation reward (mean@1) rises from 0.25 early in training to $0.44$ later in the observed training window, while training-score and trajectory-reward proxies also trend upward. In a fixed-configuration memory benchmark, the optimized attention path reduces peak VRAM from 28.06GB to 22.52GB at 4096 tokens, a $19.7\%$ reduction, and runs the measured 8192-token configuration using $25.53$~GB where the eager baseline runs out of memory. These results illustrate the value of integrating environment interfaces, RL dataflow, and attention-kernel design for memory-feasible long-horizon agent training.

</details>


### [217] [Invertible Logits Transformation for Accuracy-Preserving Post-Hoc Uncertainty Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10372)
*Lening Zhao,Qipeng Zhan,Li Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: InvLT proposes a post-hoc calibration method that applies a shared scalar MLP element-wise to logits, achieving nonlinear calibration with parameter count independent of class count, while softly preserving prediction rankings via a paired inverse network.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing post-hoc calibrators suffer from a trilemma: temperature scaling is too inflexible (only linear in logit space), expressive parametric methods (e.g., matrix scaling) introduce parameters that scale with the number of classes C, and other expressive alternatives (e.g., histogram binning, Dirichlet calibration) can alter the argmax prediction. The authors aim for a calibrator that simultaneously achieves nonlinear expressivity, parameter efficiency independent of C, and rank-preservation of original predictions.

Method: InvLT learns a scalar function f: R→R implemented as an MLP, applied element-wise to all logit dimensions. Since f is shared across all C classes, the parameter count is O(1) relative to C. Monotonicity of f is encouraged via a paired inverse network (g ≈ f⁻¹) and a reconstruction loss, rather than enforcing it strictly via numerical integration (as in prior monotone calibrators like Isotonic Regression or Neural Calibration). This soft monotonicity constraint empirically preserves argmax predictions without computational overhead.

Result: Across standard image classification benchmarks and multiple architectures, InvLT consistently outperforms a broad set of post-hoc calibration baselines on standard calibration metrics (e.g., ECE, reliability diagrams), while maintaining the original classification accuracy in all evaluated settings.

Conclusion: InvLT resolves the expressivity–scalability–rank-preservation trilemma in post-hoc calibration by using a shared scalar MLP with a soft monotonicity constraint via inverse network pairing, offering a practical and consistently superior calibration method that scales to large label spaces without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Post-hoc calibration aligns a classifier's predicted confidences with its empirical accuracy without retraining. An ideal calibrator should correct nonlinear miscalibration, scale gracefully to large label spaces, and preserve the original predictions; existing methods typically violate at least one of these properties---temperature scaling lacks expressivity, more flexible parametric alternatives introduce parameters that grow with the number of classes $C$, and other expressive methods do not preserve the rank ordering of class scores and may alter the predicted class. We propose \textbf{Invertible Logits Transformation (InvLT)}, which applies a learned scalar MLP $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ element-wise to the pre-softmax logits. Sharing $f$ across all logit dimensions makes the parameter count independent of $C$. Monotonicity of $f$---and hence preservation of the argmax prediction---is softly encouraged via a paired inverse network rather than enforced through the numerical integration required by prior monotone calibrators; this avoids their computational overhead while empirically preserving the original classification accuracy in every setting we evaluate. Across standard image classification benchmarks and a range of architectures, InvLT consistently outperforms a broad set of post-hoc baselines on standard calibration metrics.

</details>


### [218] [Your LLM, Your Style: Behavioral Mode Axes for LLM Behavioral Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10703)
*Haoze Liu,Run Liu,Haiying Xu,Jiahui Han,Siyuan Fang,Siyu Yan,Huiqi Deng,Guanchu Wang,Na Zou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit stable, model-specific behavioral profiles in situated scenarios, but these profiles shift across registers (first-person, advice-giving, task execution). Behavioral Mode Axes derived from thought traces provide cleaner control over these behavioral styles than response-derived axes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM personality studies rely on self-report questionnaires that are sensitive to surface elicitation choices and poorly grounded in concrete behavior. A behavioral-data framework is needed to study personality as measurable, situated behavioral patterns rather than abstract self-report traits.

Method: The authors construct 3,200 contrastive behavioral scenarios across 20 behavioral patterns and four prompt registers, grounded in psychometric facets (BFI-2, DOSPERT, HEXACO). They introduce Behavioral Mode Axes (BMAs) — activation-space directions from contrastive behavioral traces — and compare thought-derived versus response-derived BMAs for controlling behavioral styles.

Result: LLMs display stable, model-specific behavioral profiles with register-dependent shifts. Thought-derived BMAs more faithfully capture intended behavioral mechanisms and provide cleaner control over situated behavioral styles than response-derived BMAs, which are more prone to trait drift.

Conclusion: LLM personality-like tendencies are better understood as measurable and controllable behavioral modes grounded in concrete interaction contexts rather than as abstract self-report traits.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act in interactive settings where their behavioral styles affect user experience, safety, and downstream decision making. Existing LLM personality studies largely rely on self-report questionnaires administered in first-person settings, making the resulting profiles sensitive to surface elicitation choices and poorly grounded in concrete model behavior. In this work, we introduce a situated behavioral-data (B-data) framework for studying and controlling LLM behavioral personality. We construct 3,200 contrastive behavioral scenarios spanning 20 behavioral patterns and four prompt registers, grounded in validated psychometric facets such as BFI-2, DOSPERT, and HEXACO. Using this framework, we find that LLMs exhibit stable and model-specific behavioral profiles, while also revealing register-dependent shifts across first-person decisions, advice-giving, and task execution. We then show that these behavioral patterns can be controlled through Behavioral Mode Axes (BMAs), activation-space directions derived from contrastive behavioral traces. Compared with response-derived BMAs, which are more prone to trait drift, thought-derived BMAs more faithfully capture the intended behavioral mechanism and provide cleaner control over situated behavioral styles. Our results suggest that LLM personality-like tendencies are better understood not as abstract self-report traits, but as measurable and controllable behavioral modes grounded in concrete interaction contexts. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/lhz191/LLM-Behavioral-Personality.

</details>


### [219] [Fisher8: Stabilizing Neural Heteroscedastic Regression via Output-Layer Fisher Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10374)
*Sumedh Vemuganti,Nickvash Kani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training neural networks for joint mean-and-uncertainty prediction is unstable due to gradient steps misaligned with loss landscape geometry. The authors derive Fisher8, a Fisher-geometry-based output-layer gradient correction that stabilizes training with only a learning-rate hyperparameter, outperforming prior stabilizers across regression and representation-learning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural networks trained to jointly predict both mean and uncertainty estimates from noisy data suffer from training instability. Multiple independent stabilization methods have been proposed, but the authors argue these all point to a shared root cause: gradient updates are poorly aligned with the intrinsic geometry of the loss landscape (i.e., using Euclidean rather than Fisher geometry). A principled geometric solution is needed.

Method: The authors derive Fisher8, a closed-form gradient correction applied at the output layer. It reorients and rescales parameter updates according to Fisher information geometry rather than standard Euclidean gradient descent. The correction introduces no data-dependent hyperparameters beyond the learning rate and naturally admits an approximate KL-divergence trust radius between successive predictive distributions. The authors also show that components of prior stabilizers converge on overlapping elements of this single geometric correction.

Result: Across multidimensional regression and representation-learning benchmarks, Fisher8 achieves superior likelihood–error tradeoffs, produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, and learns rich, uncertainty-aware feature representations compared to existing stabilization methods.

Conclusion: Training instability in joint mean-and-uncertainty prediction stems from misalignment with Fisher geometry. Fisher8 provides a principled, hyperparameter-efficient geometric correction that unifies prior stabilization efforts and yields consistent improvements in predictive uncertainty quality and feature learning.

Abstract: Training neural networks to jointly predict mean and uncertainty estimates from noisy observations can be unstable, prompting a series of independent stabilization efforts. We argue that these interventions highlight a common underlying issue where gradient steps are poorly aligned with the geometry of the loss landscape. To better align updates with local curvature, we derive Fisher8, an output-layer gradient correction that reorients and rescales updates using Fisher geometry rather than Euclidean geometry. Unlike past stabilizers, Fisher8 introduces no data-dependent hyperparameters beyond learning rate and admits an approximate KL trust radius between successive predictive distributions. We show that prior stabilizers converge on overlapping components of this geometric correction. Across multidimensional regression and representation-learning tasks, Fisher8 obtains superior likelihood--error tradeoffs, predicts calibrated uncertainty estimates, and learns rich uncertainty-aware feature spaces.

</details>


### [220] [Generator-Guided Inverse Sampling for Lévy-Driven Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10384)
*Tianfu Qi,Jun Wang,Jun Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a structured reverse sampler for Lévy-driven generative models by decomposing dynamics into diffusion, small jump, and large jump components, and applies it to OFDM-SISO channel estimation under mixed Gaussian and impulsive noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional diffusion models cannot handle Lévy-driven dynamics because the reverse process is nonlocal due to infinite jump activities, making naive score-based reversal inadequate. The paper aims to characterize and operationalize the reverse-time generator for such processes.

Method: The authors analyze forward and reversed Markov generators to derive that the reversed jump component becomes a state-dependent Markov jump process governed by a nonlocal density ratio. They propose a structured reverse sampler decomposing dynamics into diffusion, small jump, and large jump components. For isotropic linear Lévy SDEs with symmetric α-stable jumps, a neural network amortizes only the large-jump rate, while jump amplitudes use analytically derived conditional distributions. Efficient implementation techniques avoid costly high-dimensional integration and sampling.

Result: Simulations demonstrate robust channel estimation performance under mixed Gaussian and impulsive noise in OFDM-SISO systems, with a favorable complexity-performance tradeoff.

Conclusion: Lévy-driven generative models can be practically reversed by decomposing the jump structure, enabling tractable sampling and effective application to robust channel estimation under impulsive noise.

Abstract: This paper studies inverse sampling for Lévy-driven generative models from the perspective of Markov generators. Unlike conventional diffusion models, Lévy-driven dynamics involve infinite jump activities, which makes their reverse process nonlocal and difficult to characterize using score information alone. We address this challenge by analyzing the forward and reversed generators.
