It is derived that the reversed jump component generally becomes a state-dependent Markov jump process governed by a nonlocal density ratio. This observation motivates a structured reverse sampler that decomposes the dynamics into diffusion, small jump, and large jump components. Based on this characterization, we develop a computationally tractable sampler for a class of isotropic linear Lévy SDEs with symmetric $α$-stable jump components. For the jump component, the neural network is used only to amortize the rate of large jump activities, while jump amplitudes are generated from analytically derived conditional distributions, which improves interpretability and controllability. Efficient implementation techniques are further introduced under this setting to avoid expensive high-dimensional integration and sampling. The sampler is further adapted to approximate observation-guided sampling and applied to OFDM-SISO channel estimation under mixed Gaussian and impulsive noise. Simulations show robust estimation performance with a favorable tradeoff between complexity and performance.

</details>


### [221] [Dreamer-SAC: Off-Policy Learning in Latent World Models for Sample-Efficient Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10386)
*Jiazhuo Li,Linjiang Cao,Qi Liu,Xi Xiong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dreamer-SAC integrates a recurrent world model with SAC in latent space, using short-horizon rollouts and n-step targets to achieve sample-efficient autonomous driving that outperforms DreamerV3, SAC, and PPO while revealing an inverted-U relationship between rollout horizon and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sample-efficient RL for autonomous driving faces a trade-off between data efficiency (requiring world models) and model bias (policy degradation from imperfect learned dynamics). Existing approaches either rely on costly real interactions or suffer from compounding prediction errors during long-horizon imagination.

Method: Dreamer-SAC combines: (1) a recurrent state-space world model for latent dynamics learning, (2) an off-policy SAC agent trained directly in latent space, (3) short-horizon generated trajectories blending real and imagined data, (4) n-step target estimation for value learning, and (5) multi-objective supervision covering driving efficiency and safety.

Result: Dreamer-SAC consistently outperforms DreamerV3, SAC, and PPO baselines in autonomous driving scenarios with substantially fewer real environment interactions. An inverted-U relationship between rollout horizon and policy performance was identified, with short horizons providing the optimal trade-off. N-step targets proved more effective than one-step TD targets for exploiting imagined experience.

Conclusion: The proposed Dreamer-SAC framework demonstrates that combining latent-space world models with off-policy actor-critic methods, short-horizon rollouts, and n-step estimation yields significant improvements in sample-efficient autonomous driving, highlighting the critical role of horizon length and target estimation in mitigating model bias while leveraging generated data.

Abstract: Sample-efficient reinforcement learning for autonomous driving is often limited by the trade-off between data efficiency and model bias. While world models reduce the reliance on costly environment interactions, policy optimization over learned dynamics remains sensitive to prediction errors. This paper proposes the Dreamer-SAC framework, which integrates a recurrent state-space world model with an off-policy soft actor-critic algorithm trained directly in latent space. The framework uses a combination of real interactions and short-horizon generated trajectories with n-step target estimation and multi-objective supervision. Evaluated in autonomous driving scenarios with objectives encompassing driving efficiency and safety, the proposed framework consistently outperforms representative reinforcement learning baselines, including DreamerV3, SAC, and PPO, while achieving improved performance with substantially fewer real environment interactions. Experiments reveal an inverted-U relationship between rollout horizon and policy performance, where short-horizon latent rollouts achieve the best trade-off between additional training signals and accumulated model bias. Furthermore, n-step target estimation demonstrates more effectiveness over one-step temporal-difference targets in exploiting predicted experience for value learning.

</details>


### [222] [Share First, Route What Remains: A Unified Framework for Token-Adaptive MoE Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10392)
*Gongli Zhang,Zhulin Liu,C. L. Philip Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UniF-MoE proposes a unified MoE framework based on the principle "share first, then route what remains." By decomposing experts into key-value channels, the authors observe that shared computation reduces residual expert demand, leading to a design that jointly optimizes shared blocks, content selection, and dynamic expert routing for improved efficiency and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MoE designs treat expert sharing, fine-grained computation, and dynamic routing as independent decisions, ignoring the fundamental dependency that extracting reusable computation alters both what remains and how much expert capacity is needed. This gap motivates a unified approach.

Method: UniF-MoE partitions each expert into aligned key-value channel blocks. A shared-demand score determines the number of shared blocks and pathway weights; key prototypes select shared content; complementary demand sets residual expert count via cumulative routing mass. A Gram regularizer separates and normalizes router embeddings to promote diverse routing directions, sparse overlap, and simple routing geometry.

Result: Experiments on DomainBed and GLUE demonstrate that UniF-MoE improves predictive performance over representative static and dynamic MoEs while reducing activated computation, inference latency, and memory.

Conclusion: The "share first, route what remains" principle effectively captures dependencies between shared and residual expert computation, and the unified UniF-MoE framework yields consistent gains in both accuracy and efficiency across benchmarks.

Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have recently moved beyond routing a fixed number of complete experts. Shared-expert designs preserve reusable knowledge, fine-grained methods vary computation within experts, and dynamic routers adapt the number of active experts. Yet these decisions are usually made independently, overlooking a basic dependency: extracting reusable computation changes both what remains and how much expert capacity the remainder needs. We study this dependency by decomposing sparsely upcycled feed-forward experts into key-value channels. Co-activated experts align at a subset of value positions; removing these positions changes expert preference; and greater shared coverage is associated with lower residual expert demand. These observations lead to one principle: share first, then route what remains. We instantiate it in UniF-MoE, a unified framework for token-adaptive MoE computation. Each expert is partitioned into aligned blocks. A shared-demand score sets the shared block count and pathway weight, key prototypes select the shared content, and the complementary demand determines the residual expert count through cumulative routing mass. A Gram regularizer separates and normalizes router embeddings, promoting diverse routing directions, sparse expert overlap, and a simple routing geometry. Experiments on DomainBed and GLUE show that this unified design improves predictive performance over representative static and dynamic MoEs while reducing activated computation, inference latency, and memory. Code is available at https://github.com/existence0420/UniF-MoE.

</details>


### [223] [ELVAE: Evidential Learning-Based Variational Autoencoder for Uncertainty-Aware Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10398)
*Ge Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ELVAE extends VAEs with an evidential normal-inverse-gamma posterior over latents, yielding explicit input-dependent uncertainty for each latent coordinate. This uncertainty can be used as a control variable during generation: low-uncertainty anchors produce more reliable samples, while high-uncertainty anchors enable stress testing. Experiments on MNIST confirm that learned latent-location uncertainty stratifies semantic reliability of generated digits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard VAEs conflate uncertainty about the latent location (epistemic) with variability around it (aleatoric). The authors aim to explicitly separate these, producing a learned latent-location uncertainty that can actively control generation quality — not merely be reported post-hoc. This enables both more reliable synthesis from confident anchors and deliberate exploitation of uncertain anchors for stress testing.

Method: ELVAE (Evidential Learning VAE) places an input-dependent normal-inverse-gamma (NIG) posterior over each latent coordinate. The NIG hierarchy naturally decomposes into a Gaussian for the latent mean and an inverse-gamma for the variance, yielding explicit location uncertainty. Training uses an exact evidence lower bound (ELBO). The authors show that direct regularization of the full hierarchical posterior is necessary — marginalizing out the uncertainty collapses the decomposition. Evaluation uses a frozen external classifier on MNIST to assess semantic reliability under uncertainty-stratified generation.

Result: Learned latent-location uncertainty clearly stratified semantic reliability of generated MNIST digits. A zero-displacement control experiment decomposed the effect: most of the reliability stratification stems from how consistently an anchor can be re-generated, with a smaller but distinct component from uncertainty-scaled perturbation. The effect holds only under within-class uncertainty ranking and varies in magnitude across random seeds.

Conclusion: The learned latent-location uncertainty serves as a practical control variable for uncertainty-aware generation, successfully separating anchor reliability from perturbation-induced failure. This supports ELVAE as a meaningful framework for producing controllable, uncertainty-informed generative models.

Abstract: Variational autoencoders generate samples from probabilistic latent representations but do not distinguish uncertainty about the latent location from variability around it. We formulate ELVAE, an evidential learning-based VAE in which each latent coordinate is governed by an input-dependent normal-inverse-gamma posterior. This hierarchy yields an explicit latent-location uncertainty that can be used during generation, not merely reported after inference: low-uncertainty anchors support more reliable synthetic samples, while high-uncertainty anchors can be deliberately exploited for stress testing. The objective is an exact evidence lower bound, and we show that direct regularization of the full hierarchy is required, since the marginalized latent law alone cannot identify the uncertainty decomposition. In an MNIST generation pilot with a frozen external classifier, this uncertainty clearly stratified the semantic reliability of generated digits. A zero-displacement control revealed that most of the effect reflects how reliably an anchor can be re-generated, while a smaller but distinct component is attributable to uncertainty-scaled perturbation itself. The effect holds only under within-class uncertainty ranking, and its magnitude varies across seeds. These findings support the learned latent-location uncertainty as a practical control variable for uncertainty-aware generation, separating anchor reliability from perturbation-induced failure.

</details>


### [224] [Do Judges Behave Like Algorithms?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10400)
*Riya Manchanda,Eric Chen,Chloe Zhu,Cynthia Rudin,Brandon Garrett,Songman Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether judges in Harris County misdemeanor bail hearings already behave algorithmically. Using ML models trained per judge, the authors find judges' decisions are generally predictable via small interpretable formulas, but significant inter-judge inconsistency exists, leading to unequal treatment of similar defendants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rather than debating whether algorithms *should* be used in judicial contexts, the authors flip the question: do judges already follow predictable, formula-like rules? If yes, judicial behavior may be more amenable to improvement through algorithmic tools. If judges instead rely on nuanced, individualized information invisible to court data, then understanding and improving standards-based decision-making becomes more difficult.

Method: The authors use court data from misdemeanor bail hearings in Harris County, Texas. They train machine learning models specific to each magistrate judge, compute variable importance metrics to identify which factors drive each judge's decisions, and analyze case outcomes to assess consistency — both within-judge (self-consistency) and between-judge (inter-judge agreement on similar cases).

Result: Judges generally behave algorithmically: their bail decisions can be captured by small, interpretable formulas based on discrete, static factors (e.g., criminal history, age, charge type). However, substantial inter-judge differences emerge in some cases, producing surprising inconsistency and unequal treatment across similarly situated defendants.

Conclusion: Identifying where algorithms fail to explain judicial decisions can improve the justice system by directing attention to cases where individualized standards — rather than rigid rules — better account for outcomes, ultimately highlighting areas of inconsistency and potential disparity.

Abstract: What if judges already behave like algorithms? As artificial intelligence and algorithms are deployed in many settings, including the judicial system, many have debated whether judges should be allowed to rely on them. Instead, we ask whether judges follow predictable, algorithmic-like rules already. If judges already follow consistent, formula-like rules based on discrete and static factors such as criminal history, age, and charge type, then judicial behavior may be improved. However, if judges rely on individualized information that cannot be identified through court data, then standards-based decision-making may be more challenging to understand or improve. This work explores these questions by studying judicial decision-making in misdemeanor bail hearings in Harris County, Texas. Using available court data, we investigate whether magistrate judges follow what resembles an algorithm; whether they consider the same variables in their decision-making; and whether they are consistent with themselves and with each other. To do this, we train machine learning models for each judge, measure variable importance metrics to determine important variables for each judge's decision-making, and analyze outcomes of similar cases for judges. Our results reveal that these judges generally behave algorithmically: their decisions can be captured by small, interpretable formulas. However, in some cases, judges differ substantially, leading to surprising inconsistency and unequal treatment across similar defendants. Identifying cases where algorithms do not explain judicial decision-making can improve the justice system by focusing attention on decisions where individualized standards, rather than rules, better explains outcomes.

</details>


### [225] [TideRL: Boosting Agentic RL Goodput with Readiness-Aware Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10402)
*Yanyu Ren,Xizheng Wang,Xiao Liu,Bowen Lv,Hanchen Zhang,Shudan Zhang,Hanyu Lai,Shuai Wang,Li Chen,Dan Li,Jie Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TideRL is an elastic RL system for multi-turn LLM agentic workloads that improves training goodput by up to 5.6× over synchronous and 33% over asynchronous baselines through three techniques: Continuous Task Batching, Resource-Aware Ref-Actor Pipelining, and Elastic Resource Scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL training for LLMs is shifting toward multi-turn agentic tasks where rollouts pause for external environments, resume with growing contexts, and finish at variable times. In this setting, GPU waiting and repeated prefill recomputation become pure overhead, making training goodput (throughput) more critical than raw GPU occupancy.

Method: TideRL introduces three complementary techniques: (1) Continuous Task Batching (CTB) preserves useful rollout state across pauses; (2) Resource-Aware Ref-Actor Pipelining (RA²P) dynamically selects between decoupled streaming and colocated aggregation based on ready backlog and arrival intervals; (3) Elastic Resource Scaling (ERS) moves ranks between rollout and training using readiness signals.

Result: Across text-only and multi-modal agentic workloads, TideRL achieves up to 5.6× training goodput improvement over synchronous baselines and over 33% over asynchronous baselines, with similar task performance. KV cache hit rate improves by 1.58×, per-step training time drops by up to 44.3%, and total waiting time is reduced by up to 77.6%.

Conclusion: TideRL demonstrates that readiness-aware scheduling, elastic resource allocation, and state-preserving batching can substantially improve RL training efficiency for multi-turn agentic LLM workloads without sacrificing task performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is moving toward multi-turn agentic workloads, where rollout tasks repeatedly pause for external environments, resume with growing contexts, and finish at highly variable times. In this setting, RL training goodput, measured by training throughput, matters more than raw GPU occupancy: GPU waiting and repeated prefill recomputation are pure overhead. We present TideRL, a readiness-aware elastic RL system with Continuous Task Batching, Resource-Aware Ref-Actor Pipelining, and Elastic Resource Scaling. CTB preserves useful rollout state, $\textrm{RA}^2\textrm{P}$ selects between decoupled streaming and colocated aggregation from the ready backlog and arrival interval, and ERS moves ranks between rollout and training using the same readiness signals. Across text-only and multi-modal agentic workloads, TideRL improves RL training goodput by up to 5.6$\times$ over synchronous baselines and over 33% over asynchronous baselines, while reaching similar task performance. It also improves KV cache hit rate by 1.58$\times$, reduces per-step training time by up to 44.3%, and cuts total waiting time by up to 77.6%.

</details>


### [226] [Actionable Hallucination Detection: Translating Latent Uncertainty into Agentic Critique](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10430)
*Sanidhya Vijayvargiya,Rahul Lokesh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The Latent Critic is a lightweight LoRA adapter that, during LLM generation, restructures the transformer's residual stream to amplify grounding signals and produce localized natural-language feedback. It detects and localizes agent hallucinations (e.g., ungrounded tool-call parameters) in real time with high accuracy (0.966 AUROC, >80% localization), and acts as a low-latency guardrail for self-correction in ReAct agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based AI agents frequently commit specification-grounding failures—executing hallucinated, undesired actions rather than expressing uncertainty. Existing detection methods either fail to localize hallucinations or impose prohibitive inference latency, making real-time, actionable correction infeasible.

Method: The authors introduce a low-rank adapter (LoRA) that runs concurrently with a frozen base LLM's autoregressive generation. It actively manipulates the transformer's residual stream to amplify latent grounding signals and convert them into localized, natural-language feedback within a single forward pass—eliminating secondary inference loops. Mechanistic analysis via activation patching and layer-wise probing reveals that this process restructures pre-existing uncertainty geometry into linearly separable representations that transfer robustly across contexts.

Result: Evaluated on tool-calling hallucinations across Qwen- and Llama-based models, the Latent Critic achieves 0.966 AUROC and >80% accuracy in localizing ungrounded elements (e.g., hallucinated dates). It significantly outperforms equivalent-scale fine-tuned external detectors, semantic entropy baselines, and passive internal probes. In a closed-loop ReAct setting, it provides negligible-latency interception of hallucinations before execution, enabling efficient agent self-correction.

Conclusion: Manipulating the latent space via a lightweight LoRA adapter yields reliable, real-time hallucination detection and localization without secondary inference costs. The approach's linear separability of restructured uncertainty representations transfers effectively, and its deployment as a guardrail in agentic systems prevents undesired actions while facilitating self-correction.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed as AI agents frequently exhibit user specification-grounding failures, executing hallucinated, undesired actions to force a resolution rather than expressing uncertainty. Existing detection methods fail to provide actionable, real-time correction as they either do not localize the hallucinations, or incur prohibitive inference latency. We introduce the Latent Critic, a lightweight low-rank adapter (LoRA) that operates concurrently with a frozen base LLM's generation to actively restructure the transformer's residual stream---amplifying latent grounding signals and translating them into localized, natural language feedback within a single sequence. By refining the base model's native uncertainty signals, this manipulation of the latent space enables reliable, granular detection without the overhead of secondary inference loops. Mechanistic analysis via activation patching and layer-wise probing shows that this rank-invariant behavior restructures pre-existing uncertainty geometry into a linearly separable representation that transfers more reliably than base model representations alone. Using tool-calling as an instantiation of granular hallucinations, we validate the detection and downstream improvements enabled by the Latent Critic architecture across Qwen and Llama-based models. Demonstrating superior real-time efficacy, our approach significantly outperforms equivalent-scale fine-tuned external detectors, semantic entropy baselines, and passive internal probes in isolating hallucinations, achieving 0.966 AUROC and >80% accuracy in localization (e.g., ungrounded: date). When deployed in a closed-loop ReAct environment, the Critic acts as a negligible latency guardrail, intercepting hallucinations before execution to prevent undesired actions while simultaneously leveraging this specific localized feedback to enable efficient agent self-correction.

</details>


### [227] [Do Time-Series Forecasters Use the Right History: Recoverability, Recovery, and Functional Use of Temporal Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10433)
*Qipeng Qian,Yuntao Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A good forecast with a correct delay report does not imply the model used the right historical inputs. The paper distinguishes delay recoverability, reporting, and actual usage, and shows through theory and experiments (N-HiTS, TCN) that models often functionally ignore their own reported delay even when forecast accuracy is near-oracle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecast accuracy alone cannot reveal which past inputs produced a prediction. This motivates a rigorous decomposition of three distinct questions: (1) can the true delay be recovered from data, (2) does the model report the correct delay, and (3) does the forecast actually use that reported history? The gap between reporting and actual usage is the central concern.

Method: The authors derive input-conditioned recoverability measures that separate intrinsic data ambiguity from model error. They prove theoretically that delay reports can become arbitrarily reliable while forecast risk approaches the oracle, even when the predictor uses the wrong lag. Empirically, they introduce a matched masking test to detect whether the reported history is functionally used, and apply it to N-HiTS and TCN models on a point-delay task. They also propose routing the prediction through the reported history and enforcing hard one-hot control to eliminate off-report bypass paths.

Result: On the point-delay task, among forecasts with correct delay reports and normalized excess risk within 10% of the oracle, the matched masking test reveals that the reported history is functionally unused in 55.4% of N-HiTS cases and 92.7% of TCN cases. Routing prediction through the reported history and applying hard one-hot control achieves exact fixed-report alignment.

Conclusion: Even a correct delay report combined with near-oracle forecast accuracy provides no guarantee that the model used the correct historical inputs. Explicit architectural constraints (routing + one-hot control) are necessary to enforce faithful delay usage.

Abstract: Forecast accuracy does not tell us which past inputs produced a prediction. We separate three questions for time-series models with known delay structure: can the true delay be recovered from the observed data, does the model report it, and does the forecast actually use the same history? We first derive input-conditioned recoverability measures that separate intrinsic ambiguity from model error. We then prove that a delay report can become arbitrarily reliable while forecast risk approaches the oracle even though the predictor still uses the wrong lag. This failure also appears in finite samples on the point-delay task: among forecasts with a correct delay report and normalized excess risk within 10\% of the oracle, the reported history is functionally unused under our matched masking test in 55.4\% of N-HiTS cases and 92.7\% of TCN cases. Finally, we show that routing the prediction through the reported history removes off-report bypass paths; a hard one-hot control achieves exact fixed-report alignment. The main conclusion is simple: a good forecast, even with a correct delay report, does not show that the model used the right history.

</details>


### [228] [A Joint-Distribution Route to Fair Representations with Continuous Sensitive Attributes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10470)
*Yijin Ni,Xiaoming Huo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes evaluating independence in fair representation learning via a single joint discrepancy between the joint distribution of representation and sensitive attribute and the product of their marginals, rather than averaging per-value conditional discrepancies. Using HSIC as an instance, it achieves better statistical efficiency (O(n⁻¹/²) vs O(n⁻²/⁵)) and comparable fairness-accuracy tradeoffs with faster training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fair representation learning methods enforce independence between representation Z and continuous sensitive attribute S by averaging per-value discrepancies between conditional law P_{Z|S=s} and marginal P_Z. This requires nonparametric estimation of conditional distributions at each sensitive value, which is statistically inefficient and computationally burdensome. The authors seek a more direct, sample-efficient approach.

Method: The authors propose measuring dependence via a joint discrepancy d(P_{Z,S}, P_Z ⊗ P_S) between the joint distribution and the product of marginals. They prove a disintegration identity showing that on decomposable witness classes, this joint discrepancy equals the conditional-integral functional used by EIPM and generalized demographic parity. They adopt the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) as a specific instance, which yields a closed-form O(n²) estimator converging at the O(n⁻¹/²) rate. They also prove equivalence between this HSIC-based approach and the conditional MMD integral up to an explicit spectral tail.

Result: The HSIC estimator converges at O(n⁻¹/²), substantially faster than the nonparametric O(n⁻²/⁵) rate of conditional-route estimators. The algorithmic implementation, FRHSIC, achieves fairness-accuracy tradeoffs comparable to conditional-route baselines while reducing per-epoch training time.

Conclusion: Fair independence can be enforced more efficiently through a joint discrepancy rather than conditional smoothing. The HSIC-based approach provides both statistical and computational advantages without sacrificing fairness-accuracy performance, making it a practical alternative for fair representation learning with continuous sensitive attributes.

Abstract: Fair representation learning with a continuous sensitive attribute $S$ requires a representation $Z$ that is statistically independent of $S$. Existing criteria, including generalized demographic parity, the expectation of integral probability metrics (EIPM), and mutual information, enforce this independence by averaging a per-value discrepancy between the conditional law $P_{Z \mid S=s}$ and the marginal $P_Z$ over the law of $S$. This approach requires a nonparametric surrogate for the conditional law at each sensitive value. We propose evaluating independence through a single joint discrepancy $d\left(P_{Z, S}, P_Z \otimes P_S\right)$ between the joint law and the product of its marginals. We establish a disintegration identity; on decomposable witness classes it equals the conditional-integral functional that EIPM and generalized demographic parity instantiate. By reaching the same target without the conditional law, this discrepancy can be estimated directly from samples via a dependence statistic rather than conditional smoothing. We take the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC) as an instance of the joint discrepancy $d$ to investigate the statistical efficiency of replacing the conditional formulation. The HSIC estimator is a closed-form $O\left(n^2\right)$ statistic that converges at the $O\left(n^{-1 / 2}\right)$ rate, in contrast to the nonparametric $O\left(n^{-2 / 5}\right)$ rate of the conditional-route estimators. We prove this instance is equivalent to the conditional maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) integral up to an explicit spectral tail. The corresponding algorithmic implementation, i.e., FRHSIC, attains fairness-accuracy tradeoffs comparable to conditional-route basel es while reducing per-epoch training time.

</details>


### [229] [Critic-Free Pretraining for Efficient Online Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10473)
*Daoyi Li,Yixian Zhang,Chao Yu,Wenbo Ding,Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Critic-Free Pretraining (CFP), a paradigm that discards offline-trained critics in O2O RL and instead initializes a fresh critic during online fine-tuning, preventing misaligned value estimates and improving performance across diverse tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In offline-to-online (O2O) reinforcement learning, reusing an offline-trained critic during online fine-tuning can be detrimental. As the policy and data distribution shift rapidly online, the inherited value estimates become misaligned with the new environment, causing inaccurate policy improvement and inefficient exploration.

Method: CFP completely abandons offline critic training. Instead, the critic is freshly initialized at the start of online fine-tuning, while only the offline-pretrained policy (actor) is retained. This allows the critic to adapt without inheriting biased estimates from the offline phase. CFP is designed as a plug-and-play paradigm compatible with various mainstream O2O algorithms.

Result: CFP consistently matches or improves upon conventional O2O algorithms across a diverse set of tasks, with particularly pronounced gains on several challenging tasks.

Conclusion: Abandoning the offline-trained critic in favor of a fresh initialization is an effective and broadly compatible strategy for O2O RL, addressing a key failure mode caused by value estimate misalignment during the offline-to-online transition.

Abstract: Offline-to-online (O2O) reinforcement learning aims to leverage policies pretrained on static datasets while improving them through online interaction. However, directly reusing an offline-trained critic can hinder online fine-tuning: as the policy and data distribution change rapidly, value estimates inherited from offline training may become misaligned with the online environment, leading to inaccurate policy improvement and inefficient exploration. To address this problem, we introduce \textbf{C}ritic-\textbf{F}ree \textbf{P}retraining: an efficient paradigm that completely abandons the approach of offline critic training, allowing a freshly initialized critic to adapt without inheriting biased estimates. CFP is compatible with various mainstream O2O algorithms and consistently matches or improves upon conventional O2O algorithms across a diverse set of tasks, with particularly pronounced gains on several challenging tasks.

</details>


### [230] [Exploration-Driven Personalized Federated Reinforcement Learning via Intrinsic Motivation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10499)
*Md Rafid Islam,Rafsan Jany,Zahid Hasan,Ratun Rahman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EDPFRL-IM introduces an exploration-driven personalized federated reinforcement learning framework that uses intrinsic motivation (Random Network Distillation) at each client to promote local exploration in sparse-reward environments, while the server coordinates exploration via global priors and minimal novelty summaries—all without accessing raw client data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PFRL methods rely heavily on extrinsic reward signals, neglecting exploration in non-stationary or sparse-reward environments. This limits policy discovery in challenging settings where rewards are delayed or absent.

Method: The framework (EDPFRL-IM) combines: (1) curiosity-driven exploration at each client via intrinsic motivation, specifically adding an intrinsic Random Network Distillation (RND) signal to the extrinsic reward; (2) a privacy-preserving server that sends global exploration priors and collects only minimal novelty summaries (not raw experiences or gradients) from clients to enable diverse yet coordinated exploration.

Result: Experiments in benchmark environments demonstrate that EDPFRL-IM outperforms average PFRL baselines in both policy personalization and sample efficiency, particularly in delayed and sparse reward systems.

Conclusion: EDPFRL-IM successfully integrates a flexible exploratory learning structure into federated reinforcement learning while preserving client privacy, offering a practical solution for personalized policy learning in challenging reward environments.

Abstract: Personalized Federated Reinforcement Learning (PFRL) takes a decentralized approach to storing and accessing information based on past experiences while keeping each client's data private during the learning of each client's policy. Many current methods for PFRL rely heavily on exploiting existing reinforcement learning reward signals to derive an optimal policy for each client, thereby neglecting exploration in non-stationary or sparse-reward environments. In this work, we introduce a new exploration-driven framework, Exploration-Driven Personalized Federated Reinforcement Learning via Intrinsic Motivation (EDPFRL-IM), that leverages an inherent curiosity-driven exploration at each client to promote local exploration and protect client privacy. Furthermore, to facilitate policy discovery via exploration in previously unexplored state spaces, clients add an intrinsic random network distillation (RND) signal to their extrinsic reward. Additionally, the server does not have access to clients' raw experiences or local gradient estimates; instead, the server sends global exploration priors and collects minimal novelty summaries from each client to enable both diverse and coordinated exploration among clients. Experiments in benchmark environments show that our framework outperforms average PFRL benchmarks in policy personalization and sample efficiency, primarily in delayed and sparse reward systems. Overall, EDPFRL-IM enables the integration of a flexible exploratory learning structure into federated reinforcement learning systems while preserving client privacy.

</details>


### [231] [Coordinating the Unknown Lipschitz Constant in Multiplayer Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10526)
*Ricardo Parada,Chenzhang Zhao,William Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies cooperative multi-agent bandits with continuous (Lipschitz) action spaces and unknown Lipschitz constant, designing algorithms for three information structures and proving regret guarantees that show agreement on discretization is achieved either freely (via common rewards or observed actions) or at no leading-order cost (via dithered quantization).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decentralized multi-agent applications (e.g., federated learning, distributed sensor networks) require agents to cooperate without communication. In continuous action spaces with unknown smoothness (Lipschitz constant), agents face the challenge of discretizing the action space consistently from only local data, as mismatched discretizations degrade cooperative learning.

Method: The authors consider three information structures: (A) unobserved actions with common rewards, (B) observed actions with independent rewards, and (C) unobserved actions with independent rewards. For each, they design an algorithm that estimates the unknown Lipschitz constant, chooses a discretization of the joint action space, and applies a cooperative bandit method. The key technical challenge—achieving identical discretizations without communication—is solved using: (1) common rewards naturally synchronizing estimates in case A, (2) observed actions enabling agreement in case B, and (3) dithered quantization of the Lipschitz estimate in case C to probabilistically align discretization choices.

Result: Regret bounds are proved for all three settings. Common rewards (A) and observable actions (B) each provide discretization agreement "for free." In the hardest case (C), dithered quantization achieves agreement without increasing the leading-order regret term, meaning coordination is bought at negligible asymptotic cost.

Conclusion: Cooperative multi-agent Lipschitz bandits are feasible without communication even when both actions and rewards are private. The regret guarantees match the leading-order dependence of the centralized or easier decentralized cases, demonstrating that dithered quantization is an effective tool for achieving implicit coordination in decentralized learning.

Abstract: Motivated by decentralized applications, we study cooperative multi-agent bandits in continuous (Lipschitz) action spaces when the Lipschitz constant is unknown. We consider three information structures: (A)~unobserved actions with common rewards, (B)~observed actions with independent rewards, and (C)~unobserved actions with independent rewards. In each case we design and analyze an algorithm that estimates the Lipschitz constant, chooses a discretization of the joint action space, and applies a cooperative bandit method to the induced discrete problem. Players never communicate once learning starts, so the central difficulty is that they must reach the \emph{same} discretization from their own data. We prove regret guarantees showing that common rewards and observable actions each supply this agreement for free, and that in their absence agreement can still be bought, through a dithered quantization of the estimate, at no cost in the leading order of the regret.

</details>


### [232] [Robust Multi-Agent Bandits with Heavy-Tailed Rewards and Information Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10529)
*Daphne Feng,Ricardo Parada,Lily Jiang,Sophia Yi,William Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies multi-agent multi-armed bandits with heavy-tailed rewards under three distinct information-asymmetry regimes. The authors develop robust decentralized algorithms for each setting and prove regret bounds that nearly match centralized heavy-tailed rates, with experiments on Pareto-distributed rewards validating the theoretical results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classic multi-armed bandit literature focuses on sub-Gaussian reward assumptions, but real-world sequential decision-making problems (e.g., finance, network routing, online advertising) frequently exhibit heavy-tailed reward distributions. Furthermore, many practical scenarios involve multiple decentralized agents with asymmetric access to information — some agents observe others' actions while others do not. Bridging the gap between heavy-tailed rewards and decentralized multi-agent coordination under varying information structures motivates this work.

Method: The authors design robust decentralized algorithms tailored to three information-asymmetry regimes: (1) unobserved actions with common rewards, (2) observed actions with independent rewards, and (3) unobserved actions with independent rewards. The algorithms incorporate robust estimators (e.g., truncated mean or median-of-means) to handle heavy-tailed noise, combined with carefully designed communication/synchronization protocols that balance exploration-exploitation across agents while accounting for each regime's informational constraints. Regret analysis is conducted for each algorithm.

Result: The proposed algorithms achieve regret guarantees that nearly match the lower bounds of centralized heavy-tailed bandit settings, despite operating in decentralized and information-asymmetric environments. Experiments using Pareto-distributed rewards confirm the theoretical findings and reveal practical trade-offs among synchronization overhead, coordination efficiency, and exploration effectiveness across the three regimes.

Conclusion: Decentralized multi-agent bandit learning under heavy-tailed rewards is feasible and can approach centralized performance, provided algorithms are appropriately designed for the specific information-asymmetry structure. The three regimes exhibit distinct trade-offs: action observability improves coordination but may require more communication, while common rewards enable implicit collaboration even without action visibility.

Abstract: The multi-armed bandit problem is a central framework in sequential decision-making, extensively studied under sub-Gaussian reward assumptions. However, real-world applications often involve heavy-tailed reward distributions and decentralized, information-asymmetric interactions. We study multi-agent multi-armed bandits with heavy-tailed rewards under three information-asymmetry regimes: unobserved actions with common rewards, observed actions with independent rewards, and unobserved actions with independent rewards. We develop robust decentralized algorithms for each setting and derive regret guarantees that nearly match centralized heavy-tailed rates. Experiments on a Pareto-distributed reward environment validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the trade-offs between synchronization, coordination, and exploration across the three regimes.

</details>


### [233] [Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction for Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10553)
*Sangjin Jin,Kangmin Kim,Junhyeong Lee,Yongjae Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RCCP combines retrieval of similar past residuals with a scalar conformal correction to produce locally calibrated prediction intervals for time series. Retrieval provides local evidence, while conformal correction ensures coverage guarantees. The method achieves target coverage, lowest Winkler scores, and scales efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard conformal prediction is inefficient for time series because forecast errors are temporally dependent and non-stationary. Existing methods that use recent, weighted, or localized residuals for local calibration often dilute the most relevant evidence through broad weighting or extra adaptation steps, making calibration indirect.

Method: RCCP retrieves similar past one-sided residuals as local evidence, constructs an asymmetric prediction interval from them, and then applies a scalar conformal correction to the normalized retrieval error to achieve the desired coverage. The method is retrieval-augmented calibration.

Result: Across standard benchmarks and backbone forecasters, RCCP attains target coverage in every setting, achieves the lowest Winkler scores with fewer severe misses, and maintains low calibration and inference overhead.

Conclusion: Retrieval-corrected calibration is an effective, scalable approach to uncertainty quantification in time series forecasting, combining the strengths of local evidence retrieval and conformal correction.

Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free prediction intervals for fixed forecasters, but its standard calibration procedure is often inefficient for time series data, where forecast errors are temporally dependent and change across time and operating conditions. Recent time series CP methods improve local calibration using recent, weighted, or localized residuals. Yet local calibration can remain indirect, since broad residual weighting or additional adaptation procedures may dilute the evidence most relevant to the current prediction. This motivates a simple retrieval and correction strategy that selects similar past residuals as local evidence and then corrects the coverage error left by retrieval. In this paper, we propose Retrieval--Corrected Conformal Prediction (RCCP), a retrieval-augmented calibration method for time series prediction intervals. RCCP builds an asymmetric interval from retrieved one-sided residuals and calibrates its normalized retrieval error with a scalar conformal correction. Thus, retrieval provides local residual evidence, while conformal correction determines the final scale needed for coverage. We provide a coverage-gap bound based on the stability of the normalized retrieval error distribution. Across standard benchmarks and backbone forecasters, RCCP attains the target coverage in every setting and achieves the lowest Winkler scores, with fewer severe misses. RCCP also achieves low calibration and inference overhead, showing that retrieval-corrected calibration is an effective and scalable approach to uncertainty quantification in time series forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/jinsaaang/rccp.

</details>


### [234] [MARCO: Click-Intent Decomposition for Calibrated Ads Conversion Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10562)
*Shiwen Shen,Xiru Huang,Liang Luo,Jianbo Sun,He Lyu,Zihang Fu,Ivonne Xu,Zhizhuo Li,Zhengyu Zhang,Pei-Ju Sung,Yunmiao Wang,Zixuan Wang,Zhengli Zhao,Qiang Jin,Mike Jermann,Mingda Li,Yang Xiao,Bhavana Challa,Brooke Bian,Yang Li,Ashish Chamoli,Bibek Bhusal,Danning Di,Yuan Jin,Meet Raval,Zhiwen Chen,Boyao Sun,Shuguang Wang,Yunlong He,Yantao Yao,Sagar Chordia,Wenlin Chen,Santanu Kolay,Qin Huang,Ellie Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MARCO decomposes ad clicks by intent to correct systematic over/under-prediction in post-click conversion rate models. Using free behavioral labels (click types), it trains per-intent CVR heads and composes estimates at serving time, yielding +2.80% conversions per click and +0.98% topline gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard industrial ad ranking treats all clicks identically when modeling post-click conversion rate (CVR), but different click types exhibit up to a 4× difference in actual conversion rates. This conflation causes systematic bias: high-intent clicks are under-predicted and low-intent clicks are over-predicted, masked by deceptively good aggregate calibration. The authors aim to resolve this hidden miscalibration.

Method: MARCO uses logged click type as a free behavioral label to train separate per-intent CVR prediction heads, each on a homogeneous sub-population. At serving time, it predicts a distribution over intents and composes per-intent CVR estimates accordingly. Theoretical analysis proves decomposition never raises population risk and quantifies headroom under squared loss. For multi-impression, multi-click scenarios, the framework casts attribution as a credit-assignment problem with a bias-variance tradeoff analogous to RL return estimation, adopting last-impression, first-click attribution with three end-to-end consistency conditions for production.

Result: At binary intent granularity, MARCO achieves near-perfect per-intent calibration (~100%), lifts conversions per click by +2.80%, and delivers +0.98% cumulative improvement in topline business metrics. Both offline and online validation confirm gains stem from finite-capacity estimation and calibration effects.

Conclusion: Click intent decomposition rectifies a pervasive yet hidden bias in CVR estimation. By leveraging freely available behavioral signals, MARCO improves both fairness of prediction across intent classes and overall ranking performance at scale, with principled theoretical grounding and practical attribution mechanisms suitable for production deployment.

Abstract: Not all clicks are equal. Industrial ads ranking decouples conversion probability into click-through rate (CTR) and post-click conversion rate (CVR), yet treats every click as the same event. In reality, users provide a free, self-generated signal of intent through their physical UI interactions. Different click types on the same ad exhibit a 4-fold difference in actual conversion rates. By conflating these signals, the standard CVR model under-predicts high-intent clicks and over-predicts low-intent ones, which is a bias masked by near-perfect aggregate calibration. We propose MARCO (Multi-intent Ads Ranking Composition Optimization), a framework that resolves this bias by decomposing each click by intent. Using the logged click type as a free behavioral label, MARCO trains per-intent CVR heads on homogeneous populations, and at serving time composes their per-intent CVR estimates under a predicted distribution over intents. Theoretically, we prove that decomposition never raises population risk, give the exact headroom under squared loss and non-negativity under the deployed loss, and show through a routing-efficiency dial how much of it reaches serving. Because the population-optimal score is unchanged, any gain is a finite-capacity estimation and calibration effect that we validated both offline and online. For deployment at scale, we further cast multi-impression, multi-click attribution as credit assignment with a bias-variance tradeoff analogous to RL return estimation, showing last-impression, first-click attribution is the low-bias, low-variance, deterministic choice under production constraints, and derive three consistency conditions enforced end-to-end at scale. Deployed at binary intent granularity, MARCO corrects per-intent calibration to approximately 100%, lifts conversions per click by +2.80%, and drives +0.98% cumulative improvement in topline metrics.

</details>


### [235] [BREAD: Baseline-Referenced Explanations for Anomaly Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10587)
*Jiaqi Qiu,Rob Goedhart,Jannis Kurtz,Inez M. Zwetsloot*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a scalable, baseline-referenced diagnosis method for AI-based prospective anomaly detection that uses both anomalous observations and normal baseline information. It provides mathematical guarantees of higher faithfulness than LIME under mean-shift anomalies, validated through simulations and a real-world case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-based prospective anomaly detection methods (e.g., AI-SPM) lack general-purpose diagnosis tools to identify which features cause detected anomalies. Existing model-agnostic XAI methods like LIME suffer from scalability issues and assign relevance to noise features, reducing diagnostic accuracy. A method that integrates baseline normal behavior is needed.

Method: The authors propose a scalable, baseline-referenced diagnosis method that leverages both the anomalous observation and normal baseline information. They provide mathematical guarantees demonstrating superior faithfulness in identifying causal features under a mean-shift anomaly setting compared to LIME. The approach is model-agnostic.

Result: Simulation studies and a real-world case study show the proposed method generates more faithful and accurate diagnosis results than existing approaches, with mathematical guarantees of higher faithfulness under mean-shift anomaly conditions.

Conclusion: The proposed baseline-referenced method addresses key limitations of existing XAI-based diagnosis for anomaly detection—namely scalability and noise sensitivity—and offers a theoretically grounded, practically effective solution for identifying features responsible for anomalies in high-dimensional, nonlinear settings.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based prospective anomaly detection methods are increasingly deployed in high-dimensional and nonlinear settings. Among these approaches, AI-based statistical process monitoring (SPM) is widely used, providing a structured framework for prospective monitoring. Once an anomaly is detected, a diagnosis method is needed to identify the features driving the flagged observation away from normal behaviour. Traditional SPM diagnosis methods are typically designed for specific detection models and cannot be directly applied to AI-based methods. Model-agnostic explainable AI (XAI) offers a general framework for feature relevance explanation. However, existing methods suffer from scalability limitations or assign relevance to noise features, reducing diagnosis accuracy. We propose a scalable, baseline-referenced diagnosis method that uses both the anomalous observation and normal baseline information. We provide mathematical guarantees that under a mean-shift anomaly setting, the proposed method achieves higher faithfulness in detecting the features causing the anomaly compared to LIME. Simulation studies and a real-world case study validate the effectiveness of the proposed method and show that it generates more faithful and accurate diagnosis results for AI-based prospective anomaly detection methods.

</details>


### [236] [$β$-VAEs as Effective Theories: Tolerance-Dependent Dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10599)
*Johannes Hirn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In nonlinear VAEs, increasing β regularization still acts as a spectral cutoff that collapses low-utility latent dimensions in order of their reconstruction utility, matching the known PCA-governed behavior of linear VAEs. However, nonlinearities broaden collapse transitions, creating a head–tail tradeoff between concentrated utility and tail fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether the clean correspondence between β-VAE regularization strength and spectral cutoff known from linear Gaussian VAEs — where latent coordinate collapse order exactly follows PCA utility ranking — persists in fully connected nonlinear VAEs. The goal is to understand how nonlinearity affects the effective-description logic of β-VAEs.

Method: Train fully connected nonlinear VAEs on the WorldClim dataset with varying β regularization strengths. Analyze latent coordinate collapse behavior, comparing collapse thresholds against reconstruction utility rankings, and derive effective-dimension curves to characterize the utility distribution across latent ranks.

Result: Nonlinear interactions shift and broaden the collapse onsets, so individual thresholds no longer exactly coincide with utility values. However, the common ordering between collapse sequence and utility ranking is preserved over resolved ranks. Effective-dimension curves reveal a head–tail tradeoff: stronger regularization (larger β) concentrates utility into the first few latent coordinates at the cost of degraded tail fidelity.

Conclusion: The spectral-cutoff interpretation of β-VAE regularization survives nonlinearity in terms of ordinal structure (collapse order matches utility order), even though exact threshold alignment breaks. The head–tail tradeoff provides a practical framework for understanding how β controls the effective latent dimensionality and fidelity distribution.

Abstract: In a $β$-VAE, increasing the regularization strength acts as a spectral cutoff by collapsing low-utility latent coordinates.
  In the linear Gaussian VAE, the collapse order matches the ranking of reconstruction utilities exactly, because both are set by the PCA spectrum. We ask which parts of this picture survive in fully connected nonlinear VAEs trained on WorldClim.
  We find that nonlinear interactions shift and broaden collapse onsets, so thresholds no longer coincide exactly with utilities. However, the common ordering is preserved over the resolved ranks, so the spectral cutoff still acts as a utility cutoff and the effective-description logic carries through.
  The resulting effective-dimension curves reveal a head--tail tradeoff: increasing depth concentrates utility into the first few coordinates but worsens tail fidelity.

</details>


### [237] [Compute-Optimal Is Not Cluster-Optimal: Systems-Aware Scaling for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10605)
*Soumajyoti Sarkar,Yuxin Tang,Sheng Zha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MOSAIC formalizes architecture-systems co-design as an optimization problem. Using sparse MoE language models, it shows optimal sparsity only emerges under hardware constraints, not from scaling laws alone. This argues for unified co-design rather than sequential architecture-then-systems optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In large-scale pretraining, architecture selection (via scaling laws) and systems optimization are done separately, leading to suboptimal decisions. The authors hypothesize that optimal model architecture depends on hardware constraints, and that coupling these stages yields better frontier models.

Method: MOSAIC combines a predictive scaling law with a calibrated performance model capturing MFU, communication cost, memory footprint, and optimal parallel layout. Applied to sparse MoE models, it sweeps scaling dimensions including sparsity factor (fraction of parameters inactive per token). The scaling law spans 104M–2.7B active parameters and up to 79B total parameters.

Result: Under a pure model-FLOPs budget, no interior optimal sparsity exists — loss decreases monotonically with sparser models, pushing the optimum to the sparsity upper bound. However, when cluster systems constraints are incorporated via MOSAIC, an interior optimal sparsity emerges.

Conclusion: Optimal MoE architecture is inherently tied to hardware constraints. A unified architecture-systems co-design approach is necessary for frontier language model training, challenging the conventional two-stage paradigm.

Abstract: In large-scale pretraining, the algorithm, architecture, and systems decisions are conventionally made in disconnected stages. A scaling law stage selects an architecture and training recipe, optimizing loss under compute constraints, and a separate systems stage then optimizes the implementation for hardware efficiency. In this work, we develop MOSAIC, which formulates model architecture and systems co-design as an optimization problem. MOSAIC couples a predictive scaling law with a calibrated performance model that estimates Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU), communication cost, memory footprint, and the best parallel layout. We instantiate the framework for sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models, where expert count, routing sparsity, and other MoE layer dimensions affect both the loss and systems efficiency. We fit a scaling law on sparse MoE models trained on text data, whose scaling dimensions include the sparsity factor, which is the fraction of model parameters inactive per token in a forward pass. The scaling law sweeps in our work span active parameters from $104$ million to $2.7$ billion and total model sizes reaching $79$ billion parameters. We show that, within the calibrated sparsity range, an efficiency-agnostic model-FLOPs budget admits no interior optimal sparsity. The fitted loss decreases monotonically with sparser models and the compute optimum lies at the upper boundary of the data support. An optimal sparsity in MoE models instead emerges under the cluster's systems constraints, as captured by MOSAIC. Our results argue for a shift towards unified architecture and systems co-design for frontier language model training.

</details>


### [238] [Pair-Centric Graph Rewiring for Over-Squashing via Optimal Transport-Guided Communication Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10619)
*Yan Wang,Chuan-Xian Ren*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PairAlign is a pair-centric graph rewiring framework that addresses over-squashing in MPNNs by explicitly quantifying the mismatch between communication demand and topological support for node pairs, then using Optimal Transport to allocate rewiring budget effectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MPNNs suffer from over-squashing when long-range information must be compressed through bottlenecks. Existing rewiring methods use edge-level or graph-level heuristics but fail to explicitly identify which specific node pairs most need structural support, especially under a limited rewiring budget.

Method: PairAlign introduces a demand-support shortage score: the ratio of original-graph structural demand to current-graph finite-hop propagation support. This score serves as a computable proxy for Jacobian-based over-squashing measures with pair-level interpretability. The framework accounts for a two-sided edge insertion effect (creating useful walks vs. diluting transition mass) and optimizes shortage to select beneficial additions. It then employs an Optimal Transport-guided allocation mechanism to coordinate the finite edge budget, matching candidate edges to shortage targets for broader and more effective coverage than greedy-local assignment.

Result: Experiments on standard graph benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvement across multiple message-passing backbones, validating that pair-level repair is an effective strategy for mitigating over-squashing.

Conclusion: Pair-level rewiring guided by demand-support shortage and Optimal Transport allocation provides a principled and effective approach to alleviating over-squashing, outperforming existing edge-level and graph-level rewiring strategies across diverse MPNN architectures.

Abstract: Message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) often struggle when task-relevant information is distributed across distant regions of a graph, since local propagation must compress remote signals through limited structural interfaces. Graph rewiring provides a structural response to over-squashing. Most existing methods rely on edge-level bottleneck scores or graph-level connectivity surrogates. With a limited rewiring budget, the key question is which pairwise communications most need structural support. This paper proposes PairAlign, a pair-centric graph rewiring framework that makes this question explicit through demand-support shortage. Specifically, PairAlign combines original-graph structural demand with current-graph finite-hop propagation support; their ratio highlights interactions whose communication demand is poorly supported by topology, and our theory shows that this score provides a computable proxy for the corresponding Jacobian-based shortage with a pair-level interpretation of over-squashing. Our theory reveals a two-sided effect of edge insertion: a new edge can create useful walks and simultaneously dilute existing normalized transition mass. Guided by this observation, PairAlign optimizes shortage to favor edge additions that alleviate over-squashing. Beyond selecting useful additions, PairAlign further introduces an Optimal Transport-guided rewiring mechanism to coordinate the finite edge budget for pair-level structural compatibility and shortage-target coverage. It formulates communication alignment between the candidate edge budget and the shortage targets, and the theory shows that this allocation covers shortage targets more broadly and effectively than a greedy-local assignment. Experiments on standard graph benchmarks show PairAlign's improvement across message-passing backbones, validating pair-level repair as an effective route for alleviating over-squashing.

</details>


### [239] [ProbGuard: Calibrated Safety Risk Estimation from LLM Output Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10621)
*Xinzhe Huang,Biwu Yao,Kedong Xiu,Mengnan Zhao,Di Wang,Puning Zhao,Tianhang Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProbGuard is a probabilistic, architecture-agnostic guardrail that leverages early LLM output distribution signals to estimate and calibrate safety probability, enabling early stopping of unsafe generations and achieving state-of-the-art calibration and jailbreak defense with minimal decoding steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM guardrails treat safety assessment as deterministic classification, which overlooks two issues: (1) safety assessment is inherently uncertain, especially early in generation; (2) discrete token classification discards rich probabilistic information in the LLM's output distribution. These limitations motivate a probabilistic approach that exploits distributional signals for early, calibrated safety estimation.

Method: ProbGuard formulates safety risk as the unsafe probability of continued generation dynamics given an LLM's generated prefix distribution. It estimates this risk via Monte-Carlo sampling of future trajectories. The model is post-trained on distributional signals with calibrated safety risk, operating in a fully probabilistic, architecture-agnostic manner.

Result: ProbGuard achieves the best calibration across all nine model–dataset combinations, reducing average Brier score by 79.6% and ECE by 71.9% over the best baseline. It also limits the attack success rate to at most 1% across six representative jailbreak attacks using only the first ten decoding steps of early output distributions.

Conclusion: ProbGuard demonstrates that probabilistic modeling of LLM output distributions enables highly calibrated, early-stage safety detection, significantly outperforming deterministic guardrails in both calibration quality and robustness against jailbreak attacks.

Abstract: Recent research on Large Language Model (LLM) safety has widely adopted guardrails to identify unsafe LLM outputs. Existing guardrails typically formulate safety assessment as a deterministic classification task, mapping a discrete token sequence to a discrete safety label. However, this paradigm has two limitations: First, safety assessment is inherently an uncertain problem, particularly during the early generation state. Second, relying solely on discrete token sequences discards the rich probabilistic information embedded in the LLM output distribution. To address these limitations, we propose the first completely probabilistic architecture-agnostic guardrail \textsc{ProbGuard} to leverage the LLM early output distributional signals for estimating and calibrating the safety probability, thereby enabling early stopping of unsafe ongoing outputs. Specifically, given an LLM's generated prefix distribution, we formulate the safety risk as the unsafe probability of its continued generation dynamics and estimate this risk by Monte-Carlo sampling. Through post-training on the distributional signals and calibrated safety risk, \textsc{ProbGuard} achieves the best calibration performance across all nine model--dataset combination settings, reducing the average Brier score and ECE by 79.6\% and 71.9\%, respectively, over the best baseline. \textsc{ProbGuard} further limits the attack success rate to at most 1\% across six representative jailbreak attacks after observing the LLM early output distributions from only the first ten decoding steps.

</details>


### [240] [IADD-TR: Intervention-Aware Dynamics Decoupling with Targeted Regularization for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10634)
*Zefeng Liang,Jie Qiao,Ruichu Cai,Weilin Chen,Zhifeng Hao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IADD-TR is a model-based RL framework that decouples transition dynamics into action-intervention and action-free evolution stages (IADD) and uses a targeted regularization loss derived from efficient influence functions for doubly robust policy-gradient estimation (TR), achieving improved sample efficiency on MuJoCo tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MBRL methods treat the transition model and critic as monolithic predictors, ignoring policy-induced data bias. This causes action to become entangled with environmental evolution, and uneven action coverage distorts counterfactual value estimates, hindering policy improvement.

Method: The authors propose IADD-TR, a unified framework with two components: (1) IADD factorizes transitions into an action-intervention stage and an action-free natural evolution stage using a zero-action anchor for robust generalization, with latent and state-aligned components identifiable up to invertible within-block transformations and pointwise, respectively. (2) TR derives a critic correction from the efficient influence function of a replay-state policy-gradient functional, augmenting the critic with action-density-scaled residual correction and optimizing a targeted loss for doubly robust policy-gradient estimation.

Result: Extensive experiments on five MuJoCo tasks demonstrate that IADD-TR achieves competitive returns with improved sample efficiency.

Conclusion: IADD-TR effectively addresses policy-induced data bias in MBRL by decoupling dynamics and employing targeted regularization, leading to more robust and sample-efficient policy learning.

Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), which learns environment dynamics to generate synthetic experience, is a promising approach to sample-efficient decision making. Numerous methods have been developed to improve dynamics prediction and policy optimization for MBRL through uncertainty estimation, model regularization, and conservative value learning. However, these methods typically treat the transition model and critic as monolithic predictors, overlooking the policy-induced data bias. Consequently, action can become entangled with environmental evolution, while uneven action coverage may distort the counterfactual value estimates used for policy improvement. To address this, we propose IADD-TR, a unified framework combining Intervention-Aware Dynamics Decoupling (IADD) and Targeted Regularization (TR). IADD factorizes transitions into an action-intervention stage and an action-free natural evolution stage, using a zero-action anchor to resolve the non-uniqueness of this two-stage factorization for robust generalization. Its latent and state-aligned components are identifiable up to an invertible within-block transformation and pointwise, respectively. For policy learning, we derive TR from the efficient influence function of a replay-state policy-gradient functional. TR augments the critic with an action-density-scaled residual correction and optimizes a targeted loss, yielding doubly robust policy-gradient estimation when either the critic or the replay action density is consistently specified. Extensive experiments on five MuJoCo tasks show that IADD-TR achieves competitive returns with improved sample efficiency.

</details>


### [241] [Optimize Cheap, Deploy Strong: Cost-Aware Cross-Tier Transfer for Evolutionary Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10694)
*Tal Oved,Roi Pony,Oshri Naparstek,Udi barzelay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes decoupling the three LLM roles in evolutionary prompt optimization (answering, reflection/variation, and deployment), placing the high-volume answering role on the cheapest tier while reserving stronger models for rare reflection/variation operations. This cross-tier approach achieves 5.6-54x search cost reduction with over 96% of tokens on cheap tiers, while matching or exceeding same-tier optimization quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evolutionary optimization of LLM prompts and agentic programs is bottlenecked by fitness evaluation costs, where each candidate must be scored by running an LLM over a validation set. The evaluator's pricing tier dominates total search cost, making it prohibitively expensive when strong models are used. The authors seek to reduce this cost without sacrificing optimization quality.

Method: The method restructures evolutionary search by decoupling the three roles an LLM plays: (1) the answering role (high-volume fitness evaluation) runs on the cheapest tier; (2) the reflection/variation operator (rarely invoked) uses a strong model; (3) the final evolved prompt is deployed on a stronger target model via upward cross-tier transfer. The approach characterizes when cheap-tier search can substitute for target-tier search and identifies failure modes.

Result: Across four tasks (HotpotQA, IFBench, LiveBench-Math, HoVer) and eleven models spanning four model families, the method matches or exceeds same-tier optimization quality. Over 96% of search tokens are placed on the cheapest tier, yielding 5.6-14x lower search cost overall, rising to 25-54x savings when reasoning-tier models emit long chain-of-thought tokens on every fitness evaluation call.

Conclusion: Decoupling LLM roles in evolutionary prompt optimization enables dramatic cost reduction without quality degradation. Cheap-tier search effectively substitutes for target-tier search in most cases, with clear characterization of where it succeeds and fails. Upward cross-tier transfer allows cheaply evolved prompts to be deployed on stronger models, making large-scale prompt optimization economically practical.

Abstract: Evolutionary optimization of LLM prompts and agentic programs (e.g., GEPA) is dominated by fitness evaluation: scoring each candidate runs an answering LLM over a validation set, so the evaluator's price tier dictates total search cost. We restructure that search by decoupling the three roles an LLM plays, running the high-volume answering role on the cheapest tier, reserving a strong model for the rare reflection/variation operator, then exploiting upward cross-tier transfer to deploy the cheaply evolved prompt on a stronger target. We contribute a cost-controlled characterization of when cheap-tier search substitutes for target-tier search, and where it fails. Across four tasks (HotpotQA, IFBench, LiveBench-Math, HoVer) and eleven models in four model families, the resulting prompt matches or exceeds same-tier optimization while placing over 96% of search tokens on the cheapest tier, at 5.6-14x lower search cost, rising to 25-54x where reasoning tiers emit long chains of thought on every fitness call.

</details>


### [242] [ProTAGAD: A Foundation Model for TAG Anomaly Detection with Decoupled Topological and Textual Prototypes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10699)
*Ziyan Wang,Liwen Wu,Cheng Xie,Song Gao,Zhenli He,Xin Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses the Blurred-Anomaly-Boundary (BAB) issue in Text-Attributed Graph (TAG) anomaly detection, caused by deep cross-modality coupling of topology and text in GNNs. The authors propose a foundation model with decoupled topological and textual prototype banks to independently model structural normality and semantic consistency, achieving SOTA cross-domain performance on 14 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GNN-based anomaly detectors use holistic message-passing that indiscriminately fuses topological structure and textual semantics, causing deep cross-modality coupling. This entanglement amplifies noise, obscures subtle anomalous signals, and produces the Blurred-Anomaly-Boundary (BAB) issue — where normal and anomalous decision boundaries become poorly separable. The problem is exacerbated for graph foundation models requiring cross-domain generalization.

Method: The authors propose a foundation model for TAG anomaly detection that decouples topological and textual representations. It constructs dual prototype banks: one modeling structural normality (topological prototypes) and another modeling semantic consistency (textual prototypes). These independent representations effectively isolate anomaly cues that are otherwise diluted during conventional coupled aggregation in message-passing GNNs.

Result: Extensive experiments on 14 diverse benchmark datasets show the proposed method consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain settings. Ablation studies corroborate the prevalence of the BAB issue in conventional coupled TAG anomaly detectors and demonstrate that the decoupled prototype design effectively mitigates this challenge.

Conclusion: Decoupling topological and textual representations via dual prototype banks effectively resolves the BAB issue in TAG anomaly detection, enabling robust cross-domain generalization. The work establishes a new foundation model paradigm for TAG anomaly detection.

Abstract: Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs), endowed with abundant textual content along with topological structures, have emerged as a versatile backbone for real-world anomaly detection spanning large language model security, social network moderation, and cyber threat identification. Unlike conventional Graph Anomaly Detection (GAD), which relies primarily on structural irregularities, TAG anomaly detection must jointly leverage both topological patterns and fine-grained textual semantics to capture nuanced anomalous behaviors. The current GNN-based anomaly detectors adopt holistic message-passing schemes that indiscriminately fuse structural proximity and textual semantics during propagation, leading to deep cross-modality coupling. This entanglement acts as a noise amplifier, obscuring subtle anomalous signals and directly giving rise to the Blurred-Anomaly-Boundary (BAB) issue by rendering normal-anomalous decision boundaries poorly separable. This challenge is further amplified for graph foundation models that require robust cross-domain generalization. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel foundation model for TAG anomaly detection featuring decoupled topological and textual prototypes. Our framework constructs dual prototype banks to independently model structural normality and semantic consistency, effectively isolating anomaly cues that are otherwise diluted during coupled aggregation. Extensive experiments across 14 diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain settings.
