Motivation: Existing probabilistic forecasting methods face a trade-off: parametric methods like MVE sacrifice point accuracy under joint NLL training, while flexible generative models (Normalizing Flows, Diffusion Models) require costly Monte Carlo sampling and may produce suboptimal means. A method is needed that achieves both distributional flexibility and accurate mean prediction.

Method: TORF uses two stages: (1) a pre-trained deterministic model produces an accurate mean forecast; (2) a Restricted Normalizing Flow composed of strictly odd functions models the residual distribution centered on that mean. The oddness constraint guarantees the flow preserves the first-stage mean exactly, eliminating the need for Monte Carlo sampling to estimate the mean.

Result: TORF achieves state-of-the-art deterministic accuracy (measured by NMAE) and strong density estimation performance (measured by CRPS) on both short- and long-horizon forecasting tasks.

Conclusion: Decoupling mean forecasting from uncertainty estimation via odd residual flows effectively resolves the accuracy-flexibility trade-off in probabilistic forecasting, delivering top performance in both point and distributional metrics without sampling overhead.

Abstract: Probabilistic forecasting plays an essential role in risk-sensitive decision-making, particularly in long-horizon settings. However, existing approaches often face a fundamental trade-off between distributional flexibility and accurate mean prediction. Traditional parametric methods, such as Mean Variance Estimation (MVE), can suffer from degraded point accuracy when trained under joint Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) objectives, while modern-flexible generative models, including Normalizing Flows and Diffusion Models, typically rely on costly Monte Carlo sampling and may yield suboptimal mean estimates. To address this limitation, we propose Two-stage Odd Residual Flows (TORF), a framework that decouples mean forecasting from uncertainty estimation. In the first stage, a pre-trained deterministic model is used to produce an accurate mean prediction. In the second stage, a Restricted Normalizing Flow, with strictly odd functions learns flexible residual distributions around the point forecast, guaranteeing mean preservation from the first stage without sampling. Experiments show that TORF achieves state-of-the-art deterministic accuracy (NMAE) while providing strong density estimation performance (CRPS) on short and long-horizon forecasting.

</details>


### [266] [A Recommendation System Approach for Interference-Robust Sensor Subset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11143)
*Kaan Buyukkalayci,Kyle Pak,Merve Karakas,Christina Fragouli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Two-Tower MLP architecture using frequency-band acoustic features outperforms RSSI-based methods by ~20% for recommending optimal sensor subsets in vehicle tracking, while maintaining low computational cost for real-time selective sensing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RSSI-based sensor subset selection for tracking is computationally efficient but suffers from acoustic interference. There is a need for a robust, low-overhead alternative that maintains real-time performance.

Method: A recommendation-system-inspired framework using a Two-Tower Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture that scores candidate sensor subsets based on frequency-band acoustic features, replacing RSSI measurements.

Result: The proposed method achieves approximately 20% improvement in tracking accuracy over the RSSI baseline on outdoor vehicle-tracking deployments, while preserving the low computational overhead necessary for real-time operation.

Conclusion: Leveraging frequency-band acoustic features with a Two-Tower MLP architecture provides a more interference-robust and accurate solution for sensor-subset recommendation, enabling effective real-time selective sensing for tracking applications.

Abstract: This paper develops a method for sensor-subset selection for tracking. Prior work showed that low-cost acoustic Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements can be used to recommend subsets of sensor nodes whose expensive sensing modalities, such as cameras, can achieve high tracking accuracy. While efficient, RSSI-based approaches are challenged by acoustic interference. We propose a recommendation-system-inspired framework that instead leverages frequency-band acoustic features and a Two-Tower Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture to efficiently score candidate sensor subsets. Experimental results on outdoor vehicle-tracking deployments show that the proposed method can improve accuracy by around 20\% over the RSSI baseline while maintaining the low computational overhead required for real-time selective sensing.

</details>


### [267] [DACRI: Decision-Aware Causal Intervention Ranking for Critical Supply Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11154)
*Shiqi Huang,Jiani He,Dingyan Shang,Yihua Xu,Jize Li,Yan Lyu,Lashimi Muraleedharan Nair*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces CriticalSCM-Bench v1, a synthetic benchmark with causal ground truth for evaluating supply-chain disruption interventions. LambdaMART improves net value by 5.7–16.2% over a static baseline in two of three domains but underperforms a simple constant-buffer policy in digital infrastructure, demonstrating that algorithmic complexity is not uniformly beneficial. Partial-information and stress-test analyses further characterize when adaptive ranking adds value.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches conflate disruption detection/attribution with intervention selection, yet the optimal recovery action depends on net-value maximization rather than merely identifying disruptions. There is a lack of controlled benchmarks with causal ground truth, factual/counterfactual rollouts, and explicit value objectives to rigorously compare intervention policies across supply-chain regimes.

Method: The authors construct CriticalSCM-Bench v1, a synthetic benchmark spanning three supply-chain archetypes (semiconductor, critical materials, digital infrastructure) with known causal structure and paired factual/counterfactual trajectories. They evaluate LambdaMART — a learning-to-rank model — against a full-information train-selected static benchmark and a domain-informed constant-buffer policy under full, partial, and delayed information conditions. Stress tests probe intervention fidelity, timing, cost, held-out disruptions, and out-of-distribution generalization. A guarded explanation study validates decision preservation under deterministic validation and template fallback.

Result: LambdaMART achieves a median normalized net-value improvement of 5.7–16.2% (paired, statistically supported) for semiconductor and critical-material archetypes but not for digital infrastructure, where a constant-buffer policy dominates. Under partial/delayed information, LambdaMART retains 33–75% of full-clamp value. Stress tests reveal that policy ordering is sensitive to intervention fidelity, timing, cost, and disruption type; critical materials exhibit the weakest out-of-distribution retention. The explanation study preserves all fixed intervention decisions across 540 generations despite wording instability.

Conclusion: The paper delineates clear regimes where adaptive ranking via LambdaMART yields net-value gains and where simpler structural policies (e.g., constant-buffer) remain preferable. Greater model complexity is not uniformly justified across supply-chain domains. The benchmark enables rigorous, causally grounded comparison of intervention policies, and the findings caution against one-size-fits-all deployment of learning-based methods in supply-chain disruption management.

Abstract: Detecting or attributing a supply-chain disruption is not the same as selecting the intervention that maximizes recoverable net value. We present CriticalSCM-Bench v1, a controlled synthetic benchmark with causal ground truth, paired factual/counterfactual rollouts, and an explicit net-value objective. Relative to a full-information train-selected static benchmark, LambdaMART improves median normalized net value by 5.7--16.2\%, with paired statistical support on the semiconductor and critical-material archetypes but not on digital infrastructure. On digital infrastructure, a domain-informed constant-buffer policy remains stronger, showing that greater model complexity is not uniformly justified. Across partial and delayed settings, LambdaMART retains 33--75\% of full-clamp value. Stress tests further show that intervention fidelity, timing, cost, and held-out disruptions can alter policy ordering. Critical materials show the weakest out-of-distribution retention. Separately, a guarded explanation study over 540 generations preserves every fixed intervention decision after deterministic validation and template fallback, although exact wording remains unstable. Within this controlled setting, the results identify regimes in which adaptive ranking adds value and those in which simpler structural policies remain preferable.

</details>


### [268] [The Gaussian-Multinoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machine: A Potts Model Extension of the GRBM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11635)
*Nikhil Kapasi,Mohamed Elfouly,William Whitehead,Luke Theogarajan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The GM-RBM replaces binary hidden units in Gaussian-Bernoulli RBMs with categorical (Potts) units, creating a richer discrete latent space. Evaluated under capacity-matched and parameter-matched setups, it achieves competitive or improved recall on analogical and structured memory tasks at comparable training cost, using only Gibbs sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many real-world tasks (associative memory, symbolic reasoning) require discrete, structured representations that standard continuous latent models and even binary-latent RBMs struggle to express. The authors aim to provide a richer latent state space using multivalued categorical units while maintaining tractability and avoiding state collapse.

Method: The GM-RBM extends the GB-RBM by replacing binary hidden units with q-state categorical (Potts) units. Training uses contrastive divergence with temperature annealing and intra-slot diversity constraints to prevent state collapse. Evaluation is performed under both capacity-matched and parameter-matched setups against GB-RBM baselines on analogical recall and structured memory benchmarks.

Result: GM-RBM achieves competitive, and in several regimes improved, recall compared to GB-RBM at equal capacity with comparable training cost, using only Gibbs updates. The categorical formulation is also amenable to efficient implementation.

Conclusion: Categorical hidden units offer a simple, scalable alternative to binary latents for discrete inference in tractable RBMs, particularly when multivalued concepts benefit from richer per-unit representations.

Abstract: Many real-world tasks, from associative memory to symbolic reasoning, benefit from discrete, structured representations that standard continuous latent models can struggle to express. We introduce the Gaussian-Multinoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machine (GM-RBM), a generative energy-based model that extends the Gaussian-Bernoulli RBM (GB-RBM) by replacing binary hidden units with q-state categorical (Potts) units, yielding a richer latent state space for multivalued concepts. We provide a self-contained derivation of the energy, conditional distributions, and learning rules, and detail practical training choices (contrastive divergence with temperature annealing and intra-slot diversity constraints) that avoid state collapse. To separate architectural effects from sheer latent capacity, we evaluate under both capacity-matched and parameter-matched setups, comparing GM-RBM with GB-RBM configured to have the same number of possible latent assignments. On analogical recall and structured memory benchmarks, GM-RBM achieves competitive, and in several regimes improved, recall at equal capacity with comparable training cost, despite using only Gibbs updates. The discrete q-ary formulation is also amenable to efficient implementation. These results clarify when categorical hidden units provide a simple, scalable alternative to binary latents for discrete inference within tractable RBMs.

</details>


### [269] [Hierarchical Empirical-Bayes Naive Bayes: Minimax Smoothing and Calibration with AODE Extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11162)
*Nguyen Thai Anh,Truong Viet Vu,Tran Thien Thanh,Vo Nguyen Quoc Bao,Ngo Hoang Tu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HEB-NB introduces a data-adaptive hierarchical empirical Bayes smoothing for Naive Bayes, replacing fixed smoothing rules. It learns Dirichlet prior concentration via Type-II maximum likelihood, enabling information sharing across classes. The method yields closed-form inference, extends to AODE, and provides theoretical guarantees including a finite-sample strict separation from Laplace smoothing. Empirically, it achieves superior probabilistic accuracy and calibration across 31 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard NB smoothing rules (Laplace, Lidstone, KT, m-estimate) use fixed smoothing strength that ignores feature cardinality, sample size, and class imbalance. This causes non-vanishing bias on modern high-cardinality tabular data, degrading probabilistic predictions and calibration.

Method: HEB-NB places a Dirichlet prior on class-feature conditional probabilities and learns the concentration parameter via Type-II maximum likelihood (empirical Bayes). This enables hierarchical information sharing across classes. The method retains closed-form inference. The approach is extended to HEB-AODE for structural relaxations of NB. Theoretical analysis provides non-asymptotic ℓ₁ error bounds, a Laplace-tight lower bound, plug-in excess Bayes-risk bounds via total-variation tensorization, and a population top-1 ECE corollary.

Result: HEB-NB achieves best average Friedman rank on probabilistic metrics across 31 UCI/OpenML benchmarks, with up to 22.1% log-loss reduction on high-cardinality datasets. HEB-AODE consistently improves over vanilla AODE. With mutual-information weighting, top-1 ECE is reduced by 41%–70%. Theoretically, HEB-NB matches the empirical-distribution minimax rate plus a vanishing data-adaptive bias, with strict finite-sample separation from Laplace smoothing.

Conclusion: Adaptive empirical-Bayes smoothing substantially outperforms fixed smoothing rules for NB on high-cardinality tabular data, both theoretically and empirically. The approach generalizes to structural relaxations like AODE and combines effectively with mutual-information weighting for calibration gains.

Abstract: The Naive Bayes (NB) classifier remains a standard choice for categorical data, yet its widely used smoothing rules, such as Laplace, Lidstone, Krichevsky-Trofimov, and the $m$-estimate, all prescribe a fixed smoothing strength that ignores feature cardinality, sample size, and class imbalance, inducing a non-vanishing bias on modern high-cardinality tabular data. We propose hierarchical empirical-Bayes Naive Bayes (HEB-NB), in which each class-feature conditional probability is smoothed by a Dirichlet prior whose concentration is learned data-adaptively via Type-II maximum likelihood, enabling principled information sharing across classes while retaining closed-form inference. We further introduce HEB average one-dependence estimators (HEB-AODE), showing that the adaptive smoothing transfers cleanly to structural relaxations of NB. Theoretically, we establish a non-asymptotic $\ell_1$ error bound for HEB-NB matching the empirical-distribution minimax rate plus a vanishing data-adaptive bias, together with a matching Laplace-tight lower bound that yields a finite-sample, risk-level strict separation from Laplace. We further derive a plug-in excess Bayes-risk bound via total-variation tensorization and a population top-1 expected calibration error (ECE) corollary. Empirically, across 31 UCI and OpenML benchmarks, HEB-NB attains the best average Friedman rank on probabilistic metrics, with up to 22.1% log-loss reductions on high-cardinality datasets and consistent improvements of HEB-AODE over vanilla AODE. Combining HEB-NB with mutual-information weighting reduces top-1 ECE by 41%-70%, demonstrating substantial gains in probabilistic accuracy and calibration.

</details>


### [270] [Beyond a Bag of Features: Set-Level Instability in Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11197)
*Nikolai Bolik,Lennart Stöpler,Artur Andrzejak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges recent claims about LLM representations aligning with human concepts by analyzing SAE latent activations. The authors find that SAE active sets fail to recover human category boundaries or typicality better than dense embeddings, instead tracking model-internal similarity. They demonstrate a substantial mismatch between human conceptual-change judgments and SAE set changes, arguing that SAE features do not exhibit simple bag-of-features semantics outside idealized settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Shani et al. (2026) claimed LLM dense representations broadly recover human category boundaries but miss fine-grained typicality. This paper questions whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) latent sets — a more interpretable, transparent similarity measure — might better capture human conceptual structure, and more broadly tests whether SAE features compose via simple set-level semantics.

Method: The authors first validate that SAE latent-set overlap is a meaningful similarity measure using controlled toy models (testing union-like composition) and natural text (testing semantic neighborhood coherence). They then extend the human-concepts analysis from Shani et al. to SAE set similarities, comparing SAE activation sets against dense embeddings and residual-stream states on category boundary recovery and typicality. Finally, they probe the gap via controlled semantic modifications, measuring alignment between human judgments of conceptual change and changes in SAE active latent sets.

Result: SAE latent-set overlap recovers compositional structure in toy models and induces coherent neighborhoods in natural text, validating the measure. However, SAE activation sets do not outperform dense embeddings or residual-stream states at recovering human category boundaries or within-category typicality; they instead reflect model-internal similarity. Controlled semantic modifications reveal a substantial mismatch between human conceptual-change judgments and SAE active-set changes, indicating that SAE features do not compose via simple bag-of-features semantics outside idealized settings.

Conclusion: SAE latent activations, despite their interpretability advantages, do not close the gap between model representations and human conceptual structure. The failure of bag-of-features semantics in realistic contexts suggests that SAE-based interpretability methods require more sophisticated compositional models to align with human conceptual judgments.

Abstract: Shani et al. (2026) show that LLM representations broadly recover human category boundaries, while failing to reflect fine-grained typicality structure. Their analysis uses cosine similarity over dense model representations. We revisit their approach using overlap over active sparse autoencoder (SAE) latent sets as a more interpretable similarity measure. We first verify that this set-level measure is meaningful: SAE latent sets can recover union-like compositional structure in controlled toy models and induce semantically coherent neighborhoods in natural text. Extending the human-concepts analysis to SAE set similarities, we find that SAE activation sets do not recover human category boundaries or within-category typicality more faithfully than dense embeddings or residual-stream states, but instead track model-internal similarity structure. To probe this gap further, we study active latent sets under well-controlled semantic modifications, revealing a substantial mismatch between human judgements of conceptual change and change in the SAE active set. We interpret this as evidence that, outside idealised settings, SAE features do not compose via simple bag-of-features semantics.

</details>


<div id='cs.MA'></div>

# cs.MA [[Back]](#toc)

### [271] [Beyond Cash Flows: A Multi-Agent AI Framework for Valuing Clinical-Stage, Cross-Border Biotechnology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10175)
*Yuhan Fang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper proposes a specialized multi-agent framework for clinical-stage biotech investment, addressing the failure of traditional cash-flow-based valuation. It features a science-to-valuation layer, cross-market coordination, and a conflict-fusion mechanism. The architecture is grounded in a manually executed strategy that yielded 127.17% vs. 50.67% benchmark over 16 months.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based multi-agent investment systems assume companies can be valued via traditional discounted cash flows. This assumption collapses for clinical-stage biotech, where enterprise value hinges on binary scientific/regulatory milestones (e.g., FDA approvals, trial results), not cash flows.

Method: The framework comprises three layers: (1) a valuation layer that maps qualitative scientific judgment onto defensible valuations for pre-revenue assets; (2) a cross-market coordination layer that reconciles pricing discrepancies across international trading venues simultaneously; and (3) a conflict-fusion mechanism that systematically arbitrates between bullish scientific conviction and cautious regulatory constraints. The architecture encodes a method previously executed manually by the author as portfolio manager of China's first cross-border biotech fund.

Result: No AI implementation is evaluated. The paper cites the author's prior manual execution of the encoded method, which returned 127.17% against a 50.67% benchmark over sixteen months, as evidence for the validity of the underlying method rather than for any AI system.

Conclusion: The paper establishes foundational architectural design principles for extending agentic investment systems into complex, event-driven asset classes like clinical-stage biotech, where current multi-agent frameworks perform poorly due to their cash-flow-centric paradigm.

Abstract: A new class of software systems is transforming investment analysis. Large language model agents assembled into collaborative team structures including analysts, researchers, and risk managers are increasingly deployed across financial markets. Yet current multi-agent frameworks share a critical limitation: they rely on the foundational assumption that companies can be valued through traditional cash flows. This paradigm fails in clinical-stage biotechnology, where enterprise value depends entirely on binary scientific and regulatory milestones. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a specialized multi-agent framework. Its valuation layer translates qualitative scientific judgment into defensible valuations for pre-revenue assets; its cross-market coordination layer reconciles pricing across international venues simultaneously; and its conflict-fusion mechanism systematically arbitrates between bullish scientific conviction and cautious regulatory constraints in a domain-specific manner. Crucially, the architecture is not a speculative design: it encodes a method the author first executed by hand as sole portfolio manager of China's first dedicated cross-border biotechnology fund, a human practice that returned 127.17% against a 50.67% benchmark within sixteen months. That record is evidence for the underlying method rather than for any AI system; no implementation is evaluated here. This paper presents the framework at the architectural level, establishing foundational design principles for extending agentic investment systems into complex, event-driven asset classes they currently serve poorly.

</details>


### [272] [The Deliberative Deficit: An Empirical Critique of LLMs in Democratic Discourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10186)
*Maurice Flechtner*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: LLM groups show procedural discourse quality comparable to humans on pluralistic reasoning tasks, but fail to replicate human convergence dynamics, exhibit low perspective diversity, and cannot yet be treated as autonomous deliberative agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM benchmarks focus on verifiable tasks (math, coding), but real-world deployments increasingly require collective reasoning on pluralistic, value-laden problems with no objectively correct answer. The authors argue that neither verifiable-task benchmarks nor procedural evaluations of discourse quality suffice to assess LLM reasoning on such problems.

Method: The authors apply the Deliberative Reason Index (DRI)—a political science measure validated in citizen assemblies—to evaluate group-level reasoning. They synthesize evidence from 1,980 five-agent LLM runs across 12 citizen-assembly topics and 11 frontier model configurations, comparing LLM deliberation against human baselines on procedural quality, intersubjective consistency, perspective diversity, and convergence dynamics.

Result: LLM groups match human procedural discourse quality. However, gains in intersubjective consistency are small, topic-dependent, and limited to tractable rather than ethically contested questions. LLM groups show roughly one-third the perspective diversity of human assemblies. Critically, LLMs reverse the human convergence pattern: human deliberation decreases dispersion as views synthesize, whereas LLM deliberation increases it. Persona-prompted diversity does not restore the human dynamic and instead inverts which component of deliberative reasoning gets updated.

Conclusion: LLMs can serve as tools to support human reasoning on pluralistic problems, but current evidence does not support treating them as autonomous deliberative agents.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed in settings that require collective reasoning on complex, value-laden problems. Confidence in these deployments rests largely on benchmarks for verifiable tasks (mathematics, coding, coordination games), yet many of these applications concern problems where no objectively correct answer exists and where decision quality instead depends on integrating pluralistic perspectives to find mutually acceptable solutions. We argue that LLM reasoning capacity on this class of problems cannot be fully inferred from verifiable-task benchmarks, and that procedural evaluations of LLM discourse (respectfulness, justification, engagement) are systematically insufficient. We apply the Deliberative Reason Index (DRI), a measure developed in political science and validated across citizen assemblies, as a tool for evaluating reliable group-level reasoning on pluralistic, non-verifiable problems. Synthesizing recent evidence across 1,980 five-agent LLM runs on 12 citizen-assembly topics across 11 frontier model configurations, we find that LLM groups produce discourse with procedural quality comparable to human deliberation, while gains in intersubjective consistency are small, topic-dependent, and concentrated on tractable rather than ethically contested questions. LLM groups exhibit roughly one-third the perspective diversity of human assemblies and reverse the human convergence pattern: human deliberation decreases dispersion as diverse views synthesise, whereas LLM deliberation increases it. Engineering diversity through persona prompting does not restore the human dynamic but inverts which component of deliberative reasoning is updated. Our conclusion is constraining rather than prohibitive: LLMs can function as tools supporting human reasoning on pluralistic problems, but current evidence does not license treating them as autonomous deliberative agents.

</details>


### [273] [Not a Monolith: Lab-Level Divergence in the Cooperative Equilibria of Chinese Frontier LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10262)
*Francisco León Zúñiga Bolívar*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Four Chinese frontier LLMs (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM) were tested in an Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with a fixed code-converter to isolate strategic disposition. Within-ecosystem variation in aggression exceeded the East-West gap; the four labs are not monolithic. Cooperative bias generalized partially, and the lab—not the national ecosystem—is the relevant unit of analysis for cooperative alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work documented a cooperative bias in Western frontier LLM agents but left two open questions: (1) whether this bias extends to Chinese models from a different alignment lineage, and (2) whether Chinese models should be analyzed as a monolithic bloc or as distinct laboratories. The authors also aimed to remove a methodological confound where models convert their own strategies into code, conflating strategic reasoning with coding proficiency.

Method: Four Chinese frontier models (DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen3-Max, Kimi K2.5, GLM-5.1) were tested in an evolutionary Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma framework. A fixed lightweight converter (GPT-5.4 Mini) was used across all models to isolate generation capability from coding ability. The protocol included all-play-all tournaments and a Moran process with n=500 runs per condition, spanning three prompt styles and four population regimes. Two pre-registered hypotheses (H5, H6) were evaluated with pairwise comparisons corrected via Holm-Bonferroni.

Result: H6 (non-monolithic): supported. Aggressive-equilibrium proportion (P_A) ranged from 1% (Qwen3-Max) to 9% (DeepSeek V4 Pro), with four of six pairwise comparisons significant. Within-ecosystem spread (8pp) exceeded the East-West ecosystem mean difference (both 5.0%). H5 (cooperative-bias generality): consistent but qualified. A cooperative plurality held in 6/12 lab-prompt combinations versus 9/12 for Western models, but this rose to 9/12 under an alternate converter, so no firm difference is claimed.

Conclusion: The lab, not the ecosystem, is the unit at which cooperative disposition is set. Treating "Chinese models" as a monolith is unsupported. Within-ecosystem variation exceeds the East-West gap, meaning alignment lineage does not determine cooperative behavior in a uniform way.

Abstract: Does the cooperative bias documented for Western frontier LLM agents extend to a different alignment lineage, and should the Chinese models that embody it be treated as a single bloc or as distinct laboratories? We study four frontier-tier Chinese models - DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen3-Max, Kimi K2.5 and GLM-5.1 - in an evolutionary Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, under a design that removes a confound present in prior work. Rather than letting each model convert its own natural-language strategies into code, which entangles strategic disposition with coding ability, we hold the converter fixed (GPT-5.4 Mini) across all labs, so every cross-lab comparison is a comparison of generation alone. We run the full protocol: all-play-all tournaments and a Moran process at n=500 runs per condition, across three prompt styles and four population regimes. Two pre-registered hypotheses are evaluated. H6 (not monolithic) is supported: the four labs differ significantly in aggressive-equilibrium proportion, P_A running from 1% for Qwen3-Max to 9% for DeepSeek V4 Pro, with four of six pairwise comparisons surviving Holm-Bonferroni. The spread across the four labs (P_A range 8pp) is larger than the difference between the Chinese and Western ecosystems' mean P_A (5.0% vs 5.0%): on this measure, within-ecosystem variation exceeds the East-West gap. H5 (cooperative-bias generality) is consistent but qualified: a cooperative plurality holds in 6 of 12 lab-prompt combinations against the 9 of 12 reported for Western models, a difference we do not treat as firm, since the count rests on Cooperative-Neutral near-ties and rises to 9/12 under an alternate converter in our pre-registered robustness check. The lab, not the ecosystem, is the unit at which cooperative disposition is set; treating "Chinese models" as a monolith is not supported by the evidence.

</details>


### [274] [ASCon: A Direction-Aware Reciprocal Agent--Step Contextualization Model for Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10646)
*Shuyu Jiang,Yue Ran,Kaiyu Xu,Xingshu Chen,Yi Zhang,Hao Ren,Rui Tang,Tianwei Zhang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: ASCon proposes a unified graph-based model that jointly contextualizes agent and step representations using shared trajectory evidence, enabling multiple failure attribution tasks (faulty agent, faulty step, failure mode) with lightweight task-specific heads, achieving substantial gains over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing failure attribution methods for LLM-based multi-agent systems treat each attribution target (agents, steps, failure modes) in isolation with dedicated models, ignoring the shared diagnostic evidence (task constraints, roles, histories, interactions) and evidential dependencies among these targets. This fragmentation motivates a unified model that leverages common trajectory evidence.

Method: ASCon is a direction-aware reciprocal Agent-Step Contextualization model. It employs three key mechanisms: (1) direction-aware graph attention to model execution context from MAS trajectories, (2) masked step-to-agent attention to build behavior-aware agent representations, and (3) agent-conditioned step contextualization to inject agent context back into step representations. Lightweight target-specific prediction heads are then applied to the resulting contextualized representations for each attribution target.

Result: ASCon improves faulty-agent detection by 5.83%+ in micro-accuracy, faulty-step detection by 10.63%+ in micro-accuracy, and failure-mode detection by 14.73%+ in Macro-F1. It also substantially enhances LLM-based methods' attribution capabilities in out-of-domain scenarios.

Conclusion: Unifying agent and step representations through reciprocal contextualization over shared trajectory evidence is an effective paradigm for multi-target failure attribution in LLM-based MAS, outperforming both dedicated models and LLM-based baselines, especially in generalization to out-of-domain settings.

Abstract: Failure attribution in LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) aims to answer who caused failures, when they occurred, and why by identifying responsible targets including faulty agents, erroneous steps, and failure modes. Existing methods have primarily focused on developing dedicated models for specific attribution targets, with limited attention to the evidential dependencies among them. Despite these attribution targets are different, they rely on common diagnostic evidence from MAS trajectories, including task constraints, agent roles, behavioral histories and inter-agent interactions. This commonality motivates us to develop a unified representation model that aggregates the trajectory evidence into individual agent and step representations, which can subsequently be adapted to different attribution targets. Accordingly, we propose ASCon, a direction-aware reciprocal \textbf{A}gent--\textbf{S}tep \textbf{Con}textualization model for multiple failure attribution targets. ASCon introduces direction-aware graph attention to model execution context, masked step-to-agent attention to construct behavior-aware agent representations, and agent-conditioned step contextualization to incorporate agent context back into step representations. The resulting contextualized representations enable different attribution targets through lightweight target-specific heads. Experiments show that ASCon can improve faulty-agent detection by 5.83\%+ in micro-accuracy, faulty-step detection by 10.63\%+ in micro-accuracy, and failure-mode detection by 14.73\%+ in Macro-F1. Meanwhile, it can also substantially enhance the LLM-based methods' attribution capabilities in out-of-domain scenarios.

</details>


### [275] [Reifying Research Logic: AI-Assisted Workflow Construction and Incremental Refinement for Quantitative Syntax](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10662)
*He Wang,Jingbo Chen,Yuqiao Lai,Nan Yang,Hanwen Zhang,Wei Yuan*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: QLWF is a visual workflow platform that uses AI to translate natural-language research descriptions into reproducible, executable workflows for quantitative syntax research, achieving 98.4% output plausibility and supporting efficient incremental refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantitative language research relies on complex computational pipelines whose logic is opaque, buried in scripts, making inspection, sharing, and revision difficult. There is a need to make the reasoning behind computational analyses visible, deterministic, and incrementally modifiable.

Method: QLWF implements a five-stage AI-assisted pipeline that converts natural-language descriptions into executable workflows via two key principles: reification (making research logic visible as a workflow graph) and formalization (giving workflows deterministic execution semantics via a fixed node library and engine). The LLM is used only during construction; execution is fully reproducible via the engine. Saved workflows support incremental refinement—only changed parts are rebuilt, not the entire workflow.

Result: On a 64-task benchmark (QL-Bench) derived from quantitative-syntax literature, QLWF produced structurally valid, executable workflows for all tasks with a mean output-plausibility rate of 98.4%, significantly outperforming prompt-based baselines. On a 12-task lifecycle benchmark, incremental refinement succeeded in every case while using roughly one-third the tokens of full regeneration.

Conclusion: QLWF demonstrates that separating LLM-based construction from deterministic execution yields highly reproducible workflows. The approach is robust across diverse quantitative-syntax tasks and supports efficient revision. The authors release the node library, benchmark, workflow templates, and platform as reusable community resources.

Abstract: Quantitative language research often depends on long chains of computational steps, yet the logic connecting those steps usually remains buried in scripts. This makes analyses harder to inspect, share, and revise than they need to be. Focusing on quantitative syntax, we present QLWF, a visual workflow platform that turns natural-language research descriptions into executable workflows through an AI assisted five-stage pipeline. In this setting, reification makes the research logic visible as a workflow, while formalization gives that workflow deterministic execution semantics. The language model is used only during construction. Execution is handled by a fixed node library and engine, which keeps the resulting workflows reproducible. QLWF also supports incremental refinement, so saved workflows can be revised by changing only the parts that need to change rather than being rebuilt from scratch. To evaluate the approach, we build a 64-task benchmark called QL-Bench from the quantitative-syntax literature. Across three runs, QLWF produces structurally valid and executable workflows for every task and reaches a mean output-plausibility rate of 98.4%, well above the prompt-based baselines. On a separate 12-task lifecycle benchmark, this refinement process succeeds in every case and uses roughly one-third of the tokens required by full regeneration. The paper also releases the node library, benchmark, workflow templates, and platform as reusable resources for quantitative-syntax research.

</details>


### [276] [Who Are You Explaining To? A Multi-Agent System for Audience-Aware XAI Narratives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11033)
*Francesco Musicco,Danilo Danese,Giuseppe Fasano,Angela Lombardi,Alberto Carlo Maria Mancino,Tommaso Di Noia*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: XstrAI is a multi-agent LLM framework that generates audience-appropriate natural language explanations of SHAP feature attributions for medical AI predictions, using specialized agents for planning, realization, and validation to ensure grounding, consistency, and risk mitigation across patient, clinician, and data scientist audiences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing feature-attribution explanations like SHAP produce numerical outputs that are not directly suitable for diverse audiences (patients, clinicians, data scientists). Naive LLM-based verbalization suffers from weak grounding, inappropriate causal language, and persuasive-but-unfaithful outputs. There is a need for audience-aware explanation generation that preserves fidelity to the underlying model evidence while adapting communication style to the target reader's expertise and risk profile.

Method: XstrAI encodes each prediction case as an immutable structured representation shared across audiences. Generation is decomposed across three specialized LLM agents: (1) an audience-aware planning agent, (2) a linguistic realization agent, and (3) a validation agent that checks for grounding, attribution consistency, communicative risk, and audience appropriateness. A bounded revision loop is triggered when inconsistencies are detected. The framework is evaluated on diabetes and stroke risk prediction tasks against 11 baselines including direct verbalization and a state-of-the-art narrator reimplementation.

Result: In intra-narrative evaluation (fidelity to SHAP evidence), XstrAI narratives maintained strong grounding. In extra-narrative evaluation (audience appropriateness via reference corpora, multi-family LLM judges, and a target-reader survey), XstrAI's narratives were consistently assigned to their intended audience by independent judges and were preferred over all baselines for Clinician and Patient audiences. For Data Scientist audience, audience-conditioned single-prompt baselines performed competitively.

Conclusion: XstrAI demonstrates that factoring explanation generation into specialized agents with explicit validation and revision yields audience-appropriate, grounded narratives. The immutable evidence representation ensures attribution consistency across audiences, and the multi-agent architecture with bounded revision effectively mitigates risks of unfaithful or misleading verbalization.

Abstract: Feature-attribution methods such as SHAP provide useful evidence about individual model predictions, but their numerical outputs are rarely sufficient for audiences with different expertise, goals, and risks of misinterpretation. In medical AI, the same local explanation must reach patients, clinicians, and data scientists through markedly different forms of communication, and naive verbalization through large language models (LLMs) is prone to weak grounding, conflation of attribution with causal language, and outputs that are persuasive without being faithful to the underlying model evidence. We introduce XstrAI, an audience-aware multi-agent framework that treats local explanations as fixed evidence and structures how it is communicated to each target reader. Each prediction case is encoded as an immutable structured representation, shared identically across audiences so the underlying evidence remains fixed. Generation is factored into three specialized LLM agents responsible for audience-aware planning, linguistic realization, and validation for grounding, attribution consistency, communicative risk, and audience appropriateness, with a bounded revision loop triggered on detected inconsistencies. We evaluate XstrAI on diabetes and stroke risk prediction against 11 baselines, ranging from direct verbalization to a re-implementation of a state-of-the-art narrator. The evaluation combines an intra-narrative regime measuring fidelity to SHAP evidence with an extra-narrative regime assessing audience appropriateness through reference corpora, multi-family LLM judges, and a survey with target readers. In both evaluations, XstrAI's narratives are consistently assigned to their intended audience by independent judges, and preferred over all baselines on Clinician and Patient audiences, with competitive performance on Data Scientist, where audience-conditioned single-prompt baselines lead.

</details>

# cs.HC [[Back]](#toc)

### [277] [How to Dogfood Your AI Chat Agent: A Three-Layer Evaluation Framework with Goal-Directed NPC Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09939)
*Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A three-layer dogfooding framework for QA of production LLM chat agents, combining canonical testing, random-walk multi-turn evaluation, and a goal-directed NPC simulator. The NPC simulator achieves 77% goal achievement at $0.17/run, enabling daily CI/CD integration with automated release decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation tools for LLM chat agents either test individual responses or simulate social interactions, but none systematically verify whether real users can achieve their goals through multi-turn conversation — creating a critical quality assurance gap for production teams.

Method: A three-layer dogfooding framework: Layer 1 uses canonical question-bank testing; Layer 2 employs random-walk multi-turn evaluation; Layer 3 introduces a goal-directed NPC simulator with five structured goal types and a ten-category failure taxonomy. Evaluated via a longitudinal case study over ~3 months with 257 evaluation runs and a 108-scenario NPC suite. Cross-layer correlation analyzed using Spearman rho.

Result: Cross-layer correlation for response quality is weak within synchronized runs (Spearman rho: -0.15 to 0.14) and negative longitudinally (rho down to -0.46), confirming canonical correctness does not predict goal-directed conversation success. NPC simulator achieves 77% goal achievement at $0.17 per run, 6,272× cheaper than human evaluation.

Conclusion: The three layers provide complementary regression signals; the NPC simulator is cost-effective enough for daily CI/CD integration with automated PROMOTE/HOLD/ROLLBACK decisions. Framework artifacts are released publicly for adoption by other teams.

Abstract: Production teams deploying LLM chat agents face a specific quality assurance gap: existing evaluation tools test individual responses or simulate social interactions, but none systematically verify whether real users can achieve their goals through multi-turn conversation. We introduce a three-layer dogfooding framework that bridges this gap by combining canonical question-bank testing (Layer 1), random-walk multi-turn evaluation (Layer 2), and a goal-directed NPC (Non-Player Character) simulator with five structured goal types and a ten-category failure taxonomy (Layer 3). In a longitudinal case study on a production multi-agent system over roughly three months (257 evaluation runs; a 108-scenario NPC suite), we find that the three layers produce complementary regression signals: cross-layer correlation for response quality is weak within a synchronized run (Spearman rho between -0.15 and 0.14) and negative across the longitudinal series (rho down to -0.46), confirming that canonical correctness does not predict goal-directed conversation success. The NPC simulator achieves 77 percent goal achievement at 0.17 dollars per run (6,272x cheaper than human evaluation), enabling daily CI/CD integration with automated PROMOTE/HOLD/ROLLBACK release decisions. We release full prompt templates, the failure taxonomy, and a Python-first replicability guide so that other teams can adopt the framework for their own LLM chat agents.

</details>


### [278] [The impact of design factors of virtual and augmented reality on tertiary students user experience in Metaverse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09940)
*Julius G. Garcia,Alvie Simonette Q. Alip*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study investigates how visual elements, environmental design, and communication features in VR/AR Metaverse platforms influence user experience (UX) among 321 tertiary students. Environmental design and visual elements significantly predict UX (explaining 47.3% of variance), while communication features show no significant effect, challenging assumptions about virtual connectedness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the Metaverse's rapid growth in education (market projected from $65.5B to $1.3T by 2030), the specific contributions of visual elements, environmental design, and communication features to user experience remain underexplored, limiting evidence-based design and resource allocation.

Method: Correlational research design with 321 purposively sampled tertiary students from engineering and computer science departments across four institutions. A structured questionnaire using validated 5-point Likert scales measured UX, visual elements (FOV, resolution, color, complexity, style), environmental design (interactivity, cohesiveness, naturalness, complexity), and communication features (text/audio/video tools, avatar interaction, spatial audio). Multiple regression analysis assessed independent and combined effects.

Result: Environmental design (β=0.424, p<0.001) and visual elements (β=0.298, p<0.001) emerged as primary UX predictors, jointly explaining 47.3% of variance with a strong inter-correlation (r=0.792). Communication features showed no significant influence on UX (β=0.053, p=0.196).

Conclusion: Well-designed, interactive virtual spaces are critical to UX in Metaverse platforms. Developers and educational institutions should prioritize environmental design and visual elements over communication features. The non-significance of communication features challenges prevailing assumptions and suggests communication design requires rethinking to better support social interaction in immersive learning contexts.

Abstract: The Metaverse is a convergent space integrating virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) technologies, with market projections rising from \$65.5 billion in 2022 to \$1.3 trillion by 2030. Despite rapid adoption in education, the specific contributions of visual elements, environmental design, and communication features to user experience (UX) remain underexplored, limiting evidence-based design and resource allocation. This study examined how these design factors in VR and AR environments influence UX in Metaverse platforms. Using a correlational research design, data were collected from 321 purposively sampled tertiary students from engineering and computer science departments across four higher education institutions, all familiar with Metaverse platforms. A structured questionnaire with validated 5-point Likert scales measured UX; visual elements (field of view, resolution, color, complexity, and style); environmental design (interactivity, cohesiveness, naturalness, and complexity); and communication features (text/audio/video tools, avatar interaction, and spatial audio). Multiple regression analysis assessed the independent and combined effects of these factors on UX. Results show that environmental design (b=0.424, p<0.001) and visual elements (b=0.298, p<0.001) are the primary predictors of UX, jointly explaining 47.3% of its variance, with a strong correlation between them (r=0.792). Communication features did not significantly influence UX (b=0.053, p=0.196), challenging assumptions about virtual connectedness and indicating that communication design should better support social interaction. These findings highlight the importance of well-designed, interactive virtual spaces and suggest that developers and educational institutions prioritize environmental design to advance immersive learning and broader Metaverse applications.

</details>


### [279] [EweAcT: Ewe behaviour aligned to accelerometer data for activity monitoring in extensive grazing systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09943)
*Lucile Riaboff,Ny Aina Andriamampandry,Jean-François Bompa,Mathias Aletru,Christian Durand,Sébastien Douls,Gaëtan Bonnafe,Morgane Costes-Thiré,Guillaume Delosières,Jean- Marc Mongrelet,Enzo Niro,Némuel Tadi,Séverine Deretz,Sara Parisot,Margot Lamarque,Dominique Hazard,Emilie Cobo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A dataset of 79 hours of tri-axial accelerometer data from neck-collars on 120 Romane ewes, manually annotated with five grazing behaviours (Grazing, Ruminating, Resting, Moving, Other), collected under extensive rangeland conditions in southern France for developing AI-based behaviour classification models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monitoring livestock behaviour under extensive conditions is valuable for assessing animal adaptation to environmental perturbations (heat waves, parasitism, predator attacks), but developing reliable AI models requires large, annotated accelerometer datasets collected across diverse representative conditions — which are currently scarce for extensive systems.

Method: Tri-axial accelerometer data were collected from neck-collars on 120 Romane ewes (from divergent genetic lines selected for social attractiveness and human tolerance) reared outdoors on 280 ha of rangeland. Data were acquired in two batches: (1) March–July 2024 under extensive conditions including sloping pastures and heat waves, with simultaneous CCTV video recording and manual behaviour annotation using BORIS software; (2) November 2025, capturing deliberate Moving activity during herd transitions. Time-synchronized alignment of annotations and accelerometer sequences was performed using Python.

Result: A merged, ready-to-use dataset comprising 79 hours of labelled tri-axial accelerometer data covering five behaviours (Grazing, Ruminating, Resting, Moving, Other) from 120 ewes under extensive grazing conditions, suitable for training AI classification models.

Conclusion: The dataset fills a critical gap by providing annotated accelerometer data from sheep in real extensive systems across varied environmental conditions, enabling development of robust AI models for automated behaviour monitoring in agroecological contexts.

Abstract: Monitoring livestock behaviour under extensive conditions would provide valuable insights to assess animal adaption to environmental perturbations in agroecological systems (e.g., heat waves, parasitism, predator attacks). Animal behaviour can be monitored using accelerometer data collected from neck-collars combined with artificial intelligence models. However, large amounts of accelerometer data aligned with annotated behaviours are necessary to develop accurate models of behaviour prediction. In particular, developing reliable models for extensive systems requires data collected across a wide range of representative conditions. The dataset includes 79 hours of tri-axial accelerometer data aligned with behaviours manually annotated from video recordings for 120 Romane ewes born between 2021 and 2024. The ewes were derived from two divergent genetic lines after three and four generations of selection started 10 years ago: low and high social attractiveness, noted S-and S+, and low and high tolerance towards humans, noted H-and H+. They were reared under the extensive system applied to the Experimental Unit of La Fage (UEF, INRAE, Saint-Jean-et-saint Paul, Aveyron) where 250 sheep were reared exclusively outdoors on 280 hectares of rangeland in southern France. First batch of data was collected on March, June and July 2024 at the UEF under a range of extensive conditions, including sloping pastures and heat-wave periods. Ewes were equipped with accelerometer neck-collars specifically designed for young sheep on pasture. They were grouped on experimental paddocks for 4 to 8 hours and provided with fresh grass and ad libitum access to water. The animals were simultaneously video-recorded using an elevated CCTV camera. Behaviour annotation was carried out using Behavioral Observation Research Interactive Software focusing on the main behaviours on pasture: Grazing, Ruminating, Resting, Moving, and ''Other'', grouping all remaining activities. Annotations and corresponding accelerometer sequences were aligned using Python language, based on a time synchronization procedure. A second batch of data was acquired on November 2025 to supplement the dataset with the moving activity. For that purpose, ewes were equipped with the accelerometer collars and moved on tracks from the housing area to the pastures, corresponding to an approximately 10 minute-walk. The start and end times of the moves for each ewe were used to align the corresponding accelerometer data with the moving activity. These data were then merged with the dataset from the first batch. The resulting dataset is ready to use for applying artificial intelligence models to classify the 5 main behaviours of sheep under extensive grazing systems from accelerometer data.

</details>


### [280] [Navigation Alone Is Not Enough: Evaluating Explanatory Assistive UI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09944)
*Santosh Patapati*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: NeXUI is a benchmark for evaluating assistive agents that navigate modern web interfaces for blind and visually impaired users, requiring agents to not only complete tasks but also generate grounded explanations of their actions, with current state-of-the-art models achieving only 44% success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern web interfaces are increasingly inaccessible to screen readers due to dynamic updates and visual-layout-dependent structure. Existing benchmarks only measure task completion without assessing whether agents can explain their actions or support user oversight — capabilities essential for assistive agents to function as collaborators rather than opaque tools.

Method: The authors introduce NeXUI, a benchmark pairing realistic user goals with instrumented interface states. Agents must navigate interfaces using both visual context and structural information, producing natural-language explanations for each step. Evaluation spans task success, safety, efficiency, and explanation groundedness — measuring whether explanations accurately reflect the actual interface state.

Result: NeXUI proves challenging for state-of-the-art models. Gemini-3.5-Flash achieved only a 44% task success rate and scored poorly on explanation quality, indicating significant room for improvement.

Conclusion: By jointly evaluating navigation, explanation, and user control, NeXUI provides a robust foundation for developing and benchmarking assistive agents that genuinely support blind and visually impaired users in modern computing environments.

Abstract: Modern web interfaces are increasingly difficult to use with screen readers, particularly when pages update dynamically or hide important structure behind visual layout. Recent UI agents can act on such interfaces; however, for assistive agents to be truly useful, they must behave as collaborators that keep users informed and in control, rather than as tools that simply take actions on users' behalf. Most existing benchmarks judge systems primarily by task completion, without assessing how well they explain their actions or support user oversight. We introduce NeXUI, a benchmark for assistive agents that must navigate interfaces while explaining each step in clear language for nonvisual use. NeXUI pairs realistic user goals with instrumented interface states, enabling agents to reason from both visual context and structural information. Its evaluation measures safety, efficiency, and task success, while also checking whether explanations are grounded in the interface state. In our experiments, we find that NeXUI remains challenging even for state-of-the-art foundation models, with % Gemini-3.5-Flash achieving only a 44\% success rate and poor explanation scores, making it a useful foundation for future research and development. By focusing on navigation, explanation, and user control, NeXUI provides a clearer way to study agents that can support blind and visually impaired users in modern computing environments.

</details>


### [281] [Co-Lecturing With the DED: Explaining Circuit Design via the Draw Encode Display Loop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09945)
*Alasdair Lambert,Guillaume Allais,Conor Mc Bride*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper presents the Draw-Encode-Display Loop (DED), a pedagogical method supported by an educational HDL called Syrup, that bridges hand-drawn circuit diagrams and formal hardware description by teaching students to systematically translate natural language specifications into testable digital circuits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hand-drawn 2D circuit representations offer intuitive reasoning and explicit structure but lack precision and testability. Conversely, HDL-based representations are well-defined and testable but lack visual intuitiveness. Students struggle to connect these two modalities, creating a pedagogical gap in digital circuits education.

Method: The authors propose the DED Loop: (1) Draw visual intermediate representations (truth tables, characteristic tables) to produce structured circuit diagrams; (2) Encode the diagram by labeling inputs, outputs, and intermediate values for direct code translation; (3) Display the code using an in-house diagrammatic renderer. This is implemented in Syrup, an education-focused HDL enabling circuit definition, experimentation, and visualization, evaluated via survey data from two student cohorts.

Result: The paper is supported by survey data gathered from two cohorts of students, though specific quantitative outcomes are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: The DED Loop combined with Syrup effectively bridges intuitive visual circuit reasoning and formal, testable hardware description, providing students with a systematic methodology for tackling digital circuit specifications.

Abstract: When representing digital circuits, 2 dimensional hand drawings free us from the linear structure of hardware description languages, enabling intuitive reasoning and making structure explicit. However these drawings are imprecise and inert: they do not enforce that the circuits are well defined and cannot be tested. We want both intuitive visual representations and well defined testable ones but students can struggle to link one to the other.
  To bridge this gap we present the Draw Encode Display Loop (DED), a Co-Lecturing dynamic which equips students with a systematic method to tackle natural language specifications:
  1. Draw: visually informative intermediate representations (truth tables, characteristic tables) to generate a structured circuit diagram.
  2. Encode: the diagram by labelling inputs, outputs and intermediate values which can be directly converted to code.
  3. Display: the code using an in-house diagrammatic renderer.
  This is supported by Syrup, an education-focused hardware description language which allows students to define, experiment with and display their own circuits. We support these approaches with survey data gathered from two cohorts of students.

</details>


### [282] [HoosierHelp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Social Service Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09946)
*Yiyang Li,Weixiang Sun,Tianyi Ma,Kaiwen Shi,Zheyuan Zhang,Yanfang Ye*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: HoosierHelp is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on conversational social service navigation with realistic, non-ideal simulated users. Experiments show current LLMs are unreliable, especially on complex interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks fail to capture the interaction complexity and constraint-grounding demands of real-world social service navigation, where help-seekers have varied needs, constraints, and non-ideal communication behaviors.

Method: The authors introduce HoosierHelp, an interactive benchmark grounded in 3,971 Indiana public social service resources. Agents interact with simulated users that vary in need structure, constraint satisfiability, and behavior patterns (impatience, rambling, unsupported requests, self-contradiction). Agents must issue structured resource-search calls, handle non-ideal interactions, and select final resources.

Result: Experiments on 240 samples across seven LLMs reveal that current agents are substantially unreliable for social service navigation, with sharp performance drops on fallback-required and self-contradictory conversations.

Conclusion: More robust agents are needed to handle the complex, non-ideal user interactions characteristic of real-world social service navigation scenarios.

Abstract: Social service navigation requires connecting help-seeking individuals to resources that satisfy their needs and specific constraints. Although LLM agents offer a promising interface for conversational resource navigation, existing benchmarks do not capture the interaction complexity and constraint-grounding demands of this setting. We introduce HoosierHelp, an interactive benchmark grounded in 3,971 Indiana public social service resources. Agents interact with simulated users, issue structured resource-search calls, handle non-ideal interactions, and select the final resources returned by the tool. HoosierHelp enhances the realism of simulated users by varying their need structure, constraint satisfiability, and behavior patterns, including impatience, rambling, unsupported requests, and self-contradiction. Experiments on 240 samples across seven LLMs show that current LLM agents remain substantially unreliable for social service navigation. Performance drops sharply on fallback-required and self-contradictory conversations, highlighting the need for agents that are more robust to complex and non-ideal user interactions.

</details>


### [283] [Mapping Multimodal Pilot Stress and Fatigue During Flight Sessions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09947)
*Atandrila Chowdhury,Sudip Vhaduri,Julius Keller,Debra Henneberry,Mark Wilson*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Student pilots exhibit accumulating workload-related fatigue across flight training, evidenced by rising EDA and skin temperature trends, event-specific heart rate spikes, and increased post-flight self-reported exhaustion. Combining physiological and subjective measures offers a robust approach for monitoring pilot stress and fatigue in real-world settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how stress and exhaustion manifest and accumulate in student pilots throughout real-world flight training, addressing the need for objective, data-driven methods to monitor pilot well-being beyond self-report alone.

Method: Longitudinal data collection from student pilots: Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) administered pre- and post-flight; continuous in-flight recording of heart rate (HR), electrodermal activity (EDA), skin temperature, and acceleration. Physiological signals were preprocessed and analyzed across flight stages to identify recurring arousal and workload patterns.

Result: Steady increases in EDA and skin temperature across flights indicated cumulative workload-related weariness. Heart rate showed event-specific spikes during high-demand phases. Post-flight self-reported exhaustion increased over time, corroborating the physiological trend toward accumulating fatigue.

Conclusion: Combining physiological signals with subjective self-reports is effective for detecting stress and fatigue patterns during actual flight training. Data-driven approaches show strong potential for real-time monitoring of pilot well-being and could inform interventions to mitigate cumulative fatigue.

Abstract: This study analyzes patterns of stress and exhaustion among student pilots throughout flight training using a combination of physiological and self-reported measurements. The Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) was used to measure perceived stress and exhaustion before and after each flight, while physiological data, including heart rate (HR), electrodermal activity (EDA), skin temperature, and acceleration, were continuously recorded during flight sessions. To identify recurring patterns in arousal and workload, physiological signals were preprocessed and analyzed across the flight stages. The findings indicate a buildup of workload-related weariness over time, as evidenced by steady increases in EDA and skin temperature across flights, as well as post-flight increases in self-reported exhaustion. Heart rate responses were more event-specific, with brief spikes during high-demand phases of flight. Overall, the findings demonstrate the value of combining physiological signals with subjective reports to identify patterns of stress and fatigue during real-world flight training and highlight the potential of data-driven approaches for monitoring pilot well-being.

</details>


### [284] [Immersive Micromanipulation Integrating Pipette and Injector Operations with McKibben-Based Haptic Sensations for Workload Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10033)
*Kenta Yokoe,Sumiwa Saito,Yuki Funabora,Tomoko Isomura,Tadayoshi Aoyama*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: An immersive micromanipulation system for ICSI that unifies pipette and injector control into a single-handed interface with McKibben-based haptic feedback, demonstrating reduced cognitive workload and improved speed over conventional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional ICSI relies solely on visual feedback and requires frequent switching between pipette movement and injector control interfaces. Existing haptic systems only address pipette puncture forces, neglecting injector state feedback. There is a need to unify these interfaces and provide comprehensive haptic feedback to reduce operator burden.

Method: The authors developed an immersive micromanipulation system integrating McKibben-based pneumatic haptic actuators. The system provides haptic sensations representing three key states: aspiration, discharge, and oocyte-pipette contact. Crucially, users operate both the pipette and injector with a single hand through a unified interface. Evaluation was conducted via a human-participant experiment comparing the system against conventional methods.

Result: The immersive interface significantly improved micromanipulation speed and reduced cognitive workload compared to conventional methods. McKibben-based haptic sensations additionally enhanced overall system usability scores.

Conclusion: The proposed immersive micromanipulation system successfully unified operational interfaces and reduced operator workload through McKibben-based haptic sensations, offering a meaningful advancement over conventional ICSI setups.

Abstract: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) requires advanced micromanipulation techniques but relies solely on visual feedback and involves frequent interface switching between pipette movement and injector operations. Existing haptic feedback systems primarily focus on pipette puncture forces and do not provide feedback on injector states. We developed an immersive micromanipulation system that unifies operational interfaces and provides McKibben-based haptic sensations to represent aspiration, discharge, and contact between the oocyte and pipette. Users operated both the pipette and injector with a single hand while receiving haptic sensations. A human-participant experiment revealed that the immersive operation interface improved micromanipulation speed and reduced cognitive workload of the micromanipulation compared with conventional methods. Additionally, McKibben-based haptic sensations improved overall system usability. The immersive micromanipulation system with McKibben-based haptic sensations successfully unified operational interfaces and reduced operator workload.

</details>


### [285] [Outer Limits: An Experimental Approach to Controlled Content Manipulation within the Reddit Interface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10115)
*Chenchen Mao,Hanjing Shi,Haiyan Jia,Daniel Unhuryan,Eric Baumer,Dominic DiFranzo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Outer Limits is a browser-based system enabling controlled social media experiments within the live Old Reddit interface, with local content rendering and contained interactions. A 219-participant study found no significant effects, and equivalence tests confirmed perceptual fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Independent researchers lack access to intervention capabilities on live social media platforms, making controlled experiments difficult. Existing approaches offer only partial solutions: precise content control, realistic platform interfaces, or containment of experimental interactions — but not all three simultaneously.

Method: The authors developed Outer Limits, a browser-based system that operates within the existing Old Reddit interface. It renders content locally, records study events, and confines voting/commenting actions so that neither constructed content nor experimental write interactions reach Reddit's servers. A 219-participant perceptual-fidelity study was conducted using ART ANOVAs (Post Type × Participant Awareness) and exploratory TOST equivalence tests (d = ±0.50 criterion). A factorial illustration study varied post frame, comment frame, and comment stance.

Result: ART ANOVAs revealed no significant main effects for Post Type, Participant Awareness, nor their interaction. Exploratory TOSTs met the d = ±0.50 equivalence criterion for marginal contrasts and for Post Type within the forewarned subgroup, supporting perceptual fidelity.

Conclusion: Outer Limits uniquely combines three key properties — precise control over experimental content, an existing platform interface, and containment from the host community — enabling ecologically valid controlled experiments on social media without requiring platform operator cooperation.

Abstract: Independent researchers often lack access to intervention capabilities for controlled experiments on live social media platforms. We present Outer Limits, a browser-based system for controlled content experiments within the existing Old Reddit interface, rather than in a reconstructed simulation. The system renders content locally, records study events, and contains configured voting and commenting actions so that neither constructed content nor experimental write interactions reach Reddit. In a 219-participant perceptual-fidelity study, ART ANOVAs found no significant Post Type, Participant Awareness, or interaction effects. Exploratory TOSTs met the d = plus-minus 0.50 equivalence criterion for the marginal contrasts and for Post Type within the forewarned subgroup. We also illustrate the system with a factorial study varying post frame, comment frame, and comment stance. Outer Limits combines three properties that the approaches considered here provide separately: precise control over experimental content, an existing platform interface, and containment of experimental content and interactions from the host community.

</details>


### [286] [Predicting affective connotation of visualizations from their constituent colors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10169)
*Karen B. Schloss,Halle C. Braun,Kushin Mukherjee,Anna L. Chinni,Seth R. Gorelik*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study investigates whether the affective connotation of whole data visualizations can be predicted from the emotional associations of their constituent colors. Results support both an additivity hypothesis (mean color associations predict whole-visualization affect) and a data-dependence hypothesis (weighting by color area improves predictions when underlying datasets are biased). Findings generalized across colormaps, dot plots, and bar charts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Affective connotation is a critical aspect of visual communication, yet methods to predict the emotional associations of whole visualizations from their design components are lacking. Understanding how individual design properties (here, color) combine to determine overall emotional impact is essential for automating affective visualization design.

Method: Three experiments tested whether affective connotation of whole visualizations could be predicted from constituent colors. Experiment 1 tested the additivity hypothesis using colormaps with well-distributed colors. Experiment 2 tested the data-dependence hypothesis using colormaps with biased underlying datasets, comparing unweighted vs. frequency-weighted means. Experiment 3 generalized findings to dot plots and bar charts.

Result: In Experiment 1, mean estimated associations of individual colors effectively predicted whole-colormap emotional associations (additivity). In Experiment 2, a weighted mean accounting for color frequency better predicted associations when datasets were biased toward one end of the color scale (data-dependence). Experiment 3 confirmed both effects generalized to dot plots and bar charts.

Conclusion: It is viable to predict the affective connotation of whole visualizations from individual design components like color. This has important implications for developing automated systems that can design visualizations with specific emotional tones to enhance visual communication.

Abstract: With increasing evidence that affective connotation (emotional association) is an important aspect of visual communication, there is a need for methods to predict affective connotation of visualizations. Many aspects of visualization design, including colors, textures, and shapes, can contribute to affective connotation, and a key question is how multiple design properties combine to determine the emotion association of a whole visualization. In this study, we focused specifically on color and tested whether it is possible to predict the affective connotation of whole visualizations by aggregating the emotion associations of the individual, constituent colors (additivity hypothesis). We also tested whether accounting for the size of colored regions, as determined by the underlying dataset, improved predictions (data-dependence hypothesis). We found that for colormap data visualizations in which colors were well-distributed across all colors in the color scale, the mean estimated associations of individual colors effectively predicted emotional associations of the maps as a whole (additivity; Exp. 1). For colormaps whose underlying datasets were biased to map more to colors at one end of the color scale, emotional associations were better predicted by a weighted mean that accounted for color frequency in the colormap (data-dependence; Exp. 2). Effects of additivity and data-dependence generalized to dot plots and bar charts (Exp. 3). These results suggest it is viable to predict affective connotation of whole visualizations from their individual design components, which has important implications for automating affective visualization design to support visual communication.

</details>


### [287] [Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Codebook-Guided Coding of Students' Mathematics Metaphor Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10276)
*Liang Zhang,Stephen Hwang,Yue Ma,Jinfa Cai*

Main category: cs.HC
